News.title: Turkish Airlines flight makes emergency diversion as passengers scream 'we will die'
News.content:
Turkish Airlines flight makes emergency diversion as passengers scream 'we will die'

The Airbus A321 took off from Istanbul and attempted three landings at Tunis Carthage International Airport before turning to Enfidha-Hammamet Airport

View 2 Images The flight made three attempts to land in Tunis before turning to the airport in Enfidha (Image: Flight Radar)

Passengers on a Turkish Airlines flight were left shouting "we will die" when the aircraft battled severe turbulence as it approached a popular holiday destination.

‌



The terrifying approach took place as flight THY663 attempted to land at Tunis Carthage International Airport (TUN) in Tunisia on Thursday. Footage shows the Airbus A321, which has a capacity of 220, shaking violently as thick storm clouds and rain engulfed the aircraft.

‌



According to data from flight tracking website Flight Radar, THY663 left Istanbul at 3.40pm local time (1.40pm BST). About two hours and 20 minutes later, the aircraft started approaching the airport, making three unsuccessful attempts to land.

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

DWP confirms State Pension age increase for anyone born after April 6 1960 READ MORE :

The ordeal lasted about 30 minutes before the Airbus A321 turned to Enfidha-Hammamet Airport (NBE), which is located south of Tunis. The flight eventually landed at NBE at 4.50pm local time (4.50pm BST), three hours after taking off from Istanbul.

Video shared online shows passengers screaming in fear, with some shouting "we will die, we will die". One person on board claimed she felt the aircraft "fall down a few seconds, like free falling".

‌



The video shows her crying with relief after landing, as other passengers clapped. The same aircraft then took off from NBE at 10.10pm local time (10.10pm BST), landing at TUN 24 minutes later.

Mirror Online has approached Turkish Airlines for comment.

View 2 Images A full map of the flight's route (Image: Flight Radar)

‌



This comes after a Lufthansa flight bound for Washington DC was forced to abort its journey after declaring a mid-air emergency over the UK.

Lufthansa Flight LH418, operated by an Airbus A340-600, left Frankfurt Airport at 1.30pm local time on Thursday, and was roughly two hours into its journey at around 34,000ft when it issued a squawk 7700 alert over northern Scotland.

Flight tracking data shows the flight descended from its cruising altitude and diverted towards Glasgow Airport, landing there on runway 23.

Article continues below

The flight initially appeared to be heading towards Dublin Airport in Ireland, where emergency ground crews were reportedly on standby.

The exact nature of the incident remains unclear as a squawk 7700 alert can refer to anything, from a medical issue on board to a technical problem with the aircraft.

News.title: Lucy Letby allowed jail telly and choc binges as she grieves death of doctor 'boyfriend'
News.content:
Lucy Letby allowed jail telly and choc binges as she grieves death of doctor 'boyfriend'

The convicted former nurse is said to have been excused from prison classes and workshops while staff monitor her wellbeing following the death of former colleague and "love" Mark Deakin

View 3 Images Letby and Dr Deakin exchanged more than 1,300 messages (Image: PA)

Killer nurse Lucy Letby has reportedly become increasingly reclusive in prison following the death of a doctor she once described as her “love”.

‌



The convicted serial baby murderer is said to have been allowed to miss prison classes and workshops while staff monitor her wellbeing at HMP Bronzefield. After the death of Consultant Mark Deakin, 53, who worked alongside Letby at the Countess of Chester Hospital and the pair exchanged more than 1,300 Facebook messages over three months in 2016.

‌



He later gave evidence during her trial, where he was referred to as Doctor A after successfully applying for anonymity. His identity was revealed earlier this month after the order protecting his name was lifted at the Court of Appeal.

‌



Letby, 36, is now said to be spending increasing amounts of time alone in her cell, where she has been watching reality TV and comfort-eating.

View 3 Images Mark Deakin gave evidence during Letby's murder trial

Families say government must fully implement findings of inquiry into killer nurse Lucy Letby READ MORE :

Harry and Meghan not on guestlist for posh wedding as only William and Kate invited READ MORE :

A source said: “It is pretty obvious Letby is devastated and the staff have been giving her the equivalent of compassionate leave. She has become more reclusive and spending hours in her cell.

‌



“She has been watching shows including Four in a Bed and Dinner Date and comfort-eating, with chocolate including Galaxy Ripples and Kinder Buenos her favourites. When officers come and call her for something, Letby often says ‘one more episode’ and stays in her cell on her own.

The source told the Sun “Staff are taking it easy on her and have to monitor her state of mind as she is currently classed as vulnerable because of what’s happened. Although the doctor was not related to her, they are treating it like a bereavement. Staff are also doing things like removing newspapers from the wing, which might mention the story.

"The only person Letby wants to mix with is Sara Sharif’s Mum Beinash Batool – she is leaning on her for support. They play chess and cards together for hours on end and there’s a view that it helps Letby take her mind off things.”

‌



Dr Deakin worked with Letby at the Countess of Chester Hospital in 2016 during the period in which she was later accused of attacking babies on its neonatal unit.

View 3 Images Letby is serving a while-life order at HMP Bronzefield (Image: PA)

During a dramatic moment of her trial, Letby broke down in tears and tried to leave court as the doctor confirmed his name while giving evidence from behind a screen after handwritten notes found at Letby's home referred to him as her "best friend" and "love."

‌



Prosecutors referred to the doctor as Letby’s “boyfriend” during the 10-month trial, which ended in August 2023 where they said Letby attacked babies to create “crisis situations” because she knew he would be called to attend.

At the later Thirlwall Inquiry into the deaths of babies at the hospital, Dr Deakin said he had been “misled” and “maybe manipulated” by Letby.

He later moved to Alder Hey Children’s Hospital in Liverpool where he was sacked over messages he and Letby had exchanged while they both worked at the Countess of Chester Hospital. He was later found unconscious in his car at a retail park the day after his dismissal and died nine days later.

Article continues below

Letby was convicted of murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven others between 2015 and 2016 and is serving a whole-life order. The former neonatal nurse, from Hereford, maintains her innocence and has twice failed in attempts to challenge her convictions.

The Criminal Cases Review Commission is considering evidence submitted on her behalf which claims natural causes and poor care were responsible for the deaths and could refer her case back to the Court of Appeal.

News.title: Met Office names areas facing heavy rain on Monday with 14 counties at risk
News.content:
Met Office names areas facing heavy rain on Monday with 14 counties at risk

Met Office weather forecasters say Monday will bring bright spells and potential 26C highs for some areas, while others could face spells of heavy rain

UK weather: Muggy cloud for the south with sunshine in the north

Heavy rain is expected in some parts of the UK on Monday, while other regions should see bright and pleasant conditions.

‌



Met Office forecasters say southern regions could see potential highs of 26C in the sunshine, but conditions further north are expected to be rather miserable.

‌



Speaking in this morning’s Met Office video forecast, meteorologist Kathryn Chalk explained that it will be a humid start to the week, with overnight temperatures set to remain in the mid to high teens.

‌



However, rain looks set to sweep across Northern Ireland and Scotland as we head into Monday afternoon. These showers could turn heavy at times.

View 2 Images Met Office outlook for midday on Monday (Image: Met Office)

UK weather maps show 30C heat surge with 20 counties reaching 28C or more – list READ MORE :

Ms Chalk said: “A warm and humid start to Monday, we’ve got cloud and outbreaks of rain arriving across the north-west of Scotland, and later on in the afternoon is when we’ll see some heavier spells of rain arriving into Northern Ireland.

‌



“Elsewhere the cloud will break. We will see some sunnier spells developing - especially across northern England and into the Midlands, the far south and west.

“Temperatures will be rising in that sunshine. It’s still going to be feeling warm with highs possibly up to 25-26C. It will be cooler where we have the outbreaks of rain across the far north and west.”

View 2 Images Met Office outlook for 3pm on Monday (Image: Met Office)

‌



The Met Office maps show heavy rain could hit 14 counties in total. They are all in Northern Ireland or Scotland.

UK counties facing heavy rain on Monday

Northern Ireland

Antrim

Armagh

Down

Fermanagh

Londonderry

Tyrone

Scotland

Wigtownshire

Kirkcudbrightshire

Ayrshire

Buteshire

Renfrewshire

Dunbarton

Argyllshire

Inverness-shire

Article continues below

BBC Weather forecast

The BBC Weather forecast paints a similar picture. It states: “Tomorrow, the north-west will be cloudy and breezy with showery rain continuing to move in, heavy in places. Elsewhere, variable cloud cover, sunny spells and a few showers in spots.”

It adds for the rest of the week: “Rain will push across the south early on Tuesday, before clearing away. Behind this, sunny spells, but also some showers in the north-west.

“Sunny spells and the odd shower on Wednesday, but turning windy and wet in the north-west later on. Rain will spread south-eastwards overnight and into Thursday, clearing to leave sunny spells but also blustery showers for the north-west.”

News.title: X Files star Gillian Anderson says she's pansexual and reveals relationships with women
News.content:
X Files star Gillian Anderson says she's pansexual and reveals relationships with women

The actress, 58, explained that appearing on Netflix's Sex Education was a turning point for her.

View 4 Images Gillian Anderson has opened about her sexuality in a new interview (Image: Getty Images)

Actress Gillian Anderson has opened up about her sexuality, saying she is pansexual. The star, used the term 'pan' about herself in a new interview - describing an attraction to people of all genders.

‌



In an interview with The Australian the 58-year-old said that "in my younger years I was in relationships with women" but is now in one with a man.

‌



The former X Files star explained that her attitude had become more sex positive since appearing on Netflix's Sex Education as Jean Milburn, where she plays a well-known sex therapist and mother of the main character, Otis. She said: "It all came from that character."

‌



Anderson has been married twice, first to Canadian TV art director Clyde Klotz and then to filmmaker and foreign correspondent Julian Ozanne.

4 View 4 Images Gillian Anderson in The X Files with David Duchovny in 1998 (Image: BBC) 4 View 4 Images Gillian said: 'I'm not a big flirter - I don't put it out there very much' (Image: Getty Images for G Spot/MUBI/Picturehouse)

‌



She has daughter Piper, 31, with Klotz and sons Oscar, 19, and Felix, 17, with businessman ex Mark Griffiths. The star is thought to be an a relationship with The Crown creator Peter Morgan but has never confirmed it.

The told the paper: "I'm not a big flirter. I don't put it out there very much. I do hear of a lot of women around our age who are rediscovering their sensuality and their desire for sex.

"It certainly sounds like they're in the dating field. That they're having a lot of fun, a lot of opportunities, but also being approached on these apps by much younger men."

‌



Gillian's new book More: Sexual Fantasies by Anonymous, a follow-up to her 2024 Want, features intimate letters submitted by woman from around the world and comes out next week.

View 4 Images She said playing Sex Education's Jean Milburn changed her attitude (Image: Handout)

She said: “I’m incredibly honoured to be at the other end of such vulnerability and trust. I’m so grateful for the courage and honesty, and just the beautiful, beautiful writing. It feels like a real honour to be entrusted with these pieces.”

Article continues below

Last month Gillian spoke about being voted the Sexiest Woman in the World by readers of FHM in the mid-Nineties, around the time the X Files was at the peak of its powers, but said she felt "anything but".

She told Vogue: 'In 1996 I was voted 'Sexiest Woman in the World' by FHM readers – a title that arrived with all the certainty of a cultural verdict.

'How 'sexy' I felt inside – or indeed looked – when the accolade was announced is another story... The ludicrous irony, of course, is that when the 'world' declared me its sexiest woman, I felt anything but.'

News.title: Andy Burnham taking part in Great North Run to raise funds for homeless charity
News.content:
Andy Burnham taking part in Great North Run to raise funds for homeless charity

The Prime Minister, who is making a charity contribution from his own salary, has taken part in the world-famous run before - finishing with an impressive time of 1:55:24 - before heading to the pub

View 2 Images PM Andy Burnham is taking part in the Great North Run (Image: Getty Images)

Andy Burnham has become the first serving Prime Minister to take part in the world’s greatest half marathon - The Great North Run.

‌



The event is celebrating its 45th anniversary with its biggest-ever field of 63,000 competitors. Organisers estimate it has raised more than £450m for good causes since 1981, and that figure is likely to reach to half a billion pounds in the next two years.

‌



View 2 Images The PM is joining 63,000 others taking part in the Great North Run (Image: Getty Images)

‌



The event already holds the world record from 2014 as the biggest half marathon in history, when 41,615 crossed the finishing line; it will set a new record this year.

The PM has take part in the run before - finishing with impressive time 1:55:24 two years ago, before heading to the a pub, wearing his medal, for a well deserved post-race pint.

He is raising money for Changing Lives, which supports over 14,000 people each year facing the challenges of homelessness.

‌



The PM wrote on his fundraising page: "I'm running the 45th Great North Run for Changing Lives because I've seen the difference they make with my own eyes.

"A few weeks back I visited Alex's Place in Newcastle to launch our drive to offer everyone a route off the streets by Christmas. I sat down with residents over a cup of tea and heard what it actually takes to rebuild a life once you've lost everything - not just a roof, but people who stick with you while you find your feet again.

"That's what Changing Lives does. Tackling homelessness is a moral mission for me. It's why I promised to end rough sleeping on my first day as PM, and why I'm proud to pull on a Changing Lives shirt today. If you can spare a few quid, please chip in and support them."

‌



The PM has already announced he will give away 15% of his salary as to homeless charities after pledging to end rough sleeping.

First staged in June 1981, the race was founded by ex-athlete Sir Brendan Foster, 78, after he was inspired by taking part in New Zealand's Round the Bays Race in 1979.

Sir Brendan said: "It has been the biggest mass participation event in the UK for some time and we entered the Guinness Book of Records many years ago. This will be our biggest run yet. In around two years, the money raised for charities will hit the half-billion-pound mark."

‌



The former long-distance athlete said he is looking forward to England and Newcastle United star Dan Burn starting their biggest ever event on Sunday.

Other famous faces are expected to be out in force including Jake Quickenden, Joe Wicks, Chris Kamara, Ben Shephard, Joe McElderry, Helen Skelton and Peter Reid.

Burn is following in a fine Toon tradition after Kevin Keegan ran the first 1981 event in a top that was half in Newcastle United's colours and half in those of Sunderland.

Article continues below

Thousands of people are expected to line the streets for another huge event on Tyneside with a display from the Red Arrows also expected.

The weather is expected to be fine for the run, with the Met saying: "A fine day, with early cloud in places breaking up to leave some warm sunny spells. Temperatures will be near average with mainly light winds. Maximum temperature 20 °C."

To support the PM's charity visit https://justgiving.com/page/andy-burnham-1.

News.title: Oncologist warns common stomach infection may be linked to bowel cancer
News.content:
Oncologist warns common stomach infection may be linked to bowel cancer

A new study has led a professor of biomedical sciences to warn that 'serious investigation' is needed

View 3 Images (Image: Luis Alvarez via Getty Images)

A leading oncologist has warned that a common stomach infection we get in childhood may have an unexpected link to bowel cancer. A new study suggests that exposure to Helicobacter pylori (H pylori) could be associated with more than one in five cases of bowel cancer across the globe.

‌



Professor Justin Stebbing describes this as a striking figure, particularly given how widespread H pylori actually is. The Professor of Biomedical Sciences at Anglia Ruskin University, said: "The wider significance of this research may be what it tells us about the causes of cancer. We tend to think of bowel cancer mainly in terms of genes, ageing and lifestyle. But some cancers also have an infectious component.

‌



"The possibility that an infection acquired in childhood could influence the risk of bowel cancer decades later therefore deserves serious investigation." The NHS says H pylori is a type of bacteria that can infect the lining of the stomach and the first part of the small intestine.

‌



One NHS trust says: "Around 40% of people in the UK have H. pylori in their stomach. For most, it causes no problems at all and doesn’t require treatment. Only around 1 in 10 people with H. pylori will experience symptoms or complications."

The professor stressed the study does not prove H pylori causes bowel cancer, but rather estimates how many bowel cancer cases might be connected to the infection. Bowel cancer, also known as colorectal cancer, develops in the colon or rectum and is amongst the most commonly diagnosed cancers worldwide, affecting approximately 1.9 million people every year.

Risk factors for bowel cancer

He noted that several risk factors for bowel cancer are already well established, including advancing age, family history, smoking, obesity, alcohol consumption and diets rich in processed meat. However, researchers are increasingly focusing on another potential contributing factor: the trillions of microorganisms residing in our digestive system, known as the microbiome, and the infections that can disrupt this delicate environment.

‌



Writing in The Conversation, the professor, who specialises in oncology and cancer research, highlighted H pylori as a particularly compelling candidate. Not only has the bacterium evolved to survive in the stomach's highly acidic conditions, but it is also already known to trigger gastric cancer.

He said: "It's thought around half of the world's population are infected with H pylori– although rates vary greatly between countries. Infection often occurs during childhood.

View 3 Images The professor says the study shows serious investigations are needed (Image: FemiHouse via Getty Images)

‌



"Most infected people never develop symptoms. But in some, H pylori causes long-term inflammation of the stomach lining. This can lead to ulcers and, in a small proportion, stomach cancer. The evidence that H pylori causes cancer is strong enough that it's classified as a carcinogen. But the bacterium's relationship with bowel cancer is less clear."

Previous studies have shown that people infected with H pylori have a higher risk of developing colorectal cancer. He said the latest study attempted to contextualise these findings. It gathered data from 43 studies involving almost 49 million people and combined it with information about the prevalence of both H pylori and bowel cancer globally.

He said: "Overall, people exposed to H pylori had about a 1.6 times greater risk of being diagnosed with bowel cancer compared to those without evidence of infection. Using these figures, the researchers calculated that approximately 22% of bowel cancers worldwide could be associated with H pylori.

‌



"This doesn't mean H pylori has been shown to cause one in five bowel cancers. The calculation depended heavily on the studies included – and, crucially, assumes that at least some of the observed association is causal."

View 3 Images The professor has spoken in detail about H pylori (Image: Anchalee Phanmaha via Getty Images)

He added that when the researchers narrowed their analysis to 14 population-based and cohort studies — designs generally considered more reliable for examining how risk develops over time — the estimated proportion of bowel cancers linked to H pylori dropped to around 12%.

‌



The professor noted it is also conceivable that some of the apparent connection reflects other distinctions between those who contract H pylori and those who don't – including diet, smoking, physical activity levels, socioeconomic conditions and healthcare access. He continued: "Nevertheless, there are several plausible ways H pylori might influence bowel cancer."

What happens when H pylori infection is treated

H pylori may also have an impact on hormones and other molecules involved in digestion and cell growth. While a fascinating possibility, there is currently no evidence of the chain of events that leads from a stomach infection to cancer in the colon or rectum.

The professor said: "Perhaps the most interesting finding from the study concerns what happens when the infection is treated. H pylori can usually be eradicated using a combination of antibiotics and medicines that suppress stomach acid. Across four observational studies included in the analysis, people who received treatment for H pylori appeared to have a lower subsequent risk of bowel cancer – with the difference becoming apparent after ten years.

‌



"Yet he said these were observational studies, not trials in which people were randomly assigned to treatment or no treatment, so we cannot yet conclude that eliminating H pylori prevents bowel cancer." He asked: "So should people now ask to be tested for H pylori to reduce their bowel cancer risk?

"On the evidence available today, no. We need stronger evidence showing that detecting and treating H pylori actually reduces colorectal cancer incidence. "

Best ways to lower bowel cancer risk

He stressed that, currently, the most effective methods of reducing your bowel cancer risk remain those backed by robust evidence. This encompasses bowel cancer screening, which can detect cancers at an earlier, more treatable stage and can occasionally prevent cancer by identifying and removing precancerous growths known as polyps.

‌



Keeping a healthy weight, staying physically active, not smoking, moderating alcohol consumption and cutting down on processed meat can also lower the risk.

Warning signs such as blood in the stool, a persistent change in bowel habits, unexplained weight loss or prolonged abdominal discomfort should never be ignored, although they are frequently brought about by conditions unrelated to cancer.

NHS symptoms list for bowel cancer

‌



The NHS website lists a number of symptoms to be aware of:

needing to poo more or less often than is usual for you

often feeling like you need to poo, even if you've just been to the toilet

tummy pain

bloating

changes in your poo, such as having softer poo, diarrhoea or constipation that is not usual for you

blood in your poo, which may look red or black

losing weight without trying

feeling very tired or short of breath – these are signs of anaemia, which can be caused by bowel cancer

bleeding from your bottom

a lump in your tummy

For more information, visit the NHS website.

Article continues below

The Conversation website is updated regularly with articles on health, science and many other topics.

News.title: Charlie's Angels star Jaclyn Smith at 80 – 4 marriages, cancer shock and legacy
News.content:
Blending high octane crime fighting with kooky fashion, fast cars and enough hairspray to punch a hole in the ozone layer, Charlie’s Angels took 1970s audiences by storm. Celebrating the US show’s 50th anniversary this year, Jaclyn Smith, who played Kelly Garrett, reveals the series was originally meant to be about three leather clad women wearing whips and chains, living in a sleazy alley.

Now 80, Jaclyn says: “The original title was meant to be The Alley Cats. The idea was framed around our co-star Kate Jackson, as she had worked with US television producer Aaron Spelling before and he wanted her for his new project. When Kate went into Aaron's office one day her eyes drifted to a painting on his wall which had some angels in it and she said, ‘alley cats are out...the Angels are in’”.

As well as influencing the show’s concept, Jaclyn says of Kate: “She also came up with the show's central idea of having the famous speaker box on the desk where a man, our boss, would talk to you, but you would not see his face. Kate was very smart and very shrewd."

Red carpet dresses that changed the world of fashion from Princess Diana to Lady Gaga READ MORE :

Launching on September 22, 1976, the show followed the crime fighting adventures of three sassy investigators. Originally played by Farrah Fawcett, Kate Jackson and Jaclyn, they worked at an LA private detective agency for their unseen mysterious boss, Charlie Townsend, voiced by former Dynasty star John Forsythe.

‌



View 6 Images Farrah Fawcett, Jaclyn Smith, Shelley Hack, Cheryl Ladd, and David Doyle on the set of Charlie's Angels. (Image: Corbis via Getty Images)

Debuting on the ABC network, Charlie’s Angels was a game changer for actresses working in American TV. Jaclyn says: "You had never seen undercover female officers before. The network thought it would bomb, as they thought we had invaded the male genre.

“But Aaron Spelling was clever and he knew beauty was not enough, so he wanted enough danger to keep you leaning forward. People thought on Charlie's Angels we were exploited, but our characters were moral and loyal. We were girlfriends who stood by each other. We were three women in the lead roles instead of three men. Before, women were just seen as the nurse or the secretary.

"I did not understand why people thought we were just Barbie dolls. Yes, we had pretty clothes and fancy hairstyles, but it was more than that. The show was about fellowship and sisterhood. I am a breast cancer survivor. Yes your family suffers right along with you, but who sees you through? The power of girlfriends. They are the ones who take you to lunch and you talk it out."

‌



At first, the producers didn’t want the women to be armed. But, after a while, they changed their minds and Jaclyn and Farrah, who’d never handled a gun, had to learn how to hold one. Jaclyn says: “Aaron decided ‘they are cops, so they are going to carry guns’.

View 6 Images Jaclyn Smith with her new memoir, which is out on October 8 (Image: Getty Images)

"Pretty soon we were taking down 200lb men and none of us weighed more than 110lb. There was magic and Aaron understood what the public wanted to watch."

Famous for their edgy style, pin-up Farrah often went braless, wearing sheer blouses, for her character Jill Munroe - while Jaclyn wore sharp jackets, furs, silk shirts and tailored suits. Jaclyn says Kate, who played Sabrina Duncan, kept to turtle necks and was never seen in a swimsuit.

‌



But she adds: “Our clothes were fantastic. Our designer loved silks and gowns from the 1940s. The clothes were eye-catching, but the seventies was a melting pot of fashion. It had the Boho style and we wore everything on that show."

Yet, despite the liberating roles, Jaclyn says Farrah, who died of cancer aged 62 in 2009, had it written into her contract that she could leave at 7pm - to go home and cook her husband’s dinner. She says: "Farrah was supposed to be able to leave at 7pm, because she was married to the actor Lee Majors, who played The Six Million Dollar Man on TV. Lee wanted her home in time to cook dinner.”

View 6 Images (L-R) Kate Jackson, Jaclyn Smith and Cheryl Ladd attended the Charlie's Angels 50th Anniversary Celebration earlier this year (Image: Getty Images)

Regularly pulling in 20 to 23 million viewers per episode, Jaclyn says: "There was no cable TV like there is today, so half the televisions in America were tuned into our show. We were in every magazine, in every grocery store.”

‌



And, despite often working 18 hour days, she says she “loved it.” But, despite its runaway success, at the end of its first season Farrah quit, feeling creatively stifled.

Cheryl Ladd replaced her as her little sister, Kris Munroe, but Jaclyn feels Farrah regretted leaving. She says: "She did come back for three seasons as a guest star. But Cheryl came in and was amazing. It was a winning concept. I always used to say Farrah Fawcett's hair was the fourth Angel."

Charlie’s Angels was finally cancelled in June 1981 after five years, following declining ratings, cast changes and changing tastes in TV. Then, 19 years later in 2000, a Hollywood movie reboot starring Drew Barrymore, Cameron Diaz and Lucy Liu, won a new generation of fans.

View 6 Images Jaclyn Smith and Cheryl Ladd in a tense scene from Charlie's Angels season three (Image: Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

‌



And in 2003, Jaclyn took a cameo in the sequel, Charlie's Angels: Full Throttle, as well as making a guest appearance in the 2019 Gen-Z remake, starring Kristen Stewart, Naomi Scott and Elizabeth Banks. She says: "The story of Charlie's Angels just had some magic. I had to turn down a few roles because of it, like Mrs Robinson in The Graduate on Broadway, but the show was a threshold for me and opened many other doors."

After the original series ended, Jaclyn became a "face" for make-up giant Max Factor, before launching her own clothing and home goods line through the shopping giant Kmart. To date, more than 100 million women across America are said to have bought her branded clothing.

Speaking at an 92Y Talks event in New York, she says Charlie’s Angels helped make her business a success. Mum to son Gaston, 44, and daughter Spencer, 40, by her third husband, British cinematographer Anthony B. Richmond, the grandmother-of-three was married for the fourth time in 1997, to Dr Brad Allen.

View 6 Images Jaclyn Smith as Kelly Garrett in Charlie's Angels, circa 1978 (Image: Getty Images)

‌



She met the paediatric heart surgeon in 1990 when he operated on her father, Jack - dating him for seven years before getting hitched. She says: "The greatest love comes when you are not looking for it. We lived apart for 17 years. He had to win my family over, but he is the best stepfather for my children I could ever dream of."

Putting her glamorous appearance at 80 down to healthy living, sleep and being loved Jaclyn adds: "People ask me how I stay looking young and the answer is eating well. I don't drink, I don't do drugs. I am a goodie two shoes.

"I am still the girl from Texas who sweeps the driveway and, at my age, I am still fortunate enough to be still doing it. I am still fortunate to do a movie now and then. After all these years. It is fun to be still challenged and go towards the fear. I say ‘go where the fruit is’".

But Jaclyn sees Charlie’s Angels as her legacy. She says: "We all miss Farrah. I was close to her at the end of her life. She never lost hope and had courage. She was funny until the end and laughter sees you through so much.”

‌



Now, five decades after the Angels launched, she says: “I think it gave women a chance to imagine themselves as brave and think outside a conventional role. We paved the way for women in television.”

*Jaclyn Smith's new memoir, I Once Knew A Guy Named Charlie, is released October 8, priced £20.

News.title: Harry and Meghan not on guestlist for posh wedding as only William and Kate invited
News.content:
Harry and Meghan not on guestlist for posh wedding as only William and Kate invited

Lady Amelia Windsor's wedding plans emerged as Harry and Meghan prepare to settle back into life in Britain, while questions continue over their place within the wider Royal family

View 3 Images William and Harry are unlikely to cross paths at the wedding (Image: AP Photo/Martin Meissner)

Prince William and Prince Harry are set to avoid a potentially awkward reunion at their cousin Lady Amelia Windsor’s wedding.

‌



Amelia, 31, is engaged to property developer Ollie Lewis and is due to marry next May in London. The ceremony could have brought the estranged brothers together for the first time since they both attended their father’s coronation in May 2023.

‌



But the Prince and Princess of Wales are understood to have received save-the-date notices, while Harry and Meghan are not currently expected to be among the guests. A source said: “Amelia has curated her guestlist for her big day and news of Harry and Meghan’s arrival in the UK came after she had drafted her list."

‌



View 3 Images Lady Amelia was "snubbed" from the Duke and Duchess of Sussex's wedding (Image: Dave Benett/Getty Images for Mit)

Prince William launches £250,000 fund to regenerate Dartmoor village near prison READ MORE :

The source quoted by the Sun continued: “She isn’t close to the couple, but maybe it’s for the best as it saves an awkward run-in between the brothers at an otherwise special day. Of course she was snubbed from Harry and Meghan’s wedding so she doesn’t owe them anything.”

The wedding comes at a time of major change for Harry and Meghan, who have recently returned to Britain with Archie, 7, and Lilibet, 5.

‌



Meghan was recently spotted at luxury retreat Soho Farmhouse having n coffee, however she has yet to make a public appearance since the family’s return and is said to be concentrating on helping the children settle into their new schools and home. She could remain out of the spotlight for several weeks, while Harry is preparing for a string of appearances in the UK.

Their move has also put fresh attention on where the Sussexes now stand within the Royal Family. William is understood to remain opposed to Harry and Meghan resuming an official role, while the King has made clear that the couple will continue to live as private citizens.

View 3 Images William is believed to be remain opposed to the Sussexes return (Image: AP)

Article continues below

Guidance issued on behalf of the King states that the Sussexes should not use their HRH styles, which remain in abeyance, and that they “do not represent the sovereign” when making public appearances. The letter was issued under the King’s instruction by the Lord Chamberlain after requests were made for clarity over the couple’s status.

Amelia, the Duke of Kent’s granddaughter, is 45th in line to the throne and is expected to put her own stamp on the celebrations and has agreed an exclusive magazine deal with Hello! for photographs from the wedding after being seen enjoying Notting Hill Carnival last month.

Her grandmother, the Duchess of Kent died last year aged 92. Her funeral was a private Catholic Requiem Mass at Westminster Cathedral – a historic first for a senior royal – and was attended by the King, the Prince and Princess of Wales, and other senior members of the family.

News.title: AI staff 'genuinely frightened' for humanity's future, ex-Anthropic researcher tells BBC
News.content:
An artificial intelligence researcher who quit AI firm Anthropic has said people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity.

Jacob Coxon told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg on Saturday about his viral resignation post in which he raised concerns about out-of-control AI.

"I believe that if we don't slow down at the current rate of progress, there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future," he said.

His resignation comes amid growing safety concerns in the industry, including from his former boss, Anthropic head Dario Amodei, who in an essay argued for development to slow down.

The bosses of two rival AI firms, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk of xAI, have both said they agree with Amodei's proposal for industry-wide deceleration and regulation, as well as independent monitoring of AI model development.

Amodei said developing the technology was not in question, but the risks associated with it were "serious", and that companies and governments must be given time to address them.

The 27-year-old Coxon - who worked at OpenAI before joining Anthropic - welcomed the suggestion of a slowdown but said it would need to be co-ordinated with China to avoid "a race at an international scale".

"The people who work at these companies are completely serious when they ask for regulation because they find themselves trapped in a race. And they're scared of the outcomes of that race," he told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg.

News.title: Reform's £72m donations 'entirely in line with law', Jenrick says
News.content:
Robert Jenrick has said Reform UK believed that Â£72m in donations it has received from two cryptocurrency billionaires were "entirely in line with the law".

The party's economic spokesman told the BBC that he did not expect that it will have to return any of the money from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, who are both British and have spent time living overseas.

The government is seeking to change the law on donations to UK political parties from British expats, including a Â£100,000 cap backdated to 25 March.

"These two donations are entirely in line with the law as it is and, as far as we know, the law as it's going to be in the future," Jenrick said.

Jenrick also told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: "It might be that [Housing Secretary] Angela Rayner or the government keep trying to change the law to make it even harder for people to donate to Reform, nothing would surprise me.

"But, as it stands, we believe these are entirely in line with the law."

BBC News has been told that both Delo and Harborne have returned to the UK. Delo is understood to have been back in the country since last year.

Jenrick said Delo had returned to the UK "in part so that he can comply with the changes to the law".

As well as limiting how much British citizens can donate to political parties from overseas, the government has proposed limiting how much those who move back to the UK can give to Â£100,000 in the remainder of the calendar year and the following calendar year after they return.

News.title: Will the Thirlwall report change the debate about Lucy Letby?
News.content:
The quick take is this. The report won't change the narrative about Letby's guilt or innocence because it didn't examine that subject at all. That wasn't its remit.

Lady Justice Thirlwall said she had "approached the inquiry on the basis that Lucy Letby is guilty of the crimes of which she has been convicted".

She emphasised that it was not her role "to set about reviewing the convictions", telling the inquiry: "The Court of Appeal has done that, with a very clear result."

But there is also a longer, more complex answer.

Whatever the report's conclusions, Letby's convictions will stand. However, the inquiry hasn't operated in a vacuum. There are other parts of the legal system which will have an eye on its findings.

And the chairwoman of the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) - the only organisation with the power to send Letby's case back to the Court of Appeal - has told the BBC the CCRC will be paying close attention to Thirlwall.

Dame Vera Baird said: "We will be looking at the report with interest to assess whether it has any bearing on our review of the case."

The CCRC has given no indication of when it will make its decision.

But while questions over Letby's convictions weren't within the scope of the Thirlwall Inquiry, it didn't stop the subject making itself felt within the hearing room.

Just as the inquiry was wrapping up, the hospital's former executives applied for it to be delayed until the CCRC has made its decision.

Letters pushing for a delay were also written to the inquiry by Letby's lawyers and Sir David Davis, an MP who has campaigned on her behalf.

Sir David argued that an inquiry "predicated on the presumption that Lucy Letby's conviction is safe, when there is now a wealth of authoritative voices questioning that conviction, will only undermine the conclusions arrived at by your inquiry and potentially lead to more babies dying unnecessarily".

Lady Justice Thirlwall refused the requests to pause the inquiry. She said that she was not scrutinising Letby's actions, but those of the officials and managers who were responsible for responding to the crisis.

News.title: Student loan terms to be made clearer in England following repayment row
News.content:
University applicants in England will be given clearer information about student loans before they take them out, the government has said.

Ministers said they would spell out that governments can change repayment rules and that different career choices can affect how much borrowers repay.

They agreed to some but not all of the recommendations made by MPs after an inquiry into student loans, and did not say whether they would reverse a freeze to the repayment threshold for some graduates.

The inquiry found the way loans had been presented to teenagers amounted to mis-selling, after the BBC revealed the Department for Education (DfE) had compared repayments to Â£30-a-month phone contracts.

The recent debate has centred around Plan 2 loans, which were issued in England between September 2012 and July 2023, and are still issued in Wales.

The interest rate on those loans is the Retail Prices Index (RPI) measure of inflation plus up to 3% depending on earnings, and borrowers repay at a rate of 9% of everything they earn over a repayment threshold, which is meant to rise with inflation every year. The loans are written off after 30 years.

Campaigners want a lower interest rate, a lower repayment rate and for the government to reverse a decision last year to freeze the threshold at Â£29,385 for three years in England.

Freezing that threshold means graduates start repaying their loans sooner and, once they do, they pay more than they would have done if it had risen with inflation.

MPs on the Treasury Committee called for a U-turn on that decision as part of a series of recommendations after an inquiry this summer.

The Treasury and the DfE did not say whether ministers would unfreeze the threshold in their response, but said: "We keep all aspects of the student finance system under review."

News.title: Europe must endure winter of hardship to keep pressure on Putin, says PM's security adviser
News.content:
Powell said "we cannot turn that into an advantage for Putin", adding that pressure on Putin was working "and that means we have to keep the pressure up".

"It will require some real hardship and difficulties on our parts," he added. "But we will have to swallow that and we have to keep the economic, military, political and diplomatic support going for Ukraine."

While admitting that things in Ukraine did "feel a bit difficult at the moment", with a lack of Patriot air defence missiles, strikes on businesses and the governments budget deficit, Powell insisted "there are strong reasons for optimism".

He said Trump â who has blown hot and cold on Ukraine â was "in a very different place".

"He sees that Ukraine is doing better and therefore he is not leaning in the direction of Putin in the way that he was previously. I think that's a really big asset."

Powell said Russia was no longer claiming the US had agreed that Ukraine should give up territory and hopes of Nato membership at last year's Trump-Putin summit in Alaska.

"The so-called Anchorage compromise is firmly dead," he said. "We can stop worrying about it. It's finished."

This meant "we can look for serious ways of getting to a negotiated settlement, rather than waiting for the Ukrainian people to hand over territory the Russians have not been able to conquer", Powell said.

Ukrainian commanders had successfully held the front line on the ground while Russia had reached 1.5 million casualties, Ukraine had increasingly struck deep within Russian territory while Europe's resolve remained solid, he noted.

"The strategy is to apply enough pressure to make [Putin] want to get into negotiation," Powell said.

"And I think that the escalation we hear talk about is not a problem - it's a sign of success, because what's happening is the pressure that we are putting on Putin is finally paying off."

Putin himself has given little sign he is feeling under pressure, telling journalists earlier this month: "I have no doubt that the enemy will crumble."

Meanwhile, Ukrainian authorities have begun evacuating some residents in Slovyansk and Kramatorsk, the biggest cities still under full Ukrainian control in the eastern Donbas region. Russia claims sovereignty over the Donbas and fully capturing it is a key objective for Moscow.

Powell said the war was "not about territory" but about "the right of Ukraine to be independent", adding that "to the extent that [Putin] gains another 10km of land or loses another 40km of land, this war is already won".

"That's the threat to him at home. There is a free, independent and European Ukraine, and people in Russia are going to notice that."

The national security adviser said it was a "mug's game" to predict when the war might end, but said Europe had to be prepared to negotiate a settlement.

"Where we least expect it, Putin will be ready to negotiate... It's all about getting him to be serious in that negotiation. And I think that strategy is beginning to work."

Powell, who helped negotiate the Good Friday Agreement in Northern Ireland, said the US and Europe should maintain contact with Putin â despite describing the Russian leader as a "terrorist".

"What we don't want is miscalculation - that they don't understand where our red lines are. That's why I think it's important the CIA went to Moscow as well."

News.title: Flattened molars and facial pain: Why are more young people grinding their teeth?
News.content:
Ella can't remember when she first started grinding her teeth at night, but she can vividly recall the excruciating jaw ache, the headaches, and being told her molars were disappearing.

"I was in so much pain," Ella says. "My face was changing shape and my teeth were at risk of breaking - I knew I had to do something about it."

The 31-year-old has bruxism, a condition which can cause regular and often intense teeth grinding, but says the treatment she's recently had has "without a doubt" changed her life.

Bruxism affects millions like Ella across the UK, external. Some studies suggest nearly one in four people experience the condition, although many may be unaware until symptoms appear.

According to the British Dental Association there is some anecdotal evidence that bruxism is becoming more common, but no specific figures. However, some dentists have told the BBC they are worried about the increasing number of young people they're seeing with dental problems caused by incessant gnashing.

"It is definitely on the rise," Dr Aditi Desai, president of the British Society of Dental Sleep Medicine (BSDSM), says. "And it's no surprise given that life itself nowadays can be so stressful."

News.title: Diljit Dosanjh makes history under the famous Wembley arch
News.content:
On Saturday night, under the world-famous Wembley arch, five words rang out: "Punjabi Aa Gaye Wembley Oye!"

Indian megastar Diljit Dosanjh famously starts all his concerts by announcing that "the Punjabis have arrived".

But this time, it was a play on the usual catchphrase.

Dosanjh is the first ever Punjabi singer to headline Wembley Stadium, the music venue has said.

Addressing his fans, he reflected on the significance of the occasion. "This moment will go down in the history books," he said.

And as Bhangra beats blared out, fans erupted with cheers while Dosanjh launched into his biggest hits, from Born to Shine to Lover.

Over two decades, Dosanjh has built a huge global fanbase, topping charts and singing with the likes of Ed Sheeran.

He has even busted Bhangra moves with Jimmy Fallon, external, with the US talk show host labelling him "the biggest Punjabi artist on the planet".

His landmark concert at Wembley further cements his status as a global star.

Ahead of the show, the singer spoke exclusively to the BBC backstage, describing the moment as "a dream" for him.

News.title: Tom Felton: I'm so excited to see Rupert Grint play Ron Weasley again
News.content:
Every night on Broadway, Tom Felton walks on stage to a roar from the audience. He had expected the reaction to die down after the first week, but it never did.

Almost 15 years after his final appearance as Draco Malfoy on screen, Felton has spent the past 10 months playing the character again in the Broadway production of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child.

I meet the actor in a dressing room at NBC Studios, just off Times Square in New York. He's just finished a live television appearance and in a few hours will be back on stage for his next performance.

He greets me with a hug and says he is excited to speak to BBC News because his mum and 100-year-old grandfather will see it. His family are some of his biggest supporters - his mum has seen the show five times already, while his dad is due to visit next month.

That support mirrors the enthusiasm Felton has encountered from Harry Potter fans, which he says still surprises him more than two decades after he first played Draco.

"I thought the applause would stop in the first week and it has not.

"It's very humbling and lovely to know how much the characters still mean to people now and if it brings them to the theatre, that's the best."

He is also struck by how many of the fans now approaching him were not alive when the first Harry Potter film was released.

"There are fans that approach me shouting 'Draco' who weren't even born when I was in the first film," he says.

News.title: Garcia crushes overmatched Benn in two rounds
News.content:
Ryan Garcia crushed Briton Conor Benn with a ruthless second-round stoppage to retain his WBC welterweight crown in a world title mismatch in Las Vegas.

The American dominated from the opening bell, repeatedly punishing Benn as the 29-year-old charged forward with a wild and increasingly desperate approach.

Benn was dropped by a flush right hook in round two but managed to beat the count. before Garcia continued the onslaught with Benn backed against the ropes until the referee stepped in.

"I knew he would bring the pressure, I felt the shots and though 'I'll let him have his way', but I knew his was reckless and you can't do that with me," Garcia told DAZN.

"147lb is my division. I'm here, you can trust me as a champion."

It was a sobering - and, for many in the sport, unsurprising - conclusion to the biggest night of Benn's life in boxing.

Few gave the Essex fighter much chance, with Benn, who fell to the second defeat of his 10-year professional career, having never faced an opponent of Garcia's calibre and some questioning whether he had done enough to earn a world title shot in the first place.

Benn was fighting at welterweight for the first time in more than four years and had already said this would be his final appearance in the division, regardless of the result.

Garcia, 28, stayed true to his promise to stop Benn inside five rounds as he made a successful first defence of the title with his 26th win from 28 professional contests.

News.title: Major fire at derelict Peaky Blinders mill
News.content:
Another major fire has broken out at a derelict mill complex where Peaky Blinders was filmed.

The blaze at Dalton Mills in Keighley started at about 20:00 BST on Saturday and at its peak required 12 fire engines to tackle it.

West Yorkshire Fire and Rescue Service (WYFRS) confirmed that due to the severity of the incident a number of nearby residents were evacuated and at 23:00 BST, 10 fire engines were still in attendance.

A spokesperson added: "Members of the public are still advised to avoid the area to allow emergency services to operate safely and effectively."

News.title: Reform receives second £36m donation in two days as crypto investor matches record
News.content:
Harborne has already donated millions to Reform and Farage, who is currently under investigation by the parliamentary standards commissioner over whether he should have declared a Â£5m cash gift from Harborne ahead of the 2024 election.

Farage has argued that he was under no obligation to register the "purely private" gift, as it was unrelated to his parliamentary or political activities.

The party is also facing scrutiny after a broadcast by Channel 4 News last week showed two senior Reform aides apparently suggesting a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations.

The Metropolitan Police has said it is investigating, while the party denies any wrongdoing.

The force is also looking into donations given to the party by Fiona Cottrell, mother of longstanding Farage ally George Cottrell, as well as a company controlled by Tice.

Harborne wrote on Saturday that he had "already accumulated enough wealth for the rest of my life", while Reform was a "start-up party" that lacked "the benefit of hundreds of years of patronage".

"A start-up party needs more money than can be provided by membership fees alone, to build and sustain itself and be ready for government," he said.

Harborne and Delo's donations mark the largest sums received by a UK political party since they had to begin declaring them in 2001.

Delo, who also announced his donation in a Telegraph op-ed, said he was giving the money away because he wanted a "fair fight and a level playing field". He said in April he was moving back to Britain from Hong Kong.

Addressing the recent scrutiny of Reform's finances, he said: "My conclusion from Reform's recent troubles is that they should spend less time trying to raise funds to compete on equal terms and more time preparing for government."

Last year, he was given an unconditional pardon by US President Donald Trump over a breach of anti-money laundering laws at his crypto trading platform, BitMEX, to which he had pleaded guilty in 2022.

There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties.

However, the Labour government has introduced a Â£100,000 cap on donations from British citizens living overseas, and plans to introduce a similar one for those who have recently returned to the UK.

There were nine donations of Â£1m or more to political parties in 2025. The largest was Â£9m given to Reform UK by Harborne.

Labour had five donations of Â£1m or more - totalling nearly Â£10m - and the Conservatives had three of Â£1m each.

Labour said Reform and Farage still had "serious questions" to answer about their finances.

Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said Reform were "drowning" in "sleaze and scandal".

She added: "It's time Farage and Reform came clean with the public, fully co-operated with the ongoing police investigations and prove they're not just in it for themselves."

Rachel Millward, deputy leader of the Green Party, told BBC News it wanted a cap on donations from individuals of Â£500,000.

She said the donations to Reform were "absolutely staggering amounts", adding: "What I am very frustrated about is the influence of extreme wealth and the super rich. What I want to see is people in politics representing the needs of their communities and ordinary people."

Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart called for the government to introduce emergency legislation to cap donations.

She said: "These are eye-watering amounts of money. This is real emergency for our democracy. It presents a very clear and present threat."

Labour MP Stella Creasy and other backbenchers had proposed an amendment to the Government's Representation of the People Bill that would stop donors giving parties over Â£100,000 a year.

But the amendment was never debated in the Commons after the government said it would set up a task force to investigate the issue. The bill will be debated in the House of Lords on Monday.

Duncan Hames, Director of Policy and Programmes at campaigning charity Transparency International UK, said: "This is a watershed moment, with two billionaires pledging Â£72m to one political party in less than 48 hours.

"This situation is now completely out of control, and makes an irrefutable case for government to bring forward an annual cap on political donations, and fast."

News.title: Shocked walker finds SUV blocking route on Wales Coast Path
News.content:
Stunned walker Canberk Beker could not believe his eyes when he came across a car blocking his way on the Wales Coast Path.

The 31-year-old was out for a stroll with wife Bethan Jones, also 31, when they saw the blue Kia Sportage on Saturday morning between Mumbles and Langland Bay.

The driver had managed to wedge the SUV between a concrete fence post on one side and a bench on the other.

Canberk, from Langland, in Swansea, said: "It was completely covering the path. I was looking inside the car."

South Wales Police said it did not attend the scene, while a local councillor believes the driver mistakenly drove down a walking path believing to be a road before getting stuck.

News.title: A united Ireland would be 'fantastic' says Trump during Irish visit
News.content:
The Good Friday Agreement says the secretary of state must hold a border poll if it appears likely that a majority of people in Northern Ireland would vote for Irish unification - and the circumstances of when that could happen is the subject of constant debate in Northern Ireland and the Republic.

Earlier this week, Martin said there needed to be more clarity on when a border poll can be called, while Burnham ruled out calling a referendum, describing a poll as "off the table".

Sinn FÃ©in leader Mary Lou McDonald said she acknowledged Trumps comments on a united Ireland and said the onus is on the Taoiseach to begin planning.

Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Gavin Robinson said Trump "knows better than most that elections matter".

"Northern Ireland's constitutional future will be decided by the people of Northern Ireland, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington," he said.

Former DUP MP Ian Paisley and close friend of the Trump family said: "everyone is allowed a personal opinion even when it's wrong".

Welcoming his comments, the leader of the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) Claire Hanna said there was something "fairly extraordinary" about Trump standing in Dublin and talking openly about Irish unity.

"When even Donald Trump has clocked that Irish unity is no longer some distant or theoretical prospect, it tells you something about just how far this conversation has shifted."

The Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) leader Jon Burrows said while America is an "important ally," Northern Ireland's future will be decided by its people".

The Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) leader Jim Allister said Trump "is not the first US President to meddle in the affairs which don't concern him".

Ireland's Foreign Minister Helen McEntee said: "Something to this magnitude can only happen where there's consent from the Irish people.

"It's something that that we have to work on and we have to work towards."

Later, while attending an event at the US Ambassador to Ireland's residence, Trump said there is "no good answer" to a question about a united Ireland.

Recalling the moment, he said: "Oh that's a nice question, I have a nice answer, I think, we'll read about it tomorrow."

News.title: Three arrests at rival protests in Portsmouth
News.content:
The new powers came into effect at 10:00 BST. Participants on both sides were not seen to be wearing any face coverings when the marches started.

The city centre protests follow disorder on 6 September, when police attended Eastney Marina as hundreds of demonstrators blocked roads in an attempt to stop coaches carrying 120 migrants, who had crossed the Channel in a dinghy, from leaving the city.

On Saturday, up to 500 anti-migrant protesters held Union and St George flags while some wearing Portsmouth Patriot branded clothing gathered outside All Saints Church on Commercial Road shortly before midday on Saturday.

The crowd chanted "stop the boats" as they marched to Guildhall Square.

About 300 people joined the counter-protest.

Both sets of demonstrators were kept apart by police when they arrived at the square.

Speaking before the march, Simon Magorian, of Stand up to Racism Portsmouth, described the demonstrations in Eastney as a "horrible spectacle".

He said: "Portsmouth is actually a good functioning multi-cultural city.

"We are now organising to have the broadest possible opposition to what we see as a fascist street movement and we're not going to allow them to get a grip on Portsmouth or any other town - this is quite terrifying."

News.title: 'Skimpflation' warning as tinned mackerel alternative hits more supermarket shelves
News.content:
A growing trend of supermarkets selling a cheaper, less nutritious alternative to tinned mackerel is an example of "skimpflation", a consumer group has said.

Princes - which supplies major supermarkets - has substituted jack mackerel, an entirely different species, for mackerel, with similar tins also being sold by Lidl.

The switch has been spurred by dwindling stocks of Atlantic mackerel after years of overfishing, with its Chilean counterpart more sustainable and a third of the cost.

"It's a real concern when manufacturers quietly downgrade everyday staples like these as shoppers can end up paying the same price for a product that delivers significantly less nutritional quality," Sue Davies, head of food policy at Which?, said.

Jack mackerel contains about half as much omega-3 and around a third as much vitamin B12 as traditional mackerel.

The shift has prompted complaints from some consumers over differences in taste and texture, as well as concerns about how clearly the replacement fish is being labelled.

Princes announced last October, external that it was changing all of its tinned mackerel products to jack mackerel, saying the species meets the Marine Stewardship Council's sustainability standards.

The firm said its jack mackerel products were "clearly identified" and had been introduced following extensive product and consumer testing, describing it as having a "milder flavour and meatier texture".

Lidl is selling jack mackerel under its house brand. Lidl GB said it was "committed to sourcing fish and seafood from responsibly managed fisheries".

Davies from Which? said: "While manufacturers face genuine supply chain pressures and sustainability challenges, they have a responsibility to shoppers to be completely upfront when they change a product's recipe."

She added: "Skimpflation - quietly changing ingredients to cut costs - has become increasingly common, but it can feel particularly sneaky as shoppers may not realise a product has changed until they get it home and eat it."

News.title: Watch: Is the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition worth the hype?
News.content:
Visitors flocked to the British Museum in London on Thursday as the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition opened its doors to the general public.

The Bayeux Tapestry is an embroidery almost 70m (230ft) in length and nearly 1,000 years old. It tells the story of the Norman conquest of England and the Battle of Hastings in 1066.

Adult tickets to see the tapestry are priced at Â£33 during peak times and Â£27 at off-peak times, with an additional Â£3.50 donation.

The BBC's Katie Razzall asked the first visitors if it was worth the price.

News.title: Saturday Night Live UK review – Jeff Goldblum will do anything for attention
News.content:
Your support helps us to tell the story Read more Support Now From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. Your support makes all the difference. Read more

When it was first announced that Saturday Night Live would transfer to the UK, I called the show “doomed”. I was writing on a heady wave of confidence. British audiences are derisive about importing American formats, the show’s cast of young comics seemed absent of the necessary star power, and the series was due to air on Sky One, a channel that no one (except, perhaps, Richard Branson and the Duke of Westminster) can afford. It looked doomed. And yet the show is back now for a second series, which kicked off last night with renewed vigour. So, is SNL UK turning into a bit of a sleeper hit?

“I’m the new PM,” Andy Burnham (George Fouracres) announces during the season-opening sketch, “and I’m nothing like the last one!” The line is delivered with a wink. Back in March, Fouracres raised the curtain on the first series playing Keir Starmer. Times have changed, but the sources of comedic inspiration are reliable. The royal family make an appearance (“don’t tell me you’ve spent all your Netflix money!”, Charles (Larry Dean) laments to a returning Harry and Meghan, as does Celeste Dring’s Claudia Winkleman impression (the return of The Traitors in a couple of weeks will likely prove irresistible to the writers’ room). The only new cast member – Freddie Meredith – debuts in a passable scene in which he plays a young man being fed pick-up lines by Jeff Goldbum, who hosts this episode.

Without wishing to demean the enormous charisma of Mr Goldblum, one does sometimes have the sense that he will do anything for attention. After Tina Fey opened the first series, there seemed to be a dearth of A-listers willing to cross the pond for this SNL franchise. And so, Goldblum (who was also the top line guest on the first episode of Claudia Winkleman’s ill-fated chat show) is, at least, a genuine international star. “Well I’m hoping to be,” he warbles at a piano during a sing-song opening monologue, “your precise cup of tea!” The problem with Goldblum as a host is that he is both incredibly game yet also has the dramatic range of a hyperactive toddler. He plays, well, Jeff Goldblum in each of his sketches, the highlight of which is a musing on imaginary friends with a genuinely heart-breaking punchline.

SNL sketches are always spotty, and this season opener is more miss than hit. There’s a good gag at the heart of Gregor J Dupont (Fouracres, again), a thespian who dresses up as a baby to prepare expectant parents, yet the delivery rips off Brian Butterfield, Peter Serafinowicz’s business guru, and the tone feels cadged from Ollie and Archimedes, a pair of verbose British tots who appeared on Very Important People. Ania Magliano and Paddy Young (who should be incorporated into more of the main sketches, in my opinion) return to Weekend Update, and the material continues to be enjoyably edgy. Magliano muses that Germany’s Alternative für Deutschland is really more of an “old classic for Germany”, while Young observes that Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu might’ve thought that “Burnham was just something you do to refugee camps”. While the gags in this section are largely quite sharp, the delivery is a tad stumbling.

Because the cast are good and growing in confidence (some, like Ayoade Bamgboye and Hammed Animashaun get almost no screen time in this episode, though that will likely be evened out over the series), the show has legs. Yet it remains unpolished and, squirreled away on Sky One, is unlikely to find the sort of audience necessary to make it a major talent factory for UK comedy. Ultimately, the show will live or die on its virality, its clippability (to coin a horrible word), yet the YouTube channel currently has just 196k subscribers (for reference, ThomasWoodenRailway, a channel dedicated to a man’s Thomas the Tank Engine model rail set, has 215k subscribers). Since it first aired, the British comedy scene has been talking a lot about SNL UK, yet it doesn’t seem to have the breakout potential of Taskmaster, Have I Got News for You, or even a podcast like Off Menu.

The cast of 'SNL UK' ( Sky )

And so, yes, it still feels a bit doomed. There are exogenous pressures beyond the control of Daran Johnson and his team of writers, or the cast. The fact that the next two episodes will be hosted by Jamie Demetriou and Amelia Dimoldenberg (both funny, yet hardly household names) suggests that the producers are struggling to pitch the project to Hollywood stars on the publicity trail. It makes the show feel parochial when it should be a showcase for the deep reserves of untapped talent still bubbling away under British soil.

From exercise snacking and vibration plates to the 75 Hard Challenge, the health and fitness landscape is constantly overflowing with viral crazes, with new routines gaining momentum almost weekly.

Among the latest practices earning praise from online influencers is the Japanese walking method.

But what does the technique actually involve, and is it a worthwhile addition to a daily routine?

To clarify how the approach works, as well as its main advantages and possible drawbacks, expert advice comes from Steve Chambers, a certified personal trainer and gym manager at Ultimate Performance.

Understanding the Japanese walking method

"It’s a cardiovascular training method, but it’s a little bit more focused than just going out and trying to do more steps because there’s a bit of a protocol to it," says Chambers.

Formally known as Interval Walking Training (IWT), the routine centres on structured changes in pace rather than passive movement.

open image in gallery Interval Walking Training (IWT) centres on structured changes in pace rather than passive movement. ( PA )

"It involves alternating between three minutes of walking at a slower, more relaxed pace, followed by three minutes of faster, more purposeful walking, repeated in cycles for around 30 minutes," explains the personal trainer.

"So, the effectiveness of this workout comes from the changes in intensity over this half-hour period, rather than the number of steps."

open image in gallery The routine centres on structured changes in pace rather than passive movement. ( Alamy/PA )

Chambers suggests completing a suitable warm-up prior to beginning. He explains that practitioners can monitor their pace using the Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE) scale, which ranges from 1 to 10.

"For the slower three-minute periods, you want to be on the lower end of the scale, so I would recommend nothing more than a five out of 10," advises Chambers. "If you do this with someone else, you should be able to hold a conversation during this three-minute window.

"However, for the faster three-minute periods, you want to try and push that up to a seven or an eight out of 10. So, you’re not quite maxing it because you want to be able to repeat this multiple times over the half-hour period, but your heart rate should go up quite a lot."

Minimal equipment required

"You can do it either on a treadmill or outdoors on foot," says Chambers. "All you need is a stopwatch or a phone to help time the three-minute cycles."

Accessible for beginners

"This training method is accessible to lots of different types of people, including those who are brand new to training and don’t know where to start," says Chambers.

"The entry level for it is really low because your seven out of 10 versus somebody else’s will be completely different, so it’s accessible for different fitness levels."

Gentler on joints

"Running has a high impact on your joints when your feet hit the floor. However, the surface impact of walking is a lot lower, so this walking method of training is much more friendly on the joints," says Chambers.

open image in gallery You just need something to time the three-minute intervals ( Alamy/PA )

"Therefore, from a longevity perspective and an injury prevention perspective, this is a massive win."

Activates multiple muscle groups

"All the lower body muscles – such as your glute muscles, quadriceps, hamstrings, and calf muscles – are engaged during this interval walking method," says the personal trainer.

"Even the smaller muscles, ligaments and tendons in and around the feet will all be working while you walk."

He notes that walking naturally recruits both the core and arms as well.

Enhances cardiovascular health

"During the faster intervals, you heart will be working a little bit harder and will be pumping more blood around the body, which will improve your cardiovascular fitness," says Chambers.

Social potential

"I would recommend asking a friend or family member to join you, as it can be a great opportunity to catch up with somebody," suggests Chambers. "Sharing this journey can help boost enjoyment and motivation, which makes people more likely to keep going and do it more regularly."

Highly time-efficient

"Everyone is so busy these days, so if you haven’t got a lot of time in your diary for training, you can just do this in a half an hour slot that you have spare," says Chambers. "So, this is a really time-efficient training method which is another big win."

Potential drawbacks to keep in mind

"One drawback is that there’s a limit of how much muscle growth, definition and strength that somebody could get out of following this walking training method," says Chambers.

open image in gallery ( Alamy/PA )

"This is because although the muscles are working whilst you are walking, there isn’t that external load that needs to be there to further increase strength levels and improve muscle definition. Therefore, I would recommend doing it in conjunction with other forms of training such as resistance training."

He adds that online trends should always be approached with a degree of healthy scepticism.

"I’ve seen many fitness trends come and go over the years, and while some are gems, some have no research to back them," says Chambers. "So, if you see a fitness trend on social media I would recommend doing your own research and it might be worth consulting a personal trainer too to see if they know anything about it."

Marcus Trescothick believes it is important for England’s Test team to keep a homegrown influence in their new coaching set-up, though his own future remains unclear.

Trescothick completed his interim stint in charge of the side by wrapping a 3-0 whitewash over Pakistan and will immediately join up with Brendon McCullum’s white-ball side for their forthcoming series against Sri Lanka on Sunday.

Incoming red-ball head coach Stephen Fleming is due to arrive in England in the coming days, leaving both squads in the hands of New Zealanders.

open image in gallery Stephen Fleming arrives in England soon to take over the Test team (Nick Potts/PA) ( PA Wire )

Fellow Kiwis Tim Southee and Jeetan Patel are also involved with the bowling group, Australian Marcus North is a recent arrival as national selector and his compatriot Mike Hussey was reportedly sounded out by Fleming as a possible Test batting mentor.

Trescothick has been the most senior English figure in the regime for the last four and a half years but is in the dark about how, or if, he will be involved in the next chapter.

“There’s another transition to happen with Stephen coming in to work with Joe Root and plan how they are going to move things forward,” he said.

“We’ll see how it pans out. Within the next couple of weeks we’ll probably know a little bit more. I’ve spoken with Rob Key (director of men’s cricket) a little bit over the last couple of weeks, had bits of discussions on what might happen. When Stephen is over, he and Rob and Brendon can really get together and thrash out how it’s going to look.

“I probably do (have a preference) but it’s probably best I don’t mention it at the moment because it may not be what happens. I love doing both formats. It’s been brilliant and a privilege.”

open image in gallery Former England wicketkeeper Sarah Taylor has impressed in a temporary role this summer (Mike Egerton/PA) ( PA Wire )

Trescothick is not the only English voice in contention for a role, with Sarah Taylor earning positive reviews for her work as a fielding consultant this summer and Michael Yardy temporarily promoted from his role with the under-19s in recent weeks.

And retaining a local influence is something Trescothick hopes for, regardless of his own status.

“Yeah, I’d like to think so. There’s nothing better than working for your own national country,” he said.

“Within the course of the coaching system you want someone within that who can highlight things that are important to England players, England teams, England series. They are different to other countries and unique in their own way.

“We want to try and promote our own from within and get them up to the top because there’s nothing better if you can get to that point. It’s not the be-all and end-all but if we can have representation in there the better it will be.”
