The visitors remained dangerous on the counterattack and Alisson pushed away a King effort that was heading for the top corner. King’s replacement, Rodrigo Muniz, let a decent chance run away from him inside the area and the substitute Kevin dragged a shot wide from 18 yards. Isak finally escaped Bassey’s attentions in stoppage time but his flicked header from a Szoboszlai corner sailed wide.

Arbeloa said: “When you are not winning games it’s not so easy for your players to believe in your ideas. But they believe in the way we have been working and I showed them the things that we were doing so well. We were more balanced and controlled the transitions well. I’m happy with the point but more with the performance of my players and the character, the personality and the ambition they showed in this stadium.”

Sports.title: European football: Dortmund win again but Freiburg top after Gladbach rout
Sports.content:
Felix Nmecha scored twice and Fábio Silva grabbed another as Borussia Dortmund won 3-0 at home to promoted Paderborn to continue their perfect start in the Bundesliga. Dortmund’s win made it three from three in the league this campaign, their best start in 11 seasons, dating back to Thomas Tuchel’s time.

Starting up front alongside Serhou Guirassy for the first time this season, Silva converted a clever pass from the Guinean to give the hosts the lead after five minutes. Guirassy had two goals disallowed for offside in the first half but Dortmund were rarely troubled by the toothless visitors, who are yet to score since returning to the top flight.

Nmecha came off the bench to score twice, wrapping up victory for the hosts with a stunning late bicycle kick.

Dortmund captain Nico Schlotterbeck made his first appearance since picking up an ankle injury at the World Cup and told Sky Germany he kept his comeback under wraps. “We just hadn’t communicated that much yet because I didn’t want to,” Schlotterbeck said, adding “I missed it terribly. It was a serious injury but I’m glad to be back now.”

Freiburg thumped a poor Borussia Mönchengladbach 5-0 at home to climb to the top. Yannik Engelhardt and Igor Matanovic netted twice each and Maximilian Eggestein added a late fifth as the hosts sent Gladbach, who finished with 10 men, to the foot of the table.

View image in fullscreen Freiburg’s Matthias Ginter (centre) congratulates Igor Matanovic on the opening goal against Borussia Mönchengladbach. Photograph: Philipp von Ditfurth/DPA/AP

A 2-2 home draw with Bayer Leverkusen ended Augsburg’s short stint as leaders. Augsburg were top after the last matchday for the first time in their history but were held by Leverkusen despite a double from Michael Gregoritsch.

Eintracht Frankfurt won their first match of the campaign with a 3-1 victory at neighbouring Mainz, with Can Uzun’s double either side of a Jonathan Burkardt goal. Frankfurt’s goalkeeper Noah Atubolu kept his remarkable penalty-saving record alive when he stopped a first-half effort from Nadiem Amiri. Atubolu’s save was his sixth in a row, extending his own Bundesliga record.

West Ham loanee Niclas Füllkrug kept his excellent run of form since returning to the Bundesliga going, scoring the equaliser for Werder Bremen in a 1-1 draw at Cologne. Thijs Dallinga missed a penalty after eight minutes but teammate Linton Maina put Cologne ahead moments later.

Füllkrug’s goal came in the 69th minute and is his third in four games since returning to Germany. He only found the net three times in 29 matches for West Ham and scored just once in 20 games on loan at Milan last season.

Elsewhere, Hoffenheim won 2-1 at home against Stuttgart thanks to a double from Adam Hlozek. On Sunday, Bayern Munich travel to promoted Elversberg – who have a 100% record – while RB Leipzig host Hamburg.

In Spain, Kylian Mbappé scored twice ⁠as Real Madrid enjoyed a 4-1 victory over Rayo Vallecano ⁠in La Liga ⁠at ​the Santiago Bernabéu. Goals from Álvaro Carreras and Jude ⁠Bellingham made the result comfortable for José Mourinho’s side.

View image in fullscreen Kylian Mbappé celebrates scoring Real’s fourth against Rayo Vallecano. Photograph: Manu Fernández/AP

A 14th-minute ⁠penalty from Mbappé was followed three minutes ​later by ‌a simple finish ‌from Carreras, with Mbappé turned provider ‌this time. A relaxed Real found little resistance from Rayo thereafter and, 11 minutes before half time, Vinícius Júnior raced down the left to set up ‌Bellingham for a neat finish into the corner.

Six minutes into the ​second half, Sergio Camello pulled a goal back for Rayo following sloppy Real Madrid play. Despite whistles from the ⁠home crowd, Real kept Rayo at ​bay, ​before closing out the ​game with a 90th-minute goal ​from ‌Mbappé.

The result ​moved ​Real on to 12 points, level with leaders Barcelona, who have a game in hand. Barça are at Levante on Sunday afternoon. Alavés missed the chance to go top overnight with a 2-1 defeat at Racing Santander.

In Italy, Diego Moreira scored twice as Milan came from two goals down to hold early season Serie A pacesetters Lazio 2-2 in Rome on Saturday. Moreira came off the bench at half-time and hauled Milan level after Matteo Cancellieri and Tijjani Noslin had given the hosts the lead at the interval.

Despite losing their 100% record having started the season with three wins, Gennaro Gattuso’s side move to the top of the table. Ruben Amorim’s Milan are fourth on eight points, after also drawing last weekend at Juventus.

View image in fullscreen Milan’s Diego Moreira celebrates scoring in his side’s 2-2 draw with Lazio. Photograph: Riccardo Antimiani/EPA

Cancellieri opened his account for the campaign after 10 minutes when he connected with a Mattia Zaccagni cross. A dominant Lazio had good chances to pull further clear before Noslin doubled their lead after 39 minutes with a close-range finish.

Amorim attempted to stem the tide by making three substitutions at half-time, bringing on playmaker Christian Pulisic and Moreira. His changes bore fruit after 65 minutes as Moreira volleyed home to halve the deficit. Less than two minutes later, the former Strasbourg player equalised with a fierce strike from outside the box, but neither side could find a late winner.

Atalanta slumped to a 2-1 defeat at home to Cagliari, with Sead Kolasinac handling the ball in the box to concede a second-half penalty that gave the visitors the win. Cagliari took the lead in the 19th ⁠minute when 19-year-old forward Paul Mendy rattled in the opener off the underside of the crossbar, ​but Gianluca Scamacca levelled for the home side ​four minutes before the break.

Mendy had the ​ball in the net again early in the second half only for the goal to be ruled out ​for a narrow offside, but ‌they took the lead ​again after Kolasinac was penalised, ​Daniel Maldini firing home from the spot to secure the three points.

The result moved Cagliari up to fourth in the table with nine points from their four games, while Atalanta are in ninth spot on six points. Earlier, hosts Genoa, who have yet to win this season, were held 1-1 by newly promoted Frosinone, who have seven points.

Champions Inter host Udinese on Monday, with Roma heading to Torino and Como at home to Parma. Inter and Roma have both won each of their first three matches.

Sports.title: Farke’s blueprint for revitalised Leeds continues upward trajectory
Sports.content:
Eleven years have passed since Daniel Farke mounted a magnificent palomino horse and rode round the perimeter of the pitch at Lippstadt, waving farewell to a capacity crowd. It seemed a fun way for the lower-tier German club’s centre-forward turned manager and sporting director to say goodbye. Yet few in the stands knew Farke was scared of horses and hauled himself into the saddle only out of politeness towards his chair, who had arranged this special surprise.

“I couldn’t deny him,” he said. “But it cured my fear – it was enjoyable.”

These days the Leeds manager is demanding similar bravery, as well as instant adaptability, from his players. “We want to be hard to predict,” said Farke as he prepared to welcome his compatriot Matthias Jaissle’s rapid counterattacking Newcastle team to Elland Road on Monday night. “We have different approaches. For example, if a team has two very good centre-backs who dominate aerially it makes sense to build with more low passes.

“It’s always in our DNA that we want to be on the ball and, in the buildup, we always want to be brave. Also it’s possible to break the [opposition] pressing by playing good football out from the back.”

View image in fullscreen Daniel Farke says ‘anything is possible’ for Leeds this season ahead of match with Newcastle on Monday. Photograph: Matthew Childs/Action Images/Reuters

Not that Leeds are averse to taking the direct route. This season only Hull and Nottingham Forest have played a higher percentage of their passes long than a Leeds XI invariably spearheaded by the formidable Dominic Calvert-Lewin. As Farke says: “We very often have a physical target player up front that we can be a bit more direct into.”

If such tactical variety is designed to keep rivals guessing, a fusion of alternative styles also befits a coach who admires the contrasting approaches of his close friends Pep Guardiola and Jürgen Klopp.

Adaptability almost certainly saved his job last season. From 4 October to 29 November Leeds played seven Premier League games, losing six. They have since completed 28 league fixtures, losing five, while reaching an FA Cup semi-final.

Farke is negotiating from a position of strength as he discusses extending a contract that has less than a year to run. “Daniel’s done great,” the Leeds managing director, Robbie Evans, said this week. “We want him to be here long term and we’re working on it.”

View image in fullscreen Daniel Farke’s half-time changes against Manchester City in November transformed Leeds’s fortunes. Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

Everything changed on 29 November. Leeds lost 3-2 at Manchester City but Farke’s half-time switch to a back three, allied to Calvert-Lewin’s introduction, provided him with a timely lifeline. The changes enabled the visitors, trailing 2-0, to level in a transformative second-half performance spoiled only by Phil Foden’s stoppage-time winner.

It marked the start of an upward trajectory that has continued this season as Leeds, alternating between three and four at the back, have remained unbeaten, like Newcastle.

A watershed perhaps came when England’s James Trafford arrived this summer from City for £40m – a record fee for a British goalkeeper. Given Newcastle had tried to buy Trafford on three occasions his signing represents something of a coup for Leeds. Throw in the abundance of diggers, hard hats and hi-vis vests on view at Elland Road as the stadium is expanded from a capacity of just under 38,000 to 53,000 and the sense of a club on the up is almost palpable.

“Something’s going well here,” Trafford said after signing. “They [the owners, 49er Enterprises] want to take the club back to where it has been historically and I think everyone here believes that is going to happen.

“With the energy, physicality and quality in this team anything is possible this season. The spirit is incredible. It’s really, really good and that can take you a long way.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

If such harmony can be attributed to Farke’s “no dickheads” policy when it comes to potential signings and the midfielder Ethan Ampadu’s impressive embrace of the captaincy, astute recruitment is steadily raising the team’s calibre.

The Bosnia and Herzegovina centre-half Tarik Muharemovic is proving an outstanding defender and a fine distributor. The £34m buy from Sassuolo is emblematic of the amalgam of robust athleticism and technical ability that increasingly characterises a Leeds team further enhanced by Harry Wilson’s arrival from Fulham.

View image in fullscreen Tarik Muharemovic scored for Leeds against Chelsea in the Carabao Cup and has already proved to be an astute summer signing. Photograph: Adam Davy/PA

Not that Farke is getting carried away. After seeing Trafford’s deputy, Michael Zetterer, overwhelmed as a rotated Leeds lost 6-3 at Chelsea in the Carabao Cup on Wednesday he was not in the mood for excuses.

“Let’s be honest, it was a nightmare debut,” Farke said on Thursday. “You feel a bit for him, but sometimes in life you have the worst possible start. He will have pressure next time, but he’s a good goalkeeper. They live a privileged life and he’s playing for a big club.”

On Monday, he will offer Jaissle a somewhat warmer greeting. They share a friendship with Klopp and Thomas Tuchel, but the Newcastle manager’s recent posting in Jeddah with Al-Ahli helped ensure that, until now, their paths have not crossed.

“He’s made a bright start,” Farke said. “Newcastle are very dangerous, especially counterattacking and it will be difficult. But we want to be on top of their challenge. We want as many points as possible.”

Sports.title: Why Conor Benn's 85-second humiliation against Ryan Garcia was the inevitable consequence of his fast-tracked career - and how the Brit became a sacrificial pawn in boxing's power struggle, writes JEFF POWELL
Sports.content:
Why Conor Benn's 85-second humiliation against Ryan Garcia was the inevitable consequence of his fast-tracked career - and how the Brit became a sacrificial pawn in boxing's power struggle, writes JEFF POWELL

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

The Wizard Of Oz is now a spectacular fantasy production encompassing the inside of the giant globe called The Sphere which looms large over the Las Vegas Strip.

Where the yellow brick road leads for Conor Benn after his one round, one minute and 25 seconds destruction by the fastest gun in Sin City is a question to which nobody had the answer as he was being ferried to hospital for precautionary checks. And may not have for some time to come.

There is no clear pathway back to the heights to which he was thrust all too prematurely and without justification this Saturday night.

Benn had no place being in the same ring as world welterweight champion Ryan Garcia, who is emerging as the golden goose saviour of American and Mexican boxing. Nor had he done anything like enough in his patchwork career thus far to qualify for the honour of topping the bill at an arena as grand as the T-Mobile in as hallowed a home of boxing as Las Vegas.

This was a match made far away from fight heaven, deep in the casino vaults. Benn Jr leaves here millions of dollars the richer but with not so much as a scintilla of evidence that he will ever be able to mix it with the royalty of the ring, in which King Ry sits upon the throne. He has the payoff but not the legacy he craved.

For the second time in as many months English sport comes home from America with its tail between its legs. Only this clinical beat-down of an inferior boxer was aeons more humiliating than the retreat of our footballers from the World Cup. His defeat more comprehensive than that by Argentina.

Conor Benn was beaten inside two rounds by Ryan Garcia in their welterweight championship fight

Benn's humiliating defeat came after he thrust all too prematurely and without justification into the title fight

Benn had no place in being in the same ring as world welterweight champion Ryan Garcia

Little did Benn know, in his delusion of self grandeur, that in return for securing his family’s financial future he was used as a sacrificial pawn in the power struggle for control of big-time boxing between the houses of Queensberry and Matchroom against the arrival of UFC promoter Dana White on their doorstep.

Garcia, younger of the two by a year but a decade wiser, knew. He tried to cushion Benn’s fall from grace by calling him a ‘good dude who I hope can come back from this.’

But as a man who likes to tell it as it is he felt compelled to add: ‘ I knew exactly how the fight would go. Rushing in against me from the start is not a good idea. Not the way to go. You need patience in this game.’

When it was pointed out to him that Benn has not stopped an opponent for more than four years he added: ‘I must be honest. I did not feel any power in his punches.’

Not that there were many of them. Benn’s charge from the first bell was suicidal against the best, fastest and hardest counter puncher in the world. He ran headlong into a hail of Garcia’s trademark left hooks. To note that he lost the first round is as understated as saying that Goliath had a bad day at the office against David. And when in the second Garcia brought into play the right hand which is now almost as deadly as the left Benn was gone in 85 seconds.

Gone crawling on the canvas and still so unsteady when reeled to his feet that the referee let him continue only so far as the next battering.

Garcia observed: ‘It could have been stopped after the first knock down. I looked into his eyes down there and they were glazed over. He was already gone.’

He echoed the pre-fight fears of many of us that Benn could be in critical jeopardy if this went on too long, saying: ‘It would not have been good for Conor if this lasted any further.’

Benn appears to have been a sacrificial pawn in the power struggle for control of big-time boxing between Queensberry and Matchroom against the arrival of UFC promoter Dana White

Has he lived to fight another day? Dana White sounded less than totally convinced: ‘I’ve told Conor to go on holiday with his family and call me when he’s ready to come back. Then we can try to find the right fight for him.’

That would not be at welter after his ‘hellish’ struggle to cut his poundage. But if he can be hammered into oblivion by a 147-pounder what will become of him if he goes back up two divisions to middleweight?

No such doubts hang over Garcia. Having been saluted to the reverberating rafters of the T-Mobile by his half-brother Mexicans in the delirium of their Independence weekend celebrations, this Californian will resume his American love affair in more world title fights against the likes of Devin Haney and Teofimo Lopez.

He, not Conor Benn in his wildest dreams, is the face and the future of boxing over here.

Sports.title: Ollie Robinson is England's most lethal bowler for more than a century - tougher tests are to come, but here's why - and how - he's grabbed his second chance by the horns, writes LAWRENCE BOOTH
Sports.content:
Ollie Robinson is England's most lethal bowler for more than a century - tougher tests are to come, but here's why - and how - he's grabbed his second chance by the horns, writes LAWRENCE BOOTH

The coffee machine was on the blink at England's team hotel on Friday morning, with Ollie Robinson – his four-week-old daughter Evie cradled in his arms – waiting patiently at the head of the queue. It felt like one of the few times this summer he had been held up by circumstances beyond his control.

Even after Pakistan's No10 Razaullah put a small dent in his figures that evening with his six-laden innings of 81, Robinson finished the home Test season with numbers once thought possible only in the era of uncovered pitches and rudimentary batting techniques.

After taking seven wickets at 11 in his only Test against New Zealand at Lord's, including a first over that turned into a triple-wicket maiden, he hoovered up 21 at under nine against Pakistan.

It all added up to 28 at 9.32, making him the first seamer to take 20 wickets in an English summer at an average below ten. And no English bowler of any hue has achieved the feat since Tony Lock with his left-arm spin ran through New Zealand in 1958.

'It'll probably never happen again,' he said with a smile as he awaited his latte. The Australians, due here next summer to defend the Ashes, will be hoping he's right.

One of the kneejerk responses on social media to his success has been to decry the quality of Pakistan's batting, or to point out the assistance Robinson has received both from the pitches and from a Dukes ball that England are convinced is staying harder for longer.

The sensational Ollie Robinson finished the summer with 28 Test wickets at a 9.32 average

Yet, faced with exactly the same factors, none of his team-mates has matched his feats. Josh Tongue's 27 wickets this summer have come at 26, Jofra Archer's 23 at 24, and Gus Atkinson's 14 at 30. Good numbers, certainly – but nothing to touch Robinson.

Equally, there have been bowler-friendly summers before, but Robinson is nudging his way into some serious statistical company.

Only three England bowlers have taken more than his 104 Test wickets at an average lower than his 19: SF Barnes took 189 at 16, Johnny Briggs 118 at 17, and George Lohmann 112 at ten. Of those, Barnes played most recently – in 1914. There is a case, then, for arguing that Robinson is England's most effective bowler for 112 years.

Plenty has been said about his long absence from the side under Brendon McCullum and Ben Stokes – essentially because of his relaxed attitude to fitness, which drove the management to distraction and eventually, in India in 2023-24, tipped them over the edge.

And history appeared to be repeating itself when the Bazballers didn't trust him to get through the decider against New Zealand at Trent Bridge in June, after he missed the Oval Test because of a knee niggle.

But, under Joe Root, Robinson was straight into the side against Pakistan, and took a wicket with the first ball of the series, nipping one back into the pads of Azan Awais at Headingley, and rarely pausing for breath.

Of his 28 victims this summer, 12 have been leg-before, and another five bowled. Nine have fallen for ducks, 11 more in single figures. He has been relentless.

'I've been trying to set the tone and land it on the spot,' he told Ian Ward on Sky Sports before play on Friday. 'Luckily, the batters are either nicking it or missing it.'

He has been thrown into the deep end under Joe Root after a lack of trust from Ben Stokes

He was being unduly modest. Robinson worked on his fitness while playing grade cricket for the University of Sydney over the winter, and was then made captain of Sussex's red-ball team – a move he said had given him the 'drive and motivation to love the game again'. England now use him to select which ball to pick from the box of options supplied by the umpires.

He has also been tweaking his skills and his action, working on his wobble-seam deliveries, while passing on advice to Tongue, and standing up a fraction taller at the crease. That has reduced his pace, from an average of nearly 83mph against South Africa four years ago to 78 against Pakistan.

Previously, England might have held that against him. But he has been so accurate that it hasn't mattered. Besides, the speed is provided by Archer, Tongue and Atkinson. They dovetail nicely, even if Razaullah made them look pedestrian for two hours on Friday evening.

He has been helped, too, by the wicketkeeping of Jamie Smith and, in Pakistan's second innings at Edgbaston, Jordan Cox, who were both excellent standing up to the stumps and creating a sense of claustrophobia from which the batsmen rarely escaped.

Above all, it all feels like a second chance for a 32-year-old who thought his time had gone. 'I thought I'd never play for England again,' he said after Root's team sealed a 3-0 win. 'But I've got a new ambition to keep going and push on. There's still a lot of hard work to do, but I'm just getting started.'

The three-match series in South Africa starting on December 17 will present a different challenge, with pitches in Johannesburg, Centurion and Cape Town less likely to do his bidding. For now, though, he can reflect on a job done so remorselessly that the record books have had as little respite as Pakistan's batsmen.

Sports.title: Rooney's overhead kick, Hinchcliffe's bullet header, Balotelli's T-shirt - and Owen's dramatic late winner: The greatest Manchester derby moments in history as Enzo Maresca's side gear up for huge clash at Old Trafford
Sports.content:
Rooney's overhead kick, Hinchcliffe's bullet header, Balotelli's T-shirt - and Owen's dramatic late winner: The greatest Manchester derby moments in history as Enzo Maresca's side gear up for huge clash at Old Trafford

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

United host Manchester City on Sunday in the 199th Manchester derby - 135 years after the clubs first faced off, way back in 1891.

With both sides hoping to add another memorable chapter to one of the most storied rivalries in English football, here, Daily Mail Sport's writers recount their favourite moments so far...

The biggest shock of them all?

I was in the Platt Lane End at Maine Road with the United fans when Sir Alex Ferguson’s team went there on September 23rd 1989. Few expected City to win but they battered United 5-1.

It was the sense of shock about the scale of the victory I remember most. City’s left back, Andy Hinchcliffe, scored the fifth right in front of us, a bullet header from a David White cross, still the best goal I’ve ever seen in a Manchester derby.

OLIVER HOLT

Andy Hinchcliffe celebrates his goal in City's 5-1 win in 1989 alongside Ian Brightwell (left) and Paul Lake (right)

Last-gasp Owen

Michael Owen's winning goal in Man United's 4-3 win in 2009. By his own admission, Owen's career was on the decline by this stage. This, then, was a rare sighter of the supreme talent that he had been 10 years previous, and he produced it on the biggest stage. The pass from Ryan Giggs to set him clear was also a reminder of his class, at 35 years old.

CRAIG HOPE

Another vote for a seven-goal thriller...

I’ll go with the Manchester derby at Old Trafford in 2009. A seven-goal thriller that was all about the strikers. Wayne Rooney scored after two minutes. Carlos Tevez, booed on every touch, was the architect of the Gareth Barry equaliser. Craig Bellamy scored a screamer to make it 2-2, and then punished Rio Ferdinand for his second and City’s third. Then came one of the most iconic Manchester derby goals ever scored… by Michael Owen.

NATHAN SALT

And it was a birthday treat ...

Sunday September 20, 2009, was notable largely because it was my 40th birthday weekend but there was also a thrilling football match at Old Trafford that day.

Manchester City were only a year into Abu Dhabi ownership but were already making their presence felt and nowhere was that noise being heard more than across town.

Mark Hughes brought his new look team to the place he once called home and gave United the scare of their lives. Rio Ferdinand in particular will never forget the day that Craig Bellamy took him to the cleaners with two goals.

But with a thriller locked at 3-3 six minutes into added time, Ryan Giggs picked out Michael Owen with a pass that was controlled with one perfect touch and finished with another. For a day at least, the Stretford End had a new an unlikely hero.

And I was late for my own party.

IAN LADYMAN

Michael Owen keeps his cool to stroke the ball past Shay Given deep into added time in 2009

Mourinho and milkgate

The pint of milk being used as a missile during a melee inside the Old Trafford tunnel after the derby in December 2017 will take some beating. Aimed at Jose Mourinho but splattering over another member of United’s staff, the culprit has never been found and reprimanded. Mourinho had been irked at City's celebrations outside their dressing room and it kicked off from there.

JACK GAUGHAN

Why always Mario?

Mario Balotelli's 'Why Always Me?' T shirt during City's 6-1 win at Old Trafford in 2011. You could write a book on Balotelli at City and he made a ton of mistakes, but I miss his unpredictable, unvarnished presence in today's Premier League.

TOM COLLOMOSSE

Mario Balotelli's 'Why Always Me?' T-shirt was typical of his unpredictable nature

Rooney's overhead kick

Wayne Rooney. The bicycle kick. 2011. I wasn’t there but we all remember it. Easier to forget with time was the context – this was a few months after Rooney said he wanted out. Not only that, he was entertaining the idea of crossing to City. Hooligans in balaclavas went to his house to share a few feelings on the situation. This goal was the most perfect bookend imaginable to that saga. It doesn’t matter that it came off his shin.

RIATH AL-SAMARRAI

Wayne Rooney's acrobatic effort in 2011 got the nod from Riath Al-Samarrai

A Cup final classic

Wayne Rooney’s overhead kick? Michael Owen’s last-gasp winner? For me, it’s Kobbie Mainoo’s goal in the 2024 FA Cup final. United fans returned to Wembley fearing a repeat of their club’s defeat to City a year earlier, but a vibrant performance was encapsulated by the move which ended with Bruno Fernandes cleverly teeing up Mainoo to score.

CHRIS WHEELER

Kompany's winning goal

I interviewed Vincent Kompany in 2023 and spent the chat thinking about how that forehead single-handedly won City the Derby in 2012. I remember the goal like it was yesterday, watching in my mate Alex’s living room (he is a United fan). It was a goal that defined the next 15 years and nearly as important as Sergio Aguero’s against QPR a few weeks later. If not for that, there was no ‘Aguero moment’ and who knows how many titles City would go on to win.

LEWIS STEELE

Sports.title: Shocking moment Shane Lowry is caught on hot mic saying spectators 'deserve to get hit' after errant tee shot at the Irish Open
Sports.content:
Shocking moment Shane Lowry is caught on hot mic saying spectators 'deserve to get hit' after errant tee shot at the Irish Open

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Shane Lowry has come under fire after being heard saying a group of spectators 'deserve to get hit' after an errant tee shot in their direction at the Irish Open.

Lowry, who leads his home tournament heading into Sunday's final round, struck the errant tee shot on the 18th on Saturday.

The 39-year-old Irishman pulled his tee shot way to the left on the course, inadvertently sending it in the direction of spectators stood behind the ropes in a viewing area.

Lowry could be heard urgently shouting 'fore, fore' in a bid to warn the spectators that the ball was heading in their direction.

Footage showed the spectators, who were near a group of marshals, remaining stationary despite his warning.

Lowry was then caught by microphones stating: 'They deserve to get hit.'

Shane Lowry will want this one back, for a few different reasonspic.twitter.com/H39UYnNUHJ — Balls.ie (@ballsdotie) September 12, 2026

Shane Lowry came under fire from fans after appearing to suggest a group of supporters 'deserve to get hit' at the Irish Open

Several fans hit out at Lowry for the remark on social media, calling for the Irishman to apologise to the fans.

'He would never have said that when he was starting his career off? Paying punters cheering him on. How dare he. The fans deserve an apology. Who does he think he is?' one fan wrote.

'He should apologise or be fined. Horrible comment to make,' another said.

'An absolute disgrace, some role model,' a third said, while another wrote 'Your man wishing spectators and or volunteers deserved to be hit by a snap hook with a driver! Can do some serious damage.'

Some other fans were more sympathetic towards Lowry's outburst, suggesting that his comment was made in apparent frustration at the fans failing to move after his warning.

Despite the tee shot, Lowry was able to save par on the 18th to take a four-shot lead into the final round, as he looks to secure his first victory since 2022.

Lowry, who set a course-record 62 on Friday at Trump International Golf Links in Doonbeg, thanked the crowd for their support following his round.

'I feel like I did a great job today of staying in the moment and playing my own game,' Lowry said.

Lowry appeared to make the comment in frustration after fans failed to heed his warning to move clear of his errant tee shot

'I had so much fun out there on the back nine, the crowds were incredible and cheered me on the whole way home.

'Hopefully they do the same tomorrow.'

Lowry had kept his focus on a day when US President Donald Trump's arrival, which came as part of a two-day visit to Ireland, had briefly led to a halt in play.

The Irish star, whose closest challenger is Jacob Skov Olesen, will be hoping to seal victory at the tournament for the first time since 2009.

Sports.title: Furious Ruben Neves hits back at fans after being targeted by disgraceful Diogo Jota chants during Saudi Pro League match: 'I hope they don't go to prayer later'
Sports.content:
Furious Ruben Neves hits back at fans after being targeted by disgraceful Diogo Jota chants during Saudi Pro League match: 'I hope they don't go to prayer later'

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Ruben Neves has hit back at supporters attempting to provoke him by chanting the name of his late friend Diogo Jota during a Saudi Pro League match.

Footage shared on social media showed Neves responding to Al-Taawoun supporters repeatedly chanting Jota's name in the direction of the Portugal and Al-Hilal midfielder.

Neves appeared to signal to the fans that 'God is watching', as he pointed first to the sky, then to his eyes and finally in their direction.

The Portuguese star could be seen repeating the gesture before returning to the game.

Neves briefly referenced the incident after Al-Hilal recorded a 6-0 victory over Al-Taawoun, as he quickly walked through the mixed zone post-match.

'I hope they don't go to prayer later,' Neves told reporters, appearing to contrast the behaviour of the fans with religious teachings.

Ruben Neves responded to Al-Taawoun supporters chanting the name of his late team-mate Diogo Jota at him during a Saudi Pro League match

Neves appeared to signal to the fans that 'God is watching', as he pointed first to the sky, then to his eyes and finally in their direction

Post-match Neves told reporters 'I hope they don't go to prayer later, appearing to contrast the behaviour of the fans with religious teachings

Neves had been the best friend of the late Liverpool star Jota, who tragically died at the age of 28 alongside his brother Andre Silva, 25, after a car crash in northern Spain in July 2025.

Neves, who played with Jota at Wolves and with Portugal, had been one of the pallbearers at Jota's funeral.

The 29-year-old last year revealed he had a new leg tattoo of him hugging his late team-mate in an emotional tribute, while Portugal decided Neves should wear Jota's No21 shirt.

Neves has also been a constant figure of support for Jota's widow Rute Cardoso, who had married the star just 11 days before the tragic car accident, which took place while he was driving back to the UK for pre-season training.

The chants from Al-Taawoun fans to Jota have been condemned in Saudi Arabia.

Waleed Al-Farraj, a prominent Saudi football broadcaster, claimed the chants lacked 'humanity'.

'For you to say "Messi" to [Cristiano] Ronaldo, this goes within the competition that exists between them, but to chant at Neves, the Al-Hilal player, with the name of his deceased team-mate Jota, this is an improper act,' Al-Farraj said.

'How do you play on people's sorrows in this way? You must have some humanity.'

Jota tragically died at the age of 28 in July last year following a car crash in Spain

Neves and Jota were close friends and played alongside each other on 164 occasions

Neves last year revealed a tattoo on his leg of him embracing his friend in a touching tribute

Saudi Arabian international Saleh Abu Al-Shamat, who plays for Al-Ahli, also labelled the chants as 'wrong and unacceptable' in a social media post.

'I wanted to draw attention to something we all witnessed today. I felt it was my duty - as a Muslim - to share this and raise awareness,' Abu Al-Shamat wrote on Instagram.

'No one is perfect, of course, but regarding the actions of some Al-Taawoun fans during the match against Al-Hilal: this isn't just about our club; it concerns our great religion, Islam.

'No matter how intense the rivalry or the situation, we should never stoop to gloating over the dead, engaging in slander, or attacking people's families or the deceased.

'We live in an Islamic country, and it is our duty to show the world what Islam truly represents—a religion of love, tolerance, and respect. I hope we can leverage the massive attention our league is receiving to project the best possible image of Islam.

'By doing so, we might foster goodwill and help others learn about our faith. That is the message I wanted to convey; I felt a personal obligation, as a Muslim living in this great Islamic nation, to speak out against what is happening—because it is wrong and unacceptable.'

Sports.title: Ryan Garcia destroys Conor Benn with brutal second-round TKO to retain WBC welterweight title in Las Vegas showdown
Sports.content:
Ryan Garcia destroys Conor Benn with brutal second-round TKO to retain WBC welterweight title in Las Vegas showdown

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Ryan Garcia sealed a stunning second-round TKO win over Conor Benn in Las Vegas on Saturday night, retaining his WBC welterweight title in the process.

Benn ran blindly to the slaughter - in a fight which was always a lunge too far - and was left groveling on hands and knees at the feet of the new face of American and Mexican boxing.

Garcia took just four minutes and 25 seconds to devastate and humiliate the upstart son of Nigel the great.

Benn’s predictable sally forth from the first bell was as pointless, desperate and doomed to disaster as The Charge of the Light Brigade.

He was stopped in his tracks by the barrage of left hooks which have taken Garcia to the welterweight championship of the world, over which he will reign for as long as he likes.

The first round was but a prelude to the carnage to come in the 85 seconds which the first round lasted. A punishment doubled by the dynamite which also explodes from Garcia's right fist.

Ryan Garcia sealed a stunning second-round TKO win over Conor Benn in Las Vegas

Garcia took just four minutes and 25 seconds to devastate and humiliate the British star

The 28-year-old retained his WBC welterweight title after the devastating display in Sin City

Conor was reduced to crawling on the canvas by a two-fisted assault to which he had no answer. When he staggered drunkenly to his feet referee Thomas Taylor looked long and hard into his glazed eyes before letting him carry on.

The kill was mercifully swift. A combination of lefts and rights which the third man in the ring could no longer ignore.

This is a warning which his handlers must not forget. This was fight too much, too soon. As Garcia had warned he done nothing to deserve the tilt at the WBC belt his father had worn with such pride.

Nor his elevation the top of a bill in the T-Mobile arena nor in this Mecca of boxing Whether he will ever be ready to mix with the company of prize-ring loyalty is doubtful.

He was not only outclassed, out-sped an out-thought but was treated to punching of almighty power with which his dad could not gift him.

The last 24 hours before the first bell had been consumed by doom-casts about Benn’s drastic weight draining to reach the welter limit of 147 lbs.

Followed by extraordinary claims that he had put on more than two stones following Friday’s weigh-in which, if authentic, would have catapulted him into the ring three divisions even heavier than the super-middleweights.

The truth would out as his robe slipped off. But if he had gorged himself between stepping on the scales and the first bell that might done him much good. Such drastic shifts in poundage are as debilitating as dehydration.

If this was another of the mind games played by Benn and Garcia throughout the wind up and build up it seemed doubtful that any of that would have a material effect on the fight itself. Would anyone in this hardest of all games risk being beaten by indigestion.

Conor was reduced to crawling on the canvas by an assault to which he had no answer

The referee swiftly waved off the bout after a barrage of punches from the American star

The substantive issue was Garcia’s boxing class and knock out power versus Benn’s frenzy and punch resistance.

For the high-paying fans – Benn’s long-haulers from the old country and Garcia’s Gen Z armies of groups from his two nations of identification the US and Mexico – what mattered most was that both delivered the barn-burner of a fight they promised.

Quite beautifully those three congregations fell silent together in commemoration of one boxer who never gave in, never gave up, never delivered a disappointing fight, never offended anyone, never betrayed a friend.

The giant screens in the 02 went into black and white mode for a nostalgic picture of Ricky Hatton who died too young as the previous British fighter to top the bill in what was until recently the fight capital of the world. Over to you Master Benn.

Garcia came to the ring to the strains of a patriotic Mexican song, wrapped in that country’s flag and to rapturous acclaim from the baying Amex majority in the house.

Unabashed and as expected Benn went instantly on the offensive only to be met by barrage of Garcia’s trademark left hooks.

Less than three minutes later it was all over.

Elena Rybakina WINS the US Open: New world No 1 dethrones racquet-smashing Aryna Sabalenka in electric three-set battle in New York

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

First, she took her status as No1, and then Elena Rybakina dethroned Aryna Sabalenka as reigning US Open champion, dissecting the two-time winner in New York 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 to win her third Grand Slam title.

For Rybakina, victory adds lustre to the top spot, earned with a quarter-final win that felt incongruous. The Kazakh knew it, and stressed that she could not celebrate this mammoth achievement yet, not with the tournament ongoing. Now, she has put herself just one major away from the full set after wins in Melbourne and Wimbledon. She has also become the third woman this century to win both of the hard-court Slams in a single season.

The second was Sabalenka. She had hoped to make history herself, as the third woman in the Open era to ‘three-peat’, and become the undisputed Queen of New York. Instead, she stuttered, unable to consistently channel the ruthlessness which has defined her run over these two weeks, and was left in tears as she vowed to 'do better' next year.

Throughout the tournament, Sabalenka has stressed the importance of maintaining focus: tuning out the noise around concerns over her form, or whether she might hold on to her ranking, and channelling everything into her performance. But yesterday, she appeared to step onto court bubbling over, frustrated with the deficiencies in her performance even in the earliest stages of the match.

Sabalenka looked unsettled as the pair exchanged opening holds, the opposite of Rybakina’s picture of calm on the other side of the net. Rybakina normally makes the sport look effortless, but this was thrown into sharper relief by the quick unravelling of Sabalenka.

With every unforced error - 15 to Rybakina’s five - there seemed to be an expression, hands thrown up, head tipped back, frantic miming to her box, but rather than offer a release, Sabalenka only wound herself tighter. After the double fault that handed her opponent the first-set break, she was given a warning for smacking a ball away, but hitting was similarly frustrated in-play as Sabalenka looked for desperate winners she couldn’t make.

Elena Rybakina is the new Queen of New York after winning the US Open in three thrilling sets

Aryna Sabalenka crashed her racquet into the court as the final set slipped away from her

Join the discussion What does Rybakina's intense victory say about the mental toughness needed to dominate tennis today?

Much has been made of the potency of Rybakina’s serve, but the Kazakh carried off the opener well below her lethal best, making only 27 per cent of her first serves. When she pulled them off, Sabalenka was flummoxed. But even when she didn’t, there was an accuracy to her second that continued to cause problems for her opponent.

Rybakina, by contrast, had the very measure of Sabalenka’s serve, and was capable of dragging out the Belarusian’s service games and bullying her into defence under-fire. The 27-year-old peppered her with four break points before the fifth finally told for 3-2.

Sabalenka stepped back onto court visibly more settled. There were fewer errors, and fewer admonishments. But there was no drop in Rybakina’s level, as she continued to play her game, and play it well. She chased Sabalenka to 5-4, and pulled off an enormous hold in the 10th game to deny her rival her first break point.

Rybakina wasn’t to hold on for long, however. The two rivals’ meetings often spill into three sets, and Sabalenka’s improved accuracy - and mood - swung the second set.

This was the fuel Rybakina needed to act more decisively in the third, and immediately, she was all over Sabalenka’s serve, looking for cracks in her game. The pair met at deuce three times before the 28-year-old could see out her opening hold, while Rybakina skipped through hers, hungry for the next attempt to break her opponent.

She would not have to wait long, with Sabalenka again the picture of fury as she crashed her racquet into the floor, sent spinning by a string of Rybakina’s forehand winners. Instead of a second code violation warning, the punishment instead was the break Rybakina snatched.

In the seventh game, 2-4 down, Rybakina reached break point again, with the gift of a double fault from across the net. Sabalenka bent down to her knees, tipped her head to her racquet, as if praying for composure. Instead, more faults, more errors, broken again. Sabalenka’s last effort was to give the court another thrashing with her racquet. She all but walked off as Rybakina sent down her championship-winning ace.

But the new champion will not have needed grace from her opponent. She has her trophy instead.

Sports.title: Marcus Rashford reborn: How the Man United forward found his smile again after Old Trafford exile, Michael Carrick's role in easing his return and the key differences staff have noticed in training
Sports.content:
It's the look of pure joy on Marcus Rashford’s face that stands out all these years later.

Leaping into the arms of Anthony Martial at the Etihad, Manchester United’s new local hero had just scored what turned out to be the winning goal 15 minutes into his first derby a decade ago.

The 18-year-old controlled a pass from Juan Mata and audaciously nutmegged Martin Demichelis to leave the Manchester City defender on his backside before sweeping the ball under Joe Hart.

‘Putting Demichelis on his a**e got as big a cheer as the goal itself,’ chuckles Dave Horrocks, one of Rashford’s first coaches at Fletcher Moss Rangers.

It crowned a quite remarkable breakthrough for Rashford at his boyhood club under Louis van Gaal in early 2016, which began with a two-goal debut off the bench against Midtjylland, at the time replacing George Best as United’s youngest-ever scorer in Europe.

Ryan Giggs, by then a coach on Van Gaal’s staff, recalled on The Debrief podcast with Rio Ferdinand this week how Rashford had convinced the Dutchman he was ready.

Rashford capped off a remarkable breakthrough at his boyhood club under Louis van Gaal in early 2016 with the winning goal against rivals Manchester City at the Eithad

Ryan Giggs recalled how he had been asked by Van Gaal to tell Rashford he had made the first team after the pair had been left impressed by him

‘I remember we got told about him,’ said Giggs. ‘The first team had finished training, so me and Louis went over and watched the reserves.

‘Marcus was playing in a small-sided game and he scored two goals: right foot, left foot, bang, bang. It was like, “what have we just seen?”. Louis turned to me and went, “you will tell him he is in my team”, and just walked off!’

Still, Rashford was only down to be on the bench in a Europa League tie against the Danes until Martial was injured in the warm-up. Horrocks was having dinner with Fletcher Moss secretary Ronny Jamieson in Didsbury as the story unfolded.

‘My phone pinged: “Marcus is in the squad”,’ says Horrocks. ‘Then ping: “He’s starting”. Ping: “He’s scored!”.’

The junior club’s membership doubled overnight, and there weren’t enough coaches to cope with all the kids.

Rashford made his Premier League debut against Arsenal at Old Trafford three days later and, incredibly, scored two more goals in another United win. A first England call-up soon followed.

Ten years on, he faces City again in Sunday's 199th Manchester derby at Old Trafford having made a fresh start at United over the summer.

Rashford has played in this fixture more than any other, and it’s one that has mirrored the ups and downs of his career.

As well as that memorable strike in 2016, his five goals to date include a late winner at Old Trafford in January 2023.

Rashford faces City again in Sunday's 199th Manchester derby at Old Trafford having made a fresh start at United over the summer

Then there was the 26th birthday bash at Chinawhite nightclub in the wake of a dismal 3-0 defeat to City in October of the same year that enraged Erik ten Hag, and Ruben Amorim’s decision to axe Rashford from the squad for the Etihad derby in December 2024 due to concerns over his attitude. Rashford didn’t play for United again before going out on loan to Aston Villa and Barcelona.

Giggs recounted the story this week of a dinner with Pep Guardiola eight years ago during which the City boss revealed that Rashford was the one United player he would like to have signed.

More recently, City were said to be hovering before Rashford agreed his current contract, although United’s insistence that their neighbours were one of only two clubs (the other was Liverpool) excluded from having the option to buy him for £40million this summer demonstrates the level of opposition to such a move inside Old Trafford.

Had things worked out differently, though, City could have got their hands on Rashford much earlier.

The youngster had joined Fletcher Moss at the age of six when his mother Melanie signed him up, and he was soon fast-tracked into one of United’s development centres.

But as the single mum worked to support her three boys and one daughter, Marcus spent his childhood moving between houses in Hulme, Moss Side, Chorlton, Withington and Wythenshawe.

When the family settled in Fallowfield, close to City’s academy on Platt Lane, a football-mad Rashford was inevitably drawn there on the nights he wasn’t training at United.

Fortunately, Horrocks agreed to drive Melanie, Marcus and his older brother Dwaine to The Cliff whenever he could because the family didn’t have a car and the journey meant taking several buses.

City are understood to have spoken to Rashford’s mother, but she had given United her word and Marcus signed at the age of nine.

‘He’s a United fan, so I don’t think City ever stood a chance,’ says Horrocks. ‘You have to understand he’s a Manchester lad, and the derby is the pot of gold for him – I hope he’s on the up again.’

Amorim axed Rashford from the squad for the Etihad derby in December 2024 due to concerns over his attitude and Rashford didn’t play for United again before loans at Villa and Barcelona

On a good run, it takes about 20 minutes to drive the ten miles from The Coffee House Cafe, where a mural of Rashford covers an outside wall in the heart of Withington, to the temporary black gates in the Mobberley countryside behind which sits the multi-million pound luxury home and golf course project that has been hindered by problems for some time.

It’s been quite the journey for the 28-year-old who was earning around £3,000-a-week when he first signed professional terms at the age of 17. Since agreeing a new contract in 2023 after a career-best 31-goal season, Rashford has been on £325,000-a-week.

The mural was daubed with racist graffiti when he missed a penalty as England lost to Italy on a shootout in the final of Euro 2020, shortly before receiving an MBE at Windsor Castle for his campaign to tackle child poverty during the pandemic.

Rashford sought the help of a sports psychologist during the darkest period of his career, and physically faced longstanding problems with his back and left shoulder.

There was the infamous tequila bender in Belfast which landed him in hot water with Ten Hag again, and the fallout with Amorim who stuck him in the bomb squad.

What hurt more than anything were the questions over his commitment to United and love of football, fuelled by concerns inside and outside the club over his demeanour.

Rashford felt sufficiently misunderstood to do an article for The Players’ Tribune titled Who I Really Am.

Perhaps leaving Old Trafford on loan has been the best thing. Had it not been for his wages, Rashford might well have joined Barcelona permanently this summer after winning the La Liga title there last season.

It’s understood he rejected interest from a dozen more clubs in England, Italy and Turkey before returning to United. Safe to say that if Amorim had still been in charge, there would have been no way back.

But Michael Carrick is a very different character. He was on the pitch that day in 2016 when Rashford scored against City, and has since been his first-team coach, caretaker manager and now head coach.

Carrick was on the pitch that day in 2016 when Rashford scored against City, and has since been his first-team coach, caretaker manager and now head coach

The two are said to have a good relationship which has eased a return that had looked so unlikely.

The rather sullen figure who left at the start of last year has been, according to sources, more cheerful than at any time they can remember from the moment he rejoined the squad at United’s pre-season training camp in Dublin. Once a poor time keeper, Rashford is now one of the first into training.

‘He couldn’t be making more of an effort on his side to make it work,’ said one insider.

Rashford was rested for Thursday’s Champions League tie against Sabah but got a good reception from the fans when he warmed up, some of whom had turned against him in the past.

He has played well enough to earn a place in Thomas Tuchel’s squad for the upcoming Nations League games, having returned to the England squad in time for the World Cup. Were it not for a minor hip problem, Rashford would probably have featured more in North America.

These are still early days, of course. With two years left on his contract at United, there are no guarantees about what will happen next.

For now, though, Rashford is back where many people feel he belongs – and City are in his sights again.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat
