For the fourth year in a row, Biscuitville has claimed the title of America's best fast-food breakfast, beating out national chains despite a footprint that remains concentrated in just three states.

The Southern breakfast chain earned the top spot in USA Today's 10Best Readers' Choice Awards, beating out larger chains like McDonald's (No. 4), Chick-fil-A (No. 5), Burger King (No. 6) and Wendy's (No. 7).

Kristie Mitchell, Biscuitville's chief marketing officer, said the recognition is particularly meaningful because of the competition in the fast-food breakfast category.

AMERICA'S FAVORITE FAST-FOOD CHAIN NAMED: MCDONALD'S WINS HEARTS BUT NOT BEST BURGER, SURVEY SAYS

"We have earned it, but we don't want to live in a space where we come to expect it," Mitchell said.

Biscuitville recently opened its 90th restaurant and currently operates in North Carolina, South Carolina and Virginia.

Mitchell said Biscuitville eventually hopes to expand into states such as Tennessee and Georgia, though the family-owned company plans to focus on growing within its existing markets for the next several years.

Biscuitville's calling card remains its scratch-made biscuits, prepared fresh every 15 minutes from a three-ingredient family recipe that Mitchell said was passed down to the company's founder by his grandmother.

FAST-FOOD GIANT DETHRONED AS CUSTOMER STUDY CROWNS AMERICA'S NEW FAVORITE RESTAURANT CHAIN

But Biscuitville's appeal, Mitchell argues, goes beyond the biscuit.

"We have no microwaves," she said. "There's no instant anything in our kitchens."

Eggs are hand-cracked, and Mitchell said nothing arrives at the restaurants partially cooked simply to be finished there. The approach requires more planning and labor, particularly when customers still expect the speed of a drive-thru window.

The result, Mitchell believes, taps into something larger than convenience.

CLICK HERE TO 

"We get comments all the time from our feedback line that says, 'Your biscuit tastes just like my grandmother's biscuit,'" she said.

"Do I agree it's the best breakfast biscuit sandwich I've ever had?" he told Fox News Digital. "Well, no, but it would come in a high second on my list."

Smith instead gives his personal top spot to Tudor's Biscuit World, a regional chain with locations including West Virginia, Kentucky and Ohio. Still, he praised Biscuitville's biscuits as tender and "super soft" and singled out its Ultimate Country Ham Biscuit as a favorite.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

For Mitchell, the enduring popularity of biscuits, grits, eggs and other Southern breakfast staples comes back to an experience that can resonate even with people who didn't grow up eating them.

World.title: Vulnerable House Republicans embrace Trump as GOP bets on defying midterm history
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

DALLAS — President Donald Trump is getting a much warmer reception from his fellow Republicans during this election cycle than his predecessor did from Democrats this time two years ago.

Conventional political wisdom dictates that the party in power will suffer losses in Congress during a midterm election year. Americans who oppose the president's party are typically more motivated to vote than people who support their agenda.

But the GOP is banking on the opposite effect. The first-ever GOP midterm convention featured back-to-back keynote addresses from the commander-in-chief, as well as speeches from his Cabinet officials, allies and members of Congress.

"I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot," Trump told his audience on Wednesday. Republican incumbents and candidates running in battleground districts this November also took the stage, and all speakers projected confidence despite Trump's own low approval numbers.

DEMOCRATS TARGETING 12 ADDITIONAL RED DISTRICTS IN MIDTERMS PUSH TO RETAKE HOUSE

"We ran together in 2024 on a ticket with President Trump, [Sen. Dave McCormick, R-Pa.] and myself — voters elected all of us to deliver real change and results, and we've actually been able to do that with securing the border and delivering historic tax relief," Rep. Ryan Mackenzie, R-Pa., told Fox News Digital on the sidelines of the convention.

"Now what we're seeing is in a midterm, we are actually going to defy the historic trends. Why is that? Because the Democrats are so far left they are totally out of touch."

Republicans believe their warnings of Democrats' socialist insurgency will help them keep their majorities in the House and Senate this year, along with touting Trump's signature tax cuts in the One Big, Beautiful Bill Act.

HOW ONE NYC SUBURB COULD DECIDE WHICH PARTY CONTROLS THE HOUSE

Mackenzie is one of Democrats' top targets in the election cycle, along with Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., in the suburbs outside New York City.

"He's the President of the United States, and whether it was Joe Biden or Donald Trump, I've always shown up," Lawler told Fox News Digital. "You have to be able to engage with the president, and, you know, frankly, this is where I think the Democrats have made a very big mistake. They could get a lot more in terms of what it is that they want if they would actually engage constructively."

Lawler, Mackenzie and Rep. Rob Bresnahan, R-Pa., are the three vulnerable incumbents who took the stage during the convention last week.

TRUMP HITS KEY BATTLEGROUNDS TO SELL TAX CUTS, BOOST GOP AHEAD OF MIDTERMS

Lawler, for his part, introduced two residents from his district whose daughter was killed by an illegal immigrant in Chicago — a poignant symbol of what Republicans say could happen more often if Democrats win.

Trump has also campaigned in each of their districts in recent months as he crisscrosses the country in a bid to keep control of Congress for the latter half of his final term.

But it was not just vulnerable incumbents who appeared in Dallas alongside Trump. The two-day affair also brought candidates from across the country, even those running in tight races.

GOP FACES BRUTAL MIDTERM HEADWINDS AS REPUBLICANS PAINT ELECTION AS ‘COMPETITION WITH COMMUNISM’

"When people say that folks are running away from President Trump, I'll tell you I'm certainly not doing that. And let me tell you why: because he has made promises to South Texas, and he has kept them, especially when we look at border security," candidate Eric Flores told Fox News Digital.

JOHNSON DOWNPLAYS GOP'S MIDTERM WOES AS DEMOCRATS EYE HOUSE TAKEOVER: 'I AM VERY BULLISH'

"My opponent, who said, you know, that the sleepy Joe Biden administration and the no-show border czar, Kamala Harris, were on the right track. Let me tell you firsthand, I was on Operation Guardian support, was a federal prosecutor on the border. It was a humanitarian crisis. President Trump, on day one, secured our border."

Flores is running in a South Texas district currently represented by Rep. Vicente Gonzalez, D-Texas.

Time will tell if the strategy pays off, but Democrats are already seizing on it in hopes that associating with Trump will sink GOP candidates like it did in 2018.

TRUMP'S APPROVAL RATING PLUMMETS TO NEW LOW AHEAD OF CRITICAL MIDTERMS: 'MORE WORK TO DO'

"Ryan Mackenzie, Rob Bresnahan and Scott Perry made their priorities clear tonight: they care more about Donald Trump’s cost-raising agenda than what’s best for the people of Pennsylvania," Pennsylvania Democratic Party Chair Eugene DePasquale said in a statement.

"After jetting all the way to Texas to champion an agenda of higher gas prices, cost-raising tariffs, and healthcare cuts, Mackenzie, Bresnahan, Perry and the entire PA GOP have proven that they’ll put Trump ahead of our Commonwealth every single time — and Pennsylvanians are ready to send them packing this November."

World.title: Sweden votes as migration, crime and economy dominate high-stakes election
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Swedes head to the polls Sunday as Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s center-right party is slightly behind the center-left Social Democratic Party led by Sweden's former Prime Minister Magdalena Andersson, with the election dominated by fears of mass migration, crime and the economy.

"Years of gang violence, Islamist extremism, persistent unemployment and pressure on public services have intensified the debate over whether integration has kept pace with immigration," foreign policy expert and author Daniel Schatz, told Fox News Digital.

DENMARK'S LEFT-WING PM WARNS: 'BIG ENEMY HAS STARTED TO GROW FROM WITHIN' AS EUROPE FACES MIGRANT RECKONING

Following on from Germany's AfD victory in a state election last week, Sweden's hard-right Sweden Democrats are in a position to enter government if Kristersson's party wins again. The Associated Press reported that the anti-immigration party has shifted toward the political mainstream and is likely to get cabinet posts. It has so far supported the Kristersson government from the outside.

The Associated Press reported that the Sweden Democrats were founded by activists in far-right-wing extremist groups, including neo-Nazis. But since then, under its leader, Jimmie Åkesson, it toned down that rhetoric and kicked out racist members. Åkesson, who has led them since 2005, is said to be responsible for the success of a once marginal party.

Sweden, once a model of the Western social welfare state, has been under economic strain as governments from both the left and the right were forced to restructure their welfare system.

While social benefits continue to be extensive, Sweden’s welfare state has changed amid rising crime rates, but the expectations for public benefits remain.

"Sweden went from being described as a ‘humanitarian superpower’ to a "humanitarian basket case.’ Discontent with migration policies extends to both foreign-born and native-born residents. Shootings have declined sharply, but fewer shootings do not mean the integration problems are solved," Schatz, who is Swedish, added.

Prime Minister Kristersson’s government took power in 2022, as the nation was experiencing a dramatic rise in gun-related violence, with the country witnessing 391 shootings resulting in 62 deaths, according to The Swedish National Council for Crime Prevention, a government agency under the Ministry of Justice.

SWEDEN JAMS SUSPECTED RUSSIAN DRONE NEAR FRENCH CARRIER AS NATO WAR FEARS RISE

The homicide rate in Sweden has been on the rise since 2013, when gun homicides contributed to a general increase in Sweden’s total homicide rate.

The Swedish National Council for Crime Prevention notes that Sweden’s homicide rate ranks very high compared with other European countries, at approximately four deaths per million inhabitants per year.

The average for Europe is approximately 1.6 deaths per million inhabitants.

The issue of immigration is another major issue that dovetails with voters’ concerns over crime and gun violence. Like much of Europe, Sweden experienced a wave of immigration in 2015 coming from those fleeing the Syrian civil war as well as the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Sweden took in over 160,000 asylum seekers in 2015, or 12% of all those who sought protection in the EU, according to Sweden’s Migration Agency.

"After the 2015 influx of asylum seekers from Syria and other war-torn countries strained its reception system, Sweden began tightening its borders. The current government has taken that shift much further," Schatz said.

ANTI-MIGRANT AFD SEEKS TO BREAK GERMANY’S POLITICAL ‘FIREWALL’ IN HISTORIC STATE ELECTION

Prime Minister Kristersson’s parliamentary ally, the right-wing Sweden Democrats, filled the void in the anti-immigration position in parliament.

Nicholas Aylott, professor of political science at Södertörn University in Stockholm, told Fox News Digital that the link between the increase in immigration and the rise in crime changed Swedish politics.

"Migration and law-and-order became much higher electoral priorities," Aylott said.

"The Sweden Democrats based their pitch on them. The other parties, rather belatedly, adapted their positions. The Sweden Democrats had at first been completely ostracized by the other parties, but they were gradually accepted as a legitimate partner by three of the other parties of the right between 2018 and 2022," he said.

As the anti-immigration backlash rose and the Sweden Democrats were more included in the policymaking process, Sweden cracked down on immigration and made it harder to seek asylum.

While asylum claims dropped and gun violence was dramatically reduced as well, with only 158 shootings and 44 fatalities to date, the government still might suffer a defeat at the hands of Andersson’s center-left coalition.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Wisconsin Republican gubernatorial candidate and U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany said he and a pilot escaped with minor injuries after their small plane lost power and made an emergency landing in a lake Saturday night.

"The pilot made an emergency water landing in Lake Wausau," Tiffany wrote on X.

COAST GUARD PLANE WITH DHS SECRETARY MARKWAYNE MULLIN ON BOARD MAKES EMERGENCY LANDING AFTER ENGINE FAILURE

The congressman explained that he and the pilot quickly called 911 after hitting the water, but the aircraft began filling and sinking into the lake before rescuers could reach them.

"As the plane began to submerge, we exited the aircraft and swam to a shallow area, where we waited until emergency responders reached us by boat," Tiffany said.

MULTIPLE INJURED AFTER FLOATPLANE MAKES EMERGENCY LANDING, CATCHES FIRE OFF WASHINGTON COAST

Tiffany and the pilot were pulled from the lake and transported to Aspirus Wausau Hospital. Both sustained only minor injuries, according to the congressman.

"I want to express my deepest gratitude to the pilot, the Wausau Fire Department, and all of the first responders who came to our aid so quickly," Tiffany said. "They got us safely off the water and transported us to Aspirus Wausau Hospital, where we received excellent care."

"God was watching over us tonight, and I am incredibly grateful to be here in the hospital with my wife, Chris, by my side," he said. "An experience like this reminds you just how precious life is."

‘COMMON SENSE AGAINST CRAZY’: TRUMP-BACKED CANDIDATE SOUNDS ALARM ON SOCIALIST HONG IN WISCONSIN RACE

World.title: Man accused in brutal motel stabbing sought as person of interest in 4 deaths, child attack
World.content:

A Louisiana man previously accused of repeatedly stabbing a woman and locking her inside a motel room is now being sought by law enforcement after four people were found stabbed to death and a child was critically wounded.

Terrebonne Parish Sheriff Tim Soignet said detectives identified 47-year-old Houma resident Kaegan Jude Solet as a person of interest in the apparent series of stabbing incidents in the Ashland Drive area of Houma.

Deputies were initially called to the 200 block of Ashland Drive, where they discovered the wounded child, according to the Terrebonne Parish Sheriff’s Office.

NORTH CAROLINA MAN BROKE INTO EX'S HOME, FATALLY STABBED HIS 5-YEAR-OLD SON BEFORE GOING TO TACO BELL: POLICE

The child was flown to an out-of-area hospital and remained in critical but stable condition after suffering "extremely significant" injuries, Terrebonne Parish Sheriff’s Office Lt. Blake Tabor told Fox News Digital.

"That’s not something that you want to see ever," Tabor said.

TWO TEEN SUSPECTS HELD AFTER 5 FAMILY MEMBERS KILLED IN 'TARGETED MASS SHOOTING'

As deputies searched the surrounding area, they made a grim discovery inside nearby homes.

At least four victims were found dead, according to the sheriff’s office. Authorities have not released their identities or disclosed what relationship, if any, they had to one another, the injured child or Solet.

SUSPECT ARRESTED AFTER MOM, PREGNANT TEEN, 12-YEAR-OLD FOUND BOUND AND MURDERED

Investigators also have not said what may have sparked the violence or whether the victims were attacked inside more than one home.

Solet has not been arrested or charged in connection with the latest deaths. The sheriff’s office stressed that identifying him as a person of interest does not mean he has been accused of a crime.

DEPUTY US MARSHAL FATALLY SHOT WHILE SERVING ARREST WARRANT IN LOUISIANA

Authorities believe Solet is likely still in the area but said they are not ruling out other possibilities.

"We’re using every investigative tool that we have," Tabor said. "Our hope is that we plan to get him in custody very quickly."

Tabor said investigators do not currently have information indicating Solet intends to leave the state or "go on the run," but added that authorities are "exploring all options."

Solet had not been located as of the latest update.

REPEAT OFFENDER RELEASED EARLY FROM JAIL NOW CHARGED WITH CAPITAL MURDER OF PREGNANT WOMAN

The latest investigation is not the first time Solet’s name has surfaced in connection with violent crime allegations.

Solet was arrested in December 2019 after allegedly stabbing a woman repeatedly and leaving her locked inside a Houma motel room, according to a police news release from the time.

Houma police responded to the Red Carpet Inn shortly after midnight on Christmas Eve 2019 and found a 59-year-old woman lying on the floor of her room with numerous stab wounds.

The woman was taken by ambulance to a medical facility with injuries considered life-threatening, police said.

Witnesses told investigators they heard someone yelling for help from inside the room. When they entered, they found the woman on the floor and unable to move.

Investigators identified Solet, then 40, as the suspect and said he had been invited into the woman’s room before the two became involved in an argument.

Police alleged the confrontation turned physical and Solet repeatedly stabbed the woman in her head and upper body. He then allegedly fled and locked the motel room door behind him, leaving the critically wounded woman inside.

MANIAC WHO STABBED BOY OUTSIDE WALMART WAS PREVIOUSLY FREED AFTER ATTACKING DAD, CHURCH RAMPAGE: REPORT

Officers located Solet approximately 18 hours later and took him into custody without incident.

He was transported to the Terrebonne Parish Criminal Justice Complex and booked on one count of attempted second-degree murder, according to Houma police.

Terrebonne Parish detectives had also obtained a warrant for Solet’s arrest on a charge of second-degree murder in January 2019, according to a separate sheriff’s office news release.

The warrant was obtained during the investigation into the Jan. 9, 2019 killing of Kemple Paul Scott Lovell. Then-Sheriff Jerry Larpenter said detectives were searching for Solet, who had last been seen in the Houma area.

The final dispositions of both 2019 cases were not immediately available.

ILLINOIS NO-CASH BAIL LAW 'UTTERLY MANIPULATED' BY VIOLENT OFFENDERS, DEM ALDERMAN SAYS AFTER COP'S KILLING

Asked why Solet was no longer in custody, Tabor said authorities were also searching for answers.

"I can’t tell you. Certainly, that’s the hot question, right? Why is he out?" Tabor said. "We’re probably just as stunned as everyone else is."

Tabor emphasized that the sheriff’s office has a strong working relationship with the Terrebonne Parish District Attorney’s Office but said questions remain about how Solet’s previous cases were handled.

"How this slipped through, I certainly don’t know, but it’s a question that probably needs to be answered," Tabor said.

Fox News Digital reached out to the district attorney’s office seeking the circumstances surrounding Solet’s release and whether he remained under any court-ordered supervision, but did not immediately receive a response.

Detectives are continuing to gather evidence and develop information surrounding the latest deadly incidents as the search for Solet continues.

The sheriff’s office urged anyone with information about his whereabouts to contact Terrebonne Parish Sheriff’s Office detectives at 985-876-2500.

The investigation remains active and in its preliminary stages. Authorities said additional details will be released as they become available.

World.title: Sam Altman backs Anthropic CEO’s call to slow down the global AI race
World.content:
The CEOs of two of the world’s leading AI companies are publicly agreeing that the race to build increasingly powerful AI systems needs to be slowed, continuing this week’s cascade of warnings from researchers working on the technology.

Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, maker of the Claude chatbot, said in essay published Saturday that AI companies should deliberately “slow the pace” at which they improve their models, arguing that AI advances are moving faster than researchers’ ability to understand and control them.

“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Amodei wrote. “Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain.”

Hours later, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman endorsed the idea and said his company would adopt one of Amodei’s proposed safeguards.

“I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier,” Altman wrote on X, saying the issue had been a major topic of discussion at OpenAI in recent weeks.

Altman has previously called for slowing AI development. In an Aug. 18 post on X, he said OpenAI had paused some advanced AI training to ensure it could meet its standards as capabilities improved.

Amodei’s call, laid out in a nearly 4,000-word essay, comes after researchers at Anthropic, OpenAI and Google publicly raised concerns about the pace of AI development and the competitive pressures that comes with it.

Amodei pointed to two developments that he said had changed his thinking: the increasing ability of AI systems to build more advanced AI, and a July incident in which autonomous AI agents powered by an OpenAI model hacked systems belonging to the AI company Hugging Face.

“It’s easy to dismiss this incident because no one was hurt and the economic damage was minimal, but in my opinion, a swarm that possessed greater capabilities but a similar level of misalignment could have caused catastrophic damage,” he wrote.

Jacob Coxon, an Anthropic safety researcher who resigned this week, told colleagues in a message obtained by NBC News that he believed the industry’s approach to developing superintelligent AI amounted to a “gamble with our lives.”

“From within, you’re just stuck in the race,” Coxon later told NBC News, describing the competitive pressures on AI companies. “You can’t change the overall structural dynamics of the situation.”

“Private companies in a race don’t allow these people to end up doing good, and we could just sleepwalk into disaster,” he said.

Two other researchers who recently left Anthropic and Google DeepMind told NBC News they had similar concerns.

Joe Benton, who used to lead a safety research team at Anthropic, warned that advances in AI could push development from its already “blistering” pace to an “uncontrollable” one. Josh Engels, a former Google safety researcher, offered an even starker warning.

“There are no adults in the room,” Engels said. “People are trying their best, but there is no one coming to save us.”

Amodei is proposing what he calls “pacing the frontier,” a three-part plan that he said would buy researchers more time without halting AI development.

He said Anthropic would begin embedding independent evaluators inside the company, giving them access to models, internal tools and researchers to assess risks. Amodei called for similar oversight across leading U.S. AI companies, backed by federal regulation and eventually for international coordination.

The goal is not to stop AI progress, Amodei wrote, but to give researchers time to develop safeguards, better understand how increasingly capable systems work and test whether they can be reliable controlled.

He estimated that slowing development could buy researchers one or two more years, time he argued could prove critical as AI systems become increasingly capable of contributing to their own development.

“The stakes are too high for pacing to be an empty exercise — we need to use the time it gives us wisely,” he wrote.

World.title: Your health insurance bills are about to go up
World.content:
Most Americans can expect to pay significantly more each month for health insurance next year, whether they get it through work, the Affordable Care Act or Medicare. In some cases, the premium increases may be the largest in decades and are driven by numerous economic pressures. But they won’t look the same for everyone. Some will pay more in the form of higher copays or deductibles.

“Healthcare costs are going up faster than they have in years, and open enrollment is when the healthcare affordability crisis is really going to hit home for people,” said Larry Levitt, executive vice president for health policy at KFF, a nonpartisan research group. “That’s true for whatever kind of insurance you have.”

Prices have shifted upward in every corner of daily life.

The rising healthcare costs stem in part from higher prices for hospital and other medical care, as well as the increased use of expensive prescription drugs — including GLP-1 weight loss medications — that are driving up spending for insurers and employers.

The pressures are unique to each type of coverage.

People who buy insurance through the Affordable Care Act marketplace, about 19 million adults, are set to face another year of steep premium increases after the enhanced federal subsidies expired last year.

On Thursday, the White House promised $500 rebate checks to an estimated 1 million ACA enrollees, alleging they were wrongly overcharged. It’s unclear where the money for the rebates would come from or whether the distribution would require approval from Congress, but experts say it’s unlikely to provide significant relief.

The $500 check “pales in comparison to the increased premiums that marketplace enrollees are facing due to the expiration of the enhanced subsidies,” said Miranda Yaver, an assistant professor of health policy and management at the University of Pittsburgh.

Workers with job-based insurance may be asked to shoulder more of their employers’ rising health costs. And some Medicare beneficiaries could see changes to their prescription drug premiums after the Trump administration ended a temporary program that helped keep those premiums in check.

Here’s what to expect.

The Affordable Care Act

People who buy health insurance through the ACA are on track for a second straight year of double-digit premium increases.

Insurers who offer ACA plans are proposing a premium increase of about 15%, on average, for 2027, according to a KFF analysis of public filings from insurers across all 50 states and Washington, D.C. For 2026, insurers upped rates by an average of 20%.

An individual earning $80,000 a year who doesn’t qualify for standard ACA subsidies could see the cost of their bronze plan — the cheapest plan — rise by roughly $80 a month, adding almost $1,000 to their annual tab.

One of the biggest reasons insurers are hiking rates is that medical care is getting more expensive, Levitt said. Insurers have pointed to higher prices for hospital stays, doctor’s visits and prescription drugs, among other costs.

Insurers generally “have felt pressure to add coverage of GLP-1 drugs for weight loss, but they’re also seeing big, big increases in costs for those drugs,” Levitt said.

The ACA marketplace is also still adjusting to the expiration of the enhanced federal subsidies at the end of 2025. Those subsidies — first put in place during the pandemic — lowered monthly premiums for millions of people in the middle class. When they expired, people either paid significantly more for coverage in 2026 or downgraded their plans.

The expired subsidies also led ACA enrollment to fall by about 3 million.

Young adults — who are generally healthier and more likely to go without insurance when it becomes too expensive — accounted for a large portion of the enrollment decrease. That left insurers with a group of customers who, on average, need more medical care, Yaver said, which was also factored into insurers rates for 2027.

Job-based health insurance

Most Americans, about 165 million people, get health insurance through their jobs. Many of them may be feeling the price increases, too.

Employers expect the cost of providing health benefits to each worker to rise 8.2%, on average, in 2027 — the largest increase since 2003, according to a survey of more than 1,800 employers by Marsh, a benefits consulting group.

That doesn’t necessarily mean workers’ premiums will rise by 8.2%, said Dr. Kevin Schulman, a professor of medicine at the Stanford University School of Medicine who researches employer-based health insurance.

Employers typically subsidize a large portion of workers’ health coverage. But when healthcare costs rise too sharply, Schulman said, employers have several ways of passing some of the increase along to employees. They can charge workers more for their monthly premiums, raise deductibles or make other changes to their benefits.

Sometimes, they slow wage increases to offset the expense.

“Because the costs are going up, the employers are trying to reduce the rate of growth, and the easiest way to reduce the rate of growth of healthcare costs is to push more of the costs onto the employee,” Schulman said.

Many appear prepared to do just that.

The Marsh survey found about two-thirds of large employers — those with 500 or more employees — said they expected to increase how much employees contribute toward their premiums in 2027.

Others may shift costs in other ways, including waiving copays and deductibles for primary care visits while charging for other kinds of care, or keeping premiums the same while raising the deductible.

For workers, that makes it important to look beyond the premium during open enrollment, Schulman said. A plan that costs less or about the same each paycheck may come with a higher deductible or require people to pay more when they seek care.

Medicare

Monthly premiums are handled somewhat differently for the roughly 70 million people enrolled in Medicare.

People on Medicare generally have more than one premium to consider: typically, a premium for Part B, which covers doctor’s visits and other outpatient care; and, for 9 out of 10 enrollees, a separate premium for Part D, which covers prescription drugs.

Prescription drug costs are where enrollees may see the biggest changes, according to Yaver, of the University of Pittsburgh.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services projected in July that the baseline monthly cost for Part D coverage will rise about 6% in 2027, from $38.99 to $41.33.

What enrollees actually end up paying varies, depending on their income and their specific plan.

The increase stems from the Trump administration withdrawing its support for a temporary federal program that helped offset premium increases for Part D plans. The program began in 2025 as Medicare’s prescription drug benefit underwent major changes under the Inflation Reduction Act. Without it, enrollees would have seen their monthly premiums nearly double, according to a report from the Government Accountability Office.

The change will hurt seniors, Yaver said, noting that the program had reduced the average premium by 40% last year. People on Medicare are often retired and live on fixed incomes.

“Though seniors don’t change their Part D plans often, this year may be an exception, potentially resulting in seniors opting into lower-quality plans, leaving them less protected,” she said.

Enrollees will still have an annual out-of-pocket cap on prescription drugs. In 2027, the cap is $2,400.

World.title: Alleged trespasser stopped outside Kamala Harris’ Malibu home
World.content:
An alleged trespasser was stopped by police on former Vice President Kamala Harris’ property in Malibu, California, Friday, officials said.

The individual entered the property, where Harris and her husband, Doug Emhoff, live Friday night, but was stopped by security personnel before they reached the house itself, Eduardo Negrón, a spokesperson for Harris, said Saturday.

“Vice President Harris and Second Gentleman Emhoff were not present. They are grateful to the security and law enforcement personnel who responded swiftly,” Negrón added.

The Malibu Lost Hills Sheriff’s deputies responded to a suspicious person call at the residence at 10:30 p.m. Friday, the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department said in a statement.

“When deputies arrived they made contact with the private security detail on the property,” the department said. “The individual who was outside of the property upon our arrival was warned and advised by deputies to leave the premises and left voluntarily without incident.”

The department added that a trespassing report was taken, but no arrests were made. The Malibu Lost Hills deputies will increase patrols in the area as a precaution, the department said.

The incident was first reported by TMZ.

The incident at Harris’ home comes after President Donald Trump revoked her U.S. Secret Service protection last year.

A senior White House official who confirmed the news last August noted that vice presidents typically only get six months of protection after leaving office.

That timeline is accurate, as Congress passed a bill in 2008 that cleared Secret Service details for former vice presidents, their spouses and their children under age 16 for up to six months, beginning after the vice president left office, though then-President Joe Biden signed a memorandum in January 2025 extending Harris’ protection to 18 months.

World.title: New York City warns of possible flash floods as thunderstorms develop along East Coast
World.content:
Federal forecasters issued flood alerts for 39 million people late Saturday into Sunday as a line of thunderstorms developed from Washington, D.C., to New Haven, Connecticut.

New York City Emergency Management warned residents of heavy rain and possible flash flooding into Sunday morning as the city opened 51 weather shelters for those vulnerable to floodwaters, including people in basement apartments.

The National Weather Service issued a slew of flood alerts, including flood watches, late Saturday through early Sunday for parts of Maryland, Pennsylvania, Delaware and New Jersey.

A flood watch for Washington, D.C., expired at 1 a.m. Sunday.

Philadelphia and neighboring counties were under a flood watch through morning. A flood watch for New York City was scheduled to start at 4 a.m. Sunday and extend through noon.

New York City Emergency Management said in a statement that 5 to 7 inches of rain could fall in Nassau and Suffolk counties, as well as in southern Connecticut, and warned that the city’s eastern boroughs could also be hit with heavy rain.

“A small shift in where the rain sets up would bring 5 to 7 inch totals and a much higher flash flooding risk into eastern Brooklyn and Queens,” it said. “New Yorkers in those neighborhoods living in basements and below grade are urged to move to higher ground tonight.”

A flood watch for parts of southern Connecticut, including northern New Haven, was in effect through Sunday afternoon, according to the weather service.

The thunderstorms are emerging as a trough of cold air high in the atmosphere moves east and clashes with warmer air, federal forecasters said.

“The combination of instability, deep moisture, and forcing, may lead to an elevated threat for excessive rainfall and severe thunderstorms,” the weather service said in a forecast discussion late Saturday.

World.title: L.L.Bean embraces its old-school roots with brick-and-mortar stores, print catalogs, no AI
World.content:
L.L.Bean’s origin story grew from the ground up — literally.

The company, which sells everything from clothing and footwear to tote bags and home goods, was first established in 1912 after its namesake founder, Leon Leonwood Bean, returned home from a hunting trip with sore, wet feet.

“He said, ‘I have an innovative solution,’” CEO Greg Elder said in an interview, part of NBC News’ “Business in America” initiative. “‘What if I developed the waterproofness of a rubber bottom and stitched on a leather upper?’”

01:47 L.L. Bean CEO on how he manages his day to day 00:00 00:00

And with that, the famous L.L.Bean boot — and a $2 billion company — was born. Since then, the brand has embraced its rugged roots and remains headquartered in Freeport, Maine, a coastal town 20 minutes north of Portland.

“It’s worked for us 100-plus years and it’s going to work for us for another 100-plus years,” said Elder, who has been at the company for nearly two decades. He emphasized L.L.Bean has no plans to relocate its operations.

“We are a family-owned, privately held company,” he said. “The family remains steadfast in their desire to keep this based in Freeport, Maine, where we’ve always been.”

It’s a legacy the brand’s flagship Freeport store has doubled down on. The famous retail location recently underwent a four-year, $50 million renovation. It’s also the only stand-alone L.L.Bean store that’s open 24 hours a day, 365 days a year.

As more retailers adopt direct-to-consumer and online-only business models, L.L.Bean maintains a significant footprint in brick and mortar across the country — around 60 store locations in 22 states.

“The customer says they love to be able to come in and touch and feel the product, they love to be able to try it on and feel the fabrics,” Elder said.

Then there’s the famous L.L.Bean catalog, a long-standing mail-order look book featuring the latest seasonal products and designs.

First launched in 1912 as the business was just getting off the ground, the physical publication has seen daily mailing volumes decline by an estimated 10% to 14% each year, according to Elder.

L.L.Bean CEO Greg Elder said the company is wary of AI's environmental footprint. NBC News

Still, he said it’s not going anywhere. “There is nothing in the foreseeable future that would suggest we’re going to eliminate the catalog.”

And it’s a catalog made the old-fashioned way — without the use of AI.

“We still believe in our hearts that old-school photography with real products on a real human is the way to go for our brand and our brand’s reputation,” Elder said.

As for how L.L.Bean is incorporating AI into its business, Elder said the company is “curious” about areas where it might “fit for our brand,” but isn’t actively searching for ways to deploy the technology.

“That’s not who we are. That’s not in our DNA. We still revolve around the personal selling experience,” he said. “We’re quite cautious about some of the risks.”

This approach differs from those of many other high-profile retailers that have rushed to embrace AI in efforts to streamline operations, improve efficiencies and boost profits.

Elder said AI’s environmental footprint, including its massive energy and water demands, has been a particular deterrent to more widespread adoption at L.L.Bean, which prides itself on being a sustainable outdoor brand.

L.L. Bean's flagship Freeport store recently underwent a four-year, $50 million renovation. NBC News

“This computing power has an impact on the environment without question,” he said. “I’m really hoping that we can find the beautiful intersection of the use of this technology that provides employee and customer productivity, [but] still takes heed to the needs of sustainability, and retains and protects the humanity that is uniquely culturally L.L.Bean.”

Until then, Elder said, the company is comfortable staying on the sidelines of the AI race.

“It may be a little atypical,” he said. “But you know, that’s who we are.”

World.title: Top Trump political adviser James Blair says he’s ‘cautiously optimistic’ about midterms
World.content:
The Republican Party is facing serious headwinds going into November. The party that controls the White House typically loses seats in Congress in the midterms. On top of that, President Donald Trump’s approval rating has hit a new low, and voters continue to express dissatisfaction with the economy and the war with Iran.

Yet James Blair, a top Trump political adviser, said he still believes Republicans can hang on to their majorities in Congress — although he knows it won’t be easy.

“‘I’m cautiously optimistic,” Blair said. “I won’t predict, you know, how many seats are going to be in either chamber come November. But, I do think there is a path for us to retain both majorities and defy history, for sure.”

Blair made his remarks in an interview with “Here’s the Scoop: Election Edition,” NBC News’ new Saturday podcast series hosted by chief White House correspondent Garrett Haake.

Listen and follow “Here’s the Scoop: Election Edition” here.

Blair served as deputy White House chief of staff until April and has been at the center of Trump’s political operations, now serving as the chief of the president’s MAGA Inc. super PAC. During the campaign, Blair was Trump’s political director and is known for his close relationship with White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, who served as a campaign manager in 2024.

Blair acknowledged that Democrats have some advantages this cycle. But he said he believes this post-Labor Day period is where the “heavy lifting” begins and that Democrats may see their polling advantages slip.

Comparing Democratic candidates to unpopular members of their party, like Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, Blair added, is a strategy he hopes GOP candidates will use. He said he views this year’s midterms as being driven by both national and local concerns.

01:38 Rep. Aguilar and James Blair weigh Iran war’s midterms impact 00:00 00:00

“There is a national backdrop against which things are being fought, and there are local considerations and sort of very specific considerations that a good campaign will be able to utilize both of,” he said.

“What they [Democrats] want a Republican to be measured against is, ‘Do you think everything is going perfectly?’” Blair said. “Our candidates, the challenge for them is to not be measured against the measuring stick the Democrats lay out for them, but to be measured against their opposition.”

On Thursday, Vice President JD Vance echoed Blair’s message at a private breakfast in Dallas for Republicans from battleground states.

“We’ve got to nationalize this election,” he said. “We’ve got to talk about all the crazy things the Democrats are doing.”

Addressing dissatisfaction on Iran and the economy

Blair’s comments come as voters’ views of Trump have sunk this year.

An NBC News Decision Desk Poll this month found that just 36% of U.S. adults approve of the way Trump is handling his job as president. On Trump’s handling of the Iran war, those polled scored the president even lower, with just 31% expressing approval.

Blair downplayed concerns about the war, saying that polling he’s seen has shown voters have begun to care less about the issue.

“As things have settled down and people see that we’re in control and are coming in for a landing, you’re seeing numbers with the voters that are sensitive to that moving back in the Republicans’ direction,” he said. “We saw that over the summer around the MOU [memorandum of understanding signed between the U.S. and Iran], and again, settling again as there’s not been, sort of, daily action.”

Earlier this week, the U.S. and Iran traded strikes, with the U.S. military hitting five Iranian oil tankers after Iran struck two U.S. warships. On Wednesday, the president told Republicans gathered in Dallas for a GOP midterm convention that the war with Iran would not end until after Election Day.

Trump has repeatedly said that the ongoing conflict has achieved its goal of preventing Iran from building a nuclear weapon, something that Blair cited as a political success, despite the president’s low marks from voters on his handling of the war.

“The president made a correct decision in the scope of history to solve a problem that has been bipartisan-agreed as a problem for 47 years in this country,” he said. “I think we can manage our way through, in September and October, to still be successful, and I think we will be.”

Another area where voters give the president low marks is on the economy and inflation.

An August Reuters/Ipsos poll found that just 32% of registered voters approved of the president’s handling of the economy. In that same poll, a slightly higher share of voters — 37% — said they believed the Democratic Party had a better plan, policy or approach to the economy than the share who said so about Republicans, 36%.

Blair downplayed concerns that views of the economy could cost the GOP its control of Congress, arguing that the president and Republican leaders were still dealing with inflation left over from President Joe Biden, who left the White House in January 2025.

“We’re still cleaning up that mess, and we need more time to finish the job,” Blair said. “That’s what we’re asking for in November.”

That message of asking for patience was reflected at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas this week.

“All of the price hikes that happened under Biden that were caused by their policies don’t just immediately drop,” Blair added.

In February 2025, the first full month of Trump’s second term, inflation was 2.8% year over year. It dipped as low as 2.4% in April 2025, the month Trump announced his “Liberation Day” tariff regime — but before those tariffs had taken effect. Fast-forward 18 months, and both tariffs and the Iran war energy crisis have helped push inflation back up to 3.4% as of August.

Trump ‘on the ballot’

In recent weeks, the president has increasingly focused on the midterms, telling reporters that he plans to travel and campaign in 35 races. He has also asked supporters to “pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot,” an idea that Blair embraced.

“Democrats are already using him as a turnout tool for their voters, whether Republicans do that or not. So that’s sort of baked into the cake,” Blair said. “The other side’s already going to, you know, attack however they’re going to attack, do whatever they think they can do to motivate their voters to win. We want to use all of the tools at our disposal to help our voters.”

Specifically, Blair pointed to low-propensity male voters, or those who don’t vote in every election, as ones whom Trump may be uniquely able to encourage to go to the polls.

He used an example of a voter who “works 40 to 60 hours a week, is not super engaged in politics. … He’s not watching this podcast. He’s not watching the news. He’s not trying to be engaged in politics on a regular basis.”

“That’s a guy who voted in the presidential race, but, historically he’s not voted in the midterms because that’s just the nature of those voters,” Blair added. “So for the president to lay out the stakes to that individual to give him a reason to come out and vote that transcends, you know, not just what he’s hearing from his local candidates, but sort of broadens out the picture nationally and what the stakes are, I think that’s very useful.”

Still, Blair said he doesn’t expect the same coalition that sent Trump back to the White House in 2024 to align with the president again this year.

“Coalitions are never exactly the same,” he said, adding: “Maybe a coalition’s core sticks, and then every election is a little different.”

He pointed specifically to Latino voters, who voted for the Republican nominee in 2024 in record numbers.

“Do I think that Republicans generically will get the same percentage with Hispanics in ‘26 as they did in ‘24? You know, probably not,” Blair said. “But will Hispanics still overperform for Republicans, you know, in broad, relative to where they did in 2018 and 2022? Yes, I think that’s likely.”

How Latinos vote this fall could be a significant factor in how many seats Texas Republicans and California Democrats win after redrawing their congressional maps. For example, Republicans’ three top targets in Texas — the 28th, 34th and 35th districts — are all overwhelmingly Latino districts. If the president’s standing with Latino voters wanes, that could jeopardize Republicans’ ability to win these seats.

MAGA Inc. begins to unload its coffers

Blair also spoke about the role that MAGA Inc. will have in the midterms. At the end of July, when its most recent campaign finance disclosure was filed, the group had a war chest of more than $400 million.

Asked about some Republicans’ concerns that Trump may not choose to spend the bulk of the MAGA Inc. cash before Election Day, Blair said simply, “I can assure that the president will leave it all on the field to keep his majorities.”

Over the summer, some members of the GOP were particularly concerned about Texas, where state Attorney General Ken Paxton ousted Sen. John Cornyn in a bruising Republican primary. Paxton had Trump’s endorsement, but much of the Republican Party backed Cornyn, known as a strong fundraiser with a record of winning in the state. Public polling has indicated a close, competitive race between Paxton and Democratic state Rep. James Talarico, who has led the state attorney general in fundraising.

On Saturday, MAGA Inc. booked $10 million worth of TV ad time in the state. Blair dismissed concerns about Paxton’s strength in the race, saying, “The fact is Ken Paxton had $100 million spent against him in the primary. Talarico had $0 spent against him in the primary, and that has an impact on candidate images that takes time to rectify. But the resources … have begun to be deployed now in earnest [and] will take care of that problem.”

On Wednesday, The New York Times reported that MAGA Inc. was funneling $49 million through a new group — No Going Back PAC — that would run TV ads in Senate races across the country.

Blair didn’t detail the group’s spending plans, but acknowledged a widening battlefield of competitive statewide races, including in Alaska’s Senate race, where former Rep. Mary Peltola is the Democratic nominee running against Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.

The race is complicated by the presence of a third candidate, also a Republican named Dan Sullivan. (In Alaska, the top four candidates in the primary, regardless of party, advance to the ranked-choice general election.) Republicans have accused Democrats of sowing confusion among voters by recruiting Dan J. Sullivan to run as a spoiler in the race against the senator, Dan S. Sullivan.

“We know that national Democrats did that,” Blair said, without pointing to specific evidence. “We know that the press release for that candidate was written by a consultant to Mary Peltola. No one even disputes this fact. That is rigging a process using ranked-choice voting against the people of Alaska.”

Democrats have not taken credit for recruiting Dan J. Sullivan, a teacher, into the race. Blair acknowledged that his presence and Peltola’s past electoral success in the state are making the race close.

“I don’t dispute that’s a competitive race,” he said. “Mary Peltola’s been elected statewide before. We know this. So I mean, I think for us, like, we’re smart enough to read numbers. We know where things are. We’re going to fish where the fish are, and we’re gonna go try to win the majority, you know, protect the majority in all these places.”

World.title: Wisconsin Congressman suffers minor injury after lake emergency landing
World.content:
Wisconisn gubernatorial candidate Rep. Tom Tiffany said Sunday he sustained minor injuries after the plane he was traveling in made an emergency landing on Lake Wausau in central Wisconsin.

Tiffany, a Republican, said in a social media post he was returning from La Crosse County Lincoln Day Dinner when the plane he was traveling in lost power on approach to Wausau Downtown Airport, forcing the pilot to make an emergency landing in the water.

As the plane began to submerge, Tiffany and the pilot exited the aircraft and swam to a shallow area where they waited for emergency responders, he said.

I want to express my deepest gratitude to the pilot, the Wausau Fire Department, and all of the first responders who came to our aid so quickly," Tiffany wrote on his post. "Thankfully, both the pilot and I sustained only minor injuries," he added.

His Democratic opponent, David Crowley, responded by saying he was "grateful to God that Congressman Tiffany and no one else was hurt in this horrifying incident, which could have been a tragedy if not for the heroism of the pilot."

CBS affiliate WSAW-TV initially reported a private plane going down in Lake Wausau at 9 p.m. local time, quoting the Marathon County Sheriff's Office, with the investigation of the incident being handed over to Federal Aviation Authority.

"God was watching over us tonight, and I am incredibly grateful to be here in the hospital with my wife, Chris, by my side. An experience like this reminds you just how precious life is," Tiffany said in his post.

World.title: Search underway for 140 people after Indonesian passenger ship overturns
World.content:
Indonesian rescuers said about 140 passengers and crew were missing after a ferry carrying more than 240 people overturned in bad weather in the Java Sea on Sunday. At least 102 people were rescued and the body of a passenger was recovered as the search operation expanded in waters around the vessel's last known position.

The ferry was traveling from East Java to South Kalimantan province, officials said.

The vessel's captain had earlier reported rough seas with waves up to 10 feet before issuing a distress message, saying the ship was listing, Sudayana said. Authorities later received information indicating the vessel had overturned, said I Putu Sudayana, who heads the Search and Rescue Office.

The rescue agency in South Kalimantan's city of Banjarmasin said it received a report two hours after contact was lost with the Virgo Transport 8. The ship had departed from Surabaya, Indonesia's second largest city in East Java province, en route to Banjarmasin on Borneo Island.

"The ship's operator reported the incident to authorities after receiving information that the vessel had encountered bad weather," Sudayana said in a video briefing.

In response, a rescue ship was headed to the Virgo Transport 8's estimated last known position, he said, and authorities were mobilizing all available personnel and assets because the vessel was carrying a large number of passengers and crew.

Initial information indicated the vessel's last known position was in the Java Sea, about 92 miles from a pier in Banjarmasin. The ship's manifest said it was carrying 243 people, including 213 passengers and 30 crew members, although it is common in Indonesia for the number of passengers to differ from the manifest.

Sudayana, who is coordinating the search, said the agency was working with maritime authorities and other relevant agencies while closely monitoring weather conditions in the area.

Search teams, assisted by nearby tugboats and other vessels, had rescued 102 people and recovered one body by Sunday afternoon, he said.

The ferry departed Surabaya, Indonesia's second-largest city, at 10:33 a.m. Saturday and was scheduled to arrive in Banjarmasin at about 2 p.m. Sunday.

World.title: Deputies respond to trespasser at Malibu home of Kamala Harris
World.content:
A trespasser was reported Friday night at former Vice President Kamala Harris' home in Malibu, California, according to Los Angeles County law enforcement officials and a Harris spokesperson.

Los Angeles County sheriff's deputies responded to her home around 10:30 p.m. after her private security detail made a "suspicious person" call, the department said.

When they arrived, they made contact with the person and advised them to leave, the sheriff's department said. The person left voluntarily without incident.

"Last night, security personnel stopped an individual who illegally entered Vice President Harris and Second Gentleman Emhoff's property before the individual reached the home," said a statement from Eduardo Negrón, a spokesperson for Harris. "Vice President Harris and Second Gentleman Emhoff were not present. They are grateful to the security and law enforcement personnel who responded swiftly."

The sheriff's department said a trespassing report was taken and deputies from the local station would increase patrols in the area as a precaution.

Former vice presidents typically receive federal government protection for six months after leaving office, while former presidents receive protection for life.

Then-President Joe Biden extended Harris' protection beyond the traditional six months, but President Donald Trump revoked the extension last August. It otherwise would have ended this summer.

World.title: Elena Rybakina bests defending champion Aryna Sabalenka to win her first U.S. Open
World.content:
Elena Rybakina came to New York and took everything that had belonged to Aryna Sabalenka.

First, it was the No. 1 ranking in women's tennis, then the U.S. Open trophy.

The tournament that for so long was a struggle for Rybakina turned into the site of her coronation.

Rybakina won her first U.S. Open title and punctuated her climb to the top of her sport by beating Sabalenka 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 on Saturday.

Elena Rybakina reacts after winning the U.S. Open final at USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center on Sept. 12, 2026, in Flushing, New York. Pete Staples/USTA via Getty Images

Rybakina had already been guaranteed to replace Sabalenka at No. 1 in the rankings next week and for good measure took the title that Sabalenka had won the previous two years.

"It's tough to find words right now, honestly," Rybakina said. "I don't expect nothing like this coming to this tournament. I've been dealing with a little bit with an injury, but somehow everything aligned together on my side."

It was the third Grand Slam title for Rybakina and the second this year — both against Sabalenka on hard courts. She opened the season by beating Sabalenka for the Australian Open title.

This time, Rybakina stopped Sabalenka's 19-match winning streak at the U.S. Open, where she hadn't lost since falling to Coco Gauff in the 2023 final.

Rybakina earned $5.5 million, the largest prize in Grand Slam history, and tied Sabalenka and French Open winner Mirra Andreeva with a tour-high three titles this season.

Sabalenka took home $2.8 million, but it was clear how little that meant to her, as she smashed her racket after a brief hug with Rybakina at the net.

Sabalenka was trying to become the first person since Serena Williams from 2012 to 2014 to win three in a row at Flushing Meadows.

"I was just out there competing, trying to do my best with what I had there today," Sabalenka said. "Not good enough."

Rybakina dethroned the champ without even having her best stuff. The WTA Tour leader in aces got less than half of her first serves in but instead put Sabalenka under constant pressure with a strong return game, racking up 12 break chances and converting three, which was all she needed.

The third meeting of No. 1 vs. No. 2 in a U.S. Open women's final since 2000 was the first to go the way of the challenger. Williams was the top seed for the other two, beating her sister Venus in 2002 and Victoria Azarenka in 2013.

The numbers didn't signify much this time, because they are going to flip Monday. Sabalenka has held the top spot for 99 consecutive weeks, but Rybakina gained enough points to unseat her simply by reaching the semifinals.

She didn't stop there.

The 27-year-old who was born in Russia but represents Kazakhstan won her first major title at Wimbledon in 2022 and now needs just the French Open to complete the career Grand Slam.

And it's clear her power — and her ability to absorb her opponent's — was something that unnerved Sabalenka.

"Her serve is amazing, the way she's able to step in and overpower you on court, and especially if it's a U.S. Open court where it's super fast, it's definitely a huge advantage for her," Sabalenka said. "A lot of things make her dangerous."

A native of Belarus, Sabalenka sometimes swings from her heels, like a golfer trying to unleash a 300-yard drive, grunting "Aaaaahhhh!" as she takes her mighty cuts.

Rybakina's power comes more easily. There is little sound coming from her side of the net besides the squeaking of her sneakers, and she rarely shows any hint of stress.

"I think Elena is probably — not nonchalant, I don't want to say that, because she's not nonchalant — but just no reaction ever," Gauff said after losing to Rybakina in the semifinals.

Rybakina did show some frustration after pulling a backhand wide with a break point in the opening game of the third set, but soon she had taken charge of the match for good.

Sabalenka had won the two other meetings this season, on the hard courts at Indian Wells and Miami, and leads their rivalry 10-8.

But her season then took a strange dip after those victories. Sabalenka fell to Naomi Osaka in the fourth round at Wimbledon, then returned to action with consecutive fourth-round exits in Toronto and Cincinnati.

Rybakina had to take a brief break after she was forced to stop playing in her quarterfinal match

against Iga Swiatek in Cincinnati because of a foot injury, but she was healthy in time for a tournament where she had never done particularly well, failing to advance past the fourth round until this year.

"I honestly was coming here for the last 10 years, and it was never successful — nothing close to that," Rybakina said. "It's just incredible. I'm falling in love with New York more and more."

Arthur Ashe Stadium, meanwhile, had been Sabalenka's house, with four straight trips to the final and six to at least the semis. Whatever troubled her during the summer seemed forgotten once she was back in New York — until Saturday.

Sabalenka repeatedly looked toward her coaches' box with her palms up, wondering why everything was going so poorly, and showed much more frustration than that when she double-faulted to hand Rybakina a 3-2 lead in the first set. Rybakina hit the serve back and the ball bounced directly to Sabalenka, who whacked it into the crowd, earning a warning from the chair umpire.

Sabalenka eventually began putting consistent pressure on Rybakina in the second set. She picked up two break points with a chance to end the set with a 5-4 lead, and though Rybakina won four straight points to get out of that jam, Sabalenka got another chance in the next service game and this time capitalized, stepping into a return to set up a miss by Rybakina.

COVER STORY: Missile crisis - The hard truths about America's military arsenal

The war with Iran was launched more than six months ago, and shows no signs of ending. In the early days of the conflict, the United States fired off thousands of long-range, precision-guided missiles. Now, with its arsenal depleted, the Pentagon is faced with the stark prospect of not having enough high-tech weapons to sustain a conflict against a true military power like China, and has ordered the defense industry onto a "wartime footing" to replenish its stockpiles. That will cost billions of dollars and require years of manufacturing. CBS News national security correspondent David Martin visited some of the plants now ramping up production to rebuild America's military arsenal.

For more info:

"Sunday Morning" looks back at historical events on this date.



WORLD: Shipwrecks and the tantalizing allure of the sea

Shipwrecks have long fascinated oceanographer Robert Ballard, who became renowned for locating the wreck of the RMS Titanic in 1985. He talks with correspondent Lee Cowan about how that discovery 12,000 feet beneath the Atlantic changed him, and about the efforts of his research vessel Nautilus to map the ocean floor. Cowan also talks with Sophie Elmhirst, author of the bestseller "A Marriage at Sea: A True Story of Love, Obsession, and Shipwreck," about human beings at their most vulnerable.

For more info:

In this preview, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told CBS News that he didn't fully anticipate the effects of rapid artificial intelligence development, while also encouraging the public not to panic. Jo Ling Kent reports.

For more info:

WORLD: Uncovering a Holocaust survival story

An oral history project organized by former schoolteacher Matthew Rozell to interview World War II veterans uncovered little-known stories from the conflict, including the liberation by American troops of 2,500 Holocaust survivors from a so-called "death train" in April 1945. Correspondent Seth Doane talks with Rozell (author of "A Train Near Magdeburg"), historian James Bulgin, and filmmaker Mike Edwards about preserving the memories of WWII vets, and the importance of society learning the stories we must never forget.

Mike Edwards



HARTMAN: A former football star's backpack becomes a lifeline

In Austin, Texas, recent Indiana University graduate Jasper Steinmetz approached a man sporting something familiar: an IU backpack. The man turned out to be Sampson James, a former Indiana University football star who had fallen on hard times, following a knee injury and a diagnosis of bipolar disorder. Steve Hartman reports on what happened when the connection made by these two Hoosiers fostered a fresh start.

Correspondent Alina Cho and designer Diane von Furstenberg in Venice. CBS News

FASHION: Diane von Furstenberg on life, love, and a wrap dress

Diane von Furstenberg has been one of the most important names in fashion for nearly 50 years, whose brand has long empowered women, with practical, feminine clothing (most famously embodied by her '70s wrap dress). In Venice, correspondent Alina Cho visits with von Furstenberg, who talks about her life's journey, which she calls a miracle thanks to a mother who survived the Holocaust.

For more info:

Getty Images

HEADLINES: Testing the ethical boundaries of surrogacy

In the United States, commercial surrogacy — paying a woman to have fertilized eggs implanted in her uterus so she can carry a pregnancy to term — is widely assumed to be closely regulated. But a yearlong CBS News investigation found that few, if any, meaningful protections exist for surrogates. Correspondent Katrina Kaufman examines the extraordinary cases of surrogates who say they experienced troubling practices in the booming U.S. industry.

For more info:



FOOD: Good gourd! A visit to the pumpkin capital of the world

In Morton, Illinois, home to the annual Pumpkin Festival, and site of the Libby's factory responsible for 85 percent of the world's canned pumpkin, correspondent Nancy Giles gets a taste of the local produce and finds out why, in Morton, orange is always in season.

For more info:



NATURE: Monarch caterpillars in New York



WEB EXCLUSIVES:

FROM THE ARCHIVES: Jay Maisel on photographing the Twin Towers (Video)

During the course of his life, New York photographer Jay Maisel, who died last month at age 95, photographed the World Trade Center thousands of times – including on 9/11, when they were destroyed. In this "Sunday Morning" report that aired Sept. 16, 2011, Maisel talked with correspondent Richard Schlesinger about the hold the Twin Towers had on the imagination, and on his camera's lens.

FROM THE ARCHIVES: How one N.J. town suffered loss on 9/11 (Video)

In this story that aired on "Sunday Morning" Sept. 16, 2001, correspondent Bill Geist reported on how his hometown of Ridgewood, N.J., was devastated by the terror attacks on Lower Manhattan, just a short commuter train ride away, and how his friends and neighbors responded to the loss of a dozen members of their community.

FROM THE ARCHIVES: 9/11, Osama bin Laden, and a safe haven in Afghanistan (Video)

After terrorists attacked the United States on Sept. 11, 2001, America's attention turned fully to the group's leader, Osama bin Laden, and his Al Qaeda network, which had found protection in Afghanistan. Correspondent Allen Pizzey reports on a country already devastated by more than 20 years of continuous warfare, which was anticipating further retaliation by Washington, in a story that originally aired Sept. 16, 2001. Pizzey also talks with Vicky and Mark Timlin, of the charity Hope Worldwide, whose head office ordered them to leave Afghanistan following the attacks on the World Trade Center and the Pentagon.

In this 1997 "Sunday Morning" profile, Wilson talked with correspondent Billy Taylor about her early influences, from her parents, to singers like Joni Mitchell and Richie Havens. FROM THE ARCHIVES: Gloria Steinem on "CBS Sunday Morning" (YouTube Video)

World.title: Anthropic CEO says "exponential" growth of AI is a "warning sign"
World.content:
Artificial intelligence technology is developing at an "exponential" rate, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told CBS News on Saturday, calling the situation a "warning sign" for the industry that requires serious safeguards.

"I don't think I fully just appreciated what it would actually be like when the progress was as fast as it was," Amodei said in an interview with senior business and technology correspondent Jo Ling Kent that will air on "CBS News Sunday Morning."

He described the development of AI as going from "one, then two, then four, then eight, then 16, then 32," saying that it currently is "on the bend" of the curve and is "starting to get steep."

"It doesn't mean we need to panic today. It doesn't mean we need to shut it all down," Amodei said, but added that it is "a warning sign that we need to slow down."

Amodei said that the technology needs safeguards that can keep up "with the pace at which the technology is happening."

The interview comes hours after Amodei published a blog post in which he called on AI companies to move forward more slowly and cautiously with the technology's development, saying risk prevention is paramount. He offered a three-point plan with the goal, he said, of "pacing the frontier."

"Carefully wielded, AI can be the latest in a long line of technological miracles that have uplifted and ennobled humanity," he said in the post. "But like many technologies before it, AI brings risks, and because it is such a powerful technology, these risks are serious."

Amodei cautioned that swarms of rogue AI agents could take over the internet in as little as six months, specifically mentioning the OpenAI-Hugging Face rogue agent incident from July.

ChatGPT maker OpenAI said an AI model went rogue during the Hugging Face incident when the company was testing two AI models — one of which hadn't been released to the public — in an isolated environment to assess their capabilities.

Amodei urged other companies to slow the pace "at which we improve the capabilities of AI models." He wrote: "Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain."

He clarified that pacing doesn't mean halting model training or technical progress but rather allowing companies to dedicate more time to testing and prioritize the alignment and safeguarding of models.

Under his three-part plan, the Anthropic co-founder said AI companies should commit to give "ongoing, employee-like access" to embedded teams of third-party evaluators whose role is to verify adherence to safety practices and commitments. He said these evaluators should have ongoing access to permissions and tools similar to internal employees who conduct comparable risk assessments.

"Anthropic is unilaterally committing to this step now," Amodei added.

He said companies within democratic countries should "coordinate to establish common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress." Finally, Amodei said that U.S. and other democratic governments should coordinate with authoritarian governments "while taking seriously the challenges of verifying compliance."

He also urged U.S. companies not to sell powerful AI chips to China, which he said will be "the main determinant of China's AI strength."

"The measures I propose to advance the frontier at a safe pace will not be easy," Amodei acknowledged. "But I believe we owe it to humanity to try."

Amodei's warning comes just days after Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic researcher, publicly resigned from the company, accusing it and rival OpenAI of "gambling with our lives" by racing to develop advanced AI models.

Coxon claimed that AI could one day threaten humanity, telling Kent in an interview Thursday that the technology development "doesn't look that different from, say, 'Terminator,' or from science fiction films."

"It really is just, if you have a super advanced intelligence, it could, it will be smart enough to kill us," Coxon added.

Coxon told CBS News he would like to see an agreement between AI companies "not to push into dangerous territory" without "transparent auditing" from third parties.

"In the future, if we keep racing, it'll be a lot harder to have completely watertight safety cases that what you're doing is safe and people will race against each other," Coxon said.

Amodei acknowledged in his blog post Saturday that people may lose control of AI, and the technology can be misused for "cyberattacks and bioterrorism, and serious economic disruption."

"A race to the bottom, spurred by commercial incentives, can make these risks more acute," Amodei wrote.

Separately, Anthropic said this week that it blocked scientists who used its Claude models "in ways that could support biological weapons development," a revelation the company shared in a lengthy report that also divulged other harmful activity involving surveillance, scams, conventional weapons development and propaganda.

On Saturday, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was quick to agree with Amodei on companies needing to "pace the frontier."

"This has been a primary topic of discussions we've had at OpenAI in recent weeks. Committing to having independent evaluators with employee-like access is a great idea, and we will do the same. We'll have more to share soon," he said in a post on X.

Meanwhile, Elon Musk, owner of SpaceXAI, while sharing Amodei's post on X, simply said: "Dario is right."

When asked Saturday by CBS News if he is communicating directly with Altman and Musk, Amodei wouldn't say, only acknowledging that he was "enormously appreciative that other industry leaders, including our competitors, have offered their agreement with this plan."

He also reiterated to CBS News the need for AI companies to jointly agree to "third-party evaluators."

"I think the next step after that is in some form, the companies need to work together to set standards, about safety standards for release, perhaps something about the pace of release," Amodei said.

Amodei stressed, however, his belief that the industry will need government regulation in order for its own safeguarding efforts to succeed.

"What we're talking about is the rate of release of products because of whether they're safe," Amodei said. "We need to have that conversation with the government in the room."

Watch Jo Ling Kent's interview with Dario Amodei on Sept. 13 on "CBS News Sunday Morning."

World.title: Indonesian passenger ship overturns, sparking search for about 130 missing
World.content:
Indonesian passenger ship overturns, sparking search for about 130 missing

toggle caption Iman Satria/AP

BANJARMASIN, Indonesia — Indonesian rescuers say about 130 passengers and crew are missing after a ferry carrying more than 240 people sank in bad weather in the Java Sea on Sunday. At least 107 people were rescued and the bodies of six passengers were recovered as the search operation expanded in waters around the vessel's last known position.

The ferry was traveling from Surabaya in East Java to Banjarmasin in South Kalimantan province, officials said.

The vessel's captain had earlier reported rough seas with waves up to 3 meters (10 feet) before issuing a distress message, saying the ship was listing, said I Putu Sudayana, who heads the Banjarmasin Search and Rescue Office. Authorities later received information indicating the vessel had overturned and then sunk.

Sponsor Message

The rescue agency in Banjarmasin said it received a report two hours after contact was lost with the Virgo Transport 8 at about 2 a.m. Sunday. The ship had departed from Surabaya, Indonesia's second largest city, en route to Banjarmasin, a city on Borneo Island.

"The ship's operator reported the incident to authorities after receiving information that the vessel had encountered bad weather," Sudayana said in a video briefing.

In response, a rescue ship was headed to the Virgo Transport 8's estimated last known position, he said, and authorities were deploying rescue teams supported by four vessels, including a navy ship, and a helicopter as the ferry was carrying a large number of passengers and crew.

Survivors are rescued and dead bodies recovered

Initial information indicated the vessel's last known position was in the Java Sea, about 148 kilometers (92 miles) from a pier in Banjarmasin. The ship's manifest said it was carrying 243 people — 213 passengers and 30 crew members — although it is common in Indonesia for the number of passengers to differ from the manifest.

Sudayana, who is coordinating the search, said the agency was working with maritime authorities and other relevant agencies while closely monitoring weather conditions in the area.

Search teams, assisted by nearby tugboats and other passing vessels, had rescued 107 people and recovered six bodies by Sunday afternoon, he said.

Sponsor Message

The Japanese-built Virgo Transport 8 is designed to transport both passengers and vehicles.

Distraught relatives wait for news at a port

Hundreds of relatives gathered at a command center in Banjarmasin's Trisakti port on Sunday, awaiting word on family members believed to be aboard the ferry. Many anxiously checked passenger manifests and rescue lists as authorities continued searching for survivors.

"I was shocked when I saw my uncle's name on the passenger list," said a woman who goes by a single name, Bunga. "But I felt relieved after officials told me he had been rescued."

Indonesia is an archipelago of more than 17,000 islands where ferries are a common method of travel. Disasters occur regularly, with weak safety enforcement often blamed.

Last month, at least 211 people were rescued from an Indonesian ferry that caught fire in rough seas near the Indonesian tourist island of Bali, while one person was found dead and four others remain missing. The incident happened less than two weeks after another Indonesian ferry, the Mutiara Sentosa 2, caught fire in waters off the main island of Java, leaving at least five people dead.

Sunday's accident comes just four days after a fire that gutted a passenger ferry in the Philippines killed at least 76 people, with at least 10 others still missing.

World.title: How a young woman became an ISIS bride — and then an informant, helping save others
World.content:
How a young woman became an ISIS bride — and then an informant, helping save others

toggle caption Illustration by Hanna Barczyk for NPR

WESTERN CANADA — Outside a tall apartment building we meet a slim, smiling woman dressed in a black shirt and jeans. She invites us inside, and we sit in a conference room, where she begins to tell her story.

We're not using her real name, or her home city, fearing her past could lead to repercussions. It's a past that led her into the arms of the Islamic State and brutal fighting in Syria. And to this day, she doesn't know how she survived.
