Both the PQ and the Liberals, however, panned the new measures. The PQ fears retaliation will hurt Quebec companies that are doing business in the U.S., while the Liberals said the plan doesn’t go far enough.

Béland said even though Fréchette can act as premier and that announcing new decisions can get her quite a bit of exposure, it also opens the door to criticism and she has to show restraint.

“If she will suspend her campaign again and there is no strong apparent trigger for it, then yes, I think she will be more vulnerable politically and that could help her opponents,” he said.

LISTEN | Trade war becomes major focus in Quebec election: Breakaway 11:49 Tariffs are taking center stage in the election campaign The election campaign is gaining speed. The leaders are preparing for a first debate. But tariffs have taken center stage in the campaign. And Christine Fréchette's decision to temporarily suspend her campaign has drawn reactions.

In the view of her opponents, the damage is already done. Milliard worries Fréchette is using her role as premier to turn the election into a one-issue campaign. He said he hopes that will change after the leaders' debates.

The main party leaders will be facing off in three French-language debates organized by Radio-Canada, TVA, Noovo and Crave. The first debate is scheduled for Sept. 15 and Radio-Canada’s French-language debate will take place Sept. 23 at 8 p.m.

Voters head to the polls on Oct. 5.

World.title: Alberta separatists expect a win, regardless of numbers that say otherwise, poll suggests
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Alberta separatists think they’re going to win a referendum that surveys suggest they are poised to lose by a wide margin, according to exclusive new polling.

And that mismatch of expectations has consequences for what comes next — including the likelihood that Albertans shouldn’t expect this issue to be put to rest with this one vote, say the pollster and a political scientist.

Abacus Data CEO David Coletto presented the results of the new poll, done during the first week of September, to CBC’s West of Centre on Friday.

On Oct. 19, Albertans will vote on a question with two choices: Option 1 is to stay in Canada, while Option 2 supports commencing the legal process to hold a binding referendum on Alberta separation.

That ballot question will be in addition to nine others that focus on constitutional and immigration issues.

Coletto’s poll found 64 per cent of respondents would vote to remain a province in Canada and 24 per cent would vote to start the separation process. Nine per cent were undecided and three per cent said they would skip the question.

But the poll also found that Option 2 supporters have surprisingly high expectations, believing that the separatist option will garner a winning 57 per cent of votes.

Coletto chalks it up to the political bubbles people live in and the natural hopefulness that comes with their strong support of the separatist camp.

Lisa Young, a political science professor at the University of Calgary, says that inflated expectation is worth noting — especially in the context of post-referendum ramifications.

"What he found, I think, should be setting off alarm bells in all of our heads," Young told West of Centre.

"If you do walk into this with the expectation that Option [2] is going to get 57 per cent and the actual outcome is 28 per cent ... the first question is going to be, 'Was this a proper result? Can we trust the outcome?'"

Premier Danielle Smith has said the upcoming referendum will be a gut-check of where Albertans stand, and that the province can hold a vote and move on .

But Young and Coletto don't see it that way.

In the event that the winning side supports remaining in Canada, the poll found many Option 2 voters expect the separatist movement to keep growing. Only six per cent of them said they expect the issue will be settled.

"There seems to be this assumption in the UCP premier's office ... that if you let this group let off steam, it will make the issue go away," Young said.

"This does not simply go away afterward. We're going to live with it one way or another for the next months, if not years."

A ballot for the Oct. 19 Alberta referendum shows the question about separating from Canada and the two options voters will choose between. (Kory Siegers/CBC)

Who is the typical Option 2 voter?

According to the polling, the typical Option 2 voter is a conservative partisan, somewhat more likely to be a man and tends to be slightly older than the provincial average.

They are more likely to live in small cities or in bedroom communities around Calgary and Edmonton. While rural Alberta contributes more than its share, the communities ringing Alberta's main metropolitan centres provide the most voters.

But the group is more distinguishable by its grievances than its demographics, the poll suggests.

It says Option 2 supporters are far more likely to put being an Albertan ahead of being a Canadian, and have a more favourable view of the United States and Donald Trump. That said, the group is split on whether Alberta should become a U.S. state.

The group also shares near-unanimous agreement that Alberta contributes more to Canada than it gets back, the province’s interests are ignored in Ottawa, and the rest of the country does not respect Alberta, the poll suggests.

Young said she wonders if the separatist camp is adequately reflected among people who were polled.

"I did start thinking back to 2016 in the United States," Young said. "People wouldn't tell a pollster that they were going to vote for Trump because it was seen as sort of socially unacceptable."

Coletto said he's confident his poll factored in as many Option 2 voters as possible, but he also acknowledged this is not a typical election.

"Partisan politics can get divisive. But this is being felt much more deeply and much more emotionally on both sides."

"Whatever side you're on, you've still got to live together no matter what happens going forward."

Do they actually want to leave?

What Option 2 voters hope to get out of a favourable result varies significantly. When asked to identify their main motivation for choosing to commence the process for a binding referendum, only 26 per cent said independence.

The rest are voting for leverage, to send a message or on principle, Coletto said.

"For many Albertans who are inclined to look at Option 2, it's not just a black or white, in and out."

That result aligns with recent messaging from the separatist camp.

“Independence isn't actually on the ballot,” Keith Wilson, with independence group Let Alberta Decide, told West of Centre last month.

“Voting Option 2 sends a message that no, we can do better. We want a more respectful and balanced and fair relationship with Ottawa.”

“Others are prepared to vote for Option 2 when they don't even support independence. And that's why I have some optimism we're going to win on Oct. 19.”

University of Calgary political scientist Lisa Young, left, and David Coletto, CEO of Abacus Data, speak to CBC's West of Centre on Friday. (Diane Yanko/CBC)

Methodology

Abacus Data surveyed 1,000 Alberta adults online from Sept. 4 to 7, 2026, six weeks before the Oct. 19 referendum. Results are weighted by region, age and gender to census data. A probability sample of this size would carry a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1 points, 19 times out of 20. For subsets, the margin of error is larger.

World.title: Canadian boxer George Chuvalo, who faced Muhammad Ali in his prime, dead at 89
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

George Chuvalo, the iron-chinned Canadian heavyweight who took the best punches from the giants of boxing without ever falling, has died. He was 89.

Chuvalo suffered from dementia late in life and had been residing in a long-term care facility in Toronto. He died Saturday according to multiple online posts by family and friends.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford, who said the boxer was a family friend, shared condolences on social media Saturday.

"My thoughts are with all of George's family and loved ones as we mourn his passing," he said.

Chuvalo went the distance with Muhammad Ali in bouts in Toronto and Vancouver, and absorbed the hardest shots sluggers Joe Frazier and George Foreman had to offer, without being knocked down.

It was unfathomable family tragedy after he retired that brought him to his knees.

WATCH | Peter Mansbridge interviews George Chuvalo: George Chuvalo | Duration 5:57 Peter Mansbridge sits down with champion heavyweight boxer George Chuvalo to talk about many of his famous fights.

"If you added up every punch I took and multiplied the total by 10,000, it wouldn't begin to equal the pain of losing three sons and a wife to drugs and suicide," he said in his 2013 autobiography Chuvalo: A Fighter's Life, co-written with Murray Greig.

The son of Croatian immigrants was born Sept. 12, 1937, in Toronto's Junction neighbourhood. He became intrigued by boxing after seeing The Ring magazine at a newsstand.

Chuvalo was 10 years old the first time he stepped through the ropes, and a growth spurt combined with an interest in weightlifting saw him develop into a six-foot, 210-pound fighter.

After a brief amateur career, he turned pro in 1956, winning notice for performances at the Jack Dempsey Tournament at Maple Leaf Gardens.

But by the early 1960s, Chuvalo's career had stagnated under ineffective guidance, until Toronto poultry magnate Irv Ungerman took over as his manager.

Chuvalo parlayed several wins into an attention-getting 11th-round stoppage over contender Doug Jones at Madison Square Garden in 1964. He returned to that mecca of boxing the next year, narrowly losing a decision to former champ Floyd Patterson in a bout The Ring named best of 1965.

'He just keeps coming and coming'

Chuvalo's style was inexorable without being reckless. He moved forward with thudding blows from both hands to the head and body, producing stoppages in 88 per cent of his wins.

"You can't believe his strength," Canadian fighter Bill Drover once told a writer. "There's no way to stop him. He just keeps coming and coming. The only way you can stop him is with a stick of dynamite."

Chuvalo would always insist his defence was better than advertised, but it was his durability that was remarkable. He was able to absorb the shots, he said, thanks to a 17.5-inch neck strengthened through exercises.

Chuvalo found himself fighting for the heavyweight title in 1966 as a replacement foe when Ali's affiliation with the Black Muslims and controversial anti-Vietnam-War stance made him a pariah in the U.S.

The challenger's prospects were described in a New York Times headline: Bettor's-Eye View of Chuvalo: A Big Bum With a Lot of Heart.

George Chuvalo, left, and Muhammad Ali go head to head as they trade blows near the rope in the fourth round of their fight in Toronto on March 29, 1966. (The Associated Press)

While Chuvalo failed to become Canada's first heavyweight champion since Tommy Burns in the early 1900s, he earned praise for a gritty performance. Ali famously called him the toughest man he had faced up to that point, but Chuvalo was ambivalent being the first to take the champ 15 rounds.

"In a crazy way, that fight is what defines me for a lot of my fellow Canadians but it took a long time before I came to appreciate how good it made me feel," he said.

Never knocked down

With wife Lynne and five children at home, Chuvalo appreciated the paydays the Ali performance begat. He would beat contenders Jerry Quarry and Manuel Ramos, losing close bouts to Oscar Bonavena and Jimmy Ellis.

Chuvalo was stopped for the first time in 1967 by Frazier, requiring a silicone implant to keep an eyeball from drooping. The loss to Foreman in the fourth round three years later was also notable, with the referee stepping in before Chuvalo's "never knocked down" streak might have been ended.

Chuvalo's loss to Ali in Vancouver in 1972 was not as compelling or as close as the first bout. He retired for good on a winning note six years later, finishing with a record of 73 wins, 18 losses and two draws, with 64 of his wins coming by knock out.

Unlike with Ali and others, the toll of concussive blows wasn't evident on the surface. Chuvalo was articulate and spoke in rapid-fire bursts, with a quip or self-deprecating joke usually at the ready.

But like many fighters, he had a tough time transitioning to the "humdrum" nature of life, as he once described it. At various points, he opened a nightclub, got his real estate licence, promoted fights, hosted a TV show and took cinema's worst ever arm-wrestling defeat in a cameo in David Cronenberg's The Fly.

WATCH | George Chuvalo's date with destiny and Muhammad Ali: George Chuvalo's date with destiny and Muhammad Ali | Duration 24:57 Chuvalo gets a shot at Ali's world title in Toronto in 1966.

Chuvalo told CBC Radio in 1968 he didn't want his four sons boxing for a living, but it was outside the ring where he couldn't protect them. The youngest, Jesse, became hooked on heroin after a prescription for pain medication ran out and was just 19 when he fatally shot himself in 1985.

Older brothers George Jr. and Steven had by then also become users of the drug and involved in petty crime to feed their habits. Steven Chuvalo described a feeling of "worthlessness" he and his two addicted brothers felt in an interview with CBC's the fifth estate in 1995.

"My dad spent quite a few years chasing us around the city, Georgie and I in particular, and dragging us out of drug houses and heroin houses and basically just trying to keep us alive," he said.

George Jr., three days sprung from jail in Kingston, Ont., overdosed on Halloween 1993.

Just four days after that, 49-year-old Lynne Chuvalo swallowed pills and left a suicide note.

"I never thought she'd do it, but I'm not surprised," Chuvalo told the New York Times a short time later, adding his wife never got over the first burial of a child.

Steven Chuvalo, who spoke on the fifth estate of wanting to make his father proud, would overdose and die eight months after that program aired.

Chuvalo would persevere, marrying again, and cherishing time spent with oldest son Mitch, daughter Vanessa, and his grandchildren. He would travel the country, speaking bluntly to students, as captured in a CBC Radio report in 1998.

"I'd like to think if you're ever tempted with the idea of doing drugs, or you ever flirt with doing drugs, I hope you think of me, George Chuvalo, and what drugs did to my family."

In 2017, reports surfaced of family drama involving Chuvalo's surviving children and the fighter's second wife, Joanne, who he was divorcing. Some of the disputes centred around the state of Chuvalo's cognitive decline and his future care.

On a podcast five years later, Mitch Chuvalo said his father no longer recognized him when he visited.

By that time, his legacy had been recognized by the City of Toronto, with the official opening in 2019 of the 7,000-square foot George Chuvalo Community Centre, located in the Junction.

World.title: With millions of dead oysters and mounting debt, P.E.I. farmers fear they'll lose everything
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LISTEN | Oyster farmer says P.E.I. industry is facing 'a massacre': The Current 21:29 Inside the PEI oyster crisis

When Kaila Richard is out on the water of her oyster farm in western P.E.I., she often thinks of her late father, who ran the farm until his sudden death in an accident in 2021.

“Being out here, I feel my father close,” said Kaila, who took over the farm in the Dock River, near Alberton, with her husband Bruce Richard.

“[When] we make mistakes, I can hear my dad saying, 'What are yous doing?!' … and when things go right I'm like, ‘Oh he'd be so proud,’” she told CBC Radio’s The Current .

The Richards took out hefty loans to upgrade the farm in recent years, installing expensive new equipment and spending long days tending their crop. But all that hard work is in jeopardy as two diseases rip through the Island’s oyster industry.

Farmers have pulled up millions of dead oysters, their shells piled high around P.E.I.

“The whole island is just a massacre at this point,” said Bruce.

“There's about a dozen farmers in this little section of river back here, and we're all in the same boat. Everybody's seeing upwards of 90 per cent, 95 per cent dead loss.”

WATCH | $100K of dead oysters dumped in a single day: P.E.I. grower throws out $100K of dead oysters in 1 day as disease devastation continues | Duration 3:03 Many oyster growers in western P.E.I. are reporting 100 per cent mortality in their cages as they pull them up after the winter. The Island has been hit hard by two oyster diseases, MSX and dermo, in recent years. CBC’s Nancy Russell has that story.

The diseases, multinucleate sphere unknown (MSX) and dermo, were detected in P.E.I. waters in 2024 and 2025, respectively. While harmless to humans, both parasites are fatal to oysters, with some growers reporting 100 per cent mortality rates .

The provincial and federal governments announced various support programs earlier this year, including financial relief, mental health support and approval for the import of disease-resistant oyster seed . Experts hope this seed could be cultivated to replenish oyster stocks on the island, but the process takes at least three years to grow from seed, with no guarantee of success.

Farmers say they need sustained financial support, and soon, to stay afloat in the interim.

“You can't hemorrhage money for three to five, [maybe] seven years … we don't have a million dollars sitting in the bank to make payments,” said Bruce, adding that at the time of his interview, his farm had not yet received any of the promised funding.

Jeff Noye, an oyster grower and the mayor of Tyne Valley in western P.E.I., said that oysters aren’t just a job on the island, but “a way of life.”

Mayor of Tyne Valley Jeff Noye said that oysters aren’t just a job on the island, but 'a way of life.' (Julie Crysler/CBC)

He worries if farmers don’t get more help, bigger corporations could come in and take over.

“Right now, the oyster industry is full of independent fishers. Men and women who work for themselves, by themselves … and we take a lot of pride in that,” said Noye, who is also the co-owner of Valley Pearl Oysters bar and restaurant in Tyne Valley.

But if those farmers can’t pay their bills, then “some of the companies with some big pockets can come in and snatch everything up,” he said.

“All of a sudden we're all working for them — and I hope that doesn't happen.”

Calls for income support

Mussel farmers in the Maritimes faced a similar issue when invasive species upended the industry 20 years ago , said Peter Warris, executive director of P.E.I. Aquaculture Alliance.

“Margins were pretty tight. We saw expenses were going up. We saw more and more growers selling out — and selling out to the big guys,” he said.

Farmers are finding that the vast majority of oysters they pull out of the water are already dead. (CBC)

In a lot of cases, he said, those same farmers were then hired by the big companies, who needed experienced workers, familiar with the waterways.

“They're going to get paid by a bigger company rather than paying themselves. Is that good? No,” he said. “But is it better than nothing? I suppose, I mean I guess that's up to the individual.”

Warris’s organization represents both smaller farmers and bigger organizations. He wants greater financial support over the next few years, arguing it would both help individual farmers stay in business — and help the industry bounce back as a whole.

In a statement emailed to The Current, Fisheries and Oceans Canada (DFO) said it is working “to support the long-term sustainability of the oyster sector,” including investments in scientific research to better understand and respond to the parasites.

DFO also pointed to a customer support program available through Farm Credit Canada (FCC).

When contacted by The Current, FCC said in an email that it will work with individual farmers to explore their options , including the potential “deferral of principal payments and/or other loan payment schedule amendments to reduce the financial pressure on those affected by oyster diseases.”

“The bottom line is we want to remain flexible and ensure producers have sufficient cash flow to get into the next production cycle,” the FCC statement said.

In a separate email statement, P.E.I.’s Department of Fisheries, Rural Development and Tourism pointed The Current to a handful of programs designed to provide “a financial safety net to eligible oyster growers.”

Peter Warris, executive director of P.E.I. Aquaculture Alliance, said 'there's no basic level of income support for growers right now.' (Jane Robertson/CBC)

Warris worries this patchwork of programs might not be enough.

“There's no basic level of income support for growers right now and … there's fuel costs, wage costs, all these other things,” he said.

“Whilst there are programs out there for some of it, there isn't anything that will just give some basic income to keep people moving for the next three years.”

Warris said that with so much uncertainty, some farmers might decide to sell to bigger operations. But financial support would mean they won’t “have to sell at fire-sale prices.”

Government is ‘giving up’

Fishers of wild oysters are also struggling with the diseases. They’ve been forced to travel further to find healthy oysters, increasing costs for an often reduced harvest.

In August, the federal government offered $40,000 to buy back 150 eligible fishing licences on a first-come, first-served basis . Recipients would not be able to reapply for an oyster fishing licence for 10 years.

It's going to be hard to keep people interested in the industry without better financial supports, said Bob Macleod, president of the P.E.I. Shellfish Association. (Julie Crysler/CBC)

Bob Macleod, president of the P.E.I. Shellfish Association (PEISA), said his organization advised the federal government to take a different approach. He thinks the buyback program should have been rolled out over three years and coupled with a wage subsidy. That would have given the worst affected fishers the option to leave, but it might have encouraged others to weather the storm a little longer, he said.

“You can't give up. You’ve got to keep trying different things. So when the government says we'll take 150 licences, they're giving up, and that is not right,” he said.

“It's going to be hard to keep enough people interested to make it bounce back.”

In its emailed statement, DFO said the buyback program aims to “help reduce pressure on vulnerable wild oyster stocks while supporting affected harvesters and coastal communities.”

DFO added that PEISA’s proposals contributed to the design of the buyback program, but the final initiative differs “due to the urgency of the situation and the government’s objective of balancing targeted support with broad accessibility.”

WATCH | Could disease-resistant seed offer a way out of the crisis?: P.E.I. oyster industry explores ways out of crisis including imported seed, new hatchery | Duration 2:31 P.E.I.'s oyster industry is looking for ways out of the current crisis brought on by two deadly diseases. One company has brought in disease-resistant seed from the U.S. Two others are building a new hatchery. They say there is no guarantee of success, but they have to do something. CBC's Nancy Russell reports.

‘A better day’

The devastation of their crop has taken a toll on Kaila and Bruce’s mental health, a sentiment echoed by many other oyster farmers and fishers on P.E.I.

“When we see each other out here, we all say, ‘Have a better day,’” Kaila said. “Because it's not ‘Have a good day,’ — just have a better day.”

For now, Bruce has taken work building lobster boats to make ends meet. He hopes the disease-resistant seed can get the industry back on track but says farmers need help “to get us between today and when those get to market.”

“It's hard to actually look at it and say, ‘Yeah, I'll still be working here in five years’ time,” he said. “Because we don't really know.”

Kaila has a tattoo of an anchor, an oyster, a line of her father’s handwriting and a compass “because he always guided me through my life.”

“It's more than just our business. It started out because of my father,” she said.

“I definitely have the fight in me, and we're gonna fight for it.”

World.title: 1 dead after Iranian commercial ship struck near Strait of Hormuz, Iranian media say
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

An Iranian commercial vessel was struck early Sunday off Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, with one person killed and four wounded, Iranian state media said, a day before Tehran seeks to brief regional countries on its contested efforts to manage shipping traffic there.

State-run IRNA news agency quoted the Qeshm governor as blaming a "terrorist enemy." He also said the person killed was among the cargo vessel's 10-member crew, and that authorities had not yet identified the projectile.

Separately, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations monitor reported a vessel was hit by a projectile while transiting the strait, with no details.

There was no immediate statement by the U.S. military, which previously has struck Iranian-flagged vessels as it keeps up a blockade of Iranian ports — while facing a new threat in recent days from Iranian ballistic missiles launched at its warships.

Qeshm Island, located about 22 kilometres from the port city of Bandar Abbas, is key to Iran asserting control over traffic through the strait.

Sunday's strike came as tensions continue around the waterway that was seen as an international one before the U.S. and Israel launched the war on Feb. 28.

WATCH | The U.S. threatens Iran with ‘economic D-Day’ : The U.S. threatens Iran with ‘economic D-Day’ | About That | Duration 3:31 The Trump administration declared 'economic D-Day' against Iran and warned global trade partners to cut all financial ties with Tehran or face severe economic consequences. Avneet Dhillon breaks down this latest push to isolate Iran's economy and why secondary sanctions threaten to put the U.S. on a collision course with China. (Photo credits: The Canadian Press, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty Images)

Global prices of oil, natural gas and related products have been sent higher, and now Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen are pressuring a key shipping alternative, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea. While the Houthis say they are targeting only neighbouring Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen's internationally recognized government, markets are wary.

Iran on Saturday said foreign ministers from regional countries will meet to discuss efforts by Iran and Oman, located on the other side of the Strait of Hormuz, to manage shipping on it.

Already, however, Bahrain has said it will not attend, and it was not clear what other nations would be there.

Iran has said reaching an agreement with Oman on the strait doesn't mean it will open for shipping. "The waterway would be opened up on the condition that the U.S. will terminate its blockade," Iran's president told broadcaster India Today TV on Saturday.

Commercial ship traffic remains low on the strait as attacks continue. Iran has expressed interest in having ships pay fees for transit. It has also said traffic into the Persian Gulf would pass through Iranian waters, while the outbound route would pass partly through Iranian waters and partly through Oman's.
