World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Exports and gas production hit record highs as patriotic spirit swells
World.content:
Listen to this article

Bilateral communications were front and center in Mexico the week of Sept. 7, with developments running the gamut from encouraging to combative. U.S. President Donald Trump’s remark that Mexico has “nothing” the United States needs beyond “hot tamales” and “tomatoes” caught fire over the weekend, unleashing a fresh round of provocations from Trump, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio in the days that followed.

Mexico, however, continued to highlight trade and security collaboration with its northern neighbor, though the PISA test results and next year’s midterm elections sparked more conversations at home. Meanwhile, the annual inflation rate ticked up to 3.26% — as expected according to Banxico, which forecasts inflation of 3.5% by the end of 2026. President Claudia Sheinbaum remained optimistic through it all, especially as her administration makes its plans for 2027. Overhead, punishing heat baked Mexico’s northern border states even as monsoon rains drenched the Pacific coast and center of the country.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

2027 budget takes shape

On Monday, Finance Minister Édgar Amador Zamora submitted a 10.6-trillion-peso (US $627.8 billion) budget proposal for 2027 to Congress, an increase of about 1% in real terms over this year. Amador framed the package around “five pillars” — economic growth, protecting government priorities, strengthening revenue, more efficient spending and fiscal discipline. The government is banking on those pillars to shrink the budget deficit to 3.9% of GDP next year from an estimated 4.1% in 2026, even as public debt climbs to 55% of GDP. No new taxes or fuel-price hikes are planned.

Health care gets a 10.9% real-terms boost to 1.1 trillion pesos, largely for IMSS-Bienestar infrastructure and medicine supply, while education rises about 7% to 1.3 trillion pesos to fund new schools. Pension and welfare programs get just over 1 trillion pesos, and debt servicing alone eats up 1.6 trillion pesos — roughly one of every seven pesos the government spends. Security agencies see an 11.6% bump to 331.4 billion pesos, while Pemex funding falls 69.2% as the state oil company pushes toward self-sufficiency.

The National Electoral Institute (INE) is the biggest percentage winner of all, with an 87.5% real-terms increase ahead of 2027 midterm elections, while the Energy Ministry, the National Human Rights Commission and the Federal Electricity Commission absorb the steepest cuts. Sheinbaum said the following day that she is “very satisfied” with the package and that growth could exceed the official forecast of 1.5-2.5%, citing anticipated stability in trade relations with the U.S. and Canada.

Homicides continue to fall

Security officials reported this week that daily homicides fell 53% in August compared to September 2024, the final month of the López Obrador administration, making it the least violent August since 2015.

More than 67,000 people have been arrested for high-impact crimes since Sheinbaum took office, though Security Minister Omar García Harfuch cautioned that “the job is not done.” Days later, from Tuxtla Gutiérrez, the president highlighted a 63% drop in Chiapas’s homicide rate since Gov. Eduardo Ramírez Aguilar took office, alongside nearly 10,000 arrests in the southern state. The same briefing revealed the discovery of a clandestine hospital the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) used to treat injured members.

Olmeca Refinery notches record month

Pemex’s Olmeca Refinery in Tabasco posted its best month yet for fuel production in July, averaging 252,498 barrels per day, a 78.8% jump over June. Gasoline output rose even more sharply, up nearly 128% month-over-month, after equipment fires forced repairs earlier in the year. Despite the milestone, the plant — which began operating approximately two years ago — is still running at roughly two-thirds of its 340,000-bpd capacity.

Fox and PRI’s Alito Moreno join forces

In a striking political reunion, former President Vicente Fox met with PRI leader Alejandro “Alito” Moreno to discuss “the need to build a strong opposition” ahead of 2027 midterms — 26 years after Fox became the first opposition candidate to sweep the once-dominant PRI out of the presidency, and years after he called the party “black vipers, vermin and tadpoles.”

Morena, for its part, dismissed the pairing as “the reorganization of the power elite,” saying in a statement that “they change the names, they invent new organizations, but behind the facade, it’s the same old faces.” The PRI, which ruled Mexico for 71 years, now holds just two of the country’s 32 governorships — the same number as the much smaller Citizens Movement (MC) party.

At her Monday press conference, Sheinbaum branded the reunion “PRIAN” politics dating to the “neoliberal” era of former President Carlos Salinas de Gortari, and called Fox a “traitor of democracy” — a jab tied to his role in Mexico’s disputed 2006 election.

Bilateral high points

Trade and security cooperation produced some of the week’s more encouraging bilateral news. Mexico’s exports to the U.S. hit a monthly record in July: US $60.55 billion worth of goods were sent north, pushing Mexico’s share of the $332.92 billion U.S. import market above 18%.

Along the border, Mexican and U.S. forces carried out “High Eagle,” a binational operation to detect and disable drones cartels use to surveil authorities near Tijuana and San Diego. And though bad weather grounded Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s flight to Mexico City on Wednesday, he and Sheinbaum still held a video call on USMCA negotiations that Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard described as “cordial” and “very useful,” with talks on steel, aluminum and automotive tariffs continuing ahead of a fourth bilateral review round.

Bilateral low points

Other exchanges were considerably more combative. Over the weekend, Trump proposed to rename New Mexico “New America,” despite having no legal authority to rename a U.S. state, drawing pushback from the state’s Democratic leaders. Later in the week, from Ecuador, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio doubled down on claims that cartels control “vast territories” of Mexico, hinting the threat may eventually have to be “confronted one way or the other.” Sheinbaum shot back on Thursday morning, telling Rubio to keep Mexico out of U.S. midterm politics and calling his remarks electorally motivated. Rounding out the week, U.S. Vice President JD Vance labeled the Mexican flag “a symbol of the far left” after a protester interrupted his convention speech in Dallas, telling the man to “get your ass over there” if he loved Mexico so much.

Poor PISA scores spark a debate over screens

New results from the OECD’s Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), given to 7,843 students across 297 Mexican schools, showed that four in 10 15-year-olds — 41.8% — scored below the basic level in science, math and reading, more than double the 19.7% OECD average and Mexico’s worst showing since 2009.

Mexican students averaged 388 points in math, 408 in reading and 414 in science, all well below OECD averages of 463, 461 and 482, and the country has shed seven points in both math and reading since the 2022 test. The decline wasn’t unique to Mexico — the OECD’s education director called it part of a “dramatic” global drop, particularly in reading — and Mexican students still reported unusually high curiosity (80%, versus a 24% global average who called school “a waste of time”). Education International, the global teachers’ federation, pinned the broader slide on shrinking attention spans, heavy AI use and a worldwide teacher shortage. China, Singapore, South Korea, Estonia and Canada topped the rankings.

Education Minister Mario Delgado blamed excessive screen use for the drop in reading comprehension — arguing that “screens make it easy to ‘read’ or consume images” — while defending the New Mexican School curriculum model and promoting traditional games like yo-yos, marbles and spinning tops as a substitute for phone time. He conceded the PISA sample was “statistically representative” even as he questioned whether the test amounts to a comprehensive evaluation of Mexican education. Sheinbaum later told reporters Mexico will roll out new math and reading textbooks next year, including poems and short stories, and push a “return to pencil and paper,” tying the effort to new national guidelines already restricting cellphone use in schools.

Education Ministry, UNESCO team up on AI in schools

Also this week, Mexico’s Education Ministry signed a letter of intent with UNESCO to guide the “responsible” rollout of artificial intelligence in classrooms, with the U.N. body offering technical assistance, teacher training and research support. Officials said the goal is to ensure AI supports, rather than substitutes for, teaching and critical thinking, and the deal also opens the door to new rules on cellphone use in schools.

Mexico prepares for El Grito and Independence Day

With the country’s 216th independence anniversary approaching, more than 18,000 members of Mexico’s armed forces are readying for the Sept. 16 military parade through Mexico City, featuring drones, horses, dogs and a float marking the country’s World Cup hosting duties this past June and July. The holiday kicks off the night before, with Sheinbaum leading the Grito de Independencia from the National Palace balcony and Tejano band Intocable headlining a concert in the Zócalo.

Festivities and gritos will ring out from cities across the country, including in Sinaloa, whose capital city of Culicán will hold a public celebration of Independence Day for the first time in two years.

Points of 🇲🇽 pride

A 20-year-old engineering student from a Chihuahua farming family, Luis Ángel Robles Morales, won a national innovation award for an irrigation filter that is already helping 500 drought-stricken farmers use water more efficiently.

Forward Julián Quiñones and Club América’s Scarlett Camberos earned historic Ballon d’Or nominations, marking the first time two Mexican players — and a Mexican club — have featured on the shortlist for world soccer’s top individual honor.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Witnessing the explosive sledgehammer ritual in San Juan de la Vega, Guanajuato
World.content:
A door in the street cracked open just enough for a hand to slip through. A kid, maybe 15, curled his fingers toward himself: come here, come here, then pulled back into the dark. I looked around the street. Nobody. I stepped inside.

The house looked like a drug kitchen. Two folding tables stretched across the room, their surfaces dusted white and yellow. On one side, a bucket of potassium chlorate. On the other, sulfur. Three kids stood around the tables, working the powders together with their bare hands. One kid looked up at me and grinned, then went back to scooping powder into small plastic bags.

Josué was the one who had waved me in from the doorway. One of the boys had no hands. Both arms ended at the wrists. I didn’t want to ask. I asked anyway. He told me it happened during the explosions, a few years back. He said it the way someone tells you about a stolen bicycle, part of life.

Don Juan David, Josué’s father, walked into the room. He greeted me with a handshake and a smile, glanced at the tables of explosive powder where their children worked, and walked back out.

A dangerous tradition

Every year, on Shrove Tuesday, the townspeople of San Juan de la Vega pack homemade explosives onto sledgehammers, carry them to the streets and open fields, and slam them against the ground. People lose limbs. This time, something was different. For the first time in the town’s history, authorities had banned the use of explosives during the carnival.

Families wanted to talk. Each family insisted theirs was the true story. The carnival, they all agreed, celebrates San Juan de la Vega, a saint who saved the town from gold robbers centuries ago. The explosives reenact the gunshots from his battles.

Every family also wanted to make sure we knew that the big explosions, the ones the town is famous for, are not the real tradition. The real tradition is small. Modest. A respectful crack of gunpowder in honor of the saint. Kids started making bigger and bigger explosives, destroying city piping. Everything breaks, they said, shaking their own heads. This is not what we are.

A man named Aquino de la Vega was moving silver shipments by mule along the Camino Real when bandits started robbing him. He prayed to San Juan Bautista. The robbers stopped. Aquino vowed he would honor the saint every year, forever, and so would his sons.

Six families still carry that vow. Each one is tied to a barrio. The families fund the music, the food, the processions. They keep the image of the saint in their home for a year.

Adrenaline and danger

The word I heard more than any other was adrenalina. The afternoon before the carnival, I found Josué sitting on a curb outside a corner store, rolling a cigarette. He was quiet.

“I’m always scared before I do it,” he told me. “But once I blow up one, I can’t stop. The adrenaline is too strong. I want to keep going.”

I asked about the dangers, and stories came easily: a man who burned, another who was paralyzed, people who lost fingers, hands, arms, legs. Accidents happen because the explosives are powerful enough to send 25-kilogram sledgehammers flying through the air. A hammer goes up, a hammer comes down, and sometimes there is a head in the way.

“Police always try to take them away,” one man said, sitting in a plastic chair outside his house, two kids playing in the dirt beside him. “But they will never stop the tradition. Nothing will change.”

On the afternoon before the main event, the streets were empty. Doors closed. No music. No voices.

Boom. The first hammer hit the ground as soon as night fell.

The sound moved through me. The ground shook under my feet. My ears whistled, even from 100 meters away. My chest vibrated. Windows cracked. The pipes beneath the street groaned and split.

Then came another. And another.

Parades took the streets. Villagers singing, dancing, playing instruments, carrying the image of San Juanito through the town. Following them in the back, kids dressed as soldiers, some in boots and gas masks, others with no gloves, no protection of any kind. Everyone carried sledgehammers and backpacks stuffed with explosives.

Defying the ban

I found Josué in the crowd. Face covered in soot, eyes wide. He swung a hammer down and the detonation threw him sideways. He got up laughing and loaded another charge.

Around midnight, the first police cars appeared.

The crowd froze. About 10 men climbed out with SWAT gear, assault rifles and bulletproof vests. They walked toward the kids with the backpacks. The boys scattered.

I saw a grandmother crack her front door open. She let the kids shove their backpacks full of explosives through the gap; she closed the door, and she stood in front of it. When the police asked to enter, she stood immobile like a statue until they were gone.

The police confiscated what they could, caught a few guys, and left. Within minutes, the parades reformed. The hammers came back out. The explosions picked up where they had stopped.

At around 3 a.m., we walked back toward town to catch some sleep. I did not sleep. The bed shook after every boom. Even with earplugs, my ears hurt. It went on until 7 a.m.

We walked outside. Over 10 police cars patrolled the town. They had shut everything down. But beyond the edge of town, we could hear it. Boom. Boom.

We followed the sound.

Moving to the tracks

The townspeople had moved to the train tracks. Flat, open land, sand, rocks and gravel, not a piece of shade anywhere. They placed explosives on the rails and waited for trains to roll over them. Between trains, they took turns blowing up hammers on steel bars laid flat against the ground.

There, away from the police, the hammers got bigger.

It was noon. The sun was directly overhead. People packed more and more powder onto the sledgehammers and took turns. Huge hammers flew tens of meters into the air.

I watched a kid swing a hammer down. The explosion threw him back onto the ground. The hammer launched upward, spinning, and came down on his head. The ring of steel on skull. He tried to stand. Blood ran from his scalp, down his face, into his eyes. His friend pulled off his own shirt, wrapped it tight around the kid’s head, and hauled him onto the back of a motorcycle. They disappeared down the road.

Nobody stopped. The next person stepped up.

The next morning, the market opened in the square as always. People walked slowly, said good morning to each other. A dog slept in a doorway. The church bell rang at 8.

Here was Josué, down the road. He waved.

I went to say goodbye to Don Juan David. He pulled me into a hug that lasted a long time. He held on. We had barely talked. When he finally let go, his eyes were wet. He thanked me. He begged me to come back next year.

“Sí, San Juanito permite,” he said. If San Juanito allows it.

Mattia Astori and Daniele Colucci make Sacratos, a documentary project on extreme rituals with photos, interviews, articles and videos. They’ve worked in Mexico, India, Bolivia, Thailand and Italy.

World.title: Turtle power: Volunteer to protect Mexico’s sea turtles
World.content:
Turtle camps can be found all over Mexico’s coastline, including the Gulf Coast, allowing volunteers to liberate baby turtles.

With the fifth-longest coastline in all of Mexico — a country that is internationally known and beloved for its beach offerings — Veracruz is certainly a sea-loving state, boasting some 450 miles of Gulf Coast access. For the record, Baja California Sur, a peninsula surrounded by water on three sides, has the longest total coastline at more than 1,350 miles of beach.

Historically, Veracruz is celebrated for its seafood and coastal tropics, as well as being the site of Mexico’s largest and oldest port with access to the Atlantic Ocean.

But what has been lost in the greater narrative is that, as part of its cultural significance along the Gulf Coast, Veracruz has also become one of Mexico’s leading states for turtle conservation.

The legacy of turtle conservationism in Mexico

The earliest federal efforts to focus on sea turtle nesting in Mexico began in 1962, led by the National Institute of Biological and Fisheries Research on both of Mexico’s ample coasts. In 1963, the Center for Turtle Culture opened on Isla Mujeres, Quintana Roo.

Shortly after, in 1966, Rancho Nuevo — located in Tamaulipas, just north of Veracruz — was among the first turtle conservation camps to formally open in Mexico. The National Commission of Protected Natural Areas outlined the importance of these efforts from the mid-1960s; the investments significantly helped to maintain the growth of Mexico’s turtle populations by increasing local awareness and participation. During that time, the National Sea Turtles Conservation Program was founded as a result.

Rancho Nuevo, along with the other turtle conservation camps that would spring up all over Mexico’s beaches — from the Gulf to the Pacific — has become a crucial element of turtle protection efforts since then, utilizing a mix of dedicated turtle conservationists and public volunteers. Responsibilities include the protection of nesting sites via monitoring and safeguarding turtle nests, and assisting (or “liberating”) fresh turtle hatchlings to ensure they make it to the sea.

Milestones in national protection rights

Since the 1960s, Mexico has become a global leader in turtle conservancy; in 2025, Mexico was recognized as an exemplar for its turtle protection efforts. Currently, Mexico federally operates 26 turtle conservation centers, in addition to various independent organizations and nonprofits extending across 13 coastal states. Officials announced a record of more than 34 million newborn olive ridley turtles that reached the ocean in a single season, in Oaxaca’s Morro Ayuta region alone.

In 1990, federally backed turtle protection rights gained further ground when then-President Carlos Salinas de Gortari decreed an end to the commercial harvesting of all sea turtles and related products. The landmark move shifted former turtle hunting communities — such as areas in Mazunte, which had among the highest rates of turtle slaughter — into epicenters of turtle conservation. Mazunte opened the Mexican Turtle Center in 1991, aiding the area’s turtle population and ecotourism alike.

Mexico’s role as a sanctuary for sea turtles

According to a 2008 report from the Secretariat of Environment and Natural Resources (Semarnat), “Mexico is the country with the largest number of sea-turtle species worldwide. Seven of the eight species known … nest in Mexican beaches, both in the Pacific and in the Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean littorals: loggerhead turtle, white or green turtle, black turtle, hawksbill turtle, Kemp’s ridley, olive ridley and leatherback turtle. Two of them, Kemp’s ridley and black sea turtle, nest exclusively in Mexican beaches.”

A more recent investigation from 2023, published in Revista Mexicana de Biodiversidad, revealed that southeastern Mexico, including Veracruz, is the most diverse region for turtle conservation in the country: “According to our results, southeastern Mexico supports three-fourths of the families — and more than half of the genera — found nationwide in Mexico. These findings highlight southeastern Mexico as a region of high importance for the composition of land and freshwater turtles at the national level … Oaxaca, Chiapas and Veracruz stand out as the states with the highest species richness and endemism, respectively. These three states are located within the region considered the richest in total herpetofauna, a result of complex orography, diverse habitats and environments, and the biogeographic history of Mexico.”

An afternoon with turtle conservationists in Veracruz

Jeanne A. Mortimer, a world-renowned marine biologist known as “Madame Torti” who specializes in sea turtle conservationism, once wrote that “The importance of the central coast of Veracruz (for turtle nesting) may be attributed to the fact that the beaches are easily accessible from the ocean without great obstacles like rocks, pronounced slopes or coastal developments that prevent the movement of the adult females along the length and breadth of the beaches.”

It partially explains why Veracruz has been able to cultivate a long-lasting ethos and engagement around turtle protection, with civic initiatives like Fundación Yépez and the Veracruzano Center for Research and Conservation of the Sea Turtle having launched decades ago. Additionally, Veracruz boasts Veracruz Reef System National Park, which played a role in a major environmental ruling by Mexico’s Supreme Court to conserve sea turtle habitats by restricting the construction of industrial ports in endangered areas (although reports that the ruling hasn’t been properly enforced have been published).

Vida Millenaria is among Veracruz’s most prominent turtle conservation groups. The project began in Tecolutla in 1974 as a personal mission for Fernando Manzano, whom locals began to call “Papá Tortuga,” or Turtle Father. Over half a century later, his efforts have expanded to include other members.

To date, the nonprofit has protected and released thousands of baby turtles each year. Visitors arrive year-round to receive public education and help to release newborn turtles into the water along the beaches on the city’s northern outskirts, about a 20-minute drive from the town’s center, along a mostly deserted dirt path.

Camping under the stars in Tecolutla

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Kate Levasseur (@katelevass)

I personally drove out to experience it for myself. Depending on your budget, you can rent a group-sized or personal tent near the beach at a campsite that includes outdoor showers, bathrooms and a common area for campers and volunteers who arrive at different hours of the day to participate in the turtle release. The camp area is shaded by palm trees and is relatively cool due to the strong coastal breeze.

The camping experience adds a layer of memory-making, as you sleep beneath the moonlight on a private, mostly isolated beach while the waves wash ashore in the near distance. A rotation of Vida Millenaria workers takes turns patrolling the area on ATVs around the clock, mostly to keep an eye on the turtles and their nests. (Note: If you decide to camp overnight, be sure to bring plenty of supplies, water and food, as a one-way trip back into town requires more than 20 minutes of off-roading to reach the edge of Tecolutla). There, you can enjoy a paradisiacal beach to yourself, undisturbed, until the next day.

A volunteer brigade assembles

Early in the morning, around 7:30 a.m., volunteers of all ages begin to arrive and assemble at the center of camp. A local expert introduces the nonprofit’s history, and a musician plays music dedicated to sea turtles. Maps and visuals are used to show and explain a brief history of turtle conservation in the state, and an adult-sized turtle replica stands in as a faux mascot for guests to take pictures with.

Afterwards, participants are escorted to the nearby souvenir shop, where everything is turtle-related (of course) and handmade. Each purchase grants a set of baby turtles for group liberation — so the more things you buy, the more turtles you’re able to liberate (prices start around 150 pesos and include turtle plushies, stuffed animals, mugs, shirts, etc.). For breakfast, a local volovanero (a savory pastry vendor common in Veracruz) brings a freshly baked batch for about 50 pesos each.

Releasing hatchlings into the wild

Then, the finale: Everyone strolls down to the beach together, lines up, and is given baby turtles to release into the ocean together. It’s a spectacular sight to see upwards of 50 small creatures — more or less, depending on the volunteer group’s size that day — crawling their way into the waves for the first time. They are swept away, their tiny heads occasionally poking out from the shimmering waters before completely disappearing into the distance by the dozens.

Of course, if you’re nowhere near Veracruz, you can search for your nearest beach. You’ll likely discover a turtle conservation group awaiting your participation. It makes a memorable weekend trip — and most importantly, it helps to keep an essential part of Mexico’s ecosystem intact.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: MND goes all in on Mexico City: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
Mexico City is having a long-overdue and well-deserved moment in the spotlight. People from all over the world of all ages are discovering the city and everything it has to offer. Entire neighborhoods are being influenced and transformed by the influx of new foreign residents and tourists. Some locals lament the changes, others celebrate them. We had one of our local CDMX writers reflect on it here.

As of late, I now hear from several people a week who have just visited the city for the first time and were blown away by how awesome it is. I can’t help but smile. When I first visited the city over 30 years ago, it was love at first sight — the history, the energy, the people, the contrasts. I would always tell people that it was one of my very favorite cities in the world and have gushed about it in articles and podcasts:

The team at Mexico News Daily is excited to announce that, starting this week, we will be further increasing our coverage of Mexico City. The idea behind this new weekly feature article is to provide the next level of news and information about the city. Perhaps most importantly, we are being very thoughtful in who we are writing for and what should be included. We hope to inspire first-timers to come check the city out, and those who have been there to come back again soon!

It is NOT written to help you understand what to do in the next 24 hours. It is NOT meant to replace local event calendars and local social media pages. It IS written to help you learn more about the city and better plan your time there. World.title: ‘Confidently Wrong About Tipping in Mexico’: A new podcast from MND
World.content:
Many people say religion, abortion and politics are topics one should avoid discussing in public. I think I would add tipping to that list! Tipping, both in Mexico and the U.S., was a pretty straightforward affair for years — that is, until the pandemic. What used to be a generally accepted 15% in the U.S. became … 18%? 21%? 24% or more? No purchase, no matter how minor, seemed free of a tip request.

Here in Mexico, tipping has also gotten more complicated for a number of reasons. Since the COVID pandemic, there has been increased awareness about the wages of service workers, and many people have raised their standard tip from 10% to 15%.

More foreigners spending more time in Mexico has also put upward pressure on tipping practices. This trend has not always been well-received by some locals who feel that they are being pressured to tip more or receiving lower quality service due to what their tip is perceived to be. Obviously, that creates an uncomfortable situation.

There is also the debate as to the rationale behind higher tips. Some people say, “If I have the money and I want to give it, who cares?” Others, meanwhile, seek to be cognizant of local norms, seeing that as a form of respect for the culture.

So who’s right? What is standard? And who else besides restaurant servers in Mexico are supposed to be tipped?

Check out our recent article here: Mexico and My Money: The tricky business of tipping in Mexico

And the latest episode of our Confidently Wrong podcast here:

Confidently wrong about tipping in Mexico: Episode 8 - Season 3

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: Angola’s Benguela Province Uses a 415-Company Trade Fair to Chase Foreign Investment
World.content:
Angola · INVESTMENT

Key Facts — What happened The 15th Feira Internacional de Benguela opened on 9 September 2026 at Estádio Nacional de Ombaka and runs until 13 September.

— How big Organisers say 415 companies are exhibiting across agriculture, industry, commerce, services, banking and fisheries.

— The theme The fair runs under the slogan the fair positions itself as fifteen years of turning opportunities into global business, linking central and southern Angola to outside markets through the Lobito Corridor.

— Who is pushing Benguela governor Manuel Nunes Júnior opened the event and called for more investment to turn the province’s potential into action.

— Why it matters The fair is part of Angola’s push to diversify away from oil and attract private capital into agriculture, fisheries, manufacturing and tourism.

The Benguela trade fair is being used as a direct pitch to national and foreign investors, with 415 companies gathered to convert the province’s economic potential into concrete business and partnerships.

Benguela opened its 15th international trade fair on 9 September 2026 with a clear message: the province wants investment, not just interest. The Feira Internacional de Benguela, known as FIB 2026, runs until 13 September at Estádio Nacional de Ombaka.

A platform built for deal-making

The provincial government is framing the Benguela trade fair as more than a showcase. It is meant to turn economic potential into signed partnerships and new business.

Organisers say the event brings together 415 companies from Angola and abroad. Exhibitors span agriculture, industry, commerce, services, banking and fisheries.

The fair’s theme, around fifteen years of connecting Angola to global markets, signals the ambition. It positions Benguela as a gateway linking central and southern Angola to global markets through the Corredor do Lobito.

The governor’s call for action

Benguela governor Manuel Nunes Júnior opened the fair and urged investors to move beyond potential. He said the province needs more capital to turn its advantages into real economic activity.

His appeal fits a wider national strategy. Angola is trying to reduce its dependence on oil by promoting private-sector investment in agriculture, fisheries, manufacturing and tourism.

For Benguela, the Lobito Corridor is central to that pitch. The port and rail logistics axis matters for regional trade and for mineral export routes that connect Angola to neighbouring markets.

Why the Lobito Corridor matters

The Lobito Corridor gives Benguela a strategic edge in the competition for foreign capital. It links the Atlantic port of Lobito to inland trade routes and mineral-rich areas.

That logistics backbone is valuable for moving goods and resources across borders. Investors looking at central and southern Africa often weigh transport costs before committing money.

The fair is therefore not only about local commerce. It is a signal that Benguela wants to be a hub for regional trade, not a stop along the way.

Competition for foreign capital

Angola is not alone in chasing investment. Other African markets are also courting the same pool of national and foreign companies.

State and business actors are backing tourism and infrastructure promotion to make Angola more attractive. The Benguela trade fair is one piece of that broader effort.

For investors, the question is whether the projects on display can deliver returns. The fair gives them a chance to meet local partners and assess opportunities directly.

What is on show

The 415 exhibitors cover a wide range of sectors. Agriculture and fisheries are prominent, reflecting Angola’s push to feed itself and export more.

Industry, commerce, services and banking round out the floor. The mix suggests organisers want to attract both productive investors and the financial intermediaries that support them.

Organisers have not published a verified deal total. The focus is on creating contacts that could lead to deals after the fair closes on 13 September.

The wider South-South angle

Benguela’s push fits a pattern of African regions using trade fairs to attract capital from emerging markets. The Lobito Corridor also connects to the broader competition for critical minerals and export routes covered in Africa: The New Scramble.

For Brazil and other Lusophone economies, Angola remains a familiar market with shared language and legal traditions. That cultural link can lower the cost of entry for companies exploring opportunities.

The fair’s international dimension suggests organisers are thinking beyond domestic demand. They want Benguela to be seen as a launchpad for regional and global business.

Frequently Asked Questions

When does the Benguela trade fair take place? FIB 2026 runs from 9 to 13 September 2026 at Estádio Nacional de Ombaka in Benguela, Angola. How many companies are exhibiting at FIB 2026? Organisers say 415 companies are exhibiting across agriculture, industry, commerce, services, banking and fisheries. What is the goal of the Benguela trade fair? The provincial government wants to convert Benguela’s economic potential into concrete business, partnerships and investment, especially through the Lobito Corridor.

World.title: Nigerian Payments Firm Will Handle Online Orders in a US$1.6 Billion Oil Refinery Share Sale
World.content:
Nigeria · EXPAT

Key Facts — What happened Flutterwave is one of 32 approved subscription channels for the Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals initial public offering, which opens on September 14 and closes on October 13, 2026.

— How big The offer covers 4.1 billion ordinary shares at 525 naira each, worth about 2.15 trillion naira, or roughly about 1.6 billion US dollars.

— The catch The minimum subscription is 10 shares, or 5,250 naira, and the process is designed for Nigerians at home and abroad, including users without an existing Flutterwave account.

— Why it matters The share sale is marketed as Africa’s biggest and sits inside Aliko Dangote’s push to finance a refinery expansion from about 700,000 barrels a day of tested throughput to 1.4 million barrels a day by 2029.

— What comes next Flutterwave’s own planned listing on the Nigerian Exchange Group remains tied to market conditions, after reports in April 2026 said President Bola Tinubu approved a 75 million US dollar state investment in the company.

Flutterwave is now an approved digital channel for the Dangote refinery IPO, letting retail and diaspora investors fund share subscriptions online through Chapel Hill Denham’s platform from September 14 to October 13, 2026.

Flutterwave offers Nigerian payments firm to handle online orders in Dangote refinery share sale

Flutterwave has been listed as one of 32 approved subscription channels for the Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals initial public offering, which is being marketed as Africa’s biggest share sale. The offer opens on September 14 and closes on October 13, 2026, covering 4.1 billion ordinary shares at 525 naira each.

How the Dangote refinery IPO works

The share sale is worth about 2.15 trillion naira, or roughly about 1.6 billion US dollars. Investors can subscribe through Chapel Hill Denham’s platform, where Flutterwave provides the payment infrastructure that lets retail and diaspora buyers fund their orders online.

The minimum subscription is 10 shares, or 5,250 naira. Reporting says the process is designed for Nigerians at home and abroad, including users without an existing Flutterwave account.

That low entry point matters for a country where retail participation in flagship assets has historically been limited. By opening the offer through digital rails, the structure aims to bring a broader base of individual investors into a national energy asset.

The money behind the refinery expansion

The offer sits inside Aliko Dangote’s push to finance a refinery expansion from about 700,000 barrels a day of tested throughput to 1.4 million barrels a day by 2029. The proposed capital expenditure plan is 14.3 billion US dollars.

That scale makes the refinery a strategic piece of Nigeria’s energy infrastructure. It reduces the country’s dependence on imported refined fuel and shifts bargaining power in a sector that matters to global energy markets.

For investors, the share sale is a direct way to gain exposure to that expansion. The offer is being positioned as a chance to own part of a flagship national asset while the refinery scales up.

Flutterwave’s own listing story

Flutterwave itself has been at the centre of a separate state-capital story. In April 2026, reports said President Bola Tinubu approved a 75 million US dollar state investment in Flutterwave ahead of a planned listing on the Nigerian Exchange Group.

Flutterwave later denied any formally executed government deal. The company said any initial public offering would depend on market conditions.

That context matters for investors watching the Dangote refinery IPO. It shows how African capital formation is increasingly tied to fintech infrastructure and state-backed strategic finance.

What this means for expats and diaspora investors

For Nigerians living abroad, the Flutterwave channel removes a common barrier to participating in domestic share sales. The digital process is built to work without an existing Flutterwave account, which simplifies onboarding for first-time investors.

The minimum of 10 shares keeps the entry point accessible. At 525 naira per share, a first subscription costs 5,250 naira before any platform or transaction fees.

That accessibility is part of Nigeria’s broader effort to deepen domestic capital markets. Wider retail participation in a flagship asset could set a template for future listings.

The great-power and regional read-through

Dangote’s refinery expansion has implications beyond Nigeria’s borders. A 1.4 million barrel-per-day facility would reshape fuel flows across West Africa and reduce the region’s reliance on imported refined products.

Flutterwave’s role in the share sale highlights how digital payment infrastructure is becoming central to African capital formation. The combination of a strategic energy asset and fintech rails reflects a wider pattern covered in Africa: The New Scramble.

For global investors, the offer is a test of appetite for large-scale African industrial assets. The outcome will signal how much capital can be mobilised through digital channels in a market where retail participation has often been thin.

What to watch next

The subscription window runs from September 14 to October 13, 2026. Investors who want exposure to the refinery expansion will need to act within that period.

After the offer closes, attention will turn to pricing and allocation. The share sale’s success or failure will shape how future Nigerian listings are structured and marketed.

Flutterwave’s own listing plans remain a separate story to follow. Any move by the company to list on the Nigerian Exchange Group would add another layer to Nigeria’s evolving capital markets.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I buy Dangote refinery shares through Flutterwave? Flutterwave provides the payment infrastructure on Chapel Hill Denham’s platform, so you can fund your share subscription online during the offer window from September 14 to October 13, 2026. What is the minimum investment in the Dangote refinery IPO? The minimum subscription is 10 shares at 525 naira each, which comes to 5,250 naira before any platform or transaction fees. Is the Dangote refinery IPO open to Nigerians living abroad? Yes, the process is designed for Nigerians at home and abroad, including users without an existing Flutterwave account.

World.title: What to Do in Rio in September 2026: Rock in Rio, the First Semana de Arte and Nine Free Things
World.content:
Rio de Janeiro · Culture

The last two nights of Rock in Rio, the first Semana de Arte do Rio, twenty-three free harp concerts, opera at the Municipal, and a long list of things you can walk into for nothing.

Rock in Rio closes at the Cidade do Rock in Barra da Tijuca on 12 and 13 September.

RIO DE JANEIRO — There is a great deal to do in Rio in September, and very little of it is written down anywhere in English. This guide is the first of a monthly selection for people who live here rather than visit: what is on, where, when, what it costs, and why it might be worth crossing the city for. Most of the entries below are free.

Two things shape the rest of Rio in September. Rock in Rio closes this weekend and moves a large part of the city west to Barra. Then, from the 16th, the first Semana de Arte do Rio pulls more than ten festivals under a single banner, with twenty-three free harp concerts running inside it. Plan accordingly.

Rock in Rio: the final night

Sunday 13 September · gates 2pm, music to 3am Rock in Rio 2026 Cidade do Rock, Parque Olímpico, Av. Embaixador Abelardo Bueno, Barra da Tijuca · Tickets through Ticketmaster only · 16+ The single biggest thing happening in Rio in September: 45 international acts, 15 of them playing nowhere else on the tour. Tonight, 12 September: Maroon 5. Sunday the 13th: twenty one pilots, and the festival closes.

Practical notes Getting in and out Cidade do Rock, Barra da Tijuca · — Gates open at 2pm. Last entry is at midnight, and the programme runs until 3am. Therefore, work out the journey home before you go: taxis at 3am in Barra are their own event. Under-16s need a legal guardian and under-fives are not admitted at all. Tickets are sold exclusively through Ticketmaster; anything offered anywhere else is not a ticket.

Running now

Photo: Clarissa Ribeiro

3 to 13 September, Thursday to Saturday 7pm, Sunday 6pm Vida de Cão — Uma Amizade Fora da Coleira Teatro Dulcina (Funarte), R. Alcindo Guanabara 17, Centro · From R$10 Pivo Maia and Claudio Amado play a man worn down by his own diary and the stray dog who interrupts it. Ten reais is the cheapest theatre ticket in Centro this month, and the Dulcina is two minutes from Cinelândia metro. In Portuguese, but it is a two-hander built on physical comedy rather than dialogue you have to catch every word of.

Also running now

Nicole Musafir’s Pra Quem Não Me Conhece opens at the Casa de Cultura Laura Alvim. (Photo: Elisa Maciel)

11 to 27 September, Fridays and Saturdays 8pm, Sundays 7pm A Pequena Prisão Teatro Laura Alvim, Casa de Cultura Laura Alvim, Av. Vieira Souto 176, Ipanema · R$30–60 · 60 minutes · 16+ Nine performances only, after more than forty at the Teatro Poeira. Vino Fragoso plays over thirty characters in the first stage adaptation of Igor Mendes’s book on the Brazilian prison system. In Portuguese, and physical enough to follow without it.

9 to 24 September, Wednesdays and Thursdays, 7pm Nicole Musafir — Pra Quem Não Me Conhece Casa de Cultura Laura Alvim, Ipanema · Price from the venue This is a short run of a one-woman show. Musafir built it out of the diaries she has kept since she was six. Blocked creatively for years, she went through the box and put what she found on stage; pianist Ceci Nery accompanies, with musical direction by Leo Valor. In Portuguese, and personal enough to reward the effort if you can follow it.

Photo: Divulgação

11 to 27 September, opening 11 September at 8pm 19º Niterói em Cena — International Theatre Festival Theatro Municipal de Niterói and venues across the city · Free Paulo Betti opens with his monologue Autobiografia Autorizada. What follows is free for seventeen days: companies from Angola, Georgia, Senegal, Mexico, Colombia, Paraguay and Peru, plus street theatre on the Praça João Saldanha. The street programme — clowning, acrobatics, the Peruvian Inka Clown Show — needs no language at all. Twenty minutes on the ferry from Praça Quinze.

16 to 27 September: the first Semana de Arte do Rio

16 to 27 September Semana de Arte do Rio — first edition Museums, cultural centres, theatres and galleries across the city · Varies; much of it free More than ten festivals come under one banner for the first time. In addition, there are exhibitions, street interventions and events in both public and private venues. Part of the Centro Cultural Justiça Federal programme falls inside it. If you have one week of Rio in September to give to the city’s art scene, make it this one.

16 to 19 September, 8pm; also Saturday 4pm Carmem — Cia. de Dança Thiago Soares Teatro Multiplan, VillageMall, Av. das Américas 3900, Barra da Tijuca · From R$110, through Sympla Thiago Soares went from hip-hop in São Gonçalo to Principal at the Royal Ballet, and now runs his own company here. His Bizet is pulled towards Latin America and mixes classical technique with urban and contemporary vocabulary. Sasha De Sola, principal at San Francisco Ballet, guests on the 17th and 19th at 8pm in her Brazilian debut. Dance, so the language question does not arise.

Wednesday 16 September, 12.30pm and 5pm RioHarpFestival opens — Walter Morato, and a harp-and-guitar duo Museu Nacional de Belas Artes, Av. Rio Branco 199, Centro; then Associação Comercial, Rua da Candelária 9 · Free The Argentine harpist Walter Morato opens the Latin American edition at the national fine-arts museum at 12.30pm. At 5pm the Paraguayan sisters Rosalía and Gabriela López play harp and guitar at the Commercial Association. Two free concerts in two buildings most visitors never get inside.

Thursday 17 September, 12.30pm XXI RioHarpFestival — Walter Morato at the Museu da Justiça Museu da Justiça, Rua Dom Manuel 29, Centro · Free The Argentine harpist plays the old jury room of the Tribunal do Júri, a courtroom turned museum that is rarely open for anything else. A hundred and twenty seats, and no ticket. Thursday 17 September, 6pm XXI RioHarpFestival — Luis Castro Centro Cultural Justiça Federal, Av. Rio Branco 241, Centro · Free The Venezuelan harpist plays the Latin American leg of the harp festival. Free, an hour long, and in the middle of the working city — the easiest good concert to walk into during Rio in September.

Friday 18 September, 12.30pm and 6pm Navy wind sextet, then the Camerata do Uerê at the Palácio Tiradentes Espaço Cultural da Marinha, Praça XV; then Palácio Tiradentes, Rua Primeiro de Março · Free The Marine Corps symphonic band sends a wind sextet to the naval cultural centre at midday, with the Brazilian harpist Giovana Sanches. In the evening the Camerata do Uerê, made up of young musicians from the Maré favela complex, plays the old chamber of deputies with the Chilean harpist Christian Rodrigues.

Saturday 19 and Sunday 20 September, 1pm and 3pm Harp weekend at the CCBB Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil, Rua Primeiro de Março 66, Centro · Free The National Symphonic Band plays the ground-floor rotunda on the Saturday and an orchestra of ukuleles takes it on the Sunday, each with a guest harpist. Upstairs at 3pm on both days, Nicolas Almada and Letícia Rodriguez sing Uruguayan candombe and milonga. Turn up and walk in.

Saturday 19 September Feira das Yabás at the CCBB Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil, Centro · Free entry; food paid A samba circle with Marquinhos de Oswaldo Cruz alongside the cooking that gives the fair its name — feijoada, angu à baiana, roast meat. The Feira das Yabás is normally a Madureira institution; catching it in Centro is the easy version.

Monday 21 to Friday 25 September, 12.30pm and 3pm Harp at lunchtime: five weekdays at the CCBB Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil, Rua Primeiro de Março 66, third-floor auditorium, Centro; and the Liceu Literário Português, Rua Almirante Barroso 118, on the 22nd · Free The quiet middle of the festival, and the easiest thing on this list to walk into on a working day. Nicolas Almada and Letícia Rodriguez sing Uruguayan candombe and milonga on the 21st, 23rd and 24th; Rafael Deboleto plays on the 21st and, at the Liceu, on the 22nd; Alessandro Aguiar pairs harp and Japanese koto with a French horn on the 23rd; the Paraguayan Júlio César Villaalta takes the 24th and 25th, and the Venezuelan Luis Castro the 25th. A hundred and six seats, sung in Spanish or not sung at all. Tuesday 22 September, 6pm Madrigal Cruz Lopes at Santa Cruz dos Militares Igreja Santa Cruz dos Militares, Rua Primeiro de Março, Centro · Free Choral music under José Machado in an eighteenth-century garrison church, with the Venezuelan harpist Jesús Suárez as guest. The building is worth the walk on its own.

24 to 27 September Mostra Violas Brasileiras: Da Raiz ao Contemporâneo Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil, Centro · Free Curated by Ivan Viela. The viola caipira is the instrument most foreigners never hear in Rio, because it belongs to the interior. Four days to correct that.

Saturday 26 and Sunday 27 September, 1pm and 3pm The RioHarpFestival closes at the CCBB Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil, Rua Primeiro de Março 66, ground-floor rotunda and third-floor auditorium, Centro · Free Harold Emert’s Camerata Viva Música takes the rotunda on the Saturday with the Venezuelan harpist Luis Castro. On the Sunday a bagpipe band closes the Latin American edition at 1pm — gaitas de foles under Maestro J. Paulo, which is not a sentence anyone expects to read about Rio — and Castro plays the last recital upstairs at 3pm with the Japanese musician Michinari Usuda.

Late September

Malize performs Baile da Saudade at the Teatro Firjan SESI Centro on the 23rd. (Photo: Thaís Monteiro)

Wednesday 23 September Malize — Baile da Saudade, live with band Teatro Firjan SESI Centro · Price from the venue The 27-year-old singer and producer from Rio’s Zona Norte performs the first single from his debut album. Alongside it, the venue screens the video that won backing from the Mosaico Rio 2026 fund. Both form part of the Mostra Firjan SESI. MPB as a foundation with everything else layered on top.

Saturday 26 September Seal — 30 years Qualistage, Barra da Tijuca · Price from the venue The thirtieth-anniversary tour. A large, comfortable room and a set of songs most people in it will know by heart.

Saturday 26 September, 6pm Tribute to Luiz Carlos de Moura Castro — Palácio São Clemente Portuguese Consulate, Rua São Clemente 424, Botafogo · Free Martin Almeida at the piano, with Jesús Suárez on harp, in a posthumous tribute to the pianist who was a long-standing partner of the series. The consulate residence opens for it, which is reason enough to go.

Tuesday 29 September, 6pm Recorders and voices at the Forte de Copacabana Museu do Exército, Forte de Copacabana, Praça Cel. Eugênio Franco 1, Posto 6 · Free The recorder ensemble Fino Som and the vocal group Vozes Encanto play international classics, directed by Nelma Pataro. The fort sits on the rocks at the end of Copacabana beach and the view alone carries the evening.

Wednesday 30 September, 12.30pm Mignone, 40 anos de saudade — the month closes at the CCBB Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil, Rua Primeiro de Março 66, 4th floor, Centro · Free Five pianists mark forty years since the death of Francisco Mignone, one of the central figures of Brazilian concert music, with video testimony from the composer between the pieces. A good last free hour of Rio in September.

Opera and orchestras in Rio in September

September Festival Oficina da Ópera Theatro Municipal, Cinelândia, Centro · Price from the box office The Municipal’s September strand brings Mascagni’s Cavalleria Rusticana and Donizetti’s Il Campanello. The building alone justifies the ticket; it was modelled on the Paris Opera and finished in 1909.

Through September 21st RioHarpFestival and Música no Museu Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil and partner venues · Mostly free Twenty-three harp concerts run from 16 to 27 September inside the Semana de Arte, all of them free — at the CCBB, tickets are handed out at the box office from 9am on the day. They sit alongside the Música no Museu series, which is in its twenty-ninth year and puts classical music into museums, palaces and churches at no charge. The September dates are listed individually above: the CCBB on the 9th and the 30th, the Museu Nacional de Belas Artes on the 16th, the Palácio Tiradentes on the 18th, the Palácio São Clemente on the 26th and the Forte de Copacabana on the 29th. One of the best-value things in the city and almost unknown to new arrivals.

Free all month in Rio in September

Until 12 October Vik Muniz — season extended Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil, Centro · Free Brazil’s most internationally recognised living visual artist, in the show that has been held over. If you see one exhibition this month, this is the one to see.

September Amazônicas — Poéticas Femininas Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil, Centro · Free Sissa Aneleh curates work by women from the North of Brazil. The reading is decolonial, and it foregrounds Afro-indigenous ancestry. Furthermore, the show uses virtual and augmented-reality elements.

September African Cinema showcase Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil cinemas, Centro · Free or low cost Ten features and six contemporary shorts. Given how little African cinema reaches Brazilian screens, this is the rare chance.

Until late September Coleção Ingá: Brasil Plural — final weeks Centro Cultural Justiça Federal, Centro · Free Around 200 works come from the Museu de História e Artes do Estado. Among them are Di Cavalcanti, Portinari, Goeldi and Mestre Guarany. The CCJF’s September programme also runs open-air cinema, short-film and Spanish-cinema seasons, choral concerts, flamenco, choro and indigenous music, literary workshops and two theatre productions — nearly all of it free.

Until 10 October, Tuesday to Saturday, midday to 7pm Inefável Presença — nine painters from one Tijuca studio Centro Cultural dos Correios, R. Visc. de Itaboraí 20, Centro · Free Nine artists have shared a studio in Tijuca for seven years. Ayla de Oliveira curates the show, and also exhibits in it. The group formed around a life-drawing class at the UFRJ fine arts school in 2017 and kept meeting on Monday evenings. Figurative painting, unfashionable for a while, now finding buyers.

Planning your Rio in September

Where we have not printed a ticket price, the organisers did not publish one — check with the venue before you travel. Programmes at the CCBB, the Theatro Municipal and the CCJF change during Rio in September, so confirm on the day.

This guide to Rio in September runs monthly, and returns in October. If you run a venue, a gallery or a production in Rio and would like to be considered, write to the newsroom with the date, the time, the address and the ticket price. Those four things are what get an event into the list.

More on living here: our Rio de Janeiro coverage and Expats in Brazil.

World.title: D1 Will Act as a Banking Correspondent for Grupo Aval
World.content:
COLOMBIA · BANKING

Key Facts — The arrangement Hard-discount chain D1 will act as a banking correspondent for Grupo Aval entities.

— What that means Customers can perform basic banking transactions at the till.

— Why it works D1 has store density in places where bank branches are not present.

— The regulator Banking correspondents are a supervised category under Colombian financial regulation.

— What this is not It is not a merger, an acquisition or a supermarket-sector combination.

Colombia has more discount-store tills than bank branches. Putting the bank behind the till is the cheaper way to close that gap.

D1 Will Act as a Banking Correspondent for Grupo Aval

The hard-discount chain D1 has agreed to operate as a banking correspondent for Grupo Aval entities, allowing customers to carry out basic financial transactions at store tills rather than at a bank branch.

What a Banking Correspondent Does

A corresponsal bancario is a non-bank business authorised to perform a defined set of transactions on a bank’s behalf: deposits, withdrawals, bill payments, balance enquiries and in some cases loan instalments.

The category is regulated by the Superintendencia Financiera and has existed in Colombia since 2006, originally to extend coverage into municipalities without branches.

The bank remains responsible for the transaction. The store provides the counter, the cash and the connectivity, and is paid a fee per operation.

Why D1 and Why Now

D1 is Colombia’s largest hard-discount chain by store count, with a footprint built deliberately in neighbourhoods and small towns rather than in shopping centres.

That footprint is the asset. Grupo Aval’s banks have branch networks concentrated in the cities, and the marginal cost of a new branch in a town of fifteen thousand people is not recoverable from the deposits it would gather.

A discount store already handles cash at volume, already has staff at a till and already has a payments connection. Adding banking transactions to that counter is close to free at the margin, which is why the model has spread across Latin America.

Aval holds Banco de Bogotá, Occidente, Popular and AV Villas.

What Aval Gets

Grupo Aval is Colombia’s largest financial conglomerate, holding Banco de Bogotá, Banco de Occidente, Banco Popular and Banco AV Villas.

What it gains is reach without capital expenditure, and a channel for the low-value, high-frequency transactions that are expensive to serve in a branch and unprofitable to refuse.

It also gains a defensive position. Colombian digital wallets have taken a growing share of exactly these transactions, and a physical cash-in, cash-out network is the part of the service a wallet cannot replicate on its own.

The Confusion Worth Clearing Up

This arrangement has been conflated in some coverage with a separate solar supply contract between the supermarket chain Olímpica and the energy company Promigas, producing reports of a supermarket-sector combination.

There is no such combination. D1 and Olímpica are different companies, the counterparties are different, and the two agreements are unrelated in substance.

The Rio Times reports each as what it is and does not state that any merger is under way, because none has been announced.

A correspondent network moves cash handling from branches to stores.

What to Watch

Transaction volumes are the only meaningful measure of whether this works, and neither party has published a target.

The second question is cash logistics. A correspondent network moves the burden of physical cash handling from bank branches to retail stores, and the cost and security implications of that fall on the retailer rather than on the bank.

Colombia’s correspondent networks are already large. Banks and their agents operate tens of thousands of points nationally, far more than the branch network, and the competition is for the retailers with the best locations rather than for the customers.

That makes exclusivity the term worth knowing. Neither party has said whether D1 will act for Aval alone or for other banks as well, and the answer determines how much of the discounter’s foot traffic Aval actually captures.

More: Colombia news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a banking correspondent?

A non-bank business authorised by the Superintendencia Financiera to perform defined banking transactions on a bank’s behalf.

What can customers do at a D1 till?

Basic transactions such as deposits, withdrawals, bill payments and balance enquiries, subject to the authorised scope.

Who is Grupo Aval?

Colombia’s largest financial conglomerate, holding Banco de Bogotá, Banco de Occidente, Banco Popular and Banco AV Villas.

Is this a merger?

No. It is a service arrangement. No ownership changes hands.

Is it connected to the Olímpica solar contract?

No. The two have been conflated in some coverage but involve different companies and different sectors.

Sources: Superintendencia Financiera de Colombia, La República, Portafolio, Valora Analítik, El Tiempo.

World.title: Olímpica Signs a Seven-Year Solar Deal With Promigas
World.content:
COLOMBIA · ENERGY

Key Facts — The contract Supermarket chain Olímpica has signed a solar supply agreement with Promigas.

— The scale One hundred and eighty stores.

— The term Seven years.

— The structure Promigas installs and operates; Olímpica buys the output.

— Why now Colombian commercial electricity tariffs have risen faster than inflation for three years.

— What this is not There is no merger or combination in the Colombian supermarket sector. Reports suggesting one are describing this contract.

A retailer buying its own electricity for seven years is a bet that grid tariffs keep rising. In Colombia that has been a safe bet.

Olímpica Signs a Seven-Year Solar Deal With Promigas

Olímpica, the Barranquilla-based supermarket and pharmacy chain, has contracted Promigas to supply solar power to 180 of its stores over seven years, under an arrangement in which the energy company installs and operates the generation.

What Was Signed

The agreement covers 180 Olímpica stores and runs for seven years. Promigas, the Barranquilla gas transporter and distributor, takes responsibility for installing and operating the generating capacity.

The structure is a power-purchase arrangement rather than a capital investment by the retailer. Olímpica commits to buy output at a contracted price; it does not put the panels on its own balance sheet.

That distinction is the reason deals of this shape have spread through Colombian commercial property. A retailer with thin margins can fix an input cost without spending capital it would rather deploy in stores.

Refrigeration is the largest operating cost after labour.

Why a Supermarket Buys Power

Refrigeration is the largest single line in a supermarket’s operating cost after labour, and it runs continuously. A chain of 180 stores on the Caribbean coast is cooling against ambient temperatures above thirty degrees for most of the year.

Colombian commercial electricity tariffs have risen faster than general inflation since 2023, driven by transmission charges and by the pass-through of hydrological risk in a system that depends heavily on reservoirs.

Fixing seven years of that cost is worth more to a retailer than the headline saving suggests, because it removes a variable that has been the principal source of margin surprise.

Why Promigas Is the Counterparty

Promigas built its business on natural-gas transport and distribution on the Caribbean coast, and has been diversifying into non-regulated energy services as gas volumes from the Guajira fields decline.

Distributed solar is the natural adjacency. The customer relationships already exist, and the commercial and industrial segment is where Colombian solar economics work best because self-consumption avoids the transmission charges that make grid power expensive.

The Story This Is Not

Some coverage this week has been read as describing a combination in the Colombian supermarket sector involving Olímpica and Grupo Aval. No such transaction exists.

What exists is this solar contract, and separately a banking-correspondent arrangement between the hard-discount chain D1 and Aval entities. They involve different companies and different sectors, and merging them produces a story that is not there.

The Rio Times states the contract as signed and does not report a supermarket-sector combination, because none has been announced.

Colombian commercial solar has grown on tariff pressure rather than subsidy.

What It Signals

Colombian commercial and industrial solar has grown on the back of tariff pressure rather than on subsidy, which makes it more durable than a policy-driven build-out would be.

If a 180-store, seven-year contract prices well for both sides, the template will be applied across the rest of Colombian organised retail within a year, because every chain faces the same refrigeration load and the same tariff curve.

The financial terms have not been disclosed, and The Rio Times does not state a contract value.

The regulatory backdrop favours it. Colombia’s Law 1715 of 2014 gives tax relief on non-conventional renewable energy investment, and the self-generation rules allow surplus output to be fed back to the grid within defined limits.

The constraint is grid connection rather than economics. Interconnection queues on the Caribbean coast have lengthened as distributed generation has grown, and a seven-year contract assumes the stores can be connected on the schedule the parties have agreed.

More: Colombia news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Olímpica sign?

A seven-year solar supply agreement with Promigas covering 180 stores.

Who owns the equipment?

Promigas installs and operates the generation. Olímpica buys the output.

Why is a supermarket doing this?

Refrigeration is a continuous load and Colombian commercial tariffs have risen faster than inflation since 2023.

Is there a supermarket merger involved?

No. No combination in the Colombian supermarket sector has been announced.

Has a contract value been published?

No. The Rio Times has not seen one and does not state a figure.

Sources: Promigas, La República, Portafolio, El Heraldo, Valora Analítik.

World.title: Cartagena’s Mayor Answers Petro With Arrival Data
World.content:
COLOMBIA · TOURISM

Key Facts — The dispute Cartagena’s mayor has rejected President Petro’s account of the city’s tourism performance.

— The mayor Dumek Turbay.

— His figures More than 4 million visitors through September, air arrivals up 3.8 percent, road arrivals up 25.1 percent.

— His line “Dato mata relato” — data kills narrative.

— Why it matters Cartagena is Colombia’s single largest tourism destination and the argument is about whether the sector is in crisis.

A mayor answering a president with arrival statistics is a familiar Colombian genre. The statistics, in this case, are checkable.

Cartagena’s Mayor Answers Petro With Arrival Data

Cartagena mayor Dumek Turbay has rejected President Gustavo Petro’s characterisation of the city’s tourism performance, citing more than four million visitors through September and double-digit growth in road arrivals.

The Exchange

Petro described Cartagena’s tourism sector in terms the city’s administration disputes. Turbay answered with arrival figures rather than with rhetoric, and closed with the phrase “dato mata relato”.

The formulation translates as data kills narrative, and it has become a standard rejoinder in Colombian political argument when one side believes the other is describing a situation rather than measuring it.

The Numbers He Cited

Turbay put visitors through September at more than four million. He gave air arrivals as up 3.8 percent and road arrivals as up 25.1 percent against the same period a year earlier.

The road figure is the more interesting of the two. Growth of 25.1 percent by land indicates domestic Colombian tourism rather than international arrivals, and it is the segment that responds fastest to exchange rates and to fuel prices.

The air figure of 3.8 percent is modest by comparison and is the number a critic would reach for, since international visitors spend more per head than domestic ones.

The walled city and Bocagrande carry the international tourism.

What Cartagena Actually Depends On

The walled city and Bocagrande carry the international tourism, and the cruise terminal adds a volume of day visitors that inflates headcount without proportionate spending.

Behind that, Cartagena is a port and an industrial city with a refinery, and tourism is the most visible part of its economy rather than the largest. That distinction is usually lost in arguments of this kind.

The city also has some of the sharpest inequality in Colombia, and the tourism boom of the past decade has not reached the neighbourhoods outside the historic centre in any measurable way.

Why the President and the Mayor Are Arguing

Turbay is not a Petrista, and Cartagena has been a point of friction between the national government and a Caribbean-coast administration for most of the term.

Colombia is also in the first year of a new presidency following Abelardo De la Espriella’s election, which makes any statement by Petro about the state of the country a statement about the record he left rather than about current policy.

The arrival data is therefore doing double duty: it is a defence of the city’s management and an argument about who should be credited with the numbers.

Cartagena is a port and industrial city before it is a resort.

What Can Be Checked

Arrival statistics for Colombian cities are published by Migración Colombia for international entries and by the aviation authority for domestic air traffic, which makes the air figure verifiable and the road figure considerably harder to audit.

The Rio Times reports the mayor’s figures as his, notes which of them can be independently confirmed, and does not present the four-million total as an established count.

Hotel occupancy is the third series that would settle the argument, and it is the one neither side quoted. Cotelco, the hotel association, publishes it monthly, and it captures paying visitors in a way that arrival counts do not.

The gap between visitor numbers and visitor spending is where most tourism disputes in Colombia end up. A city can add arrivals and lose revenue in the same year if the mix shifts from hotel guests to cruise passengers and day-trippers from Barranquilla.

More: Colombia news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is disputing what?

Cartagena mayor Dumek Turbay rejected President Petro’s account of the city’s tourism performance.

What figures did the mayor give?

More than 4 million visitors through September, air arrivals up 3.8% and road arrivals up 25.1%.

What does “dato mata relato” mean?

Data kills narrative. It is a standard Colombian rejoinder to an opponent describing rather than measuring.

Are the figures verifiable?

The air figure can be checked against aviation-authority data. The road figure is harder to audit independently.

Why does it matter?

Cartagena is Colombia’s largest tourism destination, and the argument is about whether the sector is in difficulty.

Sources: El Tiempo, El Universal, Semana, Infobae, Alcaldía de Cartagena.

World.title: Trump Rules Out Leaving the USMCA
World.content:
MEXICO · TRADE

Key Facts — The statement President Trump ruled out withdrawing from the USMCA on 12 September 2026.

— Why it was asked The agreement faces its scheduled joint review in 2026.

— The mechanism USMCA has a sixteen-year term with a six-year review that can extend it.

— What it does not settle Ruling out withdrawal is not the same as agreeing to extend.

— The stakes Mexico sends roughly 80 percent of its exports to the United States.

Ruling out an exit removes the worst case. It does not tell Mexico or Canada what the review will actually produce.

Trump Rules Out Leaving the USMCA

President Donald Trump said on 12 September that the United States would not withdraw from the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, as the pact approaches the joint review built into its terms.

What Was Said

Trump ruled out a US withdrawal from the USMCA. The statement addresses the most severe outcome available under the agreement rather than the question of what the review will decide.

The distinction matters because withdrawal and non-extension are different mechanisms with different timetables, and only one of them was addressed.

How the Agreement Is Built

The USMCA entered force on 1 July 2020 with a sixteen-year term. A joint review falls six years in, at which point the three parties can agree to extend the term by a further sixteen years.

If they do not agree, the agreement does not end. It continues to its original expiry, with annual reviews in the interval, which is a slow unwinding rather than a cliff.

Separately, any party may withdraw on six months’ notice. That is the provision Trump was asked about and the one he ruled out using.

Roughly 80% of Mexican exports go to the United States.

Why Mexico Was Listening

Roughly 80 percent of Mexican exports go to the United States, and the share has risen rather than fallen as nearshoring moved supply chains out of Asia.

Mexican industrial investment decisions run on horizons longer than the review cycle. A plant commissioned in 2027 is being financed now, and the financing prices the risk that the trade framework changes.

President Claudia Sheinbaum’s government has spent 2026 managing tariff actions taken outside the agreement, on steel, aluminium and vehicles, which has made the question of the framework itself more pressing rather than less.

Rules of origin and dispute settlement are the substantive items a review would reopen.

What Is Still Open

Rules of origin for vehicles, the labour-value content requirement and the dispute-settlement panels are the substantive items a review would reopen. None was addressed.

Tariffs imposed under separate national-security authorities are not governed by the USMCA and would survive any outcome of the review. Mexico’s exposure to those is unchanged by this statement.

Canada’s position is the third variable and has been the more difficult one through 2026, particularly on dairy and on softwood lumber.

Digital trade and the treatment of state-owned enterprises are the two chapters that were written for a 2018 economy and that both Washington and Mexico City have reason to revisit, for opposite motives.

The review is a joint process, which means no single party controls its outcome. That structural point is what makes a unilateral statement about withdrawal informative but not decisive.

How to Read It

The value of the statement is that it narrows the range of outcomes rather than that it settles one. Markets price tail risk, and removing the withdrawal tail is worth something to the peso and to Mexican corporate credit.

What it does not do is give an investor a view on the rules of origin that will apply in 2030, which is the number an automotive supply chain actually needs.

The peso and Mexican sovereign spreads are the cleanest live reading of how much that narrowing is worth. Both have been more sensitive through 2026 to tariff announcements made outside the agreement than to the agreement’s own timetable.

For Canada the calculation runs the other way. Ottawa has less to lose from a slow unwinding than Mexico does, because a larger share of its trade sits in sectors where the most-favoured-nation tariff is already low.

More: Mexico news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Trump say?

That the United States will not withdraw from the USMCA.

When?

12 September 2026.

Does that extend the agreement?

No. Withdrawal and extension are separate questions. The joint review decides the second.

What happens if the review does not extend it?

The agreement continues to its 2036 expiry with annual reviews, rather than terminating.

Does this affect existing tariffs?

No. Tariffs imposed under separate national-security authorities sit outside the agreement.

Sources: Reuters, El Financiero, El Economista, Milenio, Office of the US Trade Representative.

World.title: Pope Leo XIV Will Visit Peru From 11 to 16 November
World.content:
PERU · RELIGION

Key Facts — The visit Pope Leo XIV will visit Peru from 11 to 16 November 2026.

— The cities Lima, Chiclayo, Cusco and Pucallpa.

— The estimate Tourism Minister Rogers Valencia expects 3.1 million people to take part.

— Why Chiclayo Leo XIV served as bishop of Chiclayo before his election.

— The scale It is the largest logistical undertaking the Peruvian state will manage this year.

A pope who spent two decades in Peru is returning to the diocese he ran. The tourism arithmetic is secondary to that, but it is not small.

Pope Leo XIV Will Visit Peru From 11 to 16 November
