World.title: Inside the Karpacz Economic Forum 2026: Poland’s rise, political divides and the future of the V4
World.content:
Three days, more than 6,500 participants, hundreds of panel discussions, politicians, businesspeople, local government leaders and experts – the Karpacz Economic Forum 2026 was an impressive event by its sheer scale alone. Yet what was even more interesting on the ground was seeing how the economic and political figures of one of Europe’s most dynamically developing countries view their own situation. And also how differently the very same economic figures can be interpreted.

All this took place not in Warsaw, Kraków or another major Polish city, but in Karpacz, a mountain resort near the Czech border.

A small town that becomes one of Poland’s centres for three days

At first glance, the choice of venue may seem surprising. Karpacz is hardly a conventional conference city, yet the Hotel Gołębiewski and the surrounding infrastructure have enough capacity to host an event attended by several thousand people without major disruption.

According to the official summary by Forum Ekonomiczne, more than 6,500 participants attended the 35th Economic Forum, held between 8 and 10 September, with more than 500 debates, panels and other events taking place. The programme covered eight major thematic areas, ranging from the economy and international politics to digitalisation, artificial intelligence and healthcare.

The true scale of the event could best be appreciated on site. Conference rooms were spread across several floors of the hotel and in pavilions erected in front of the building, while gala events and banquets were held on a separate floor. According to the organisers’ official information, even the logistics centre itself was located 3.5 kilometres from the main conference venue.

According to an on-site report by wroclaw.pl, around 500 media representatives, 1,200 local government officials and 900 foreign delegates arrived in Karpacz. Although a significant part of the programme was held in Polish and focused primarily on Polish issues, interpretation was available for the more important panels, making much of the conference accessible to international participants as well.

Karpacz Economic Forum 2026. Photo by Daily News Hungary

Karpacz Economic Forum 2026: a strong economy facing serious dilemmas

One of the most interesting lessons of the three days for me was just how differently the same economic data can be interpreted.

Poland is recording particularly strong growth by European standards. The European Commission’s May forecast projected GDP growth of 3.5 percent for 2026, while unemployment remains exceptionally low. At the same time, the picture is far from problem-free: the Commission expected a budget deficit of 6.5 percent and a further increase in public debt.

The OECD’s June forecast was somewhat more cautious, projecting growth of 3 percent in 2026 and specifically highlighting risks related to energy prices, global demand and the geopolitical situation in the region.

In Karpacz, therefore, the same economic performance was presented in one discussion as proof of a successful convergence model, and in another as the starting point for examining the challenges facing a country entering a new stage of development.

Perhaps this was precisely what made the forum so interesting: within just a few conference rooms of one another, it was possible to hear entirely different conclusions drawn from the same economic reality.

Karpacz Economic Forum 2026. Photo by Daily News Hungary Karpacz Economic Forum 2026. Photo by Daily News Hungary

Both government and opposition figures turned out in Karpacz

Numerous prominent figures from Polish political life also attended the forum. The organisers highlighted the participation of, among others, Defence Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, Deputy Prime Minister and Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski, Development Minister Katarzyna Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, Science Minister Marcin Kulasek, Deputy Speaker of the Sejm Krzysztof Bosak and former Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki, while numerous state secretaries were also present.

The presence of right-wing and opposition politicians was particularly conspicuous. Morawiecki received a standing ovation, while Krzysztof Bosak’s appearance also prompted a strong reaction from the audience. According to the report, former Prime Minister Beata Szydło and former Defence Minister Mariusz Błaszczak also spoke at the event. Andrzej Duda, Poland’s president between 2015 and 2025, likewise appeared at several events.

The gala dinners were among the forum’s most spectacular occasions. This was where awards recognising outstanding achievements in the economy, business and public life were presented. Perhaps the most important of these, the 2026 Person of the Year award, went to Infrastructure Minister Dariusz Klimczak.

In case you missed it – Looking beyond price per square metre: how the new-build housing markets of Budapest, Warsaw and Bucharest differ

Morawiecki: the V4 must continue even when countries are led by different political camps

Mateusz Morawiecki’s appearance was particularly interesting to me because I also had the opportunity to put a question directly to the former Polish prime minister at the forum.

Karpacz Economic Forum 2026. Photo by Daily News Hungary

I asked whether, if he were to return to government following Poland’s 2027 election, he would continue Visegrád Group cooperation even if Hungary’s prime minister were Péter Magyar rather than Viktor Orbán.

Morawiecki gave an unequivocal yes.

According to the former Polish prime minister, the V4 must be maintained at all costs, and it must not be allowed to fall apart or lose its significance again simply because the countries concerned are governed by political forces with differing views.

The essence of his answer was that regional cooperation must survive party-political differences. Poland, Hungary, Czechia and Slovakia share numerous economic, infrastructural and geopolitical interests that remain regardless of which political camp happens to be in power.

The message is particularly noteworthy because the V4 has been on hold in recent years precisely because of foreign-policy and political differences among its member states.

Polish–Hungarian rail links: Budapest to Warsaw took ten hours 20 years ago – and still does today

A much more critical assessment of the state of Polish–Hungarian relations was heard during another panel.

Balázs Szabó, president of the Polish Nationality Self-Government of Dunakeszi and the Association of Modern Polish Thought, said that in his view the previous Hungarian government had not done enough over its 16 years in office to develop Polish–Hungarian relations in practical terms, with transport providing one of the clearest examples.

Karpacz Economic Forum 2026. Photo by Daily News Hungary

Szabó pointed out that around 20 years ago it took roughly ten hours to travel by train from Budapest to Warsaw, and that journey times have not decreased substantially since then.

He considered this particularly problematic given that Hungary undertook a major international railway investment in another direction: the Budapest–Belgrade railway line was upgraded, while no project of comparable scale was launched towards Poland.

According to Szabó, a modern Budapest–Warsaw connection would go far beyond tourism.

A north–south railway connection could also be of strategic importance for logistics, freight transport and closer links between the countries of the region. While new north–south logistics corridors and high-speed rail connections are being developed across Europe, Hungary is not yet a major player in these networks.

Szabó said, however, that some change may already be perceptible. He noted that Dávid Vitézy, transport and investment minister in Hungary’s new government, has already spoken about developing rail connections towards Poland. This does not yet amount to a concrete investment project, but he believes it is an important indication that the issue could once again make its way onto Hungary’s transport policy agenda.

Vitézy is indeed preparing a large-scale railway development programme: according to a 11 September report by 24.hu, the minister spoke about a comprehensive HUF 3.5 trillion – approximately EUR 9.6 billion – rail and transport development framework.

More than fifty Hungarians attended the forum

The composition of the participants was also interesting from a Hungarian perspective. More than fifty people from Hungary registered for the event, several of whom also spoke in panel discussions.

In previous years, the Hungarian delegation regularly included ministers from the Orbán government as well as political and public figures close to the former governing party. This year, several Fidesz politicians or participants linked to the previous period of government could again be seen at the event, while high-level representation from the new government led by Péter Magyar was much less noticeable.

Among those present was former Speaker of the Hungarian National Assembly László Kövér, who had originally been scheduled for two events but ultimately took part in one panel discussion. Péter Márki-Zay, mayor of Hódmezővásárhely, also travelled to Karpacz and attended several events. Their encounter even made it into the Hungarian press: 24.hu reported that, according to Márki-Zay, László Kövér declined to shake his outstretched hand.

The composition of the Hungarian participants was also interesting in light of the fundamental change in Hungary’s political situation a few months earlier. The personal and institutional network built up over recent years was still clearly visible at the forum, while relations between Hungary’s new government and the Karpacz Economic Forum are evidently still at the beginning of a new era.

I was invited to one of Central Europe’s largest economic forums, as the owner of DNH MEDIA GROUP Ltd., by the Warsaw Enterprise Institute Foundation to attend both the event and the press trip that followed.

Karpacz Economic Forum: much more than just an economic conference

By the end of the Karpacz Economic Forum 2026, this was perhaps my strongest impression: although it is called an economic forum, for three days it effectively becomes a Central European meeting place where economics, politics, geopolitics, infrastructure, technology and business are almost inseparable.

Karpacz Economic Forum 2026. Photo by Daily News Hungary

Conversations in the corridors and over dinner were at least as important as those taking place on stage. And across the hundreds of panels, it was sometimes possible to hear completely different answers to the same question depending on whether one was listening to a minister, an opposition politician, a businessperson or an economist.

By many indicators, Poland has every reason to look to the coming years with optimism. At the same time, Karpacz also showed that rapid economic growth does not in itself eliminate dilemmas. On the contrary: the greater the country’s economic and political weight becomes, the more important the question of how it chooses to use that strength.

From a Hungarian perspective, one of the most important lessons may have been something that emerged in two very different discussions: Polish–Hungarian relations cannot be built solely on the political friendship of whichever parties happen to be in government. Whether the issue is the V4 or a modern railway connecting Budapest and Warsaw, long-term cooperation requires relationships and infrastructure capable of surviving changes of government.

As we wrote after the election, Polish–Hungarian friendship could gain new momentum. Magyar and Tusk discussed exactly this in Warsaw.

World.title: Former PM Orbán reveals why he nominated man for high state honour later convicted for sexual abuse of many children
World.content:
Former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán has revealed why he nominated the paedophile director of the children’s home in Bicske for a high state honour.

Péter Magyar, Hungary’s prime minister, today published a document proving that the director was nominated for the award in a submission bearing Orbán’s signature. Proceedings had already been brought against him in 2011, yet the nomination went ahead on the recommendation of Zoltán Balog, then minister for human resources.

Orbán brushes off question

Asked today in Kötcse why he had nominated the director of the Bicske children’s home in 2016 – he has since been convicted of paedophile offences – Orbán replied that someone had put his name forward and that the press should ask the person responsible.

Péter Magyar speaking in the Hungarian Parliament. Photo: Facebook/Orbán Anita

Magyar had earlier published the nomination document, which bears the name of Orbán, who was prime minister at the time, as the signatory. It said the director deserved the honour for his work educating disadvantaged children and preparing them for independent lives.

If you missed – Sexual abuse, starvation, squalor and accident hazards: Orbán’s government concealed the reality of Hungary’s children’s homes

The scandal surrounding János Vásárhelyi erupted in 2016, after a former resident of the Bicske children’s home took his own life, having grown tired of nobody believing him. Vásárhelyi was convicted in 2019, but the first official complaint and police investigation against him dated back to 2011, after two employees of the home reported that several children had accused him of sexually abusing them. Police closed the investigation in 2012, citing a lack of evidence.

Nomination came from Zoltán Balog

“It was the same Zoltán Balog who recommended the paedophile director of the Bicske children’s home for a state honour to Viktor Orbán, and who later secured a presidential pardon from Katalin Novák for Endre Kónya, an accomplice in the paedophile abuse,” Magyar wrote on Facebook on Saturday.

Paedophile Hungarian director to be released from prison: one abuse victim died by suicide

World.title: Kosovo Ex-President Thaci’s Defence Seeks Acquittal in Obstruction of Justice Trial
World.content:
The defence teams of former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci and four others co-accused of obstruction of justice in Thaci’s war crimes trial at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague have called for their acquittal, accusing the prosecution of charging them based on conversations that did not result in any witness-tampering or intimidation.

The prosecution claims that that during visits at the Detention Centre in The Hague, where Thaci is being held, he told the other four defendants – Hajredin Kuci, Fadil Fazliu, Isni Kilaj and Bashkim Smakaj – to instruct certain witnesses in his war-crimes trial about what to say in court.

But Sophie Menegon, Thaci’s lawyer, told the court during closing statements on Thursday that Thaci was “on trial for having a conversation in the Detention Unit [where he is being held pending the verdict in his war crimes trial]. There is no allegation of a bribe, compulsion, or threat against witnesses.”

She added: “There is no allegation of actual interference with witnesses …There isn’t any victim in this case …The prosecution asks you to send Mr Thaci to prison for six years over conversations inside a detention unit that resulted in zero real-world impact.”

The claims are based on recordings of the visits as well as physical evidence found also at Kilaj’s home in November 2023 – less than a month after Kryeziu and Kilaj met Thaci – allegedly printed via the only printer at the detention centre that Thaci could use.

Thaci and his four-co-accused have denied wrongdoing.

Smakaj’s lawyer, Jonathan Elystan Rees, in his closing statements on Friday, called for the acquittal of all the defendants.

“You should find Mr Smakaj and all the other defendants not guilty, whether individually or collectively,” he said, because Smakaj’s actions did not obstruct or have an impact on the course of justice.

Smakaj “cannot be convicted on the allegation that he intentionally aided in disobeying court orders, because he was completely unaware of the court’s orders”, Rees said.

He added: “There is no evidence from the prosecution, nor any legal obligation, requiring my client to be aware of the operational guidelines and functioning procedures of the detention centres.”

The lawyer for Isni Kilaj, Ian Edwards, told the court on Friday that Kilaj did not take any action after visiting Thaci at the Detention Centre in The Hague, saying he “neither called nor met with any witnesses”, so showing a lack of intent to obstruct justice.

“Everything else is mud that the prosecution is throwing at Mr Kilaj, hoping that some of it will tarnish his reputation,” he added.

David Young, lawyer for Fadil Fazliu, highlighted that his client was not even questioned by the prosecution.

“We can infer that the prosecution adopted a strategic approach of not interviewing them, of not questioning these individuals regarding the allegations. Is this the right way to initiate investigations or bring charges? I believe not. I state clearly that it is not,” Young told the court.

Alexander Admiral, lawyer for Hajredin Kuci, told the court that his client had been charged based on a wrongful translation of a message he sent to one of the witnesses in Thaci’s war-crimes trial, former Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA fighter Rrustem Mustafa.

According to Admiral, the message had been misinterpreted as passing a note from a third individual when the rightful translation revealed that Kuci was passing his support to Mustafa and was basically “a man calming an old friend”.

During the prosecution’s closing statements on Thursday, it was claimed that Thaci tried to influence Mustafa and another former KLA, fighter, Bislim Zyrapi, both of whom were testifying in his war-crimes case.

The testimony of both men favoured Thaci’s defence.

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was created specifically to try former members of the KLA; it is located in The Hague and staffed by international judges and prosecutors due to doubts about the Kosovo justice system’s own ability to try former KLA fighters, many of whom are considered heroes in Kosovo. Witness-tampering has been one of its key concerns from the outset.

World.title: Kosovo Parliament Hit by Fresh Dispute Over Deputy Speakers
World.content:
Kosovo parliament session on September 11, 2026. Photo: BIRN.

Kosovo’s parliament failed to find a way out of a fresh crisis on Friday when MPs reconvened in two attempts to elect new deputy speakers.

The legislature derived from the June 7 snap partliamentary elections has not yet been inaugurated because the ruling Vetevendosje party refuses to support proposed candidates from two opposition parties, Vlora Citaku, from the Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK, and Kujtim Shala, from the Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK.

Under the constitutional rules, parliament cannot be considered inaugurated until the speaker and all five deputies are elected.

Albulena Haxhiu from Vetevendosje was elected speaker on Wednesday, Ardian Gola, from the same party, was installed as deputy on Friday.

When Citaku of the PDK received only 44 of a minimum of 61 votes on Friday, her party colleagues left the session and accused Albin Kurti’s Vetevendosje of blocking the inauguration of parliament.

“As of today, the PDK has no reason to participate in parliamentary sessions and we will take the case to the Constitutional Court,” Bedri Hamza, the PDK leader, said as soon as speaker Albulena Haxhiu interrupted the session.

In the June elections, Vetevendosje won 53 of the 120 seats in the chamber, well ahead of the next-placed PDK, which won 22 seats. The LDK came third with 18 seats.

Vetevendosje claims it can call on 62 MPs to form a new government, again relying on the support of MPs from ethnic minority communities – Roma, Ashkali, Egyptian, Turk and Bosniak – plus one of the Serb MPs.

However, the wider crisis that led to the June 7 elections has not been solved, as parliament needs to elect a new president of Kosovo within two months of its inauguration. Failure to do so would trigger another election, the fourth within less than two years.

As the post-election blockage enters its second month, Kurti and LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku agreed on August 31 to nominate Bekim Sejdiu, a former Constitutional Court judge and former diplomat, as Kosovo’s president. But, days later, six LDK MPs refused to support his candidacy, making the necessary quorum impossible.

For a president to be elected, a candidate must win at least 80 votes in the first two rounds. In a potential third round, they need a simple majority of only 61 votes.

Arberie Nagavci, head of Vetevendosje’s parliamentary group, said its MPs would not support any candidate for deputy speaker who is against the deal on the new president. Both Citaku and Shala have announced their opposition to Sejdiu’s candidacy.

“Of course, the MPs who are in favour of the Vetevendosje-LDK agreement [on the president] have the support of our 53 MPs,” Nagavci said after the interruption of the session.

Parliament will resume work on Sunday.

World.title: Bosnia Charges Seven Over Deadly Fire at Tuzla Elderly People’s Care Home
World.content:
Investigators inspect the scene after the fire at the nursing home in Tuzla, November 5, 2025. Photo: EPA/NIDAL SALJIC.

Prosecutors in Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Tuzla Canton on Friday indicted seven people over the fire at a Tuzla nursing home in November 2025 that killed 15 elderly residents and injured more than 30 others.

The indictment charges former nursing home director Mirsad Bakalovic, service head Zinaida Razic Halilovic and Mustafa Azabagic, who was responsible for fire and occupational safety at the facility.

Three employees of the Tuzla-based company Inproz, which prepared the nursing home’s 2021 fire risk assessment, are also indicted: Nedim Dzambic, Mirsad Zukancic and Jasmin Softic. The seventh defendant is Ibrahim Sarajlic, a fire safety inspector in Tuzla Canton.

The defendants are charged with serious offences against public safety. Bakalovic is also charged with abuse of office and authority, the prosecutor’s office said.

Prosecutors allege that between April 2021 and November 4, 2025, the defendants failed to implement or order legally required fire safety and general safety measures, despite knowing the facility was classified as a high-risk building.

The nursing home run by the city of Tuzla housed 180 elderly residents, 110 of whom were seriously ill, immobile or living with disabilities.

According to the indictment, the failures included inadequate supervision of residents with limited mobility, inappropriate accommodation and allocation of residents according to their health and mobility, and an inadequate fire prevention and protection system.

Prosecutors said these failures prevented the timely detection and containment of the fire, the early detection and reporting of fire and carbon monoxide in residents’ rooms, the evacuation of residents, and the removal of smoke and heat from the building.

“As official and responsible persons, by failing to install prescribed fire protection equipment and by failing to act in accordance with regulations or technical safety rules, they caused a danger to people’s lives, resulting in the deaths of several people,” the prosecutor’s office said.

The fire broke out in a resident’s room on November 4 and quickly spread. Fifteen residents died, with autopsies establishing a direct causal link to carbon monoxide poisoning or other complications related to the fire, prosecutors said. More than 30 people were injured.

The indictment has been submitted to the Tuzla Cantonal Court for confirmation.

Prosecutors have also asked the court to ban all seven defendants from holding public or professional positions or performing certain activities for 10 years.

World.title: North Macedonia Govt Finally Reveals Independence Day Celebrations’ Cost
World.content:
North Macedonia’s government spokesperson, Marija Miteva (R) and State Lottery director Aleksandar Klimovski (L) at a press conference in Skopje. Photo: BIRN.

The series of celebrations marking the 35th anniversary of North Macedonia’s Independence Day, September 8, cost a total of 5.5 million euros, of which almost 4.9 million euros came from the State Lottery, government spokesperson Marija Miteva told a press conference on Thursday.

The rest of the money, some 650,000 euros, Miteva said, came from “socially responsible” companies.

The financial disclosure followed a BIRN Macedonia report published on Wednesday showing that the government had effectively tasked the State Lottery with taking care of the events, by choosing a production company that would organise them according to the government’s requirements.

Four months ago, the government announced its plan for a series of events marking the anniversary, culminating in a September 8 concert in Skopje by world-famous DJ David Guetta. Since then, officials had repeatedly declined to say how much the events would cost, or who was paying for them.

The government at the press conference focused on its argument that the almost 5 million euros coming from the State Lottery, which is fully owned by the government, was not taxpayers’ money.

State Lottery director Aleksandar Klimovski told the press conference that the government, as the company’s sole shareholder, had ordered it to allocate the money from its undistributed 2024 profits to the celebrations.

But he insisted it should not be considered budgetary funds because it remained on the company’s account and was therefore “corporate money” until formally transferred to the state budget.

This supported the Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski’s claim on Wednesday, who, confronted by reporters, maintained that the events “cost the budget and the citizens zero denars”.

The funding arrangements raised questions about transparency. In June, BIRN reported that the government was refusing to disclose the financial details of what it described as spectacular celebrations under the slogan “Silno svetnal den” [Brightly shining day], despite repeated requests for information.

On Thursday, Boban Miloseski, the owner of Avalon production, which the State Lottery hired to carry out the celebrations, apologised for an earlier incident on September 7, at a press conference organised by Avalon and the Interior Ministry ahead of Guetta’s September 8 concert in Skopje.

Asked why the cost of Guetta’s contract had not been made public, and whether a clause prevented disclosure, Miloseski had responded: “Do I look like an idiot to you?”, calling the question a provocation. In his apology, he said he uttered these words under a lot of “stress and fatigue”, before he had time to properly think it through.

Besides Guetta, the celebrations in Skopje and across the country featured other world-famous performers and DJs, including José Carreras, Steve Aoki, Paul van Dyk and Paul Oakenfold.

World.title: Week in Review: Tests and Pressures
World.content:
The lavish funeral of the convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic, complete with military honours and attended by senior Serbian and Bosnian Serb officials, drew condemnation from EU states and renewed questions about how deeply the glorification of wartime figures remains embedded in regional politics.

Experts told BIRN that the spectacle in Serbia reflected a state-sponsored politics of memory rather than Serbian society as a whole, while warning that Mladic’s funeral has become entangled with election campaigns and could further damage already strained regional relations.

Writing from Brussels, Gjeraqina Tuhina argued that this is also a test for the EU: after years of accommodating Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic, Brussels must decide whether its opposition to war-criminal glorification will have consequences beyond strongly worded statements.

World.title: Concentration Camp to Hotel Catwalk: Montenegrin Fortress’s Makeover Puts History at Risk
World.content:
So the thought of a fashion show being staged on Mamula last month seems grotesque. What is even more worrying is how a place of suffering became a playground for luxury, with the survivors and their families witnessing the quiet obscuring of history.

Eighty years after the concentration camp was dismantled and the Italians fled, an Egyptian investor opened the renovated Mamula fort as a luxury hotel. Under the name Mamula Island Hotel, it was unveiled in 2023 and functioned briefly under this name before the Banyan Group took over and rebranded it as Mamula Island by Banyan Tree, a makeover that went into effect for the 2026 summer season.

When the news about the Montenegrin government decision to lease out the former concentration camp to be turned into a luxury hotel was first announced a decade ago, it caused an outcry, with many former prisoners speaking out against it. Many in the Montenegrin public viewed the commercialisation of this historically significant site of suffering as the loss of an important part of Montenegrin’s history.

The decision triggered international outrage as well, prompting major media outlets to write about the controversy. The government even received a letter from the then UN Secretary general Boutros Boutros-Ghali who expressed concern over the endeavour.

However, the government stood by its decision, citing that they had only two options: either let the fort and the island be abandoned to decay or find an investor who would restore it and open it for visitors. The authorities were very vocal in reassuring the public that the island’s history would be preserved and would become a crucial part of the new development.

Which it was. Sort of.

Mamula Island by Banyan Tree has an accompanying memorial gallery named Historical-Memorial Gallery Mamula, where the details of the island’s dark past along with personal artefact, testimonials and the names of prisoners are laid out on display.

For the fashion show, the invited public came, some of them even visited the memorial gallery. They posted photos, they were or tried to be respectful and then they went on to see the show, ate and slept in the soft beds of their hotel rooms, former prisoners’ holding cells where inmates slept on the hard limestone floors or improvised bunk beds, squeezed in with several dozen other people.

Supporters of the hotel project claim the site needed a curator and that history will not be erased by the renovation or the change in the function of the fortress, and that letting the fortress decay was also a form of erasure.

This last argument is true. Leaving Mamula fortress exposed to the elements and cause it to decay into ruin. But preserving a building does not necessarily preserve memory authentically.

The walls of the fortress hold the truth – bodies crammed against one another, straw mattresses on wooden boards, a gasoline barrel used as a toilet. Luxury hotel rooms do not preserve that memory.

New lives for old buildings?

World.title: Student-Led Movement Launches Election Challenge to Serbian Government
World.content:
Hundreds gathered in Serbia’s second city Novi Sad on Thursday evening for the first pre-election rally held by the student opposition movement ahead of early parliamentary elections scheduled for October 25.

Their electoral slate – called Student List – Students are Winning – will include 250 candidates chosen by students involved in the long-running protest movement triggered by the November 2024 Novi Sad railway station disaster.

The student movement has become the strongest opposition force in Serbia, and the decision to participate in the elections represents its first direct entry into electoral politics. It hopes to defeat the Serbian Progressive Party led by Aleksandar Vucic, which has been in power since 2012.

World.title: Croats more Generous Than Most Europeans: 68% Have Donated Money
World.content:
September the 13th, 2026 – Croats seem to generally be more generous than most Europeans as a new survey reveals that as much as 68% of them have donated money to various charitable causes.

Research shows that the decision to donate is influenced not only by the financial resources a person has at their disposal, but also by a sense of belonging to the community, personal values and trust in the organisations that receive donations. Ana Roksandic reports for Poslovni that Croatia is actually among the leaders in the share of income that citizens give for donations.

Croatian citizens set aside more for others than most Europeans. According to a new report by the Charities Aid Foundation (CAF), 68% of Croatian citizens donated money during 2025, whether to charitable organisations, directly to people in need or for religious purposes.

a culture of solidarity

Domestic donors most often provide direct help to people in need, while donations to organisations are mainly directed towards local and national civil society organisations, states the National Foundation for Civil Society Development, according to CAF data. Research shows that the decision to donate is influenced not only by the financial resources a person has at their disposal, but also by a sense of belonging to the community, personal values and trust in the organisations that receive donations. Countries in which citizens feel a stronger connection with their local communities also record a significantly higher level of giving. Social connectedness is important for the development of philanthropy. The share of income that residents of Croatia set aside through various forms of financial assistance places our country in second place among European Union members, behind Romania, where that share is 0.9 percent, and ahead of Ireland with 0.7 percent. Domestic organisations that we asked for comment are not surprised by such a level of generosity.

“Croatia’s high position did not completely surprise us. In Croatia there is a strong culture of solidarity and helping, especially when it comes to concrete people and needs. Over the past 10 years we have recorded greater visibility and diversity of philanthropic activities and citizens’ readiness to help. It is important to further develop this culture of giving towards longer-term forms of philanthropy,” said Smiljana Rađa, Managing Director of the European Foundation for Philanthropy and Social Development.

From Croatian Caritas they said that, although they currently do not have consolidated statistical data with which they could give a precise answer to the question about donation trends, they confirm the tendency towards mutual help. “From our everyday experience we can confirm that the solidarity of Croatian citizens and companies is extremely great, especially in moments of crisis, which coincides with the positive trends cited by CAF,” they told us from Croatian Caritas.

donations directly to those in need

Of the 0.8 percent of citizens’ income that is on average set aside for various forms of giving, as much as 0.4 percent goes directly to people in need, while 0.2 percent goes to charitable organisations and the same amount for religious purposes. In other words, Croatian citizens on average direct twice as large a part of their income directly to individuals than to organisations.

“This shows that in Croatia there is strong direct solidarity; citizens often want to help a concrete person or family. At the same time, there is room for greater trust in civil society organisations, which can turn donations into long-term and systematic support for a larger number of people,” said Rađa.

between 10 and 19 euros

Research by the National Foundation for Civil Society Development from 2024 also showed what typical Croatian donating looks like. According to the research on citizens’ donating habits in Croatia, as many as 67 percent of citizens would rather donate to local than to international organisations, while the most common donation amount is between 10 and 19 euros. Donating is at the same time strongly connected with concrete circumstances. Around 53 percent of citizens say that crisis situations prompt them to donate, while 46.3 percent with higher personal incomes would donate more. Total donations in the three largest economies of the European Union, Germany, France and Italy, in 2025 on average amounted to only 0.4 percent of income. Europeans on average donated 0.6 percent of their income, compared to the global average of one percent.

World.title: French Judiciary Prepares Warrant for Suspected Jean-Michel Nicolier Murderer
World.content:
September the 13th, 2026 – The French judiciary is currently preparing an international arrest warrant for Spasoje Petković, known as “Štuka”, the suspected Jean-Michel Nicolier murderer.

The French judiciary is preparing an international arrest warrant for Spasoje Petković, known as Štuka, suspected of the murder of French volunteer Jean-Michel Nicolier at Ovčara back in 1991. Index reports that news of progress in the investigation being conducted in Paris has brought new hope to the Nicolier family that justice will finally be served after 35 years. The family’s lawyer confirmed that the investigating judge at the War Crimes Department of the court in Paris is currently working on the warrant. Paul Nicolier, brother of the murdered Vukovar defender, told RTL that they received the news with “great satisfaction and deep emotion.”

the nicolier family will never give up on justice

“We’re extremely grateful to the French judicial authorities for all their efforts. We hope that, 35 years after the murder, all the circumstances of his death will finally be clarified and that those responsible for it will answer before the court,” said Paul Nicolier. He emphasised that this is an extremely important step that the family has been waiting for years and that sends a clear message: “Thirty-five years after the crime, the judiciary has not given up, and neither have we.” He stressed that the family has always wanted only the truth and justice for Jean-Michel. “Our lawyers Ghislain Dubois and Arnaud Bilen have our full and unconditional trust. We sincerely thank them for their commitment, determination and tireless work. For Jean-Michel, for our family and for his memory, we will go all the way,” concluded the brother of the murdered volunteer.

previous demands to serbia to extradite the suspected murderer fell on deaf ears

The Nicolier family had previously threatened Serbia with a private lawsuit and, through the embassy in Paris, demanded the urgent extradition of Štuka. According to information published by RTL, France has already questioned Petković, and the investigation is nearing its end. He told the French judge that he is not guilty, but investigators have reportedly gathered sufficient evidence against him. During the investigation, several people were questioned in Croatia and Serbia. One of the last persons questioned was someone hiding in Norway, who is suspected of having participated in the relocation of mass graves at Ovčara.

The exact location of Spasoje Petković Štuka is not known. It is only known that he lives under a changed identity at a secret location. Jean-Michel Nicolier joined the defence of Croatia in the summer of 1991 as a member of HOS. After being wounded in Vukovar, he was transferred to the hospital, where he awaited the fall of the city. From there, members of the JNA and Serbian paramilitary units took him to Ovčara. According to the testimonies of survivors, he was tortured and killed at Ovčara. His remains were only exhumed after 34 years from a mass grave. In the court proceedings for the crimes at Ovčara conducted in Belgrade, Štuka had the status of a repentant witness. He allegedly admitted guilt in exchange for freedom, and several witnesses accused him of the murder. One of them stated that Štuka, after killing Nicolier, even went as low as to steal 20 francs from his pocket.

World.title: Rijeka Gateway Establishes Cooperation With Huge Shipping Companies
World.content:
September the 13th, 2026 – In its first year of commercial operation, Rijeka Gateway has successfully established cooperation with the two largest shipping companies in the world, Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd.

Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that the terminal has received more than a thousand trains and over 80 thousand trucks since opening, and the current ratio of cargo transport from the terminal is 42 percent by rail and 58 percent by road. Rijeka Gateway is the technologically most advanced container terminal in this part of Europe, in the first year since the start of commercial operations has created a team of 422 employees, raised the terminal to a high level of operational excellence required by the global APM Terminals network, received over 100 ships and handled more than 370 thousand TEU of cargo.

Additionally, the terminal has strengthened Rijeka’s logistical position between large Asian ports and the Mediterranean within the Gemini shipping network, and new logistical routes have been opened so that Rijeka is connected by regular rail links with Serbia, Hungary and Austria, as well as with important ports on the Adriatic and in Italy, it was highlighted at a press conference organised on the occasion of the first anniversary of commercial operations of Rijeka Gateway.

In the first year of commercial operations, Rijeka Gateway successfully established cooperation with the two largest shipping companies in the world, Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd, both of which use this terminal as their transhipment hub for import and export cargo from Italy. Rijeka Gateway has additionally confirmed its role as a regional logistical hub for container traffic within the Adriatic and is currently the only terminal on the Adriatic that performs this type of operations within the Gemini network. Information indicates that the lowland railway project has finally received the long-desired “acceleration”, which is necessary due to the new phase of development of the Rijeka terminal.

the gemini network

Rijeka Gateway has also confirmed its role as a regional logistical hub for container traffic within the Adriatic and is currently the only terminal on the Adriatic that performs this type of operations within the Gemini network – an operational cooperation between the companies Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd, which covers seven main global trade routes and serves to accelerate and optimise traffic, and Rijeka Gateway is a key port of call within the Gemini cooperation on the line connecting large Asian ports with the Mediterranean. Thus Rijeka is additionally connected with Trieste, Venice, Ravenna and Ancona.

Three ships currently arrive at Rijeka Gateway weekly: one mother vessel on the Asia–Europe service and two smaller feeder vessels. The introduction of an additional feeder service for Ploče and Durrës is expected soon. The terminal has also started parallel operations, which means that two smaller feeder vessels, around 150 metres in length, can be berthed in parallel at the terminal, and operations on them take place in parallel, which enables better utilisation of the operational quay, shorter waiting times for ships and greater efficiency of terminal operations.

“Rijeka has always had a vision and the port has always been the one that carried new development moments. We are striving for the connection of the Port of Rijeka with a double-track railway to go as quickly as possible, and for the container terminals to get an exit with the most efficient part of extracting traffic from the port. This port is not only a local and national interest, it has always been a European hub, and Rijeka Gateway contributes precisely to such positioning of Rijeka,” said Nina Perko, Director of the Maritime Administration in the Ministry of the Sea, Transport and Infrastructure.

Denis Vukorepa, Director of the Port Authority of Rijeka, recalled that thanks to Rijeka Gateway the total container traffic in the Port of Rijeka in the first six months of this year increased by 66 percent, and total traffic by around 40 percent.

“A year ago here we spoke about what Rijeka Gateway would mean for Rijeka, Croatia and this transport route. Today we see concrete results. In less than a year the terminal has received its hundredth ship, opened more than 420 new jobs and confirmed that Rijeka is once again strongly written on the map of European and world logistical flows. Rijeka Gateway represents the foundation for the further development of the port and an important step forward for the economy of Rijeka and Croatia,” said Denis Vukorepa, Director of the Port Authority of Rijeka.

“Rijeka has always been connected with the port, the port is part of our identity and part of our future. That is why it is important to us that our port is competitive, well connected with European and world markets. We are especially pleased that the development of the terminal brings new jobs, new knowledge, and especially opportunities for young people and the fact that young people can build their knowledge and experience right in our city. We want a Rijeka that develops, attracts such investments, creates new opportunities, new jobs, but a city in which development takes place with respect for space and the quality of life of our citizens,” emphasised Vedran Vivoda, Deputy Mayor of the City of Rijeka.

The terminal has received more than a thousand trains and over 80 thousand trucks since opening, and the current ratio of cargo transport from the terminal is 42 percent by rail and 58 percent by road.

corridors, ecology and employees

During the first year of terminal operations, more than 92 thousand hours of education and professional training were invested in employee development. This was preceded by an intensive period of learning and preparation, during which in 2025, ahead of the terminal’s launch, 130 thousand hours of education were recorded.

“When we draw a line under the first year of operations, I must say that I am most proud of three things. The first is our team of 422 employees, and that a young team considering that the average age of employees is 35 years, but also a team in which 20 percent are women, employed in almost all functions and levels of management. In Rijeka, and even in the wider region, such a technologically advanced terminal did not exist, our jobs and processes are special and very complex, so building a team that can compete at that level with the best terminals is a source of pride not only for all of us at Rijeka Gateway, but also for Rijeka and the whole of Croatia.

The second are the new logistical corridors with which we have connected Rijeka with the region, which is a great value that our terminal has brought. The third is that we have continued to carefully monitor our impact on the environment and the community with the goal of being a good neighbour to the citizens of Rijeka. We have successfully certified the environmental management system according to the ISO 14001:2015 standard, confirming our commitment to environmental protection, and we continuously communicate with the local community on all topics related to the quality of life of citizens,” said Peter Corfitsen, President of the Management Board of Rijeka Gateway.

The terminal has received more than a thousand trains and over 80 thousand trucks since opening, and the current ratio of cargo transport from the terminal is 42 percent by rail and 58 percent by road. The entry and exit process for truck transport is fully digitised, which speeds up the truck processing process and reduces waiting times, which reduces the burden on traffic and pollution. The average truck time is around 15 minutes, and the shortest achieved truck processing time is ten minutes, and that on a day when more than 500 trucks were processed.

It is clear that the main limitation remains the railway. In this year little has changed. Nevertheless, information indicates that the project has finally received the long-desired “acceleration”, primarily bureaucratic. The project practically languished unprepared for years, only to receive the necessary acceleration in the past year. Processes have been moved from a standstill, so it is still to be expected that by the middle of the next decade we will finally see the realisation of that project.

investments for rijeka and the community

“By handling 370 thousand TEU of cargo we have significantly raised the total capacity of the Port of Rijeka and we are rapidly approaching the numbers we planned – and that is to reach a handling of 650 thousand TEU, and then in the second phase one million TEU. During the first year of operations Rijeka Gateway maintained a high level of operational reliability, with 98 percent availability of port equipment and 99 percent availability of key systems on the operational quay and storage areas, which is at the level of the best terminals.

For the full potential of the terminal, the planned increase in the capacity of rail traffic will be key and here we welcome the activities of the Government of the Republic of Croatia. We will continue to invest in the local community, especially through cooperation with the Faculty of Maritime Studies and the University of Rijeka, through various scholarship and education programmes, but also through donation programmes aimed at Rijeka kindergartens and primary schools,” concluded Tomislav Rosandić, Member of the Management Board of Rijeka Gateway.

World.title: Croatian Airports Enjoy a Record Summer
World.content:
September the 13th, 2026 – Croatian airports have enjoyed a record summer this year, with July in particular standing out.

Croatian airports recorded strong passenger traffic in July 2026. A total of 2,355 thousand passengers passed through domestic airports, which is 40 thousand more than in the same month last year. Zrinka Gabelica Toplek reports for Poslovni that when compared to July 2025, when 2,315 thousand passengers passed through Croatian airports, this year’s result is an increase of 1.7 percent. The largest number of passengers was recorded by Split Airport, through which 767 thousand passengers passed in July, thus retaining the status of the busiest Croatian airport.

It is followed by Dubrovnik Airport with 557 thousand passengers, while 465 thousand passengers passed through Zagreb Airport. In fourth place is Zadar Airport with 365 thousand passengers, and fifth place was taken by Pula Airport with 145 thousand passengers.

split comes out on top

In July 2026, 2.35 million passengers passed through Croatian airports, which is 1.7% more than in the same month last year, and Split was the busiest. The five busiest airports together recorded 2,299 thousand passenger movements, or almost the entire traffic recorded at Croatian airports during July.

According to the country of origin of passengers, the most passengers arrived from Germany, from which 380 thousand passengers were recorded. The German market was thus the most important source of passenger traffic in the Croatian air system. In second place was the United Kingdom with 376 thousand passengers, while 192 thousand passengers were recorded from Poland in July. France follows with 180 thousand passengers.

The four leading markets – Germany, the United Kingdom, Poland and France – together accounted for 1,128 thousand passengers, which shows how important a role European markets play in Croatian air traffic during the main tourist season.

World.title: This Dalmatian Island is Heavily Visited, But Few Spend the Night There…
World.content:
September the 12th, 2026 – There’s a beautiful Dalmatian island that attracts around 150,000 visitors each summer, but only 40 or so of them opt to actually spend the night there.

Gorgeous Biševo itself had only 44 registered tourists in 2025, while more than 150,000 people visited the famous Blue Cave. Putni kofer writes that at first glance, Biševo in the middle of summer is anything but a deserted island. Boats full of day-trippers arrive all day long, people wait to board the small boats that transport thousands towards the world-famous Blue Cave. According to currently available data, during the summer, over 150,000 tourists visit the cave, and one of the most famous natural attractions on the Adriatic brings a huge number of people to this small open-sea island every year.

However, most of them board the boat again after visiting the Blue Cave and leave, heading off elsewhere. Few stay to explore the rest of the island. During the whole of 2025, according to data from the Croatian Bureau of Statistics, only 44 people decided to actually spend the night on Biševo.

a contrast unlike any other on the adriatic coast

Day-trippers arrive on Biševo from nearby Komiža, but also from Split, Hvar and the surrounding islands, as well as numerous coastal tourist destinations. The visit to the Blue Cave itself lasts less than half an hour, but on the island it is also possible to visit the Visitor Centre inland, the old military tunnels, and to swim on beautiful beaches such as the one in the place of Porat. It is a real shame to reduce a trip to Biševo only to a visit to the cave. But most people visit it that way, which is confirmed by both statistics and our experience: when we continued exploring the island after viewing the most famous attraction, we met perhaps twenty people during the whole day.

This contrast between the number of visitors and those who stay on the island at least a little longer is unique in Croatia. It is not only a matter of overnight stays: after all, only about thirty beds are registered on Biševo. The island is ideal for a full-day excursion, swimming, getting to know the heritage, which many skip because they concentrate only on the famous cave. This is also confirmed by a study by the Institute for Tourism. Their research showed that only 8.3 percent of guests stay eight hours or longer on the island, and almost half said they came exclusively because of the Blue Cave.

The Blue Cave in Balun bay owes its name to the reflection of the sun’s rays which around noon, in calm seas, penetrate through an underwater opening into the cave, reflecting off the white bottom and creating the blue colour. It is 24 metres long and about 12 metres wide, and its modest depth of 3 to 20 metres and typical karst shape make it an ideal habitat for a diverse ecosystem, while divers discover its mysterious world through hidden underwater cracks. It is said that it is best to visit it between 11:00 and 14:00 on a sunny day.

no shop, no cash machine, and no maritime connections…

The island of Biševo is the most remote inhabited Croatian island. It stands proudly in the middle of the open sea, isolated and a little wild, and a holiday on it is definitely not for everyone. Neither ferries nor catamarans sail to it, and it is connected to neighbouring Vis by the only boat line, Sv. Salvestar, the so-called “pruga”, which departs from Komiža. It spans only 5.8 square kilometres, in the middle of the last century about 300 inhabitants lived on it, and today only about ten remain. Biševo was once known as the home of the Mediterranean monk seal, but that animal disappeared from the island long ago. Besides the most famous Blue Cave, on the southern side of the island, in Trešjavac bay, there is also the beautiful Medvidina Cave. The island also has its own distinctive wine: Biševo plavac.

the home of caves, military tunnels and stunning beaches

In the very centre of the island a few years ago the Visitor Centre was opened, which you can reach from Mezoporat harbour by electric cart. The Centre is really worth visiting; it presents the wonderful world of underwater, terrestrial and geological phenomena, and also showcases the rich past of the island. The surroundings are also interesting: an old village with a beautiful church that was probably once full of life. The military tunnels are located at the other end of the island, on Cape Gatula, and if you are not up for walking, you can specially arrange transport by electric vehicles to them.

A walk that is definitely worth it is the one from the Visitor Centre to the place of Porat, where the regular boat line docks and can take you directly back to Komiža from there. Porat beach is, according to many, one of the most beautiful on the Adriatic. Soft sand, enough shade, a café for refreshment… Although there are day-trippers, the crowds are practically never too big. This island is isolated and certainly not for everyone, but it is a real glimpse of genuine Dalmatian island life that is rapidly being sent to the history books on other islands.

World.title: Meet the Highest Fortress of the Dubrovnik Republic… That Isn’t Even in Dubrovnik
World.content:
September the 12th, 2026 – The highest fortress of the former Dubrovnik Republic (Ragusa) isn’t even located within the city. It’s a very unusual, irregular fortification that once played a vitally important defensive role.

Nestled against the rock sits one of the most monumental fortification systems in the south of Croatia, and it was once an important cog in the defence of the powerful Republic of Dubrovnik. Putni kofer writes that anyone who looks at Dubrovnik clearly sees that this city is teeming with incredible history. Even without any prior knowledge, the gaze will stop on the monumental walls, fortresses, palaces… Today one of the most beautiful cities on the Mediterranean, it was once a powerful force. The Dubrovnik Republic was small in a territorial sense, but politically, commercially and diplomatically, it was extremely influential.

Lovrijenac, Revelin, Minčeta, Bokar and St. John are fortresses that line up in the defensive ring of the city or next to it, but none of these fortresses was the largest defensive fortification of the powerful republic. It is located about forty kilometres from the city, among the hills of Konavle. Sokol Grad is, according to official sources, the largest single fortress from the time of the Republic of Dubrovnik.

sokol grad towers on a natural 25-metre rock

Sokol Grad was built above the small place of Dunave, on a natural rock that rises more than 25 metres above the surrounding terrain. Its walls so faithfully follow the shape of the rock and blend in colour with the karst that from a distance the fortress looks almost like its extension. The position was not chosen for beauty, although the view today is spectacular. From this point the Konavle field and an important road that led from the hinterland towards Dubrovnik were monitored, and official sources state that from Sokol one of the most complete views of the entire Konavle opens up.

a hillfort existed there all the way back to prehistoric times

The fortress did not originate in the time of the Dubrovnik Dubrovnik. Traces have been found in this area that point to much older fortification of the position, from a prehistoric hillfort through ancient and late antique fortifications. It is mentioned in written documents at the end of the 14th century, and at the beginning of the 15th century its Dubrovnik story begins. The people of Dubrovnik briefly entered the fortress in 1420, and from 1423 it came under their control again and remained part of their defensive system for the next two and a half centuries. Its task was clear: to protect Konavle from enemies who could arrive from the hinterland. Precisely for this reason the Republic of Dubrovnik did not spare on its maintenance. During the 15th century the walls were repaired, expanded and strengthened, and construction works continued in the 16th and 17th centuries. Sokol also protected an area of vital economic importance, including the area of the river Ljuta and the mills that participated in the supply of Dubrovnik.

a three-level fortress

Sokol Grad has an irregular shape and that is no coincidence. The ramparts follow the morphology of the rock, and the entire fortification is organised on three levels. The lowest part, called Kamen (Stone), was arranged as a space into which the surrounding population could take shelter in case of danger. In the outer bailey were the fortified main entrance, kitchen, food stores, rooms for soldiers and crossbowmen, a guard tower and sanitary facilities.

The safest part was at the very top. In the citadel there was a large cistern, stores of food and weapons, grain supplies, the castellan’s residence, a church, a blacksmith’s workshop and a furnace. The system for sheltering the population was precisely determined: children under the age of ten were to be housed in the upper fortress in case of danger, while women and those unfit for combat were housed in the outer bailey.

it survived the devastating 1667 earthquake

Sokol survived the great earthquake of 1667, but after 1672 it is no longer mentioned in the Dubrovnik archival records, so it is considered that it was abandoned at that time. For centuries it decayed, and the surrounding population used its stone as building material. The Society of Friends of Dubrovnik Antiquities took it over in 1966, after which decades of conservation and restoration followed. Intensive works lasted from 2007 to 2013, when Sokol Grad was reopened to visitors. Today, instead of guards on its walls, there are day-trippers, and the former military position has become one of the best viewpoints in Konavle. Sokol Grad is open to visitors, and in the current period the official website lists opening hours from 08:00 to 19:00; tickets can also be purchased online and the price is 10 euros for adults and 5 euros for children.

World.title: Croatia is the Only EU Country Without a Waste Incinerator
World.content:
September the 12th, 2026 – After the hazardous waste scandal in Lika comes the news that Croatia is actually the only EU country without a proper waste incinerator.

Croatia is facing an enormous waste management problem with nowhere left to dispose of it, and at the same time it is the only EU Member State without a single waste incinerator. Index reports that all across the rest of Europe, more than 500 of them are currently operating. Switzerland, Norway, the UK and others also have numerous incinerators. After the scandal involving improperly disposed waste in Gospić, the question of building energy plants, facilities for the thermal treatment of waste, is being raised once again.

After the horrific case in Gospić, it seems the question is no longer whether Croatia can avoid thermal treatment of waste, but where it will even carry it out. Landfills have limited capacity, and European rules require less and less landfilling of waste that can be treated differently.

croatian ministers are confused

Minister of Economy Ante Šušnjar points out that Croatian companies are building such facilities across Europe. “If all EU Member States have them, only Malta does not but is building them, and if there are 500 of them, is Croatia the smartest or is there some other issue here? When it comes to building incinerators, Croatian companies today are building them across Europe, in Iceland, Belgium, Scotland and Germany. If we can do that for the whole world, I think we should also do it here,” said Šušnjar, as reported by N1.

Energy plants burn waste and use the resulting energy to produce electricity and heating. They are not a replacement for recycling, but a solution for the remaining part of the waste. Their construction in Croatia has for years been opposed by part of the public due to concerns about emissions, impacts on health and the environment, and the disposal of residues after incineration.

Minister of Environmental Protection Marija Vučković believes that the set waste management targets cannot be achieved without energy plants. “Would I accept an energy plant in my neighbourhood? If the environmental impact assessment has shown that it is acceptable, if the conditions from the permits are regularly controlled and, of course, if the supervision system is fully functional, there is no reason not to have an energy plant in one’s neighbourhood,” said Vučković.

is the system the problem?

Nikola Grmoja from Most sees the problem in the system, not in the disposal model itself. “If we do not have a control system, if hazardous waste could be imported into Croatia without anyone noticing or doing anything about it, how will we know what is being burned there, where it is being brought from, what the by-product is and where that by-product ends up?” asks Grmoja. He believes this is a question of a non-functioning system and corrupt people in key positions. “If we talk about the model, I am not sure how incinerators fit into all the goals that the European Commission has set for us regarding waste separation,” he said.

the zagreb project and interest from other cities

Interest in building energy plants has been shown by Šibenik, Osijek and Rijeka, and Zagreb is also considering it. A feasibility projection for Zagreb was made back in 2024 and showed that such facilities pay off. President of the Zagreb City Assembly Matej Mišić confirmed the position of the city SDP to N1. “The city SDP continues to advocate the construction of an energy plant that would burn refuse-derived fuel and thereby generate thermal energy. In fact, the City Assembly already in 2024 adopted a conclusion launching the preparation of documentation for the construction of an energy plant,” said Mišić. Although the project was started, it has not been realised. If energy plants become part of the solution for waste in Croatia, the open question remains whether the need for waste disposal will ultimately outweigh the resistance to such facilities.

World.title: New 14,000 Square Metre Shopping Mecca for Croatia
World.content:
September the 12th, 2026 – A new 14,000 square metre shopping mecca for Croatia has opened up more shopping and job opportunities near Samobor.

The opening of the new complex is a significant contribution to the local labour market and new employment opportunities for the residents of Samobor and the surrounding area, stated Joško Piteša, Director of Operations for Croatia. The 22nd retail park of this type is opening in Croatia; it will offer 23 well-known brands and around a hundred jobs. Poslovni reports that Samobor has now become richer with another shopping mecca. On 14,318 square metres of sales space, the Stop Shop retail park is being officially opened. This is already the 22nd concept of this type in Croatia, and it will offer 23 well-known brands, 429 parking spaces, and it should also be noted that each new location is expected to create around 100 new jobs.

a contribution to the local market

“This is our largest location in Croatia so far, so we expect the number of jobs to be even higher than the average of our network. It is certainly a significant contribution to the local labor market and new employment opportunities for the residents of Samobor and the surrounding area,” says Joško Piteša, Director of Operations for Croatia. The doors are being opened by well-known domestic and international brands such as TEDi, Mana Moda, LC Waikiki, Plodine, CCC, BabyCenter, Sinsay, Action, Optika Anda, Vitapur, dm, Znanje, Bipa, NKD, Admiral Bar, The Fitness, Le Mas, Zoo City, s’Oliver, Vacom, Europa 92, Mambino and Sport Vision.

expansion and development

By the end of the year, projects in Bjelovar and the expansion of the park in Vinkovci will continue. This opening in Samobor is a continuation of the brand’s expansion on the Croatian market, and Piteša says that they do not view the new location exclusively through the prism of competition with the existing offer, but as its complement.

“Our advantage is in the concept of simple and practical shopping – good traffic accessibility, parking, direct access to stores and the possibility of doing different types of shopping in one location. We expect that precisely this combination of diverse offer, accessibility and practicality will make Stop Shop Samobor attractive not only to the residents of the city, but also to customers from the wider surrounding area,” he says, adding that by the end of this year they will continue with the planned projects in Bjelovar and the expansion of the existing retail park in Vinkovci.

He also emphasised that ambitions on the Croatian market do not stop there and that they intend to continue expanding the network in the coming years, especially in areas where they recognize the need for a practical retail offer. “Croatia remains an important market for us with potential for further investments and development.”

The retail park concept has proven to be extremely resilient and popular with customers, so we ask whether he sees saturation of this model in the future or room for more? “Previous experience shows that on the Croatian market there is still interest from both customers and tenants, but we believe that further development must be thoughtful and based on the real needs of each local market. We do not believe in expansion just for the sake of increasing the number of locations – each project must have a clearly defined catchment area, appropriate traffic infrastructure, a quality mix of tenants and long-term potential.”

Stop Shop in Croatia systematically chooses medium-sized cities, so we ask what they expect from Samobor? “The focus on medium-sized cities is an integral part of our concept and long-term development strategy. Precisely in cities like Samobor we see space for accessible retail content that enables residents to do a large part of their shopping in their immediate vicinity,” he says, adding that the goal is not to concentrate the offer exclusively in the largest urban centres, but to bring retail infrastructure closer to customers in smaller and medium-sized cities. “Samobor fits very well into this strategy thanks to its size, economic activity, good traffic connections and proximity to Zagreb, but also a strong local community and a wider catchment area,” he concludes.

World.title: Gallery: Tallinn hosts tenth Literary Street Festival
World.content:
The Literary Street Festival (Kirjandustänava festival) took place again on Saturday in Kadriorg, Tallinn, bringing together various organizations involved in literature. The main program focused on living classics, and this year featured an especially large number of young authors.

This year's festival keywords included "Tõde ja õigus 100", Viivi Luik and Betti Alver, the horse‑cart from "Mäeküla piimamees", a costume exhibition of Heljo Mänd's beloved characters, Tuglas's end‑of‑the‑world island, a prayer exhibition, a meditation area and much more.

The festival also featured the traditional veranda concert, with Mari Kalkun performing this year. Theatres introduced their new season programs, and the Katariina Jee library bus was present. For children, the festival offered two areas this year — one near the Tammsaare Museum and another near the Vilde Museum — where they could meet Sipsik and Lotte's friend, the travelling dog Klaus.

The festival concluded with "The Red Umbrella Journey", dedicated to Betti Alver's 120th birthday, and a poetry picnic held this year by the swan pond — considered the most fitting location given that the picnic was dedicated to Viivi Luik. The author herself was present and read poems important to her, while Kersti Kreismann performed works by Viivi Luik. Tõnis Mägi provided the musical part.
