World.title: Cowboys back in the saddle as Alice Springs Rodeo returns
World.content:
The dust was flying and cowboys were hitting the dirt as the Alice Springs Rodeo returned after a year out of the saddle.

More than 2,000 spectators in total visited the arena at Blatherskite Park on Saturday, watching competitors take on bucking bulls and horses, while some of the youngest riders tried their luck on poddy calves.



For Aileron Bush Club secretary James Christian, the response showed how much the event had been missed.

"It's electric," he said.

"People are really glad to have a rodeo back on here in town.

"There's people from all different parts of society here, all cheering … they're enjoying the spectacle."

James Christian says the rodeo brought the community together. (ABC News: Chris Murrkarany Fitzpatrick)

Mr Christian said the event drew organisers and competitors from across a huge stretch of the Territory.

"The committee comes from probably a diameter of about 1,000 kilometres," he said.

"We've all converged on Alice Springs to put on this show.





[ Young competitors took part in horse and poddy calf events. (ABC News: Chris Murrkarany Fitzpatrick) "But it takes the whole community to help make that happen."

Young riders take their turn

Among those preparing to enter the arena was 10-year-old Lucy Muenstr, who was competing on the poddy calves.

She said she was more excited than nervous about getting into the arena.

"It's pretty fun," she said.

"You can just watch everyone fall off, and that, and it's just funny sometimes — but it's not funny if someone hurts themselves."

Ten-year-old Lucy Muenstr was excited to take on the poddy calves. (ABC: Chris Murrkarany Fitzpatrick)

Another young rider, 12-year-old Ollie McKay, had travelled 300 kilometres and was also hoping to leave with a buckle.

"I enjoy it, and it's just, like, the fun and the feel," he said.

"I just like riding and just like the cattle and all that."

For a cowboy veteran, 41-year-old rider Garyshane James, who has competed in rodeos for about 25 years, seeing another generation taking part was an important part of the event.

"Kids that get here — amazing young fellas getting in and having a go and keeping the cowboy spirit going," he said.

"Rodeo was our key to get out and see our mates."

Garyshane James has competed in rodeos for about 25 years. (ABC: Chris Murrkarany Fitzpatrick)

Three competitors taken to hospital

The dangers of the sport were also on display.

Three competitors were taken to hospital after being injured during the rodeo and were reported to be in a stable condition and recovering.

Three competitors were taken to hospital after being injured during the 2026 Alice Springs rodeo. (ABC: Chris Murrkarany Fitzpatrick)

Rodeo announcer Ricky J. Morrison said injuries were an accepted risk for many competitors.

"The cliché saying for rodeo is it's not if you get hurt, it's when," he said.

"If you do it long enough, you're going to get hurt."

He said the difference in size between riders and bulls made the risks clear.

"When a cowboy weighs anywhere from 50 to 100 kilos, and the bulls weigh anywhere from 450 to 600 kilos … you're probably going to come out second best sometimes," he said.

Rodeo announcer Ricky Morrison (right) says getting hurt is an accepted risk of the sport. (ABC: Chris Murrkarany Fitzpatrick)

Animal welfare concerns remain

While the crowd cheered on the competitors, not everyone was tipping their hat to the rodeo.





Di Evans has written numerous papers on rodeo for the RSPCA (Supplied: RSPCA) RSPCA Australia senior scientific officer Di Evans said the organisation remained opposed to rodeos because of concerns about the animals involved.

"We oppose rodeos on animal welfare grounds because of the high risk of pain, injury, fear [and] stress," she said.

Dr Evans said behaviours including head tossing, showing the whites of the eyes and excessive salivation could indicate distress in bucking animals.

" Great for a spectacle, but not so good for the animals. "

She acknowledged rodeos could provide social connections and contribute to the identity and economy of regional communities, but argued those benefits could be achieved in other ways.





Sam Webb pocketed $3,000 after winning the Open Bull Ride and shoot-out. (ABC: Chris Murrkarany Fitzpatrick) "If there's other ways that people can … connect with this culture and this focus without harming animals [and] display these skills through another way," she said.

Sam Webb cleans house

In the end, the competition produced a clear winner.

Territory cowboy Sam Webb, 38, won the Open Bull Ride before taking out the final shoot-out, earning $1,500 for each victory and pocketing $3,000 in total.

Mr Webb said there was no secret to his success.

"It's just like a hard day at work," he said.

"You work hard, you get the results.

"I was due for a bit of money."

He said he was never worried about taking on the bull that ultimately delivered his win.

"That's the fella I wanted, the big red fella," he said.

Mr Webb said beyond the competition, the rodeo offered something less tangible but no less valuable.

"It just brings the community together, brings everybody together," he said.

"It's a time to meet and greet and have a good time."

After the hiatus in 2025, organisers have described the rodeo as a "peak success" and hope to get back in the saddle again next year.

World.title: Kangaroos survive Blues scare to keep AFLW record alive
World.content:
Ash Riddell racked up 39 disposals as North Melbourne survived a scare to keep its record AFLW winning run rolling with a 10-point victory over Carlton.

In other results on Sunday, Melbourne defeated Port Adelaide 11.8 (74) to 2.11 (23) at Casey Fields, Richmond beat St Kilda 9.4 (58) to 6.7 (43) at Windy Hill, Sydney got past cross-town rivals GWS 13.9 (87) to 8.8 (56) at Henson Park, and Fremantle downed Essendon 5.7 (37) to 3.4 (22).

In front of more than 3,500 supporters at Arden Street, a boilover was on the cards after the Blues kicked back-to-back goals against the breeze in the second quarter to take a three-point lead.

The match was still in the balance in the dying minutes, with Carlton's Lily Goss having the chance to close a 10-point deficit to four after taking a mark 35 metres out.

But not realising there was a player behind her, Goss played on and was immediately tackled, with the moment proving Carlton's last chance to fire a shot as the Kangaroos held on to win, 4.9 (33) to 3.5 (23).

Riddell was unstoppable throughout, while Jasmine Garner (30 disposals, five clearances, one goal) was also a significant contributor for the victors.

The Kangaroos have a 5-0 win-loss return this season.

They have won a record 32 straight matches since drawing with Geelong in round two of 2024.

Riddell said her team embraced the challenge thrown down by the Blues.

"We love it, and we had that against Brisbane a couple of weeks ago," Riddell told the Seven Network.

"We get excited by that. You could see the girls smiling as they came in at three-quarter time. We want that challenge, so it's great."

Although Carlton dropped to a 4-1 win-loss record, the strong display against the Kangaroos has fuelled their belief.

"We would have loved to have won, so we're a little bit disappointed, but also super proud," said Blues captain Abbie McKay following her 27-disposal, five-clearance effort.

"We lost by [53 points] last year, so it shows we're really growing as a team.

"We're here to win, and we're here to win a grand final. Although we lost, it shows we're improving."

Riddell was everywhere in the first term on the way to 15 disposals and four inside 50s.

Goals against the breeze to Nell Morris-Dalton and Lila Keck thrust Carlton into a shock lead early in the second term, but a 40-metre set-shot from Tahlia Randall followed by Blaithin Bogue's goal on the run ensured the Kangaroos entered the long break with a nine-point advantage.

Randall suffered a scary moment in the third quarter when she hyperextended her left elbow, but she was able to return after receiving treatment.

The stand-out moment of the third quarter was a two-bounce, tackle-busting effort from Carlton speedster Goss that helped set up a goal to Erone Fitzpatrick.

Garner's late major ensured the Kangaroos headed into three-quarter time with an eight-point lead, and there were no goals scored in a frantic final term.

AAP

World.title: Screen time to be capped for NSW students to improve results
World.content:
Students in NSW public schools will be limited to as little as 15 minutes of screen time per day, under guidelines announced by the state government.

The 15-minute limit will apply to students from kindergarten to year 2.

Students in years 3 and 4 will have up to 30 minutes of daily classroom screen time, increasing to 45 minutes for years 5 and 6.

The guidelines will become mandatory from 2028. (ABC News)

The guidelines will be introduced next year, but will not become mandatory until 2028.

Education Minister Prue Car said children needed to get back to basics, including using pens and paper.

"There's just too much screen time for our young people in our school system," she said.

"We want to make sure that at school it's not the default, that the default is pen and paper."

Screen time limits will be more relaxed for high-schoolers, with digital learning allowed to make up 25 per cent of a subject's coursework for years 7 to 10.

Students in years 11 and 12 will be able to spend half their class time on digital devices like laptops and tablets.

Ms Car says there is too much screen time in schools. (ABC News: Nick Dole)

Raising standards

The state government said the screen time limits were designed to arrest a "worrying trend" of falling academic results.

Ms Car said according to the OECD's Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), Australian students were nearly twice as likely to spend more than two hours a day learning using digital devices than the OECD average.

Global results show Aussie students' struggles Australian students have recorded their lowest-ever scores in maths and reading in international testing, but improved on their science results.

Last week, PISA data also showed reading and mathematics scores for15 year olds in NSW were going backwards.

"There's no doubt the two are linked, and they're linked around the world," Ms Car said.

Education secretary Murat Dizdar said while technology would continue to play an important role in classrooms, imposing screen time limits would help students concentrate.

"It's about backing in the research and evidence that our own students and our teachers are telling us around avoiding distractions in the learning process."

Digital detox a 'relief' for students

While mobile phones have been banned in all NSW classrooms for several years, some schools have recently been trialling their own limits on other forms of screen time.



Chatswood High School principal, Robin Chand, said since paring back the use of digital devices, staff had noticed an improvement in students' handwriting and engagement.

"I know that this will be welcomed by students because students directly tell me that they feel relieved at times when they are working directly with pen and paper and their course books," Mr Chand said.

"When screens go down, relationships go up.

"And the relationships that are the most important in our classroom are relationships between the students and their teachers," he said.

Mr Chand says that "when screens go down, relationships go up". (ABC News)

Seventeen-year-old student, Archie Newman, said learning with hard copy books, pens and paper had allowed him to slow down and think more deeply, without the temptations of a laptop or tablet.

"I was someone who could get distracted so easily with digital technology," he said.

"And [now] the emphasis on handwriting is allowing me and my learning experience to be maximised."

World.title: 71yo motorcyclist dies after hitting pothole on highway
World.content:
A motorcyclist has died after hitting a pothole on the Western Highway in Victoria's south-west this afternoon.

Victoria Police said emergency services were called to the Western Highway in Trawalla after reports that a motorcycle had struck a pothole and lost control at around 12:50pm.

The rider, a 71-year-old Ballarat man, died at the scene.

"The exact circumstances surrounding the crash are yet to be determined and will be investigated," a Victoria Police spokesperson said.

All westbound lanes were closed on the Western Freeway between Windermere and Beaufort.

It comes just days after a new report from Victoria's auditor-general found almost half of Victoria's road network is in poor condition and crumbling faster than the government can repair it.

Victoria Police has urged anyone with dashcam footage to contact Crime Stoppers.

World.title: 'Can't get boy's face out of my head': Witness retells Sydney carjacking
World.content:
A bystander who attempted to protect two children during a pursuit and carjacking in Sydney's south-west, described the moment a man allegedly lunged at him with a knife.

About 3pm on Saturday, police were called to carry out a welfare check on a 36-year-old man in Lakemba, but he fled in a vehicle with two children, who police confirmed were his sons.

Officers engaged in a short pursuit through the Campsie area, which they said was called off due to the "manner of the man's driving".

The car crashed in Lidcombe at the intersection of Parramatta Road and Bombay Street. (ABC News)

The car crashed at the intersection of Parramatta Road and Bombay Street at Lidcombe, about nine kilometres away, where members of the public attempted to intervene after the father got out of the car with the boys.

Nicholas Karagiannis was driving along Parramatta Road when he came across the crash scene.

While rendering assistance to the driver, the 46-year-old said he heard bystanders yell, "He's getting away" and "He's got children".

Mr Karagiannis said he chased after the man, who was allegedly attempting to enter other vehicles while armed with a knife.

Witness Nicolas Karagiannis. (ABC News)

Instinctively, Mr Karagiannis said he wanted to make sure the two boys were okay, but "everything happened so fast".

"He had a knife in his hand, he did not look well," he said.

" I can't get that boy's face out my head. "

Video shows Mr Karagiannis and several other men attempting to subdue the father in the middle of a busy road.

At one point Mr Karagiannis managed to grab one of the young boys "but the boy wanted to go back".

"They were just crying …in shock, my heart bleeds for those kids," he said.

Mr Karagiannis said he pleaded with the father to let the children go to no avail.

A woman was thrown out of a black Cerato. (ABC News)

In the video, the man appeared to bundle the boys into a black Kia Cerato, and moments later the female driver is forcibly thrown from the car.

Police said he allegedly threatened the woman with what they described as "a small black knife".

"I just did what I think anyone else would do in that situation [when] you see a guy with a knife and two young boys," Mr Karagiannis said.

The children, aged between five and seven, suffered minor injuries and were expected to be released from hospital on Sunday.

Second altercation

Inspector Mark Wakeham said a member of the public had unsuccessfully tried to remove the keys from the Cerato's ignition, sustaining a laceration to his hand as the father sped off with the two children inside.

The vehicle came to a stop on the M4 near the overpass of Greystaynes Road before being approached by members of the public, including an off-duty police officer, Inspector Wakeham added.

Bystanders this time managed to restrain him before police arrived.

Police praised the actions of bystanders who tried to help. (Supplied)

Inspector Wakeham described their actions as "incredibly brave".

" They did a wonderful job and we'd like to thank members of the public for assisting us with this case. "

He ruled out the incident as an act of kidnapping.

The man remained under police guard in hospital on Sunday where he was charged with three offences, including aggravated robbery with wounding, police pursuit and reckless wounding.

In the afternoon he appeared in court from hospital via a video link.

He did not apply for bail with the matter adjourned until September 24.

World.title: Broncos, Titans win to wrap up NRLW regular season
World.content:
The Brisbane Broncos have thrashed the Warriors to hit peak form before the finals, while the high-flying Gold Coast Titans beat the Newcastle Knights to wrap up the NRLW regular season.

The Broncos, defending premiers, put in a stunning seven-try second half on Sunday in a club-record 52-18 victory at Brisbane's Langlands Park.

Meanwhile, the Titans' 32-20 win in Newcastle stretched their unbeaten streak to 10 matches. They had already secured second place on the ladder behind the undefeated Sydney Roosters.

The Broncos finished the regular season in third place.

They were too classy for the Warriors, who ended a disappointing season with a fifth straight loss.

Roosters remain perfect in NRLW The Roosters come home strong to secure a second straight unbeaten NRLW season as they look to rectify last year's grand final stumble.

The New Zealanders came out of the blocks firing, but the Broncos scored first via Kerri Johnson, before former Brisbane premiership winner Gayle Broughton crossed for the visitors.

Broughton laid on another try with a deft kick for winger Tysha Ikenasio and the Warriors looked set to head into the break with a lead.

But Broncos centre Deleni Paitai scored her first NRLW try with 10 seconds left in the half to give her side a 12-8 advantage.

The Broncos extended their buffer just four minutes into the second half when Chelsea Lenarduzzi powered over.

Tries followed to Paitai, Tamika Upton, Georgia Bartlett, Julia Robinson and Lauren Dam, before Warriors centre Stacey Waaka stopped the rot.

Waaka stretched her try-scoring streak to seven matches, and Jasmin Huriwai added another for the Warriors prior to Robinson scoring her second for the Broncos.

Teagan Levi scored a double in the Titans' win over the Knights. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner)

In Newcastle, Mercedez Taulelei-Siala opened the scoring for the Knights inside two minutes.

But the Titans' response was almost immediate when Phoenix-Raine Hippi scored.

Laikha Clarke made it two tries in two minutes for the Titans, but once the match settled into an arm wrestle, it was Sienna Yeo who scored a neat individual try for the Knights to lock up the scores.

Teagan Levi scored next for the Titans to continue her stellar debut NRLW season, before Evania Isa'ako touched down to give Gold Coast a 20-10 lead at the break.

Fane Finau revived Newcastle 10 minutes into the second half with a tackle-busting solo effort, but the Titans came back six minutes later through Indie Bostock.

From the ensuing kick-off, the Titans marched up the field, and Levi brushed off three would-be defenders to score her second try.

Isa'ako sealed her double minutes later, and while Taulelei-Siala scored with eight minutes to go for Newcastle, it was too little, too late.

AAP

World.title: Funding for prostate cancer charity redirected to McGrath Foundation
World.content:
Tens of thousands of men are diagnosed with prostate cancer in Australia every year.

Martin Fisk is one of them.

"I was experiencing extreme fatigue that I couldn't work out why, so I went to the GP and she ordered a bunch of tests," he said.

" Then I got the phone call that nobody wants to get. "

It was a diagnosis Mr Fisk had been dreading; both his father and father-in-law died from the disease.

He is now receiving a combination of hormone therapy, radiation and drug treatments — all tracked and monitored with regular biopsies, tests and scans.

Martin Fisk's father and father-in-law both died from prostate cancer. (ABC News: David Sciasci )

A specialist prostate cancer nurse helps to coordinate this vital yet complex care, while supporting Mr Fisk and his family in Canberra.

"I'm having three different treatments, they each have side effects, but they also interact with each other, and [my nurse] is across all of that," he said.

"When I have a symptom I can't explain, I can go to her."

'Specialist knowledge built over many years'

Prostate cancer accounts for 17 per cent of new cancer diagnoses, with one in five men at risk.

Prostate Cancer Foundation Australia (PCFA) provides specialist nurse positions in hospitals around the country, mostly funded by the federal government.

"We have many men in touch with us who are telling us they're alive today because of the support they received by prostate cancer specialist nurses," said PCFA director of nursing Sally Sara.

Sally Sara says some nurses have already told the foundation that they are looking for other positions. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor )

But federal funding for PCFA's nursing program will be moved to the McGrath Foundation from July next year, part of a wider shift to an "all-cancer" model.

"We have had a number of nurses in our network already approach us to tell us that they are looking for alternative positions," Ms Sara said.

" I have grave concerns for men out there in the community who are dependent on this specialist level of care. "

PCFA CEO Anne Savage says the foundation has "no issues with McGrath", but the change risks losing expertise built over time.

"[The nurses] are not interchangeable with the McGrath all-cancer service," she said.

"Their specialist knowledge, trusted clinical relationships, and deep understanding of prostate cancer have been built over many years."

Move towards all-cancer model

The government says the funding change is a continuation of its "all-cancer" model which has brought multiple disciplines into the McGrath Foundation.

In a statement, Special Envoy for Men's Health Dan Repacholi told the ABC that the transition would be planned to ensure patients "continue receiving care".

"Existing nurses will have the option to move across to McGrath, keeping their location, experience and patient relationships wherever possible," he said.

"If a nurse chooses not to transition, McGrath will recruit someone to fill that position."

In a statement, Dan Repacholi said the same level of funding for prostate cancer nurses would be maintained under the changes. (ABC News: Laurence Curson)

Last month the federal government announced that $46.5 million over five years — the equivalent to 60 full-time positions — would be moved to the McGrath Foundation.

The McGrath Foundation was founded in 2005 by former Australian cricketer Glenn McGrath following the death of his wife Jane from breast cancer.

Prostate cancer support groups Michael Platts panicked when he was diagnosed with prostate cancer. Now he wants to help others break through the stigma around the condition.

After initially raising money for breast cancer nurses, it now provides care for all cancer types.

It's developed the McGrath Model of Care which the foundation describes as "a national, evidence‑based framework shaped by real‑world nursing experience".

In recent years the Labor government has shifted its funding for 14 types of cancer from a range of individual charities and foundations to McGrath, representing tens of millions of dollars.

Mr Repacholi said the latest change "maintains the same level of funding", and all the money being moved to McGrath would be used for dedicated prostate cancer nursing.

He said that nurses wouldn't lose their specialist skills or practice.

"It's not a funding cut. The contract's simply moving from PCFA to McGrath as part of the national all-cancer nursing model," he said.

Foundation to pursue 'every available avenue'

PCFA says it will pursue "every available" avenue to protect its nursing services, including "parliamentary scrutiny and examination of our contractual and legal rights".

"This is not a dispute about funding, this is about the standard of care and the survival of Australian men impacted by prostate cancer," Ms Savage said.

Through fundraising and corporate sponsors, PCFA provides an extra 24 full time nurse positions beyond the 60 funded by the Commonwealth.

"The PCFA will retain responsibility for those positions, honour its existing agreements and continue raising funds for specialist prostate cancer nursing," Ms Savage said.

Ms Savage says the change to the "all-cancer" model risks losing nursing expertise that's been built over time. (Australian Story)

Despite being in the midst of his treatment, Mr Fisk is himself now raising money for prostate cancer, with more than $16,000 raised at last count.

Mr Fisk spent much of his working life in the community and charity sector, including running the mental health organisation Menslink for more than a decade, and is no stranger to raising money for charity.

He is taking part in PCFA's annual Long Run campaign, with funds raised going towards the specialist nursing care like he and his family are receiving.

"We have people from all over Canberra and, in fact, all around the world chipping in and donating with some amazing messages of support," Mr Fisk said.

"They make me cry, but they also make me a bit stronger to go out and help more people if I can."

Martin Fisk (centre) takes a walk with this wife Sandra Fisk (left) and friend Zebunnissa Khan (right) at Lake Burley Griffin. (ABC News: David Sciasci )

Mr Fisk says support provided by his nurse for his mental health has been just as important as his physical health.

"Having a cancer diagnosis and cancer treatment is a scary journey. [My nurse] is able to be there alongside [us]," he said.

"I want to make sure [nurses] are available not just to me, but for all the other prostate cancer patients that are coming in the future."

World.title: New social rental apartment building in Perth CBD underway
World.content:
The WA government will spend more than $100 million on a new 30-storey apartment building in the Perth CBD, which it says will ease the city's housing shortage.

Set to be built on Roe Street, adjacent to the Perth Arena, the project will include 174 one- and two-bedroom rentals, 139 of which will be used for affordable housing, with 35 for social housing, according to the government.

The building is expected to be completed by 2029.

The government said the project is one of 21 currently under construction across Western Australia, with a total of 1,500 apartments set to be made available.

A render of the social rental apartment building next to Perth Arena. (Supplied: Development WA)

Housing minister John Carey said the state government was "throwing everything" at accelerating housing supply across WA, with support from the federal government's Housing Australia Future Fund.

"Never have we seen in our state's history so many build-to-rent projects underway," Mr Carey said.

"These are the kinds of projects that we want … close to amenities, close to jobs.

Housing minister John Carey says he is hopeful the project will drive activity in the Perth CBD. (ABC News: Courtney Withers )

"Ultimately the aim is to enable more than 40 build-to-rent projects across WA, only made possible by the joint investment."

Build-to-rent projects are purpose-built for the long-term rental market.

They are typically large apartment complexes developed by private capital or super funds, with only two such developments currently operational in Perth.

WA's proposed build-to-rent push explained Perth was last year declared Australia's least affordable to rent in, and now the government has launched an election pitch geared around getting more long-term rental stock. Here's how it works.

This contrasts with traditional apartment complexes, which typically do not have a single owner.

Once constructed, the apartment will then be sold to a community housing provider, according to the government.

Mr Carey said it would then be up to that provider to set the rental price.

The ABC spoke to multiple providers, none of which had heard of the new apartment building.

New project welcomed

Anglicare WA chief executive Mark Glasson welcomed the announcement, saying any additional social and affordable housing stock was "sorely needed".

"Western Australia is in the midst of a housing crisis that is unprecedented in our history," Mr Glasson said.

Mark Glasson says he welcomes the new building project. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"Every day we talk to people on low incomes who are struggling to find and keep rentals in this market ... [they] are forced to make impossible decisions to stretch their budgets thinly enough to keep their rentals.

"These apartments will benefit people who are doing it toughest, who aren't seeing the benefits of WA's strong economy and who would struggle to get a toehold in the state's private rental market."

He urged the state government to continue its Rent Relief Program and ramp up construction efforts further.

World.title: Blues fail to capitalise on key moments, ruthless Roos extend AFLW unbeaten streak
World.content:
All dynasties eventually have to end. But North Melbourne’s AFLW team are clearly steadfast on remaining immortal for, well, for as long as possible.

On Sunday afternoon 4048 fans packed into a wind-whipped Arden Street Oval, to watch the all-conquering Kangaroos’ reign continue with a tight 10-point win over Carlton – their third-lowest winning margin since their unbeaten streak began after the 2023 grand final defeat.

North have continued their winning streak but other teams are closing in. Getty Images

The ever-dominant Kangaroos also played a draw early in their 2024 premiership season.

North have advanced to a record-extending 32st-consecutive victory. They faced a tough onslaught from Carlton defenders who dimmed the Roos’ typical fast attacking style and managed to keep the margin largely to about one goal.

Carlton’s Harriet Cordner. Getty Images

North coach Darren Crocker conceded the winning margin – the closest a team has come to the Kangaroos all year – was nail-bitingly tight, and said Carlton “threw everything at us”.

“There were lots of almost moments in that game where I thought that we were going to break the game open, but we... to Carlton’s credit, we just couldn’t,” he said.

“They made it, very hard for us to score, we were able to still get there, which was really pleasing.”

Irishwoman Erika O’Shea said the reigning premiers knew “Carlton was going to give it to us”, praising the Blues’ pressure and physicality.

“They’re a young team... they’re fast, and I suppose it was an exhausting game. It was very hot, but I suppose we love the challenge,” she said with a grin.

Carlton announced their intention to challenge the Roos within the opening seconds of the first quarter. The Blues defenders brought a high level of pressure and capitalised on some relieving marks, with Harriet Cordner leading the charge with four intercepts and one intercept mark by the end of the first quarter.

The Blues’ pressure limited Talia Randall to two behinds in the opening term but couldn’t stop Alice O’Loughlin from booting North’s first goal. But two consecutive goals from Nell Morris-Dalton and Lila Keck put Carlton in front during the second quarter, earning a wild cheer from the smattering of Blues supporters in the crowd.

But Randall quickly snatched the lead back with a perfect goal from 45m out, followed by another from Blaithin Bouge.

Carlton Lilly Goss had the job on last year’s best and fairest winner Ash Riddell, dulling the midfielder’s impact briefly. Goss and teammate Erone Fitzpatrick were also at the centre at one of the game’s best moments.

In the third term Goss swooped on the Sherrin and sprinted down the field, dodging a fierce tackle from O’Shea and booting the ball towards the goal. Fitzpatrick almost did a 360-degree turn, scooping the ball up and snapping arguably the best goal of the week in AFLW.

By three-quarter time, the rowdy North Melbourne crowd were noticeably quiet as Carlton sensed a rare opportunity to unseat the Roos. The Blues were within a goal and an animated Carlton coach Matthew Buck came down from the coach’s box to shout instructions from the boundary line.

Ultimately, it was a goalless final quarter with Carlton holding North to only two behinds. But Carlton failed to capitalise on key moments and North held on to win 4.9 (33) to 3.5 (23).

Post-match Buck said his message to the group at three-quarter time was about “continued belief”.

“We felt like we took a good step forward today in the way we want to play, and the way we want to play against a really strong team,” he said.

“You love playing against the best side, and clearly the Kangaroos being the best in the competition for a long time, and they were great against today. You have to beat them, like you have to beat them in all different areas of the ground.”

North Melbourne face Hawthorn next week and the week after have a highly anticipated clash against Melbourne – a match up that could be their biggest test.

Under the stewardship of new coach Tim Wilson, Melbourne remain undefeated in 2026 and are second on the ladder. The Demons face Carlton next week – a match up Crocker said he would be tuning in to.

World.title: How to endure your syntax terror
World.content:
“Reading this morning of the predicted demise of the world by AI, I wonder what the world would look like,” ponders Garry Thomas from Oatlands. “No work, little hope and continual breadlines where one would get bread, soup and a copy of the latest C8 to keep our morale up?”

“On a brighter note than dragonflies (C8) is the delight of fireflies up here,” says Suzanne Saunders of Jiggi. “Half a dozen or so is Christmas come early. Swarms would be brilliant.”

Noted head-turner Judy Bower of Burraneer is the latest to attest to a Sydney Bee Gees sighting (C8): “Many years ago I was walking towards the Chevron Hilton in Kings Cross with my mother, grandmother and great aunt. I was 15 at the time and who should walk past me but Barry Gibb. Naturally, I turned around after he had passed, and was very thrilled to see that he had done the same.”

A muso for years, that’s no fib.

You can tell by the cut of my jib.

A long time, and yet,

I can’t say that I’ve met,

Even one of the famed brothers Gibb.

We thank Jim Dewar of Davistown.

Trevor Townson of Leichhardt was just wondering: “Are Al Gore rhythms (C8) different from the ones used by the Trumpet Ministration that runs the White House?” Not sure, but the latter is pretty good at banging his own drum.

World.title: Resident slams ‘shocking’ road following death of motorbike rider who reportedly hit pothole
World.content:
Updated NationalVictoriaRoads Resident slams ‘shocking’ road following death of motorbike rider who reportedly hit pothole Roy Ward and Alexander Darling Updated September 13, 2026 — 8:45pm ,first published 6:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A 71-year-old man died after reportedly hitting a pothole on the Western Highway and crashing his motorcycle just outside the town of Beaufort on Sunday. Emergency services responded to the stretch of highway near Trawalla Road after the Ballarat man lost control of his motorcycle just before 12.50pm. Police confirmed he died at the scene and investigations are continuing. Potholes have become a flashpoint in the leadup to the Victorian state election on November 28. Getty The state of Victoria’s roads, particularly in regional and rural areas, has become a flashpoint in the lead-up to the state election in November. Potholes have caused delays, accidents and vehicle damage for thousands of voters. The Labor member for Ripon Martha Haylett, whose seat covers Trawalla, said she had been pushing the government to fix the roads “properly”.



“I am devastated by this news. My heart goes out to the victim’s family and loved ones,” Haylett said on Sunday. Editor's pick Roads The small holes making big news: An unscientific reckoning on Victoria’s roads “Our roads are not good enough, and I have been pushing the roads minister and others to begin repair works urgently. “Works started last week, but still have a way to go. No person should ever lose their life on our roads and that’s why we have to fix them, and do it properly.” Katherine, who asked for her surname not to be used, has lived in Trawalla for more than 30 years and said the stretch of highway between Ballarat and Beaufort had “dozens on dozens” of potholes.



“The road is shocking. We’ve had problems with that stretch for years, and even when they fix [the potholes] up they’re rough,” she said.



“They come along and fix the worst of them, but usually, they don’t work weekends. Ben Carroll recently promised to come along and fix all of these [potholes], but this road needs a major upgrade sooner rather than later. I don’t understand why we’re in this position, constantly faced with the dilemma of poor roads.” The road is shocking. We’ve had problems with that stretch for years, and even when they fix [the potholes] up they’re rough. Trawalla resident Katherine Katherine did not know which pothole the rider hit, but said both directions of the highway had their dangers. “There are two lanes, but you have to swap so often,” she said. “We used to be quite fearful of kangaroos, but now potholes are the danger.” Western Region MP Joe McCracken, whose upper house seat covers the area, expressed his frustration in an Instagram post on Sunday, calling on the government to do better.



“My condolences to the family and friends of this man - a very sad fatality. It is just awful and underscores the very real safety risks potholes pose to drivers,” McCracken wrote. Related Article Roads Almost half of Victoria’s roads in poor condition, as decline outpaces repairs A report released by the Victorian Auditor-General’s Office last week found 48 per cent of the state’s government-managed roads are in poor or very poor condition and decline is outpacing repairs. Shadow roads and road safety minister Danny O’Brien said fixing the state’s roads needed to be the government’s highest priority. “This is a terrible tragedy, and my heart goes out to the deceased and his family,” O’Brien said. “This is the saddest possible consequence to have come from the terrible state of Victorian roads, and it never should have come to this.



“A government website has claimed it has completed rehabilitation works in this area, but clearly any repair job hasn’t been sustainable, and it has had fatal consequences,” he said. “These potholes need to be fixed and fixed properly as a matter of urgency. It is time for action and this needs to be the highest priority now so that no more lives are lost on Victorian roads because of government neglect.” Premier Ben Carroll announced policies on potholes and road maintenance recently, and work is set to begin on fixing scores of potholes as the weather gets warmer. In August, this masthead reported on data gathered by citizen-reporting platform Snap Send Solve that showed reports of potholes and damaged roads increased more than 46 per cent to 37,482 in the year to August 16. A state government spokesperson expressed sympathy to the 71-year-old’s loved ones, and echoed police calls for video or information about the crash.



“Our thoughts are with the family and loved ones of those involved in this horrific tragedy,” the spokesperson said. “We thank the emergency services who responded to the scene and Victoria Police who are currently investigating.” Police have appealed for anyone with dashcam, CCTV footage or information about Sunday’s fatal crash to contact Crime Stoppers at crimestoppersvic.com.au or by calling 1800 333 000. To'o swoops as Panthers book prelim spot

World.title: Roosters go down but Nawaqanitawase magic breathes life into their season
World.content:
Analysis SportNRLNRL 2026 Roosters go down but Nawaqanitawase magic breathes life into their season Tom Decent September 13, 2026 — 8:06pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Three years ago, Mark Nawaqanitawase’s finest moment at CommBank Stadium came for the Wallabies against Argentina. Out on the wing and sensing a Pumas overlap, Nawaqanitawase backed himself, bolted out of the line, took an intercept and ran 95 metres to score in front of a sea of gold late in the match. It should have been enough for victory. But the Wallabies, under Eddie Jones and just months out from their fateful 2023 World Cup campaign in France, went on to lose at the death. Much like that Wallabies game, some more individual Nawaqanitawase magic wasn’t enough yesterday for the Roosters. But he and his mates from Bondi certainly breathed life back into their season despite a 19-12 defeat to Penrith.



Nawaqanitawase made a fresh case for his greatest individual moment on the CommBank Stadium turf on a day that ultimately belonged to Penrith. His intercept, juggle and regather centimetres off the turf in the 24th minute – before sprinting 40 metres to score a try – was athleticism at its finest and gave the Roosters belief they could cause a boilover and beat the minor premiers in their own backyard (sort of). Mark Nawaqanitawase scored to put the roosters ahead. Getty Images A Nathan Cleary field goal and an ordinary Hugo Savala pass late in the match that went to ground, leading to Brian To’o’s match-winning try, were the difference in the best game of the weekend. The Roosters, slight premiership favourites a few weeks ago and now staring down the barrell of five consecutive defeats, will have to do it the hard way from here.



Next week could be Nawaqanitawase’s last NRL match and the code will miss him dearly. There is always a degree of cynicism when someone from the 15-man game switches codes, but Nawaqanitawase’s first-half highlights reel was another reminder of his class. His try-saving tackle on Tom Jenkins and another intercept with the Roosters camped on their own line were influential plays that underlined his brilliance. Mark Nawaqanitawase tackles Thomas Jenkins. Getty Images Overall, this was a fabulous game of rugby league, featuring two quality teams who could well meet again on October 4. This week’s Cleary judiciary drama is exactly what this NRL finals series needed.



Long before Penrith sewed up their victory their hopes of a headline-free week evaporated with a brain fade when Cleary hit Savala’s leg as he kicked on. With 31 minutes remaining and scores locked at 12-12, Cleary returned to the field eager to make up for his error, trying not to think about the prospect of missing a finals football. His other headache could be a potential lower-leg injury. It was abundantly clear when Cleary ran back after his field goal that he was not 100 per cent. Loading As far as the crowd went, it was an underwhelming turnout on week one of the finals.



In the upper south-western stand of CommBank Stadium, a grand total of five fans were present at the beginning of the match. If only the Penrith and Roosters fans who thought better of turning up could have predicted the tense tussle that followed. With 28,152 showing up to watch Newcastle upset Souths at Allianz Stadium on Friday night and 17,429 rolling into the same venue for the Sharks and Cowboys 24 hours later and 22,148 for the Panthers-Roosters showdown, the NRL might need to consider cheaper tickets for these corresponding fixtures next year. The thousands of empty seats at marquee games would have AFL head honchos chuckling away. There was a bit of AFL about Liam Martin’s opening try as he leapt over Victor Radley and planted the ball down with great delight. Forwards aren’t supposed to move like that.



Spencer Leniu, fresh off his stoush with Souths enforcer Keaon Koloamatangi last week, took exception to Martin giving it to Savala after the Roosters playmaker missed a penalty on the stroke of half-time. Later, Leniu set his sights on Isaiah Papali’i. This game had plenty of spice. It was two heavyweight Sydney clubs trading blows, both desperate for a week off. Related Article NRL 2026 Sharks boss says it’s time to end ‘embarrassing’ stadium debate. Even if that means defeat One got its wish and the other will have to roll up its sleeves again next weekend. But with quiet confidence that halfback Sam Walker could return at some point this season from injury, the Roosters gave the competition reason to believe they can send Nawaqanitawase off a winner before he sails into the rugby sunset.

World.title: Police release CCTV in hunt for two men after Hamilton Hill shooting
World.content:
Updated NationalWACrime Police release CCTV in hunt for two men after Hamilton Hill shooting Indigo Lemay-Conway Updated September 13, 2026 — 7:38pm ,first published 10:03am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Police have released CCTV footage as they search for two men over a shooting in Perth’s southern suburbs on Sunday morning. Residents of Hamilton Hill were put into lockdown early on Sunday after a man was shot in the stomach in bushland near Owen Place. Loading Two men who are believed to be involved in the shooting remain on the run, but police say there is no risk to the public. Police were called about 4.35am after a 37-year-old was allegedly shot by two men dressed in black clothing and wearing face masks.



Police and St John WA responded and provided emergency first aid to the victim. Detective Brian Connelly, of the serious and organised crime division, said the shooting unfolded near the intersection of Yongka Road and Karda Way, before the victim and another man ran across Forrest Street towards Owen Place. The 38-year-old man was shot at a residence on Owen Place in Hamilton Hill. Andrew Du Connelly said a member of the public was alerted to the scene and provided emergency first aid. “It was a very short incident, it was over within a matter of seconds,” he said.



The man rushed to Royal Perth Hospital in a serious but stable condition. He has since undergone surgery for his injuries and is recovering in hospital. Related Article Crime ‘There’s no defence’: Man arrested over video of three-year-old steering car Connelly said offers believed the victim and his attackers were known to each other, and that there was no ongoing risk to the public. “We strongly suspect that they were known to each other, and the person that shot the victim knew the victim,” he said. “We’re confident in saying that it is a targeted attack at one individual, and we’re treating it as such.”



Police have since released CCTV from a nearby house showing the two men sought by police fleeing the area after the shooting. Earlier in the morning, people were told to stay away from the Hamilton Hill area and residents were instructed to lock their doors and windows and remain inside. Significant police resources were deployed to the scene and are conducting a thorough search of the area. Connelly said there was no information to suggest the shooting was related to tobacco wars or outlaw motorcycle gangs. Deputy Premier Rita Saffioti said the incident was “terrifying” for all those involved.



“It sounds terrifying the type of nature of what’s happened this morning ... but we need to get to the bottom of it and we need to arrest those two that are on the run,” she said on Sunday. Detectives want to speak to anyone who saw any suspicious vehicles or activity in the vicinity of Owen Place, or the surrounding bushland between 4am and 5am on Sunday. Anyone with information or CCTV is urged to contact Crime Stoppers.

World.title: ‘We want little boys to go and young men to return’: Scotch College’s bold vision for the next generation
World.content:
Special series NationalVictoriaSchools that excel ‘We want little boys to go and young men to return’: Scotch College’s bold vision for the next generation Bridie Smith September 13, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jason Potoi Andrew can still remember arriving at Scotch College for the first time. It was 1984, and he was touring the school that his father, David, had graduated from two decades earlier. The pair were soon approached by Ron “Chesty” Bond, a revered classics teacher and vice principal who worked at the school for close to four decades and was a favourite among generations of boys who gave him a nickname that stuck for life. Jason Potoi Andrew with his sons Austin and Maximus. Wayne Taylor “He came up to Dad and said, ‘Oh, David Andrew, I remember you. I taught you Latin’,” he says. “It was a nice moment.” It’s an example of what Scotch alumni, known as Old Boys, like to call the cardinal thread – an intangible link named after the distinctive shade of red in the school’s blazer and tartan that links the past with the present.



While outsiders might see it as a network founded on privilege, entitlement and affluence, for Potoi Andrew, connections aren’t made in boardrooms or clubs, but rather in interactions like the one his dad shared with “Chesty” Bond. “I wouldn’t say that going to Scotch has smoothed a path because things have changed a lot,” he says. “You’ve got to prove yourself.” Potoi Andrew’s sons Maximus and Austin had their names put down at birth, and became third-generation “Scotchies” when they ultimately joined the school. Again, the cardinal thread played its part. “I knew maybe two people when I started,” Maximus says. “But knowing that my dad came here, and my grandpa also came here, it was easy to find friends.”



Austin’s entry was similarly linked to his Scotch heritage, but he credits playing percussion in the school’s military band, an arm of the 142-year-old cadet corps, as his cardinal connection. “You learn more about the school and its history in cadets,” he says. “Things like what we did during World War I and about key figures like [General Sir John] Monash.” Scotch College’s Memorial Hall was built to honour students and staff who served in WWI and WWII. Wayne Taylor Having started at the school as an 11-year-old before graduating equal dux in 1881, Monash is a favoured son of Scotch. His bust, left breast laden with military medals, is displayed at reception, while Principal Dr Scott Marsh has a smaller version in his office. Other references to the school’s history and legacy are scattered across the 27-hectare Hawthorn campus, one of four owned by the college.



The $32 million science centre is named after former student and governor-general Sir Zelman Cowen while a plaque on the Cardinal Pavilion rowing shed on the banks of the Yarra River states it was opened by former school vice captain and later Liberal Party leader, Andrew Peacock. “The boys are aware they are part of something incredibly special,” Marsh says. Dr Scott Marsh became principal in 2023. Wayne Taylor “They are part of a school that has made incredible contributions to Australia and beyond.” Scotch does like to talk, modestly if possible, about its high-flying graduates. They include a prime minister, eight premiers, three governors-general and four High Court justices. And that’s before you get to collegians who have headed the navy, defence force, Reserve Bank, the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation, and universities, including Oxford.



The college’s full-time archivist Paul Mishura says alumni have received more top Order of Australia honours than any other school in Australia, and more than 70 Old Boys have been knighted. When asked where the school sees itself in the Melbourne private school hierarchy, Marsh says with a pause, “Well, because we value humility, we don’t like to say.” Moments later, he’s back on message. “We like to talk about how we develop good men of good character who will go and shape a better future,” Marsh says. “That’s what we like to talk about.”



Scotch’s strategic plan, developed over more than two years and released last year, frames the school as an institution focused on instilling character and fostering boys who aim high but keep their feet on the ground. At the most recent Young Old Boys of Scotch College (or YOBS) annual dinner in June, the school’s oldest Old Boy, 110-year-old Bill Morgan, spoke via a recorded message. The 1935 school captain, who played rugby for Victoria alongside Edward ‘Weary’ Dunlop, urged the YOBS to remember the lessons that went beyond the curriculum. “Give thanks to the teachers who helped create your character,” Morgan stressed.



The school’s strategic plan also outlines a desire to look past the “narrow goal of attaining an ATAR” because, it says, there is more to school than preparing students for university. (Though an honour board with the names of 31 Rhodes Scholars hangs to the right of the altar in the Memorial Hall.) Scotch’s median VCE study score has remained above the statewide median of 30 throughout the past decade, recording a high of 36 in 2017. For the past three years, it has sat on 34. Last year, three students achieved a perfect ATAR of 99.95, with 36 students recording an ATAR of 99 or above and a further 80 students scoring 95 or above. “We’re selective in that you’ve got to be able to afford over $40,000 for fees. Yes, I accept that. People always criticise me when I don’t say that. But academically we’re not selective at all,” Marsh says.



Growing up with Melbourne Founded by Scottish-born Presbyterian minister James Forbes in 1851 – the same year gold was discovered in Victoria and just 15 years after the foundation of Melbourne – Scotch College is the state’s oldest secondary college. “We’re selective in that you’ve got to be able to afford over $40,000 for fees... But academically we’re not selective at all.” Principal Dr Scott Marsh Its history has risen and fallen as the city cycled through boom and bust. Mass migration triggered by the gold rush grew the school and the city, with migrants who could travel unassisted being largely educated and literate. Scottish Presbyterians, in particular, prized literacy because you couldn’t be a good Christian if you couldn’t read the Bible. “Right from the beginning you’ve got a mindset in Melbourne that if you’re middle class, you don’t go to state schools,” retired Melbourne University sociologist emeritus professor Janet McCalman says.



But when the 1890s and 1930s depressions hammered Melbourne, Scotch enrolments were hit too, according to McCalman’s book, Journeyings, on Melbourne’s middle class. However, while not as pronounced now, McCalman says ‘being Scotch’ was a currency that was traded and treasured even when times were tough. Initially built in East Melbourne on land gifted to the Presbyterian church by government, Scotch was known as the Melbourne Academy until 1855 and colloquially by some as “the green door school”. It was small and existed without a motto, coat of arms or uniform. “There was no need to distinguish the school from others because there was no interschool sport at that time,” Mishura says.



There was however a game played in 1858 between Scotch and its nemesis Melbourne Grammar which is considered the first recorded AFL match. The game spanned three consecutive Saturdays and ended in a draw, with each side kicking one goal. Officiating was a Scotch chemistry and natural sciences teacher John Macadam – after whom the macadamia nut is named. Between 1916 and 1926, Scotch moved to its Hawthorn hilltop. When the school bought the property, it was understood to be 20.64 hectares – but it ultimately turned out to be 27 hectares. The boundaries have since contracted to the south and expanded to the north. The school’s footprint extended northwards after the college bought all 12 houses on Morrison Street, with some demolished and others used as the school’s museum and Old Boys’ Association headquarters. To the south, a narrow strip of land next to three of Scotch’s five ovals was compulsorily acquired in 2008 when CityLink was widened.



In 2013, the then-Napthine government paid $5.4 million for the sliver of land, valued at just over $1 million by Victoria’s Valuer-General. Old Boy and former state Liberal Party MP David Kemp headed the taskforce to ensure the school got what it considered fair compensation, a campaign that included Supreme Court legal action initiated by Scotch. Scotch was again in the headlines in 2015 when it revealed former students had suffered abuse on school grounds. Several historical claims were settled, most involving sexual abuse dating back to the 1950s and 1960s. Earlier this year, one former student launched legal action over allegations of abuse that occurred during a school camp on Phillip Island in the 1970s. More recently, the school attracted attention over a controversial decision to invite an anti-abortion activist to speak to year 11 students, for which Marsh apologised.



A measure of a school’s socio-educational advantage is known as the ICSEA score which is calculated using parents’ occupation and level of education attainment – as well as the remoteness of the school and the percentage of Indigenous students, which for Scotch is 1 per cent. Data from Australia’s curriculum and assessment authority shows that an ICSEA score of 1000 is the national average score. At Scotch, it is 1188, with just over three-quarters of families in the top quarter of socio-educational advantage. The Scotch community raised half of the $40 million it cost to build the Sir Zelman Cowen Centre for Science. Wayne Taylor Like all schools, Scotch receives state and federal government funding. The most recent data shows that in 2024 it received $6.83 million from the federal government, while the state government provided $1.99 million. The active network of Old Boys and current families can also raise sizable funds at short notice.



When Cyclone Fina hit Tiwi College, Scotch’s partner school on Melville Island, last November, the remote boarding school of 77 students was left with flooded boarding houses and classrooms with collapsed ceilings and shattered windows. Within 24 hours, Scotch had raised $522,000. “It’s a very generous, humble community, despite the labels that are thrown at it,” Marsh says. The school’s foundation, which oversees fundraising, scholarships, infrastructure spending and programs generated from bequests and donations, spent more than $2.4 million on scholarships and bursaries last year alone. And with a surplus of almost $4.9 million, it can afford to dream big.



Speaking at a gathering earlier this year, president and Old Boy Paul Aberdeen pondered what future contributions the foundation could make to the school, which turns 175 this year. “It’s fun to dream, isn’t it?” he mused. “We could be talking about new grandstands and sporting facilities. New buildings. Finally bringing the Hambledon Road area to life after patiently buying up those 25 houses over the years. Scotch College owns more than 20 homes on Hambledon Road which it has purchased as part of future expansion plans. Wayne Taylor “We’re even dreaming about new institutes and facilities you’d normally only find at a university.”



The Hambledon Road houses Aberdeen referred to are residential properties to the north of the school that have been purchased over decades and are key to ambitious expansion plans the school has for its main campus. Another two properties on Fordholm Road, purchased in 2004 and 2022 for a combined $5.65 million, have already been repurposed. The homes were demolished, and the land is now a staff car park. The school is also poised to sign a $60 million deal to buy a property just down the hill on Glenferrie Road, Kooyong, from Vision Australia – an acquisition all the more satisfying because Scotch outbid long-term rival and neighbour St Kevin’s College. The deal comes three years after Scotch bought Fairhaven, a 175-hectare waterfront property bordering a UNESCO biosphere reserve in Mallacoota. It will become Scotch’s third outdoor education campus after an 80-hectare Healesville plot and a sizable beachfront property at Cowes on Phillip Island.



Like its Hawthorn headquarters, the Healesville and Cowes boundaries have expanded over decades with the purchase of neighbouring properties. However, Fairhaven will be the centrepiece. According to Aberdeen, it will be Scotch’s answer to Geelong Grammar’s prized Timbertop campus – but with an ocean view. “It’s where we want little boys to go and young men to return,” Marsh says. “I think in our society we have an epidemic of 20, 30, 40, even 50-year-old little boys; men who haven’t taken on the responsibility of being a man.” Fairhaven, a 175-acre waterfront property near Mallacoota, will become part of the year 9 outdoor education program.



Marsh was there last year when a pilot group of year 9 students visited and, as a man whose Christmas holidays are spent camping with his family, it made an impression on him. “Out of the 23 or 24 boys we had there, I think only three or four had ever been in a tent,” he says. Having led the school since 2023, Scotch College is not a world Marsh was born into. Where his alma mater had one school oval, Scotch currently has five. Arriving as both a runner-up and an outsider, his name was in the leadership mix when the 17-member college council appointed Matthew Leeds as the school’s 10th principal. But before Leeds could take up the post, a whistleblower revealed a complaint alleging misconduct was made against him in 2017 at his former school, Geelong Grammar. Two separate investigations by Geelong Grammar and the Victorian Institute of Teaching did not substantiate the claims made against Leeds.

World.title: New school playgrounds, ovals to be opened to public: Find your nearest new open space
World.content:
Residents in Sydney’s crowded urban fringe suburbs with little space to play will be given access to new playgrounds and ovals connected to public schools being built in the area, in a stopgap measure to increase liveability in the growth areas.

The NSW Labor government will on Monday announce plans to extend the state’s Share Our Space program to all new schools due to open over the next two years. The program, launched by the Coalition government as a trial in the 2017 summer holidays, has grown in recent years to allow residents to access green space and sporting facilities across 250 public schools in the state – either during holidays or after school hours.

Year 9 and 10 students Keya Patel, Ayo Okeowo and Jesnoor Khehra play basketball at Melonba High School, in Sydney’s north-west. The school has opened its basketball court to the public. James Brickwood

Ten new schools in western Sydney, and 10 more across the state, will automatically be added to the program when they open in 2027 and 2028, Deputy Premier and Minister for Western Sydney Prue Car will announce.

“Giving local families access to space and facilities in schools that would otherwise be locked up after school, over weekends and during school holidays, is something that just makes sense,” she said. “We have worked hard to find timely solutions for those communities, especially in Sydney’s north-west and south-west who have felt left behind, and expanding Share Our Space is an important part of this.”

World.title: Blues fail to capitalise on key moments, ruthless Roos extend AFLW unbeaten streak
World.content:
All dynasties eventually have to end. But North Melbourne’s AFLW team are clearly steadfast on remaining immortal for, well, for as long as possible.

On Sunday afternoon 4048 fans packed into a wind-whipped Arden Street Oval, to watch the all-conquering Kangaroos’ reign continue with a tight 10-point win over Carlton – their third-lowest winning margin since their unbeaten streak began after the 2023 grand final defeat.

North have continued their winning streak but other teams are closing in. Getty Images

The ever-dominant Kangaroos also played a draw early in their 2024 premiership season.

North have advanced to a record-extending 32st-consecutive victory. They faced a tough onslaught from Carlton defenders who dimmed the Roos’ typical fast attacking style and managed to keep the margin largely to about one goal.

Carlton’s Harriet Cordner. Getty Images

North coach Darren Crocker conceded the winning margin – the closest a team has come to the Kangaroos all year – was nail-bitingly tight, and said Carlton “threw everything at us”.

“There were lots of almost moments in that game where I thought that we were going to break the game open, but we... to Carlton’s credit, we just couldn’t,” he said.

“They made it, very hard for us to score, we were able to still get there, which was really pleasing.”

Irishwoman Erika O’Shea said the reigning premiers knew “Carlton was going to give it to us”, praising the Blues’ pressure and physicality.

“They’re a young team... they’re fast, and I suppose it was an exhausting game. It was very hot, but I suppose we love the challenge,” she said with a grin.

Carlton announced their intention to challenge the Roos within the opening seconds of the first quarter. The Blues defenders brought a high level of pressure and capitalised on some relieving marks, with Harriet Cordner leading the charge with four intercepts and one intercept mark by the end of the first quarter.

The Blues’ pressure limited Talia Randall to two behinds in the opening term but couldn’t stop Alice O’Loughlin from booting North’s first goal. But two consecutive goals from Nell Morris-Dalton and Lila Keck put Carlton in front during the second quarter, earning a wild cheer from the smattering of Blues supporters in the crowd.

But Randall quickly snatched the lead back with a perfect goal from 45m out, followed by another from Blaithin Bouge.

Carlton Lilly Goss had the job on last year’s best and fairest winner Ash Riddell, dulling the midfielder’s impact briefly. Goss and teammate Erone Fitzpatrick were also at the centre at one of the game’s best moments.

In the third term Goss swooped on the Sherrin and sprinted down the field, dodging a fierce tackle from O’Shea and booting the ball towards the goal. Fitzpatrick almost did a 360-degree turn, scooping the ball up and snapping arguably the best goal of the week in AFLW.

By three-quarter time, the rowdy North Melbourne crowd were noticeably quiet as Carlton sensed a rare opportunity to unseat the Roos. The Blues were within a goal and an animated Carlton coach Matthew Buck came down from the coach’s box to shout instructions from the boundary line.

Ultimately, it was a goalless final quarter with Carlton holding North to only two behinds. But Carlton failed to capitalise on key moments and North held on to win 4.9 (33) to 3.5 (23).

Post-match Buck said his message to the group at three-quarter time was about “continued belief”.

“We felt like we took a good step forward today in the way we want to play, and the way we want to play against a really strong team,” he said.

“You love playing against the best side, and clearly the Kangaroos being the best in the competition for a long time, and they were great against today. You have to beat them, like you have to beat them in all different areas of the ground.”

North Melbourne face Hawthorn next week and the week after have a highly anticipated clash against Melbourne – a match up that could be their biggest test.

Under the stewardship of new coach Tim Wilson, Melbourne remain undefeated in 2026 and are second on the ladder. The Demons face Carlton next week – a match up Crocker said he would be tuning in to.

World.title: How to endure your syntax terror
World.content:
“Reading this morning of the predicted demise of the world by AI, I wonder what the world would look like,” ponders Garry Thomas from Oatlands. “No work, little hope and continual breadlines where one would get bread, soup and a copy of the latest C8 to keep our morale up?”

“On a brighter note than dragonflies (C8) is the delight of fireflies up here,” says Suzanne Saunders of Jiggi. “Half a dozen or so is Christmas come early. Swarms would be brilliant.”

Noted head-turner Judy Bower of Burraneer is the latest to attest to a Sydney Bee Gees sighting (C8): “Many years ago I was walking towards the Chevron Hilton in Kings Cross with my mother, grandmother and great aunt. I was 15 at the time and who should walk past me but Barry Gibb. Naturally, I turned around after he had passed, and was very thrilled to see that he had done the same.”

A muso for years, that’s no fib.

You can tell by the cut of my jib.

A long time, and yet,

I can’t say that I’ve met,

Even one of the famed brothers Gibb.

We thank Jim Dewar of Davistown.

Trevor Townson of Leichhardt was just wondering: “Are Al Gore rhythms (C8) different from the ones used by the Trumpet Ministration that runs the White House?” Not sure, but the latter is pretty good at banging his own drum.

World.title: Resident slams ‘shocking’ road following death of motorbike rider who reportedly hit pothole
World.content:
Updated NationalVictoriaRoads Resident slams ‘shocking’ road following death of motorbike rider who reportedly hit pothole Roy Ward and Alexander Darling Updated September 13, 2026 — 8:45pm ,first published 6:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A 71-year-old man died after reportedly hitting a pothole on the Western Highway and crashing his motorcycle just outside the town of Beaufort on Sunday. Emergency services responded to the stretch of highway near Trawalla Road after the Ballarat man lost control of his motorcycle just before 12.50pm. Police confirmed he died at the scene and investigations are continuing. Potholes have become a flashpoint in the leadup to the Victorian state election on November 28. Getty The state of Victoria’s roads, particularly in regional and rural areas, has become a flashpoint in the lead-up to the state election in November. Potholes have caused delays, accidents and vehicle damage for thousands of voters. The Labor member for Ripon Martha Haylett, whose seat covers Trawalla, said she had been pushing the government to fix the roads “properly”.



“I am devastated by this news. My heart goes out to the victim’s family and loved ones,” Haylett said on Sunday. Editor's pick Roads The small holes making big news: An unscientific reckoning on Victoria’s roads “Our roads are not good enough, and I have been pushing the roads minister and others to begin repair works urgently. “Works started last week, but still have a way to go. No person should ever lose their life on our roads and that’s why we have to fix them, and do it properly.” Katherine, who asked for her surname not to be used, has lived in Trawalla for more than 30 years and said the stretch of highway between Ballarat and Beaufort had “dozens on dozens” of potholes.



“The road is shocking. We’ve had problems with that stretch for years, and even when they fix [the potholes] up they’re rough,” she said.



“They come along and fix the worst of them, but usually, they don’t work weekends. Ben Carroll recently promised to come along and fix all of these [potholes], but this road needs a major upgrade sooner rather than later. I don’t understand why we’re in this position, constantly faced with the dilemma of poor roads.” The road is shocking. We’ve had problems with that stretch for years, and even when they fix [the potholes] up they’re rough. Trawalla resident Katherine Katherine did not know which pothole the rider hit, but said both directions of the highway had their dangers. “There are two lanes, but you have to swap so often,” she said. “We used to be quite fearful of kangaroos, but now potholes are the danger.” Western Region MP Joe McCracken, whose upper house seat covers the area, expressed his frustration in an Instagram post on Sunday, calling on the government to do better.



“My condolences to the family and friends of this man - a very sad fatality. It is just awful and underscores the very real safety risks potholes pose to drivers,” McCracken wrote. Related Article Roads Almost half of Victoria’s roads in poor condition, as decline outpaces repairs A report released by the Victorian Auditor-General’s Office last week found 48 per cent of the state’s government-managed roads are in poor or very poor condition and decline is outpacing repairs. Shadow roads and road safety minister Danny O’Brien said fixing the state’s roads needed to be the government’s highest priority. “This is a terrible tragedy, and my heart goes out to the deceased and his family,” O’Brien said. “This is the saddest possible consequence to have come from the terrible state of Victorian roads, and it never should have come to this.



“A government website has claimed it has completed rehabilitation works in this area, but clearly any repair job hasn’t been sustainable, and it has had fatal consequences,” he said. “These potholes need to be fixed and fixed properly as a matter of urgency. It is time for action and this needs to be the highest priority now so that no more lives are lost on Victorian roads because of government neglect.” Premier Ben Carroll announced policies on potholes and road maintenance recently, and work is set to begin on fixing scores of potholes as the weather gets warmer. In August, this masthead reported on data gathered by citizen-reporting platform Snap Send Solve that showed reports of potholes and damaged roads increased more than 46 per cent to 37,482 in the year to August 16. A state government spokesperson expressed sympathy to the 71-year-old’s loved ones, and echoed police calls for video or information about the crash.



“Our thoughts are with the family and loved ones of those involved in this horrific tragedy,” the spokesperson said. “We thank the emergency services who responded to the scene and Victoria Police who are currently investigating.” Police have appealed for anyone with dashcam, CCTV footage or information about Sunday’s fatal crash to contact Crime Stoppers at crimestoppersvic.com.au or by calling 1800 333 000.
