World.title: Roosters go down but Nawaqanitawase magic breathes life into their season
World.content:
Analysis SportNRLNRL 2026 Roosters go down but Nawaqanitawase magic breathes life into their season Tom Decent September 13, 2026 — 8:06pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Three years ago, Mark Nawaqanitawase’s finest moment at CommBank Stadium came for the Wallabies against Argentina. Out on the wing and sensing a Pumas overlap, Nawaqanitawase backed himself, bolted out of the line, took an intercept and ran 95 metres to score in front of a sea of gold late in the match. It should have been enough for victory. But the Wallabies, under Eddie Jones and just months out from their fateful 2023 World Cup campaign in France, went on to lose at the death. Much like that Wallabies game, some more individual Nawaqanitawase magic wasn’t enough yesterday for the Roosters. But he and his mates from Bondi certainly breathed life back into their season despite a 19-12 defeat to Penrith.



Nawaqanitawase made a fresh case for his greatest individual moment on the CommBank Stadium turf on a day that ultimately belonged to Penrith. His intercept, juggle and regather centimetres off the turf in the 24th minute – before sprinting 40 metres to score a try – was athleticism at its finest and gave the Roosters belief they could cause a boilover and beat the minor premiers in their own backyard (sort of). Mark Nawaqanitawase scored to put the roosters ahead. Getty Images A Nathan Cleary field goal and an ordinary Hugo Savala pass late in the match that went to ground, leading to Brian To’o’s match-winning try, were the difference in the best game of the weekend. The Roosters, slight premiership favourites a few weeks ago and now staring down the barrell of five consecutive defeats, will have to do it the hard way from here.



Next week could be Nawaqanitawase’s last NRL match and the code will miss him dearly. There is always a degree of cynicism when someone from the 15-man game switches codes, but Nawaqanitawase’s first-half highlights reel was another reminder of his class. His try-saving tackle on Tom Jenkins and another intercept with the Roosters camped on their own line were influential plays that underlined his brilliance. Mark Nawaqanitawase tackles Thomas Jenkins. Getty Images Overall, this was a fabulous game of rugby league, featuring two quality teams who could well meet again on October 4. This week’s Cleary judiciary drama is exactly what this NRL finals series needed.



Long before Penrith sewed up their victory their hopes of a headline-free week evaporated with a brain fade when Cleary hit Savala’s leg as he kicked on. With 31 minutes remaining and scores locked at 12-12, Cleary returned to the field eager to make up for his error, trying not to think about the prospect of missing a finals football. His other headache could be a potential lower-leg injury. It was abundantly clear when Cleary ran back after his field goal that he was not 100 per cent. Loading As far as the crowd went, it was an underwhelming turnout on week one of the finals.



In the upper south-western stand of CommBank Stadium, a grand total of five fans were present at the beginning of the match. If only the Penrith and Roosters fans who thought better of turning up could have predicted the tense tussle that followed. With 28,152 showing up to watch Newcastle upset Souths at Allianz Stadium on Friday night and 17,429 rolling into the same venue for the Sharks and Cowboys 24 hours later and 22,148 for the Panthers-Roosters showdown, the NRL might need to consider cheaper tickets for these corresponding fixtures next year. The thousands of empty seats at marquee games would have AFL head honchos chuckling away. There was a bit of AFL about Liam Martin’s opening try as he leapt over Victor Radley and planted the ball down with great delight. Forwards aren’t supposed to move like that.



Spencer Leniu, fresh off his stoush with Souths enforcer Keaon Koloamatangi last week, took exception to Martin giving it to Savala after the Roosters playmaker missed a penalty on the stroke of half-time. Later, Leniu set his sights on Isaiah Papali’i. This game had plenty of spice. It was two heavyweight Sydney clubs trading blows, both desperate for a week off. Related Article NRL 2026 Sharks boss says it’s time to end ‘embarrassing’ stadium debate. Even if that means defeat One got its wish and the other will have to roll up its sleeves again next weekend. But with quiet confidence that halfback Sam Walker could return at some point this season from injury, the Roosters gave the competition reason to believe they can send Nawaqanitawase off a winner before he sails into the rugby sunset.

World.title: Wild conspiracies are not good for democracy
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Wild conspiracies are not good for democracy September 13, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Badiucao To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. ONE NATION Neil Mitchell is right, (“Four things Carroll and Wilson must do to combat One Nation”, 13/9) the major parties have not been listening to the concerns of voters for years.

The Liberal and National parties have been engaged in redundant culture wars – climate, gender, Australian history – the latest being the Ben Roberts-Smith brouhaha. Labor has largely been in the grip of vested interests – the gambling, fossil-fuel and development industries just to name a few.

The problem I have with this article is “this party gives … voters hope”. Based on what?

Conspiracy theories – the 15-minute city is about bureaucratic control, climate change is a United Nations plot, three-word slogans double as policies reflecting largely their billionaire backers’ interests, Nazi infiltration into membership, contradictory statements … I could go on.

The problem is when some in One Nation peddle what are fringe, debunked theories and ideas, they give them legitimacy.

Attracting voters based on misinformation and wild conspiracies is not good for democracy.

Craig Horne, Fitzroy North Independents good for democracy, too

While I have never been a fan of Neil Mitchell, his analysis of the current state of politics is on the mark.

However, Mitchell and other commentators make an omission, namely the role of community independents in providing answers to our state and country’s woes.

Driven by the scarce commodity of political integrity and real-life experiences beyond a political party, their current presence in Canberra has offered many solutions to problems the major parties have failed to address: gambling, education, health, AI, climate, the economy and challenges from overseas.

The Liberals still need a viable leader, clarity in values and invigorating policies. The Labor Party has squandered its opportunity for ″⁣great″⁣ reform.

The Greens fail to capitalise on their unique opportunities to effect change through intransigence.

None of these parties truly listens to us Australians. Mitchell indicates that One Nation is stepping into the breach.

However, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, with her simplistic populist views, is offering a range of ill-considered and dangerously divisive policies.

The large number of community independents on the crossbench in Canberra were elected because they listen and formulate their policies based on the direct input of their constituents and actual evidence. Their debate is civil and positive. Real democracy at work.

It is about time the media spent more time examining the real contributions and differences community independents can make to our country.

Jennifer Quigley, Balwyn



Giving disengaged voters hope

Neil Mitchell’s thoughtful views on how One Nation’s rise in voter support is having a beneficial effect on Victorian politics is timely. He refreshingly doesn’t refer to ″⁣Howard’s battlers″⁣ or ″⁣Tony’s tradies″⁣ as being the presumed crass, unthinking voters for Pauline Hanson, yet his ″⁣rednecks″⁣ reference may preclude them from his astute observation: ″⁣The party has given genuine and decent disengaged voters hope.″⁣

And I would add, for many an opportunity to vote in a strategic way, perhaps only the once, for One Nation so as to scare the political life out of Labor.

If it takes removing the opprobrium from voting for One Nation by it becoming a ″⁣genuine″⁣ decision, so be it.

Voters have been ignored for years by successive Labor premiers, and Ben Carroll’s hurried proposals to clear up the past mistakes underlines some of the neglect of potholes on Victoria’s roads.

This falls into laughable category of government if it didn’t have such serious consequences.

Des Files, Brunswick THE FORUM Easy to be hard

Easy to be proud. Easy to say no. OK, I’m a Boomer. But this much I know: our public discourse is in the gutter. No, we are not calling Andrew Hastie a traitor – it’s just satire, just a meme.

Deep in our hearts, we know the truth. These are tough times. Discontent is rife. We face many challenges, one of the biggest among them being the choice between grace and the gutter.

Don’t like the mainstream parties? Seek out an independent with a modicum of decency. That’ll do. There is so precious little of it these days.

Tony Newport, Hillwood, Tas Saying no to drugs

Pauline Hanson defends her Victorian One Nation leader’s past drug use well into his twenties, perhaps thirties, by asking us ‘Who in this country possibly has not tried drugs?’ (‘Hanson gives her support: Who has not tried drugs?’, 10/9).

Well, up goes my hand, unless you are referring to a nice glass or two of sparkling wine or a cheeky chardonnay. Drugs such as speed, amphetamines, ecstasy and marijuana? No way. Guess this means I’m not cut out to be a One Nation supporter, thank goodness.

Robyn Westwood, Heidelberg Heights Freedom when it suits

Opposition communications spokesperson Senator Sarah Henderson is using freedom of speech to justify the Coalition’s opposition to Labor’s digital care bill. However, the senator has only ever appeared interested in freedom of speech when it aligns with her own views.

I recall her maligning anti-genocide protesters as antisemitic, congratulating the Adelaide Writers’ Week for cancelling the appearance of human rights (and Palestinian) advocate Randa Abdel-Fattah, calling for police to investigate students protesting against One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, demanding ABC Americas editor John Lyons be ″⁣shut down″⁣, and demanding an inquiry into the ABC’s ″⁣impartiality failures.

Henderson might believe ″⁣freedom of speech is precious and must be protected at all costs″⁣, but her actions craft an entirely different narrative.

Neil Hudson, East Melbourne



We need AI rules

The recent article in The Age about AI “agents” escaping their “sandbox” parameters, and acting in a semi-autonomous manner, together with Michael Koziol’s article, “Could kill us all” (10/9), highlighting the serious concerns of Anthropic operatives about the potential for harm to humanity with increasing AI autonomy, constitute dire warnings and justifiable alarm about the speed and direction of this technology.

These, and other similar concerns from respected distinguished experts in the field, such as Geoffrey Hinton, appear to be ignored by the multibillion-dollar AI tech industry and governments eager to profit by hosting them.

By and large, the prevailing narrative is that AI will transform civilisation for the better. There seems to be far less focus on how to control AI before it controls us. It is not alarmist to present the real potential risks of an uncontrollable, cataclysmic event, and to attempt to establish some form of international consensus whereby this technology can be controlled.

An analogy could be the international effort to control and prevent the proliferation of nuclear weapons.

Responsibility to control AI cannot be allowed to reside solely with the companies who reap huge profits from this technology. So far, there is little evidence of government policy to address the issue.

Leslie Chester, Brighton Tea with a robot?

I have become alarmed by the infiltration of AI into our everyday lives. I am horrified that data centres are springing up like mushrooms on our east coast without a full evaluation of their consequences for our country and our people.

There seems to be a headlong rush to join this possible menace in case we miss out on financial gains. They are taking up farmland where we could grow food and land to build homes. Building permits seem to be given out willy nilly without a cohesive strategy or caution about where this will

all lead. At the micro level, The Age on Saturday was chockers with Harvey Norman s.

Alarmingly to me, seven pages are given over to promoting the sale of robotic lawn mowers, pool cleaners and window cleaners. At a time of rising cost of living and unemployment, this money could be better used to hire people to do these jobs.

You can actually have a chat and a cup of tea with these people. Kathryn Anne Feather, Aireys Inlet

Wrecking the system

Economic principles demanding maximum growth and productivity were developed in the late 1700s, when European population pressures were the imperatives for global imperialism. But now, when there are no more indigenous populations left to slaughter, or land to steal to fulfill these principles, they are still the only thing on offer.

Climate change is becoming catastrophic, governments can no longer guarantee jobs or infrastructure, resources are become scarcer and more expensive, inequality is massive and growing and productivity is a joke because rather than adding to the common wealth, it’s either seeking to recover from existing problems, making useless trinkets, or mostly, adding to the wealth of the already ultra-rich.

You don’t need a degree to work this out and aspirational advertising only rubs salt in the wounds.

Given that it would be the same whoever is in power, wrecking the system is becoming seen as the only option where disruptive change can happen.

John Laurie, Riddells Creek Superannuation benefit

Mollie Muroi’s thoughtful article (“One Nation’s super access policy is a thought bubble”, 9/12) touches on how our superannuation system reduces the cost of the age pension.

What also needs to be explored is the tax concessions that encourage investment in superannuation, and what these concessions cost compared to the cost of the age pension. Federal Treasury has predicted that the cost of these tax breaks will overtake the cost of the pension by around 2040.

Given that more than two-thirds of super tax breaks go to the top 20 per cent of earners, who would not have qualified for the pension anyway, the current system appears to be unnecessarily wasteful. A review could both benefit Treasury’s bottom line, and make superannuation cheaper and fairer.

Jan Lacey, North Melbourne Bleak in Boroondara

Another 65,000 homes in Boroondara by 2051? We’re already struggling with increased traffic and parking. Five new builds in our street are built boundary to boundary, with massive underground garages affecting the water table and not a tree to be seen. We’re facing a climate crisis and gardens and green spaces are more important than ever. The future looks bleak.

Belinda Burke, Hawthorn For the record

The 1960s exhibition at the Old Treasury Building Museum “Swinging Sixties” includes an image of me burning my draft card in 1966. While it is ironic that political protest is now deemed suitable material for a museum, the irony is doubled by the fact that this iconic photograph by The Age photographer was not published until 40 years after the event which itself went unreported by The Age, despite being the first draft card burning in Melbourne.

Protests were, in fact, rare in 1966 (though not in the years that followed). Protests are much more frequent today, but most of the media still regard fashions at the Melbourne Cup as more newsworthy than anti-war protests and efforts to repress them.

Andy Blunden, Brunswick



Entitled cyclists

For so many years now, I have walked the public paths. I have come to the conclusion that cyclists live in a totally different world to the rest of us. There are multiple signs on public paths advising ″⁣ring the bell″⁣, ″⁣warn when passing″⁣, ″⁣walkers have priority over wheels″⁣ and to what effect?

Today, I was passed multiple times with no bell, and twice made contact from a cyclist with no apology. A group of cyclists coming the other way forced me off the walking track as they would not cease riding three, yes three, abreast and I heard an under the breath “out of the way”.

If cyclists wish to have the general public stop thinking about cyclists as entitled, privileged inconsiderate people then say hello as you approach us, ring your bell or call ″⁣passing″⁣ as you come behind us rather than have us jump out of our skin as we hear you laugh when passing. And, let me not mention the time my dog was hit by a cyclist who did not stop or apologise

David Raymond, Doncaster East See you next year

The San Francisco 49’ers – they came, they saw, they conquered.

They spent a full week climatising, were generous with their time amongst the public, and made many fans.

The Los Angeles Rams, in their ‘wisdom’ chose to fly in about 25 hours before game time. They were soundly beaten 27-7. They flew out.

It was a wonderful event for Melbourne and was an overwhelming success. I still don’t understand the game, but hope it returns next year.

Geoff Lipton, Caulfield Nth Lord Trump arise

So Donald Trump, who loves to watch a good fight, now wants a united Ireland.

It’s time King Charles confers a title on his great admirer. How about “Lord of misrule”?

Jayne Lilley, Torquay AND ANOTHER THING One Nation

Neil Mitchell’s assertion that “One Nation’s rise is good for democracy” (13/9) reminds me of the apocryphal stories about surgery in the 19th century where surgeons would boast: “The procedure went incredibly well; unfortunately, the patient died”.

Richard Jamont, Williamstown



Neil Mitchell describes One Nation as giving “genuine and decent disengaged voters hope”. Wasn’t that the aim of the community independent movement?

Sarah Russell, Mt Martha How do you know a politician is telling the truth when asked if they’ve taken recreational drugs? They answer: ″⁣I can’t remember.″⁣

Patrick Alilovic, Pascoe Vale South Furthermore

It seems that King Charles, who is head of the Church of England, is unaware of the parable of the prodigal son. Bill Burke, Hawthorn Re the manosphere: My mother always reminded me, ″⁣handsome is as handsome does″⁣. Think about it. She was right, of course.

Kate Read, Canterbury Perhaps parents should think less about their own desires about going to gigs with their toddlers and more about the impact on their child who has to wear noise-cancelling headphones in a very strange environment.

Ingrid Rodger, Williamstown



When the ship sinks, Donald Trump will not go with it: he has his lifeboat always ready. But there will be no room in it for colleagues, supporters or relatives. He needs all the room for his luggage.

Rob Attrill, Balwyn North If the letters, ″⁣ap″⁣, in the Trumpapaloosa nickname for the US Republican mid-term convention was removed, the result would more than aptly describe the current the US president.

Grey Barnden, Drysdale Finally

In regard to dogs biting people (″⁣Huge spike in dog bites - and most are from pets″⁣, 13/9), some simple advice - don’t buy a Jack Russell.

Dennis Fitzgerald, Box Hill The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Police release CCTV in hunt for two men after Hamilton Hill shooting
World.content:
Updated NationalWACrime Police release CCTV in hunt for two men after Hamilton Hill shooting Indigo Lemay-Conway Updated September 13, 2026 — 7:38pm ,first published 10:03am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Police have released CCTV footage as they search for two men over a shooting in Perth’s southern suburbs on Sunday morning. Residents of Hamilton Hill were put into lockdown early on Sunday after a man was shot in the stomach in bushland near Owen Place. Loading Two men who are believed to be involved in the shooting remain on the run, but police say there is no risk to the public. Police were called about 4.35am after a 37-year-old was allegedly shot by two men dressed in black clothing and wearing face masks.



Police and St John WA responded and provided emergency first aid to the victim. Detective Brian Connelly, of the serious and organised crime division, said the shooting unfolded near the intersection of Yongka Road and Karda Way, before the victim and another man ran across Forrest Street towards Owen Place. The 38-year-old man was shot at a residence on Owen Place in Hamilton Hill. Andrew Du Connelly said a member of the public was alerted to the scene and provided emergency first aid. “It was a very short incident, it was over within a matter of seconds,” he said.



The man rushed to Royal Perth Hospital in a serious but stable condition. He has since undergone surgery for his injuries and is recovering in hospital. Related Article Crime ‘There’s no defence’: Man arrested over video of three-year-old steering car Connelly said offers believed the victim and his attackers were known to each other, and that there was no ongoing risk to the public. “We strongly suspect that they were known to each other, and the person that shot the victim knew the victim,” he said. “We’re confident in saying that it is a targeted attack at one individual, and we’re treating it as such.”



Police have since released CCTV from a nearby house showing the two men sought by police fleeing the area after the shooting. Earlier in the morning, people were told to stay away from the Hamilton Hill area and residents were instructed to lock their doors and windows and remain inside. Significant police resources were deployed to the scene and are conducting a thorough search of the area. Connelly said there was no information to suggest the shooting was related to tobacco wars or outlaw motorcycle gangs. Deputy Premier Rita Saffioti said the incident was “terrifying” for all those involved.



“It sounds terrifying the type of nature of what’s happened this morning ... but we need to get to the bottom of it and we need to arrest those two that are on the run,” she said on Sunday. Detectives want to speak to anyone who saw any suspicious vehicles or activity in the vicinity of Owen Place, or the surrounding bushland between 4am and 5am on Sunday. Anyone with information or CCTV is urged to contact Crime Stoppers.

World.title: ‘We want little boys to go and young men to return’: Scotch College’s bold vision for the next generation
World.content:
Special series NationalVictoriaSchools that excel ‘We want little boys to go and young men to return’: Scotch College’s bold vision for the next generation Bridie Smith September 13, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jason Potoi Andrew can still remember arriving at Scotch College for the first time. It was 1984, and he was touring the school that his father, David, had graduated from two decades earlier. The pair were soon approached by Ron “Chesty” Bond, a revered classics teacher and vice principal who worked at the school for close to four decades and was a favourite among generations of boys who gave him a nickname that stuck for life. Jason Potoi Andrew with his sons Austin and Maximus. Wayne Taylor “He came up to Dad and said, ‘Oh, David Andrew, I remember you. I taught you Latin’,” he says. “It was a nice moment.” It’s an example of what Scotch alumni, known as Old Boys, like to call the cardinal thread – an intangible link named after the distinctive shade of red in the school’s blazer and tartan that links the past with the present.



While outsiders might see it as a network founded on privilege, entitlement and affluence, for Potoi Andrew, connections aren’t made in boardrooms or clubs, but rather in interactions like the one his dad shared with “Chesty” Bond. “I wouldn’t say that going to Scotch has smoothed a path because things have changed a lot,” he says. “You’ve got to prove yourself.” Potoi Andrew’s sons Maximus and Austin had their names put down at birth, and became third-generation “Scotchies” when they ultimately joined the school. Again, the cardinal thread played its part. “I knew maybe two people when I started,” Maximus says. “But knowing that my dad came here, and my grandpa also came here, it was easy to find friends.”



Austin’s entry was similarly linked to his Scotch heritage, but he credits playing percussion in the school’s military band, an arm of the 142-year-old cadet corps, as his cardinal connection. “You learn more about the school and its history in cadets,” he says. “Things like what we did during World War I and about key figures like [General Sir John] Monash.” Scotch College’s Memorial Hall was built to honour students and staff who served in WWI and WWII. Wayne Taylor Having started at the school as an 11-year-old before graduating equal dux in 1881, Monash is a favoured son of Scotch. His bust, left breast laden with military medals, is displayed at reception, while Principal Dr Scott Marsh has a smaller version in his office. Other references to the school’s history and legacy are scattered across the 27-hectare Hawthorn campus, one of four owned by the college.



The $32 million science centre is named after former student and governor-general Sir Zelman Cowen while a plaque on the Cardinal Pavilion rowing shed on the banks of the Yarra River states it was opened by former school vice captain and later Liberal Party leader, Andrew Peacock. “The boys are aware they are part of something incredibly special,” Marsh says. Dr Scott Marsh became principal in 2023. Wayne Taylor “They are part of a school that has made incredible contributions to Australia and beyond.” Scotch does like to talk, modestly if possible, about its high-flying graduates. They include a prime minister, eight premiers, three governors-general and four High Court justices. And that’s before you get to collegians who have headed the navy, defence force, Reserve Bank, the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation, and universities, including Oxford.



The college’s full-time archivist Paul Mishura says alumni have received more top Order of Australia honours than any other school in Australia, and more than 70 Old Boys have been knighted. When asked where the school sees itself in the Melbourne private school hierarchy, Marsh says with a pause, “Well, because we value humility, we don’t like to say.” Moments later, he’s back on message. “We like to talk about how we develop good men of good character who will go and shape a better future,” Marsh says. “That’s what we like to talk about.”



Scotch’s strategic plan, developed over more than two years and released last year, frames the school as an institution focused on instilling character and fostering boys who aim high but keep their feet on the ground. At the most recent Young Old Boys of Scotch College (or YOBS) annual dinner in June, the school’s oldest Old Boy, 110-year-old Bill Morgan, spoke via a recorded message. The 1935 school captain, who played rugby for Victoria alongside Edward ‘Weary’ Dunlop, urged the YOBS to remember the lessons that went beyond the curriculum. “Give thanks to the teachers who helped create your character,” Morgan stressed.



The school’s strategic plan also outlines a desire to look past the “narrow goal of attaining an ATAR” because, it says, there is more to school than preparing students for university. (Though an honour board with the names of 31 Rhodes Scholars hangs to the right of the altar in the Memorial Hall.) Scotch’s median VCE study score has remained above the statewide median of 30 throughout the past decade, recording a high of 36 in 2017. For the past three years, it has sat on 34. Last year, three students achieved a perfect ATAR of 99.95, with 36 students recording an ATAR of 99 or above and a further 80 students scoring 95 or above. “We’re selective in that you’ve got to be able to afford over $40,000 for fees. Yes, I accept that. People always criticise me when I don’t say that. But academically we’re not selective at all,” Marsh says.



Growing up with Melbourne Founded by Scottish-born Presbyterian minister James Forbes in 1851 – the same year gold was discovered in Victoria and just 15 years after the foundation of Melbourne – Scotch College is the state’s oldest secondary college. “We’re selective in that you’ve got to be able to afford over $40,000 for fees... But academically we’re not selective at all.” Principal Dr Scott Marsh Its history has risen and fallen as the city cycled through boom and bust. Mass migration triggered by the gold rush grew the school and the city, with migrants who could travel unassisted being largely educated and literate. Scottish Presbyterians, in particular, prized literacy because you couldn’t be a good Christian if you couldn’t read the Bible. “Right from the beginning you’ve got a mindset in Melbourne that if you’re middle class, you don’t go to state schools,” retired Melbourne University sociologist emeritus professor Janet McCalman says.



But when the 1890s and 1930s depressions hammered Melbourne, Scotch enrolments were hit too, according to McCalman’s book, Journeyings, on Melbourne’s middle class. However, while not as pronounced now, McCalman says ‘being Scotch’ was a currency that was traded and treasured even when times were tough. Initially built in East Melbourne on land gifted to the Presbyterian church by government, Scotch was known as the Melbourne Academy until 1855 and colloquially by some as “the green door school”. It was small and existed without a motto, coat of arms or uniform. “There was no need to distinguish the school from others because there was no interschool sport at that time,” Mishura says.



There was however a game played in 1858 between Scotch and its nemesis Melbourne Grammar which is considered the first recorded AFL match. The game spanned three consecutive Saturdays and ended in a draw, with each side kicking one goal. Officiating was a Scotch chemistry and natural sciences teacher John Macadam – after whom the macadamia nut is named. Between 1916 and 1926, Scotch moved to its Hawthorn hilltop. When the school bought the property, it was understood to be 20.64 hectares – but it ultimately turned out to be 27 hectares. The boundaries have since contracted to the south and expanded to the north. The school’s footprint extended northwards after the college bought all 12 houses on Morrison Street, with some demolished and others used as the school’s museum and Old Boys’ Association headquarters. To the south, a narrow strip of land next to three of Scotch’s five ovals was compulsorily acquired in 2008 when CityLink was widened.



In 2013, the then-Napthine government paid $5.4 million for the sliver of land, valued at just over $1 million by Victoria’s Valuer-General. Old Boy and former state Liberal Party MP David Kemp headed the taskforce to ensure the school got what it considered fair compensation, a campaign that included Supreme Court legal action initiated by Scotch. Scotch was again in the headlines in 2015 when it revealed former students had suffered abuse on school grounds. Several historical claims were settled, most involving sexual abuse dating back to the 1950s and 1960s. Earlier this year, one former student launched legal action over allegations of abuse that occurred during a school camp on Phillip Island in the 1970s. More recently, the school attracted attention over a controversial decision to invite an anti-abortion activist to speak to year 11 students, for which Marsh apologised.



A measure of a school’s socio-educational advantage is known as the ICSEA score which is calculated using parents’ occupation and level of education attainment – as well as the remoteness of the school and the percentage of Indigenous students, which for Scotch is 1 per cent. Data from Australia’s curriculum and assessment authority shows that an ICSEA score of 1000 is the national average score. At Scotch, it is 1188, with just over three-quarters of families in the top quarter of socio-educational advantage. The Scotch community raised half of the $40 million it cost to build the Sir Zelman Cowen Centre for Science. Wayne Taylor Like all schools, Scotch receives state and federal government funding. The most recent data shows that in 2024 it received $6.83 million from the federal government, while the state government provided $1.99 million. The active network of Old Boys and current families can also raise sizable funds at short notice.



When Cyclone Fina hit Tiwi College, Scotch’s partner school on Melville Island, last November, the remote boarding school of 77 students was left with flooded boarding houses and classrooms with collapsed ceilings and shattered windows. Within 24 hours, Scotch had raised $522,000. “It’s a very generous, humble community, despite the labels that are thrown at it,” Marsh says. The school’s foundation, which oversees fundraising, scholarships, infrastructure spending and programs generated from bequests and donations, spent more than $2.4 million on scholarships and bursaries last year alone. And with a surplus of almost $4.9 million, it can afford to dream big.



Speaking at a gathering earlier this year, president and Old Boy Paul Aberdeen pondered what future contributions the foundation could make to the school, which turns 175 this year. “It’s fun to dream, isn’t it?” he mused. “We could be talking about new grandstands and sporting facilities. New buildings. Finally bringing the Hambledon Road area to life after patiently buying up those 25 houses over the years. Scotch College owns more than 20 homes on Hambledon Road which it has purchased as part of future expansion plans. Wayne Taylor “We’re even dreaming about new institutes and facilities you’d normally only find at a university.”



The Hambledon Road houses Aberdeen referred to are residential properties to the north of the school that have been purchased over decades and are key to ambitious expansion plans the school has for its main campus. Another two properties on Fordholm Road, purchased in 2004 and 2022 for a combined $5.65 million, have already been repurposed. The homes were demolished, and the land is now a staff car park. The school is also poised to sign a $60 million deal to buy a property just down the hill on Glenferrie Road, Kooyong, from Vision Australia – an acquisition all the more satisfying because Scotch outbid long-term rival and neighbour St Kevin’s College. The deal comes three years after Scotch bought Fairhaven, a 175-hectare waterfront property bordering a UNESCO biosphere reserve in Mallacoota. It will become Scotch’s third outdoor education campus after an 80-hectare Healesville plot and a sizable beachfront property at Cowes on Phillip Island.



Like its Hawthorn headquarters, the Healesville and Cowes boundaries have expanded over decades with the purchase of neighbouring properties. However, Fairhaven will be the centrepiece. According to Aberdeen, it will be Scotch’s answer to Geelong Grammar’s prized Timbertop campus – but with an ocean view. “It’s where we want little boys to go and young men to return,” Marsh says. “I think in our society we have an epidemic of 20, 30, 40, even 50-year-old little boys; men who haven’t taken on the responsibility of being a man.” Fairhaven, a 175-acre waterfront property near Mallacoota, will become part of the year 9 outdoor education program.



Marsh was there last year when a pilot group of year 9 students visited and, as a man whose Christmas holidays are spent camping with his family, it made an impression on him. “Out of the 23 or 24 boys we had there, I think only three or four had ever been in a tent,” he says. Having led the school since 2023, Scotch College is not a world Marsh was born into. Where his alma mater had one school oval, Scotch currently has five. Arriving as both a runner-up and an outsider, his name was in the leadership mix when the 17-member college council appointed Matthew Leeds as the school’s 10th principal. But before Leeds could take up the post, a whistleblower revealed a complaint alleging misconduct was made against him in 2017 at his former school, Geelong Grammar. Two separate investigations by Geelong Grammar and the Victorian Institute of Teaching did not substantiate the claims made against Leeds.

World.title: Rugby teams support campaign encouraging men to buckle up
World.content:
Four provincial rugby teams are getting behind the Transport Agency's campaign to encourage young men to buckle up in the car.

Young men are over-represented in death and serious injury vehicle crashes, with 1 in 7 not wearing a seatbelt, according to NZTA's crash analysis system.

Since 2020, 33 percent of drivers and passengers who died in vehicle crashes across New Zealand were not wearing a seatbelt - that's 500 lives lost.

A jersey with a strip across the front, which looks like a seat belt, was worn by the Manawatū Turbos, Taranaki Bulls, Northland Taniwha, and Waikato on Saturday at matches this week.

NZTA head of driving regulation, Chris Rodley said, "It is a sad, yet avoidable reality that men between the ages of 15-39 are dying or getting seriously injured in crashes because they're not wearing a seatbelt, especially in regional New Zealand.

The Waikato team wearing the jersey with a strip across the front, which looks like a seat belt. Graeme Murray

He said there were many reasons why young men don't buckle up, like seeing it as a hassle for a short drive.

However, half of all injury crashes occurred within 7km of home.

"Wearing a seatbelt is one of the easiest and most effective ways to protect yourself from injury in a crash."

He said wearing a seat belt reduced the risk of dying or being seriously hurt by 40 percent.

Manawatū Turbos. Graeme Murray

Paul Thompson from the Otago Rugby Football Union said there was a clear overlap between those in the wider community and the demographic that needs to be told to buckle up.

"This campaign gives us a way into this conversation because this age group are the men in our teams, our clubs and in our stands, and the statistics tell us they are among those least likely to buckle up."

The slogan of the campaign is "Who do you wear it for?", which Thompson said reflects how not buckling up doesn't just affect the person in the car.

"It affects their mates, their whānau and the wider community. We hope the jerseys serve as a reminder to buckle up for the people who expect you to make it home."

While NZTA research showed 90 percent of people think enforcing seat belt use helps reduce road deaths, 12 percent admitted to not wearing one in the past month.

World.title: Vanuatu MP criticises 30-hour search delay after ferry sinking
World.content:
Vanuatu authorities have been searching for survivors after an inter-island ferry carrying 34 passengers and 11 crew members sank in critical weather conditions.

The ferry sank while sailing between the islands of Ambae and Santo. Supplied / Tui's Shipping / Facebook

Seven people have been rescued, with an estimated 38 people still unaccounted for, as boats and a flying doctor plane search for more survivors 24 hours after the vessel sank in the north of the country on Friday (local time).

Police told national broadcaster VBCTC that MV Matui sank in rough seas on Friday while sailing between the islands of Ambae and Santo.

Police said one survivor made it to shore on the island of Santo, where a diver took him to the local community for help.

A video showing the man, named Jefferson, covered in a blanket and being offered a cup of hot tea has been shared widely on social media.

"We floated to Ambae, but the tide was too strong … I swam … until I ended up here (Santo)," he said.

There were also calls for communities on the coast of the Ambae Islands to keep an eye out and help possible survivors as the search continues.

Former foreign minister Matai Seremaiah, who was aboard the vessel LC Mahalia, rescued a number of survivors.

He posted on Facebook that two additional survivors had been spotted by a plane, though darkness made retrieval difficult.

Flying Doctor Mark Turnbull used his plane to drop life jackets and helped locate survivors for rescue vessels.

Terry Ngwele, harbour master of Luganville on the island of Santo - who was on another rescue vessel - said the search would continue tomorrow.

"We rescued two people today," he told ABC News.

World.title: Iran-US 'probably unlikely' to return to full hostilities - MFAT
World.content:
Regardless of the uncertainties surrounding the Iran war and the US administration, New Zealand officials six months on are hopeful - confident, even - that supply chains will hold. In the second of a two-part series, RNZ political reporter Russell Palmer sits down with MFAT's Taha Macpherson.

Unfortunately, responding to complex crises has become "part and parcel, and an increasing part" of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade's business.

That's the view of deputy secretary Taha Macpherson, who points to crises in the Pacific, Ukraine, Gaza and more recently Nepal.

He has led the ministry's policy group since 2024, and before that was acting deputy secretary for the Europe, the Middle East, Africa and Australia group.

The global fuel crisis may have been sparked by a notoriously unpredictable US President Donald Trump and Israel attacking Iran in February, and although attacks in both directions have resumed since then, Macpherson seems cautiously optimistic.

"We would probably say ... both parties have incentives not to return to a full-scale conflict like we saw in the initial stages," he says.

"It's probably unlikely that we see a return to full-scale hostilities."

He says Pakistan and Oman, which have facilitated talks, believe both sides feel that engagement is worthwhile - so long as a path to diplomatic resolution exists.

"With the caveat that it's very difficult to predict, what we may see is a sustained period of a new normal where you see increased tensions and maybe periodic flare-ups, probably around the Strait of Hormuz primarily."

MFAT handles sensitive global diplomacy and rarely grants interviews; keen readers will note Macpherson's language is loaded with words like 'probably' and 'unlikely'.

Concerns remain about the management of the Hormuz Strait and other key shipping routes being subject to Iran, Israeli or American influence, and Houthi attacks from Yemen and the Red Sea.

"You've got 12 to 15 percent of global oil trade going through the Red Sea and the Suez Canal so I think anything which led to ... major disruptions to those significant waterways would be of concern, because you are seeing potential supply impacts," Macpherson says.

"We've been very consistent since the outset of the conflict: we want to see de-escalation ... to see the parties return to a negotiated outcome ... the restoration of freedom of navigation."

An all-of-government response

New Zealand responded as soon as attacks on Iran began, setting up an all-of-government response group with 11 agencies, which were soon hosted in MFAT's new offices, which replaced a formerly earthquake-prone building.

"We'd only been here for about a week ... very, very helpful at the time. It was very lucky timing," Macpherson says.

Treasury is leading the fuel price response, MBIE the supply response.

MFAT also played a key role on international policy and diplomacy both at home and in embassies or 'posts' in the Middle East; in Southeast Asia, where more than 90 percent of New Zealand's fuel comes from; and with Pacific partners.

"Posts directly involved, right: we had Tehran, we had Abu Dhabi ... Riyadh, Cairo," Macpherson says.

"They're responding or assisting with the consular response, but also they're providing reporting on developments ... they're doing that at the same time as they're trying to make sure that they're safe, their families are safe."

Some staff needed to move between embassies, or provide remote support.

"You can't keep the rhythm of this type of response going relentlessly over a sustained period."

The efforts of Southeast Asian and other regional posts quickly became central. The ministry needed to know how other countries were responding, and "encouraged governments that were quite critical to us as partners in fuel supply chains ... not to take measures to introduce restrictions".

"They very quickly became expert in advocating for our interests through this crisis ... we haven't seen big supply chain disruptions from our key Southeast Asian partners.

"The posts themselves would often then go in and engage with the host governments ... to ensure that our position - New Zealand's position and priorities - were understood," Macpherson says.

"They would facilitate contacts between our ministers and relevant ministers, and also facilitate engagement with the fuel suppliers."

The government found that like New Zealand, Pacific countries at the end of supply chains relied on refined imports for 80 percent of total energy needs.

Posts were "very, very quickly" working with them to understand what those partners were doing and they understood New Zealand's priorities, he says.

Trade agreements were also key - particularly the so-called 'food for fuel' deal with Singapore.

"It sort of introduced between us and Singapore some binding commitments, which meant that countries agreed not to put restrictions on critical services or goods during a crisis like this.

"This is something that I think we'll continue to look at - whether or not that model can be used as a basis to help support our longer-term supply chain resilience."

Leadership role for NZ

The Future of Investment and Trade Partnership (FITP) group has received less attention. New Zealand, Singapore, Switzerland and the United Arab Emirates formed the grouping in September 2025 to curb trade barriers and maintain supply chains.

Macpherson says New Zealand played a leadership role, and by July this year 19 member countries were attending the https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/business/724810/largest-trade-meeting-in-20-years-underway-in-auckland biggest trade meeting New Zealand had hosted in 20 years].

MFAT, MBIE and NZ Trade and Enterprise also hosted webinars to brief businesses as the crisis went on.

"Some of these would have 800 participants on screen and we did them on quite a regular sort of tempo ... bigger businesses, smaller businesses, they were quite open," Macpherson says.

The crisis has also led MFAT to begin building a "crisis cadre", training 55 staff as "surge capacity" for future crises, he says.

"Things will stabilise somewhat, but some of these challenges are still out there and still uncertain.

"This work hasn't ended."

World.title: Mining company's equipment targeted in Panguna arson attack
World.content:
Reports from Bougainville say heavy machinery and vehicles belonging to a foreign mining company were destroyed in an arson attack at the Panguna mine site.

Armed men are alleged to have entered the site in the autonomous Papua New Guinea region this morning, and set fire to heavy haul trucks and other equipment stationed near the large open pit mine.

The machinery is understood to belong to Indian company Lloyds Metals and Energy Limited.

Lloyds was selected by the Autonomous Bougainville Government as one of the developers involved in plans to assess the future rehabilitation and possible reopening of the copper and gold mine.

The company has been in Bougainville advancing feasibility studies and exploration work.

Conflict over the former mine operations at the Panguna sparked Bougainville's civil war in 1989 - since then the mine has been closed for industrial mining.

Panguna and its large reserves of copper are seen by the ABG and others as critically important to Bougainville's aim to develop its economy as it seeks independence from Papua New Guinea.

The mine's potential rehabilitation has remained at the centre of debate in Bougainville over ongoing discussions about resource ownership and development.

But this weekend's unrest has raised concerns about security at the mine site and the future of proposed exploration and rehabilitation activities.

Details surrounding the attack, including the identities and motives of those responsible and the full extent of the damage, remain unclear.

PNG's Post Courier reports that police in Bougainville are investigating the incident.

World.title: Women's health advocates questions waitlist discrepancies
World.content:
Women's Health Action is questioning why colposcopy - or cervix scans - has seen significantly less improvement in wait times than other diagnostic services.

Colposcopy is a procedure to check the cervix for signs of precancerous or cancerous tissue.

Yesterday, Minister of Health Simeon Brown announced that waitlists for diagnostic services had reduced 21 percent overall.

Waitlists from June 2025 to June 2025 have fallen 9 percent for colposcopy and echocardiography. While CT waitlists were down 48 percent and MRI down 33 percent.

Manager of the action group, Isis McKay said, "Why has the reduction in the colposcopy waitlist been considerably smaller than the reductions seen in services such as CT and MRI scanning or coronary angiography?"

She questioned to what extent the use of private health providers contributed to the improvement.

Urgent colonoscopy services was the only service where waitlists had gotten worse, increasing two percent since June 2025.

"Understanding why some services are improving more quickly than others is crucial if we are to ensure equitable and timely access to care across the system."

McKay asked the Government for transparency around the changes, saying this will help improve trust that it can be maintained long term.

"These details matter because there is no quick fix to the challenges facing our health system.

World.title: National to set up Auckland Transport police team if re-elected
World.content:
The National Party will set up a dedicated Auckland Transport police team if re-elected.

The policy announcement coincides with the opening of the City Rail Link (CRL) on Sunday morning, which is expected to increase peak commuter capacity through the city centre by around 50 percent.

National would recruit 50 new officers for the team and police would received $7 million per year from Budget 2027.

Police spokesperson Mark Mitchell said the team would boost the visible police presence in trains, buses, ferries, stations and transport hubs.

"Police should be where people are. As more Aucklanders use public transport, it makes sense to have more police on the network.

"A visible police presence helps deter offending before it occurs, reassures passengers and transport staff, and ensures rapid intervention when something does go wrong," he said.

A policy statement released by the party said the team would focus on preventing anti-social behaviour, protecting passengers and staff, and responding quickly to incidents.

It said the team would be established in Auckland first, but could be expanded to other cities if successful.

Mitchell said it would be up to police to decide which services the team would patrol.

"They're very used to working in a way where they identify where the need is and then putting resources there.

"That's BAU (Business As Usual) for police, they gather intelligence, they look at where the work is, and then they put resources in there," he said.

New Zealand Police Association president Steve Watt said it was always good to have more police but pointed out the government had failed to meet past promises when it came to policing numbers.

"The irony behind it all is, however, is that we're still waiting for this government to fulfil its promise of 500 extra cops.

"So an extra 50, you know, who knows when that's going to actually happen."

New Zealand First and National's coalition agreement included a promise that by November 2025 the number of police officers in the force would be increased by 500.

However, the government conceded last year that the target would be missed.

Watt said it was always difficult to choose where to increase police presence but a boost in policing numbers was always a good thing.

Asked if the government had met its target of 500 new police officers, National Leader Christopher Luxon said he was confident that commitment would be met.

"We'll be delivering on that 500 extra police officers, and that's why we're confident we can push on and recruit another 50.

"With extra funding coming out of budget next year, we'll be able to get the police operationalising that funding." he said.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said National could not fulfil its promise of 500 extra officers, let alone 50 for a new transport beat.

"Why should New Zealanders believe that they're somehow going to magic up more police when they can't even fulfil the commitment they've already made?

"More police on the beat's a good thing, it would be good if this government showed up with the 500 extra police they promised to have delivered by now," he said.

Meanwhile, ACT leader David Seymour said National were trying to "solve the right problem", but more efficiencies could be found.

World.title: How world media reacted to All Blacks' loss against South Africa
World.content:
Heartbreak.

The All Blacks have suffered their third straight loss after being beaten by the Springboks 43-28 in Baltimore.

The loss concludes the Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series, with world media highlighting South Africa's dominant performance.

However, the All Blacks also received much recognition for the "pulsating, breathless and unpredictable nature" of the past six weeks.

Here's how world media reacted to the All Blacks vs Springboks series closer.

The Telegraph

"Springboks look like World Cup champions... again," The Telegraph's headline reads.

The post-match article angles in on the "long shadow" that has been cast over the All Blacks ahead of next year's World Cup in Australia.

"At key moments [the All Blacks] were let down by their discipline and turnovers in attack to gift the Springboks' transition ball, and their directness, backed by their power both in collisions and set piece, enabled them to pick up points much more easily than their opponents," the article reads.

It acknowledged the All Blacks' attempts to claw their way back into the game, but said the reality was the "Springboks always had another gear".

The Guardian

The Guardian continued with that sentiment, describing the All Blacks' loss as a thrashing.

Codie Taylor, Will Jordan, Ethan Blackadder and Beauden Barrett received honourable mentions, but the post-match article made it clear they were no match for "South Africa's total dominance at the breakdown, set piece and aerial battle".

The article acknowledged the controversy in the first half when play was held up for more than eight minutes after a failure in communication equipment between the match officials.

However, the newspaper said the Springboks "produced a devastating second-half display" to seal the Rivalry series victory.

Will Jordan of New Zealand tackled by Springboks, fourth Test, Baltimore, 2026. Dylan Davies / www.photosport.nz

RugbyPass

RugbyPass angled in on All Blacks head coach Dave Rennie's post-game heartbreak.

"Yeah, look, the boys put in a massive shift again," Rennie is quoted as saying.

"You look at all the numbers, and everything's very even, but they were electric, and when they got their opportunities, and we were trying to chase the game late and put ourselves under a bit more pressure."

The 62-year-old said coming to South Africa and the US to play the Springboks in a four-Test series wasn't easy.

"Tonight will hurt, but you know we'll wake up tomorrow, and I think be moving in the right direction."

The South African

What a game. What a series. What a tour. That is how the South African online newspaper The South African concluded the four-Test series.

The newspaper's post-match article said although the Springboks dominated the series, the All Blacks "contributed immensely to the pulsating, breathless and unpredictable nature of the past six weeks".

"Many, if not all, other Test teams would have crumbled under the sheer pressure and intensity of a tour like this; and yet, these two sets of players just kept at it and at each other for four consecutive matches."

The All Blacks will take on Australia next, in a battle for the 2026 Bledisloe Cup.

World.title: 'Gutted': All Blacks coach Dave Rennie feels the pain as Springboks win series 3-1
World.content:
All Blacks coach Dave Rennie feels the All Blacks are making making good progress, but says the loss of Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series hurts.

The Springboks rejoiced with the series trophy after beating the All Blacks 43-28 in Baltimore, taking the four-match series 3-1, with victory in the final three matches after the All Blacks won in Johannesburg.

It has been a bruising eight-match tour over more than six weeks for the New Zealanders, who were hoping to unseat the South Africans as world number one, albeit with a revamped side after skipper Ardie Savea, Luke Jacobson and Quinn Tupaea returned home injured after the third test loss.

But they could not match the Springboks' firepower and clinical approach.

The All Blacks made too many mistakes to be able to foot it with the Boks at M&T Bank Stadium, the home of NFL side the Baltimore Ravens, where nearly 70,000 people turned up. A win would have drawn the series and the Greatest Rivalry trophy would have been split in half.

When asked for his initial reaction, Rennie replied: "Gutted."

"We were confident that if we got a few things right tonight, we'd have a good chance of winning and fell short."

Siya Kolisi holds up Rugby's Greatest Rivalry Trophy Getty Images via AFP

"So, yeah, disappointing from that perspective. From a tour point of view, you know, I think I said three, four or five months ago whenever I got appointed that I was really excited about the tour coming here because we knew it was going to be tough, but we'd learn a lot about ourselves and we'd leave with a better understanding of our game model and tighter as a group.

"And we're definitely in that position. It's been awesome for us."

Rennie has found the Boks the big stumbling block in his first season as All Blacks coach, after the New Zealanders beat France in his initial test in charge on 4 July, then Italy and Ireland. Hopes were high after the All Blacks won the first test 33-16 in Johannesburg, but the wounded Springboks rebounded with victories in the next three tests.

Rennie said they were a great side.

"I thought South Africa were very good, they were electric and really clinical when they got their opportunities," said at the press conference after the Baltimore test.

"That was probably a key point tonight."

'Really excited' despite loss

Rennie said the result hurt, but with an eye on next year's Rugby World Cup in Australia he was pleased with his side's progress.

"Really excited about where our game's heading and knowing that we need to be better when you play a great side like the Springboks.

He thought on the match numbers that it was "a very even game tonight, bar the score".

"We probably conceded a little bit chasing the game late, but felt even with 15 to go we were right in it. So, yeah, disappointed, but still really proud of the effort and feel that we're tracking in the right direction.

Of areas that stung the All Blacks, he was disappointed with the performance under the high ball, saying the South Africans put them under more heat again.

"We couldn't grab a lot of those."

But he was pleased with the set pieces.

As to the near nine-minute break in the first half when officials tried to work out how to fix the broken communications system used by referee Karl Dickson and the Television Match Official, Rennie said it did not have an impact, but it should not have happened.

"I'm not sure. If comms gear goes down, you pull out of the spare set, surely. So, yeah, I'm not sure why it took so long," Rennie said.

One discipline area the All Blacks will have to work on is at the breakdown where they were pinged for illegal cleanouts and holding players down. Rennie conceded as much calling the illegalities "dumb".

Beauden Barrett has late say with try

Rennie also complimented veteran Beauden Barrett on his efforts for the team. The 35-year-old came on at fullback as a late replacement for his 145th cap and had the final say in the game, dancing in for a nifty try.

"Yeah, we're really happy with Beauden. Yeah, I mean, you guys just get to see the game. We get to see his contribution daily in meetings and in training and in leadership."

He said Barrett had been excellent in the matches he played on tour, while halfback Kyle Preston, who played in all eight tour matches, had been a strong performer who "suited our game".

World.title: Cleary plays hero and villain in NRL finals thriller
World.content:
Nathan Cleary is at risk of being rubbed out of Penrith's preliminary final after booting the Panthers to a thrilling 19-12 finals win over the Sydney Roosters.

In a cracking Sunday afternoon qualifying final, Cleary was sin-binned for collecting Hugo Savala's leg before breaking a 12-12 deadlock with a late field goal at Parramatta Stadium.

Brian To'o then iced the win with a 77th minute try after pouncing on a spilled Roosters pass.

The result means the Roosters will host Cronulla in a do-or-die semi-final on Saturday night, while Penrith are one win away from their sixth grand final in seven years.

But all eyes will be on the NRL's charge sheet on Monday, with Cleary anxiously awaiting what sanction he will face for crashing into Savala's leg after the Roosters player kicked in the first half.

The Panthers star immediately gave a worried look, before referee Gerard Sutton told him his action had "force", was "very dangerous" and "carried a high risk of injury".

If Cleary was to receive a grade-two dangerous contact charge on Monday, the game's best player would be facing a ban from the preliminary final with an early plea.

If he elected to challenge the charge, he would then risk being rubbed out of the grand final if found guilty.

A grade-one charge would only attract a fine for Cleary, and prove a massive boost in Penrith's bid for a fifth premiership of their dynasty.

Panthers coach Ivan Cleary was adamant the challenge was not worthy of a suspension.

"God no, of course not," said Cleary.

"He was just trying to make a play and he was thinking the right thing but he got the angle wrong.

"I must say though, the same thing happened to him earlier in the game, but anyway.

Cleary's challenge on Savala could have huge implications in the premiership race. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"We just had to manage our way through that period and then it was a dogfight for most of the second half, like a real semi-final.

"You could tell he was disappointed. Hugo (Savala) is not injured, it's just a black and white thing we've brought into the game."

The Roosters failed to make use of Cleary's absence, with Savala missing the ensuing penalty goal and being denied a try for a double movement after the break.

That was one of the few chances during a scoreless opening 32 minutes of the second half, before Cleary stepped up as the game's ultimate ice man.

To'o iced the game with a late intercept try. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

Sat in the attacking line after a searching Moses Leota run, Cleary was able to slot over the one-pointer with no pressure from Roosters defenders.

Daly Cherry-Evans then attempted to reciprocate moments later, but sprayed a shot from 20 metres out to the right before To'o's sealer under the posts.

"Execution of moments (cost us). It was a good contest, both teams were in there fighting," said Roosters coach Trent Robinson.

"You're looking for those little opportunities where can take advantage. Cleary took his with the one-point and we had some that we missed.

"We missed them and they got them. That's the tale of the tape really."

Cleary's boot had also wreaked havoc early on Sunday, with the Roosters unable to handle three of his bombs and Liam Martin leaping to score off one of his shallow cross-field kicks.

The Penrith halfback also changed the point of attack and went back inside to Dylan Edwards for the Panthers' second try, with the fullback swerving his way over to make it 12-12 after 38 minutes.

Mark Nawaqanitawase's freakish ability had kept the Roosters in the match in the first half, with two key intercepts.

The Roosters winger first helped deny a Penrith try when he reached out and held onto an Isaiah Papali'i ball in the third minute.

He then gave the Roosters a 12-6 lead when he stretched out to stop a Penrith break, juggled the ball three time as he fell, got up and ran 45 metres to score.

AAP/ABC

World.title: I'm ready to be Swans captain, says Gulden
World.content:
Sydney superstar Errol Gulden says he is prepared to step up as captain to help the Swans pursue an AFL premiership bid without the injured Callum Mills.

The 24-year-old has thrown his hat in the ring to deputise for skipper Mills after his midfield performance led the Swans to a stirring qualifying final win over Brisbane.

Sydney coach Dean Cox also has an experienced leader in former co-captain Dane Rampe, as well as fellow veteran Jake Lloyd, midfielder James Rowbottom and Tom Papley at his disposal.

Whoever Cox lands on could also play a key leadership role next year, with Mills facing the possibility of missing the entire 2027 season after tearing the anterior cruciate ligament in his right knee.

Swans vice-captain Isaac Heeney is among five players serving club-imposed bans after last month's post-match incident at the Pullman Hotel in Melbourne.

Star defender Mills had earned significant praise for leading the Swans through the turmoil, which past players said shattered the club's famed "Bloods culture".

Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice are the other Swans who will not play again this season.

Gulden rallied the Swans after Mills went down late in the first quarter against the back-to-back reigning premiers, finishing with one goal, 34 disposals and eight clearances.

"If it [the captaincy] was offered to me, I would love to," Gulden told AAP.

"I would feel like I'd be ready. I wouldn't change anything that I'm doing. I don't think any of us need to change anything that we're doing.

"But you're just so shattered for the person. He's [Mills] just an amazing leader.

"He is the best human being at the club. It's just not fair.

"We've just got to keep going, and it's going to be next man in."

Gulden said the 53-point qualifying final win left him with the most pride he has ever felt in the Swans across six seasons at the club.

The two-time All-Australian has played in two losing grand finals (2022, 2024), with last year's 10th-placed finish the first time he had missed finals in his career.

"I love playing with this team. The last couple of games have been so fun as a player to be a part of," Gulden said.

"There's something in having your back against the wall and trying to fight your way out of it.

"The weekend [against the Lions] was easily the most rewarding game.

"The most pride I've felt to be a part of this team in my career.

"There was obviously some respect lost for the club. It's completely fair enough.

Scans confirm ACL rupture for Swans skipper Callum Mills will be sidelined for the remainder of Sydney's finals campaign and possibly all of next season after scans revealed an ACL tear in his right knee.

"All we can focus on as players is what we can control, and that's going out there and representing the club the best way we can on and off the field.

"I'm really proud of the club and the team, everyone involved, because the last few weeks have been really difficult."

Sydney will continue its unlikely flag push by hosting minor premiers Fremantle at the SCG on Friday.

"A premiership would mean the absolute world to me," Gulden said.

"Even if what happened hadn't happened, it still would mean the world to me."

AAP

World.title: Warriors moved to Eden Park for Knights finals showdown
World.content:
The Warriors will make history when they host their first NRL final at Eden Park after the governing body announced the venue for the club's elimination final.

The NRL confirmed the Warriors would play Newcastle at Eden Park next Sunday at 6:05pm (4:05pm AEST) in week two of the finals.

The Warriors' first preference is to play at Mt Smart Stadium where their support is through the roof.

Eden Park holds 50,000 people, however, and is a more modern stadium compared to Mt Smart, where a sold-out crowd of 26,131 created a cauldron-like atmosphere in the Warriors' 26-16 loss to the Dolphins in Saturday night's qualifying final.

The Warriors have hosted five finals in their history in Auckland, but all at Mt Smart.

The Warriors have injury concerns ahead of the clash with the Knights, who they beat 46-32 in Auckland in round 25.

They lost strike centre Leka Halasima in the warm-up to the Dolphins clash with the Tonga international clutching at his right leg.

Trindall returns from shoulder dislocation to lead Sharks in finals win Four weeks after dislocating his shoulder, Braydon Trindall has returned to lead the Cronulla Sharks to a 26-16 win, advancing to the second week of the NRL finals while knocking out the North Queensland Cowboys.

"It was a hamstring in the warm-up, nothing related to what he's been having, which was an ankle injury," coach Andrew Webster said.

"He just felt his hamstring in the first stride out and reported it straight away. Yeah, couldn't go.

"I don't know any more than that right now."

Halasima is set to miss the Newcastle clash amid fears that prop Jackson Ford's injury comeback will be short-lived.

Ford, on return after a 12-week pectoral tear lay-off, limped off against the Dolphins with an ankle complaint.

"Not good," Webster said, when asked about the nature of the injury.

"We don't know much more."

The Warriors were never in full cry in attack against the Dolphins, with five penalty goals edging them to a 16-8 lead, but also denying them the chance near the opposition tryline to perhaps put the game to bed.

"We didn't get the opportunity to get a flow in to our attack," Webster said.

"That's the negative side of taking the penalty goals. But to stretch the lead out to eight points, we had to do it. It's a no-brainer.

"The negative side is there, but the eight-point gap is what every team should take."

Webster said the Warriors were in a strong position when leading 12-8 at half-time, but were unable to contain Dolphins centre Herbie Farnworth in particular as their tackles failed to stick.

"We were trying so hard … chasing contact and collision, and they were pinballing. We have to be more efficient next week."

AAP

World.title: Root says England's back from 'chaos' after Pakistan series sweep
World.content:
Joe Root admits England descended into "chaos" before he returned as the Test captain and believes things are back on track after sealing a cricket series whitewash over Pakistan on Saturday.

England survived a scare before Root and Jordan Cox scored unbeaten half-centuries to knock off the target of 130 and win the third Test at Edgbaston by eight wickets with five sessions to spare.

The dramatic retirement of Ben Stokes in June followed by coach Brendon McCullum being stripped of his red-ball responsibilities briefly left the Test side with a worrying leadership vacuum.

Root, who served as skipper for five years before standing down in 2022, accepted the captaincy again and, in concert with interim coach Marcus Trescothick, brought a hat-trick of comfortable wins at Leeds, Lord's and now Edgbaston.

The partnership steadied the ship ahead of Stephen Fleming's arrival as McCullum's long-term successor.

The Kiwi is due to arrive in the country in the coming days and Root believes he will find a team that has put its turbulent recent past to one side.

"There's been a lot of chaos around this series before a ball was bowled," Root said.

"The way we've handled it on and off the field, the way everyone understands what is expected of them, both as a player and how we want to carry ourselves, is a really good thing.

"It's been a very unusual summer, hasn't it? We had a resignation mid-series, there has been a few off-field incidents and we've got a new coach. Whether you call it chaos, whether you call it unusual, whether you call it unsettling, all of those are fair.

Root fuming after Carse nightclub incident England captain Joe Root opens up on his disappointment after finding another teammate involved in an alcohol-fuelled off-field incident.

"But ultimately, the thing that I care about and the most important thing is what happens from that. The way that we've responded to that has been excellent. And the fact that there's now clarity in what is expected of the group moving forward is quite evident. We build on that now."

Pakistan finally put England under some pressure in Birmingham after flaccid efforts in the first two games.

A stunning 81-run cameo from debutant Razaullah Khan on Friday left England chasing 130.

In Saturday's first over, the host was reduced to 2-2 when Mohammad Abbas got Ben Duckett to edge behind and Emilio Gay lbw.

"We thought this morning that anything is possible," Abbas said. "My specialty is taking wickets with the new ball … and we tried our best."

England could have been 3-35 when Root dragged on but Mohammad Ali overstepped.

Root and Cox shared an unbeaten stand of 128 with Root finishing on 62 and Cox 59 when they won at 2-133 just before lunch.

Seam bowler Ollie Robinson was named the player of the series for taking 21 wickets at an average of 8.76.

AP

World.title: New world number one Rybakina dethrones Sabalenka in US Open final
World.content:
Elena Rybakina has won her first US Open title, ending Aryna Sabalenka's hopes of a hat-trick of wins at Flushing Meadows in New York.

Rybakina controlled the first set, then was put in danger in the second, defending two set points before losing a third to allow Sabalenka back into the match.

However, the Kazakh player held her nerve, taking an early break in the third set and holding on for her third major title win, 6-4, 5-7, 6-2.

The win marked a second major triumph for Rybakina this year, after her Australian Open final victory over Sabalenka in January.

Sabalenka's loss ended her hopes of winning a third US Open crown in a row, emulating tennis great Serena Williams, who was undefeated between 2012 and 2014.

Sabalenka was increasingly frustrated through the match, smashing a couple of racquets as she struggled to find a way past her opponent.

Aryna Sabalenka's inability to crack Elena Rybakina left her frustrated at the US Open final. (Getty Images: Sarah Stier)

Rybakina stopped Sabalenka's 19-match winning streak at the US Open, where she had not lost since falling to Coco Gauff in the 2023 final.

The WTA Tour leader in aces got less than half of her first serves in but instead put Sabalenka under constant pressure with a strong return game, racking up 12 break chances and converting three, which was all she needed.

Rybakina earned $US5.5 million ($7.67 million), the largest prize in grand slam history, and tied Sabalenka and French Open winner Mirra Andreeva with a tour-high three titles this season.

Sabalenka took home $US2.8 million ($3.9 million) but it was clear how little that meant to her, as she smashed her racquet after a brief hug with Rybakina at the net.

A devastated Sabalenka found it hard to talk at the trophy presentation.

"That's the last thing I want to do now is giving a speech," she said.

"Obviously, I'm disappointed but I want to say congratulations Elena, it's a great win.

"I wish I could perform a little better, but maybe next year," she said as tears fell.

Rybakina was overjoyed and a little overwhelmed.

"It's tough to find words right now," she told the crowd.

"I didn't expect anything like this coming to this tournament. I've been dealing with an injury but somehow everything aligned together on my side.

"I want to say to Aryna, you are a great champion. It's so difficult to play you. I was diving around on court trying to get balls [back]."

Rybakina also thanked the crowd for their support, adding: "I'm falling in love with New York more and more."

It was celebration time for Elena Rybakina at the US Open after she won her second major title of 2026. (Getty Images: Julian Finney)

The second seed drew first blood to go ahead 3-2 following a Sabalenka double ⁠fault, with the frustrated Belarusian earning a code ‌violation immediately afterwards for launching ‌a ball high into the stands of the main showcourt.

A sudden drop-off in Rybakina's level midway through the second set gave the 28-year-old Sabalenka hope, and she produced a delicate drop shot and a stunning backhand crosscourt winner en route to forcing a deciding set.

However, Rybakina's quality ‌shone through as she took a commanding 5-2 lead and then ​closed out a famous triumph to leave her Belarusian rival without any major silverware in 2026.

ABC/wires

World.title: Wallaroos scare England but fail 'mission impossible'
World.content:
Australia's rugby women have given England's world champions a run for their money by leading sensationally at half-time, but the Wallaroos' dream of downing the Red Roses crumbled as they ended up losing 48-15 in Salford.

The English were stunned in the first 40 minutes of their WXV Global Series opener on Saturday (Sunday AEST) as the Australians went in to the break with a 10-5 lead but any hopes of handing the hosts their first defeat after 38 straight victories was buried after the break.

The John Mitchell-coached world champs, initially rusty in their first outing since being crowned European grand slam champions in May and struggling to adapt to the new smaller size 4.5 ball being trialled, ran in eight tries in total as their set-piece finally began to tick over to their normal high efficiency.

But Australia could be proud of their efforts, deserving their half-time lead as they controlled the breakdown and defended stoically even after being reduced to 14 for 10 minutes in the first period when halfback Samantha Wood was sin-binned for a deliberate knock-on.
